Thank you, that's very reassuring. I'll draft something over lunch and show it to you before sending it, as long as you've got a few minutes to look it over.

scenarios.scenario: Introducing a controversial speaker to a wary audience
scenarios.context: A conference chair talks with a controversial economist before introducing him to an openly skeptical audience.

speakerA.en: Dr. Lindqvist, thank you for coming, and I should be frank: the audience is divided. Not until the program was published did we realize how many people objected to your book. What I'd like to do is introduce you in a way that's fair to everyone.

Under no circumstances would I do that. I'd stress your credentials and the fact that you've invited criticism, which, by and large, academics rarely do. Be that as it may, a few attendees plan to walk out. Would that bother you?

There's a full forty minutes, and I'll moderate it myself. Should the discussion become heated, I'll step in, but I'd rather let people speak. Whatever else happens, I'll ensure everyone gets a fair hearing. Do you have a particular question you hope for?

Probably Professor Alvarez, who reviewed your book harshly. What you should know is that she's respected, and she'll ask precise questions. Not only is she well-informed, but she's also remarkably courteous. Would you like to meet her beforehand?

It might, and I'll mention it as I introduce you both. What I'd suggest is a brief handshake before the session, nothing formal. Not until the audience sees you speak civilly will the mood settle, I suspect. Is there anything about you that I should avoid saying?

Perfectly. I'll keep it short, factual and warm. Whatever the reaction, the evening will be remembered for its seriousness, not for its noise. Shall we go through the opening lines once more, in case I stumble?

speakerB.en: I appreciate the candor. Were it not for the controversy, I doubt so many would have registered, so I can hardly complain. What do you plan to say about me? I'd rather you didn't apologize on my behalf.

Not in the least. What concerns me is that people leave before hearing the argument, not that they disagree with it. Not until they've heard the whole case can they fairly reject it. Is there a Q&A, or will they be silenced?

Frankly, the hostile ones, since they reveal the weakest points of my thesis. Rarely have I learned anything from agreement. Were I to have a choice, I'd begin with the toughest critic in the room. Who's likely to be the first?

I'd welcome that, if she's willing. It's not that I expect to convince her, but that I'd like to show respect. Come to think of it, I once cited her work approvingly. Might that make an opening for conversation?

Please don't call me a provocateur, though the label may be inevitable. All I ask is that you present the argument as a serious one. Under no circumstances should the introduction sound defensive. Does that seem reasonable?
By all means. For what it's worth, I'm grateful for your integrity, as many hosts would've simply avoided the risk. Let's hear it, and I'll tell you honestly how it sounds.

scenarios.scenario: Introducing a partner to an exacting family at a milestone dinner
scenarios.context: A man prepares his partner of three years to meet his formidable extended family at his grandmother's ninetieth birthday dinner.

speakerA.en: Before we go in, let me warn you about my family. To say they're formidable would be an understatement, but not one of them is unkind. What worries me is that they'll interrogate you, not that they'll dislike you.

Quite the opposite, she's the easiest. Rarely have I met anyone so quick to forgive. It's my Aunt Margaret who requires care, since she holds strong opinions about everything. Were it not for her, family dinners would be dull, though. Shall I explain?

Gardening, mainly, and anything related to the town's history. Should she ask where you're from, mention the old harbor, since she grew up there. Little did I realize how much that would matter until I brought home my last girlfriend, who knew nothing about it.

Be honest, I'd say. It's not that we're avoiding the subject, but that we're still deciding. The last thing I'd want is for you to invent an answer under pressure. Whatever you say, I'll support you. Does that help?

That's perfect, and so like you. Were she to push further, I'd change the subject by asking about her roses. By and large, it works. What do you think of my cousin Tom, by the way? He's sure to flirt with you.
Probably, but it's a kind one. I've said nothing but good things about you, and so has my mother. For what it's worth, I'm proud to introduce you, whatever Aunt Margaret thinks. Shall we go in?

speakerB.en: That's reassuring, in a way. Had you told me earlier that there would be sixty of them, I'd have rehearsed. Who should I be most careful with? And please don't say it's your grandmother.
Please. I'd rather be prepared for her than ambushed. What does she care about most? Not that I intend to flatter her, but I'd like to avoid saying something clumsy about a topic she holds dear.
I'll remember that. Come to think of it, I've read a little about the harbor, so I might hold my own. Be that as it may, what do I say if she asks about our plans? We haven't really settled on any.

It does, thank you. Though I'd suggest we agree on a line beforehand, in case she presses us. Not only is she quick, but she's also persistent, from what you say. How about "We're enjoying the present, and the future will take care of itself"?

I haven't met him yet! Needless to say, I'll cope, as long as he's harmless. Such is the nature of big families, I suppose, that everyone arrives with a reputation. Will my own reputation be ready for me?
Yes, before I lose my nerve. Not for a moment did I imagine I'd be this nervous, but I'm also rather excited. Hold my hand, and introduce me properly, starting with your grandmother.

scenarios.scenario: Meeting unexpectedly
scenarios.context: Two friends run into each other after a long time.

speakerA.en: Mark? Is that you?
Yes! How are you?
I'm good. Where do you live now?
I still live here. Are you free for coffee?
Wow, I haven't seen you for ages!
speakerA.fa: واو، سال‌هاست تو را ندیده‌ام!

speakerA.en: How nice to see you again!
speakerA.fa: چه خوب شد دوباره تو را دیدم!

speakerA.en: What a surprise! How have you been?
speakerA.fa: چه تعجب! چطور بوده‌ای؟

speakerA.en: I thought you were in Canada. What are you doing here?
speakerA.fa: فکر کردم کانادا هستی. اینجا چیکار می‌کنی؟

speakerA.en: You look great! Have you been working out?
speakerA.fa: عالی به نظر می‌رسی! ورزش می‌کردی؟

speakerA.en: I moved to a new apartment last month. What about you?
Congratulations! Do you have time for a coffee?

speakerB.en: Oh, hi! Long time no see!
I'm well, thanks. And you?
I live in Leeds now. And you?
Yes, let's go. I'd love that!
I know, it's been too long!
speakerB.fa: می‌دانم، خیلی وقته!

speakerB.en: Nice to see you too! What's new with you?
speakerB.fa: من هم خوشحالم که تو را می‌بینم! چه خبر از تو؟

speakerB.en: I've been busy with work and family. How about you?
speakerB.fa: سر کار و خانواده مشغول بودم. تو چطور؟

speakerB.en: I came back last week. I'm here for a conference.
speakerB.fa: هفته پیش برگشتم. برای یک کنفرانس اینجام.

speakerB.en: Thanks! I've been trying to stay fit.
speakerB.fa: ممنون! سعی کردم تناسب اندامم را حفظ کنم.

speakerB.en: I started a new job at a bank. I like it a lot.
Yes, I have an hour before my train.

scenarios.scenario: Planned visit to a friend's place
scenarios.context: One friend visits the other at their home.

speakerA.en: Hi! Come in. I'm happy to see you.
Please sit down. Would you like some water?
Here you are. How was your trip?
Great. Dinner will be ready soon.
Hi, I came to see you as promised.
speakerA.fa: سلام، طبق قولم به دیدنت آمدم.

speakerA.en: Thanks for having me over.
speakerA.fa: ممنون که من را دعوت کردی.

speakerA.en: Your house looks lovely! I love the new decor.
speakerA.fa: خانه‌ات قشنگه! دکوراسیون جدید را دوست دارم.

speakerA.en: How have you been keeping? I've missed our chats.
speakerA.fa: چطور بودی؟ دلم برای گپ‌هایمان تنگ شده.

speakerA.en: I brought some cake for us.
speakerA.fa: یک کیک برایمان آوردم.

speakerA.en: I made it myself this morning. I hope you like chocolate.
Can I help you in the kitchen?

speakerB.en: Hello! Thank you for having me.
Yes, please. It's a hot day.
It was good. There was no traffic.
It smells delicious!
Welcome! Come in, make yourself at home.
speakerB.fa: خوش آمدی! بیا داخل، خودت را در خانه ات فرض کن.

speakerB.en: It's so good to see you again!
speakerB.fa: خیلی خوبه که دوباره می‌بینمت!

speakerB.en: I'm glad you like it. I just redecorated.
speakerB.fa: خوشحالم که دوست داری. تازه دکوراسیون را عوض کردم.

speakerB.en: Thank you! Please make yourself at home.
I've been well, just busy. I missed you too!
speakerB.fa: خوب بودم، فقط مشغول. دلم هم برای تو تنگ شده!

speakerB.en: Oh, you didn't have to bring anything. Thanks!
speakerB.fa: اوه، نباید چیزی می‌آوردی. ممنون!

speakerB.en: Thanks, but everything is ready. Please sit down.

scenarios.scenario: Having tea at a friend's home
scenarios.context: Two old friends sit together and talk over tea.

speakerA.en: Would you like some tea?
Here you are. How is your family?
That's wonderful. Do you like your new job?
I'm glad. Have some cake, too.
Come in and sit down. You must be tired after the trip.
Would you like green tea or black tea?
I baked these biscuits this morning. Please try one.
Of course. I'll write it down for you before you go.

speakerB.en: Yes, please. With a little sugar.
They're fine. My daughter is in school now.
Yes, I do. The people are friendly.
Thank you. It's very good!
A little. Thank you for inviting me.
Green tea, please. With a little honey.
They're delicious! Can you give me the recipe?
That's very kind. You're a great host.

scenarios.scenario: Catching up and saying goodbye
scenarios.context: The friends share some news, then the visit ends.

speakerA.en: Do you have any news?
Congratulations! Is it big?
That's great. I'm happy for you.
Okay. Thanks for coming.
How is your job going these days?
That's wonderful! Are your children still at school?
It's getting late. I need to catch the last bus.
No, thank you. I'll be fine. Let's keep in touch.

speakerB.en: Yes! I have a new house.
Yes, it has a small garden.
Thank you. It's late. I must go now.
Thanks for the tea. See you soon!
It's going well. I got a promotion in spring.
My daughter is at university now, and my son is still at school.
Already? Let me call you a taxi.
Definitely. Send me a message when you get home.

scenarios.scenario: Looking at old photos together
scenarios.context: Two old friends look at photos from their school days.

speakerA.en: Look at this photo! We were so young.
Who is the boy next to you?
Do you still talk to him?
I'm glad we're still friends.

speakerB.en: I remember that day. We went to the beach.
That's Ali. We played football every weekend.
Yes, we call each other a few times a year.
Me too. Let's take a new photo today.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing news about life changes
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about what has changed in their lives since they last met.

speakerA.en: I have a new baby now. Do you want to see a picture?
It's a girl. She's four months old.
Not really, but we're used to it. What about you?
That's a great plan. I'm sure you'll do well.

speakerB.en: Congratulations! Yes, please. Is it a boy or a girl?
She's beautiful. Does she sleep well?
I'm studying again. I want to become a teacher.
Thanks. It's hard, but I enjoy it.

scenarios.scenario: Planning the next visit
scenarios.context: Before leaving, two friends arrange to meet again soon.

speakerA.en: I had a lovely time today. Thank you for everything.
I'm free in two weeks. Is Saturday okay for you?
I'd love to. Can I bring something?
Wonderful. I'll arrive around five o'clock.

speakerB.en: I'm happy you came. When can you visit again?
Saturday is perfect. Why don't you stay for dinner?
Just bring yourself. I'll cook my special rice.
Great. Drive safely and text me when you arrive.

scenarios.scenario: Arriving after a long journey
scenarios.context: A traveler arrives at an old friend's house after a long trip.

speakerA.en: You made it! How was the trip? I was starting to worry about the traffic.
You haven't changed at all. It's been what, eight years since we last saw each other?
Come in and put your bags down. I've prepared the guest room for you.
Not at all. I've been looking forward to this visit for months.

speakerB.en: It took longer than expected, but I'm just happy to finally be here.
Closer to nine, actually. We have so much to talk about.
That's very kind. I hope I'm not causing too much trouble.
Me too. I've been telling everyone at work about my trip to see you.

scenarios.scenario: Showing an old friend around the hometown
scenarios.context: A man shows his visiting friend how their hometown has changed.

speakerA.en: Do you remember this street? It looks completely different now.
It closed about three years ago. A phone shop is there now, which is a shame.
Let's walk to the park. At least that hasn't changed much since we were kids.
Wait until you see the old tree. Someone carved our names into it, remember?

speakerB.en: I can hardly recognize it. There used to be a little bakery on that corner.
That's sad. I used to buy bread there every morning before school.
Good, because I've been thinking about it for days. We spent so many summers there.
I do! I can't believe it's still there after all these years.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing life stories over dinner
scenarios.context: Two old friends catch up on their lives during dinner.

speakerA.en: When I think about school, I can't believe how fast the years have gone.
And look at us. You're a teacher in the same town, and I'm still not sure what I want to do.
That's true. I just wish I had made my decisions with more confidence.
Thanks for saying that. It's easier to talk about this with someone who knows me so well.

speakerB.en: I know. Back then, we were sure we would both be living abroad by now.
Don't be so hard on yourself. You've changed jobs, but you've learned something every time.
Everyone feels that way sometimes. What matters is that you keep trying new things.
That's what old friends are for. Now, tell me about your plans for next year.

scenarios.scenario: Reuniting after many years apart
scenarios.context: Two friends meet again after more than a decade without contact.

speakerA.en: I can hardly believe it's you. You haven't aged a day, whereas I've gone completely gray.
I know what you mean. It's strange how quickly the old familiarity comes back.
Don't apologize. I was just as guilty. The important thing is that we're here now.
I hardly know where to begin. So much has happened that it's difficult to summarize.

speakerB.en: Flattery will get you everywhere. Honestly, it feels as if we only said goodbye yesterday.
I'm sorry we lost touch. Life got in the way, and I kept putting off getting in contact.
Agreed. Come in and sit down. We have more than ten years of news to get through.
Start wherever you like. We have the whole evening, and I've opened a bottle of wine.

scenarios.scenario: Visiting a friend who is going through a hard time
scenarios.context: A man visits a friend who has recently lost his job.

speakerA.en: I hope you don't mind me dropping in unannounced. I've been worried about you.
I was sorry to hear about the layoffs. It must have come as a terrible shock.
Have you thought about what you'd like to do next? There's no rush, of course.
You're more capable than you give yourself credit for. And if I hear of anything, I'll let you know.

speakerB.en: Not at all. To be honest, I could use the company. The days have been dragging.
It did, although in hindsight I should have seen the signs. The company had been struggling for months.
I'm considering retraining, though it's daunting to start again at my age.
That means a great deal. Right now, simply knowing someone cares makes a difference.

scenarios.scenario: Reminiscing about shared experiences
scenarios.context: Two old friends look back on their student years.

speakerA.en: Do you remember the night we got locked out of the dormitory and ended up sleeping in the library?
That's a gross exaggeration. If anything, it was your idea to take the shortcut.
Shared misfortune tends to do that. I wouldn't trade those years for anything.
We should organize a reunion. I'm sure half the old group would jump at the chance.

speakerB.en: How could I forget? We were nearly expelled, and all because of your terrible sense of direction.
Whoever's fault it was, I think it's what made us such close friends.
Nor would I, even though we were permanently short of money and slept very little.
I'll draft a message tonight. If nothing else, it will give us an excuse to relive those stories.

scenarios.scenario: Reconciling after a long estrangement
scenarios.context: Two former friends meet after years of silence following a falling-out.

speakerA.en: I wasn't sure you'd agree to see me. I wouldn't have blamed you if you'd simply let the letter go unanswered.
I owe you an apology that's long overdue. I allowed my pride to harden into something I now find indefensible.
It hardly matters now. What matters is that I let years go by when I could have reached out.
I'd like that more than I can say. Shall I put the kettle on, or have your tastes changed?

speakerB.en: I came close, I'll admit. But curiosity, or perhaps something gentler, got the better of me.
We were both guilty of that. I've replayed the argument so many times that I've lost track of who said what.
Then let's not compound the loss. I'd rather spend the afternoon rebuilding than relitigating.
Some things endure. Tea would be perfect, and I'll even tolerate your terrible biscuits.

scenarios.scenario: Visiting a friend who has changed profoundly
scenarios.context: A man reunites with a friend who has radically altered his lifestyle.

speakerA.en: You look remarkably well. I confess I was expecting a hermit, given the stories I'd heard about your retreat.
It's a striking contrast with the man who once dashed between three meetings and answered emails at midnight.
Do you ever miss the adrenaline? I find the quiet unnerving after a few days.
It's enviable, if I'm honest. I suspect I'm not brave enough to walk away from my own treadmill.

speakerB.en: I've been told I've mellowed. Living without constant noise tends to sand down the rough edges.
That man was exhausted, though he'd have sooner died than admit it. I simply couldn't sustain the pace.
Occasionally, but what I've gained outweighs it. I notice things now that used to blur past me.
Bravery had little to do with it. I simply ran out of alternatives, and that proved a surprisingly effective motivator.

scenarios.scenario: Revisiting shared history with a changed perspective
scenarios.context: Two old friends look back on a pivotal period of their youth with the benefit of hindsight.

speakerA.en: Looking back, I'm struck by how certain we were about everything. We spoke as if the world owed us a verdict.
Though much of what we were certain about turned out to be wrong, or at least wildly oversimplified.
Like the magazine, which collapsed spectacularly but taught me more than any job since.
I'd love to see them, provided you promise not to read my editorials aloud.

speakerB.en: Youth confers a remarkable immunity to doubt. I'd trade a good deal of my hard-won wisdom for a measure of that conviction.
True, yet I don't regret the fervor. It gave us the nerve to attempt things a more cautious pair would never have risked.
I still have a box of back issues in the attic. They're embarrassingly earnest, and I can't bring myself to discard them.
No promises. Some indignities are simply the price of friendship, and I intend to collect.

scenarios.scenario: Returning to a childhood home with an old friend
scenarios.context: Two friends walk through the town where they grew up, now strangely altered.

speakerA.en: I'd forgotten how small everything is. The playground that once seemed vast now looks like it was built for dolls.
Which category does the old school fall into? I can't decide whether I'm nostalgic or merely relieved I no longer have to attend it.
Remarkably, I can still recall the smell of floor polish and boiled cabbage. It's astonishing what the mind elects to preserve.
Spare me; I'll be humming it for days. Shall we see whether the bakery on the corner has survived the decades?

speakerB.en: Memory is an unreliable cartographer. We inflate the places where we were happiest and shrink the ones we feared.
Both, naturally. Nostalgia is largely the art of forgetting the unpleasant parts while retaining the smell of the corridors.
And what it discards. I couldn't tell you my locker number, yet I remember every word of that dreadful school song.
If it has, I'll be astonished and, quite possibly, moved. Let's go and find out.

scenarios.scenario: Staying with a friend who is recovering from illness
scenarios.context: A visitor tries to be helpful without being intrusive during a friend's convalescence.

speakerA.en: I hope my turning up unannounced isn't an imposition. I only wanted to see for myself how you were getting on.
Then I'll keep the talk resolutely frivolous. I've brought gossip of questionable accuracy and a rather good lemon cake.
Please don't exert yourself on my account. If anything needs doing around the house, I'm quite prepared to be useful.
Consider it done. I'd far rather pull weeds than watch you fret about them through the glass.

speakerB.en: Not in the slightest. I've been starved of conversation that doesn't revolve around my medication schedule.
You've an uncanny instinct for what a convalescent requires. Do sit down; I'll pretend to be a gracious host.
Well, since you insist, the garden has become something of a jungle, and I can only glare at it from the window.
You're a true friend. I only wish I could repay the kindness with something more substantial than tea.

scenarios.scenario: Reconnecting with a friend after a decade abroad
scenarios.context: A friend who has lived overseas for years returns and finds both of them changed.

speakerA.en: Ten years, and you walk in as though you'd merely nipped out for milk. How is it possible that you look so at ease?
I'd imagined you would return with a different accent and a vast collection of opinions about how we do things here.
Prudent. We've changed more than you'd expect; even the pub where we spent our twenties has become a gastropub.
I fear the carpet was the first casualty. Come on, I'll buy you a pint of whatever passes for bitter these days.

speakerB.en: Years of practice at being a stranger, I suppose. One learns to carry home around like a rather awkward piece of luggage.
I do have the opinions, but I've learned to keep them to myself until I've reacquainted myself with the local customs.
Don't tell me they've replaced the sticky carpet with reclaimed oak. Some institutions ought to be protected by law.
Lead on. It's the strangest thing, but I feel more at home here than I'd dared to hope.

scenarios.scenario: Picking up a friend at the station
scenarios.context: A man meets his old friend at the train station.

speakerA.en: Sara! Over here!
How was the train?
Let me take your bag.
My car is outside. Let's go home.

speakerB.en: Hi, Tom! It's so good to see you.
It was long, but it was fine.
Thank you. You are very kind.
Great. I'm hungry!

scenarios.scenario: Meeting the friend's family
scenarios.context: A visitor meets the family of his old friend.

speakerA.en: Come in! This is my wife, Mina.
Please sit down. These are our children, Lily and Sam.
Would you like some tea?
Of course. Dinner is at seven.

speakerB.en: Nice to meet you, Mina.
Hello, Lily and Sam! You are so big!
Yes, please. With milk.
That's great. Thank you for everything.

scenarios.scenario: Bringing a small gift
scenarios.context: A guest brings a gift when he visits an old friend.

speakerA.en: Hello! This is a small gift for you.
It's a book about cooking. You like to cook.
Look, I also brought some flowers.
Is your mother at home?

speakerB.en: Oh, thank you! What is it?
I love it! You remember everything.
They are beautiful. I'll put them in water.
Yes, she's in the kitchen. Come and say hello.

scenarios.scenario: Staying overnight at a friend's apartment
scenarios.context: A traveler stays one night with an old friend in another city.

speakerA.en: Thanks so much for letting me stay. I hope I'm not causing any trouble.
A shower would be great. Then maybe we could go out for dinner?
I'm leaving quite early tomorrow, around seven. I'll try not to wake you.
That's very kind of you. I'll make breakfast next time you visit me.

speakerB.en: Not at all! I've been looking forward to this for weeks. Make yourself at home.
Of course. The towels are in the bathroom, and I know a nice place around the corner.
Don't worry about it. I'll set an alarm and make you some coffee before you go.
Deal. And please don't leave it so long before you come back again.

scenarios.scenario: Catching up after ten years
scenarios.context: Two friends who lost touch meet again and talk about what has changed.

speakerA.en: I can't believe it's been ten years. You haven't changed at all!
I moved to Spain for work and ended up staying. What about you?
That sounds wonderful. Do you ever think about our old school days?
We should definitely meet more often. Let's not wait another ten years.

speakerB.en: You're too kind! Honestly, I feel like a different person. So much has happened.
Spain, really? I'd never have guessed. I've been here the whole time, with two kids now.
All the time. I still have a photo from our class trip hanging in my hallway.
Agreed. I'll send you my number, and you can call me whenever you're in town.

scenarios.scenario: Visiting a friend who has moved abroad
scenarios.context: A traveler visits a friend who emigrated and talks about how life has changed.

speakerA.en: I can't believe I'm finally here! It's been three years since you left, and the place is even more beautiful than in your photos.
Honestly, I was a little nervous about the trip, but your directions were perfect, and the train was right on time.
I'd love to see them. Tell me, do you ever feel homesick, or have you completely adapted to the new life?
That must have been difficult at the beginning. I'm sure that I wouldn't have had the courage to do what you did.
That's a lovely thought. Since I'm only here for a week, I'd like to see as much as possible with you.
Perfect. And thank you for letting me stay with you. I'll cook a traditional dinner one evening to say thanks.

speakerB.en: You made it! Welcome! I've been counting the days, and I've planned so many things for us to do while you're here.
I'm glad. Come on in. Let me take your suitcase, and then I'll show you around the apartment and the neighborhood.
Sometimes I miss home, especially around the holidays. But I've made friends here, and the people are more welcoming than I expected.
It wasn't easy. For the first six months I barely understood anything, and I cried more than once. But looking back, I'm happy I did it.
Tomorrow we'll visit the old market, and at the weekend we could drive to the lake, which is about two hours from here.
That sounds perfect. And you don't have to cook anything. Just having you here is already the best gift.

scenarios.scenario: Helping a friend after a difficult year
scenarios.context: A visitor listens to an old friend describe a difficult period and offers support.

speakerA.en: It's so good to see you. When you called last month, you sounded tired, so I decided to come as soon as I could.
I'm sorry to hear that. If you'd told me earlier, I would have come sooner. Why didn't you say anything?
I understand, but you don't have to carry everything alone. What are you planning to do about the job now?
That sounds like a good plan. Maybe a change would be exactly what you need after everything that's happened.
I'm sure you will. In the meantime, let's go for a walk. Fresh air will help you to clear your head.
Of course. Whatever you need, I'm here, and I'm not going anywhere. That's what friends are for.

speakerB.en: Thank you for coming. I really needed this. This year has been much harder than I expected.
I didn't want to worry you. I lost my job in the spring, and then my landlord decided to sell the apartment.
I've been applying for new positions, but nothing has come up yet. I might have to move to another city if I don't find something soon.
Maybe you're right. I've been trying to see the positive side, although it isn't easy when the bills keep arriving.
I think I will, but it's reassuring to know that I can count on you. Honestly, I don't know what I'd do without friends like you.
I'm so glad you came. Now let's make some tea, and you can tell me everything that's been happening in your life.

scenarios.scenario: Reflecting on how friendships change over time
scenarios.context: Two friends reflect on how their lives and values have changed since they last met.

speakerA.en: It's strange to think how much has changed since we last sat together like this. We used to talk about nothing except what we'd do when we grew up.
In some ways I've achieved what I wanted, but I'm not sure it's made me as happy as I'd expected. Success looks different when you get there.
I suppose I've realized that the things I valued most at twenty, like status and travel, matter less to me now than having time for the people I care about.
That's interesting, because I seem to have gone in the opposite direction. I used to be a homebody, whereas now I can't stay in one place for long.
I wonder whether friendships survive because people change in the same direction, or because they remain curious about how the other has developed.
I think you're right. Let's make a point of meeting more regularly, rather than letting life get in the way, as it has so often.

speakerB.en: I know. When I look at old photographs, I hardly recognize the person I used to be. Our priorities seemed so simple then, didn't they?
That's a common experience, I think. We chase certain goals for years, and when we reach them, we find that what we were really seeking was something else altogether.
I couldn't agree more. After my father fell ill, I began to reconsider how I spent my time, and I've been much more selective about my commitments ever since.
That's a perfect illustration of how unpredictable we are. If someone had told me ten years ago that you would become a traveler, I'd have laughed.
Perhaps it's a bit of both. What matters is that we've remained honest with each other, even when our opinions have diverged quite dramatically.
Agreed. Next time, I'll come to you, and we can continue this conversation over a long dinner, with no phones and no deadlines.

scenarios.scenario: Supporting a friend going through a career crisis
scenarios.context: A visitor listens to a friend who is questioning her professional path.

speakerA.en: You sounded so uncertain on the phone that I decided to come, even though I could hardly spare the time. Tell me what's been going on.
That doesn't sound like you at all. You've always been so determined. What changed? Was there a particular moment when you began to doubt it?
I can understand that. When you spend years working towards something, it's difficult to admit that it may not be what you want. It doesn't mean you wasted your time, though.
Have you thought about what you'd prefer to do instead, or is it more a feeling that something is missing than a clear idea of an alternative?
Why not treat it as an experiment? You could take a few months to try things out, without making any irreversible decisions about your future.
I'm sure you will. And whatever you choose, remember that I'm only a phone call away. You don't have to figure it out alone.

speakerB.en: Thank you for coming. I didn't want to burden you, but I'll admit that I've been feeling lost. I've started to wonder whether I chose the wrong profession altogether.
I think it built up gradually. I used to enjoy the work, but lately I dread Monday mornings, and I can't remember the last time I felt proud of something I'd achieved.
That's what I keep telling myself, but it's hard to shake the feeling that I've wasted a decade. At my age, starting again seems almost irresponsible.
Mostly the latter. I've considered going back to study, or maybe working with an organization that helps young people, but I can't tell whether that's a real passion or just an escape.
That's a sensible suggestion, although I'd need to be able to afford it. If I took a sabbatical, I'd have to rely on my savings, which wouldn't last very long.
That means more than you know. I feel less anxious already, simply because I'm talking about it. Now, let me make some tea, and you can tell me about your trip.

scenarios.scenario: Staying with a friend who is renovating
scenarios.context: A visitor stays with a friend whose house is in the middle of a renovation.

speakerA.en: Thank you for letting me stay, though I hope I'm not in the way. I didn't realize that you were in the middle of such a big renovation.
It's chaos, isn't it? How long have the builders been working on it, and are you really planning to live here while they finish?
I can imagine that it's stressful. Still, once it's done, I'm sure it'll look fantastic. What was the main reason for doing it all at once?
That makes sense. If it were my house, I think I'd have chosen to move out for a few months, but I suppose that it's impossible if you can't afford a second rent.
Honestly, I don't mind the noise or the dust. I'd rather spend time with you than sit in a hotel room. What time do the workers usually start?
I'll make sure that I'm up in time. Let me help you with breakfast, and then perhaps I can lend a hand with some painting, if you need it.

speakerB.en: You're not in the way at all, and I'm delighted that you could come. I'm sorry about the mess. We're about three weeks into what was supposed to be a six-week project.
Exactly, and the worst part is that it keeps expanding. Every time they open a wall, they find another problem, like old pipes or damaged wiring, and the budget grows.
We'd been putting it off for years, and then the roof began to leak last winter. Once we had to repair that, we decided that we might as well do the whole thing, rather than paying twice.
We did consider it, but with the children's schools nearby, it didn't seem practical. So we've set up a temporary kitchen in the living room, and we eat there on a camping table.
That's very kind of you. They start at seven thirty, I'm afraid, and the drilling is rather loud, but you'll get used to it. Earplugs are on the table beside your bed.
That's a generous offer, and I might take you up on it. We could certainly use an extra pair of hands, and I promise to pay you in food and good conversation.

scenarios.scenario: Meeting a friend's new family after years
scenarios.context: A visitor meets the friend's spouse and children for the first time.

speakerA.en: It's so wonderful to finally meet all of you. I've heard so much about your family, and it feels strange that after all these years, I'm only now seeing your home.
You must be Leo. Your father tells me that you're the best football player in your class, and that you've already scored more goals than anybody else on the team.
And you must be Chloe. I hear you've recently begun to learn the violin. I'd love to hear you play something, if you don't mind a very critical but extremely enthusiastic audience.
Thank you for having me. It would have been such a shame to let another year go by without visiting. I only wish that I'd made the effort earlier.
It's been far too long. Our lives took different directions, but when I walked through the door, it felt as though we'd seen each other only last month.
That would be wonderful. I'd be delighted to see you in the summer, and we could make it a proper reunion, with everyone from our old group.

speakerB.en: We're so glad that you could come at last. The children have been looking forward to meeting you since I told them that you'd be staying for the weekend.
Well, I'm not sure about the best player, but I do enjoy it a lot. Dad says that you used to play too, back when you lived here. Is that true, or is he exaggerating?
I'm still not very good yet, and the neighbors say that it sounds like a cat in distress. But I can play one short piece, if you promise not to laugh.
It was the same for us. We often talked about visiting you, but there was always something that got in the way. I'm just happy that you finally found the time.
That's the sign of true friendship, isn't it? After so many years, you can pick up exactly where you left off, and nothing seems to have changed between you.
We'd love that. And this time, you must come to us for a longer period. There are plenty of stories that the children haven't heard yet.

scenarios.scenario: Dropping in on a friend who has just had a baby
scenarios.context: A friend turns up unannounced at the home of someone who recently became a parent.

speakerA.en: I hope I'm not intruding. I know how exhausted new parents are, and I wish I had called ahead instead of just turning up at your door.
Thank you. I must say you look better than I expected. It wasn't until I saw the photos you sent that I realized how much your life has changed. The more I think about it, the more I admire you.

That sounds like the right approach. I wish someone had told me that when my sister had her first, since I spent months worrying on her behalf. Do you get any sleep at all, or is that a silly question?

I can imagine. Look, as long as you're comfortable with the idea, I could take over for a couple of hours this weekend, since I'm staying until Sunday. You could have a proper nap, or even go out for dinner.
To be honest, I'd say it's a small price to pay for seeing you both happy. The more time I spend here, the more I realize how much I've missed by not being around.
Then let's not waste the weekend. I'll make dinner tonight, as long as you tell me where everything is, and tomorrow we can all go for a walk, weather permitting.

speakerB.en: Don't be silly, I'm delighted to see you. If anything, I wish more people would turn up unannounced, because the days have been so long that any company is welcome. Come in, and mind the toys.
You're too kind. It wasn't until the third week that I stopped feeling completely lost. The more I tried to follow the books, the more confused I became, so I eventually just trusted my instincts.
It's a silly question, but a fair one. We take turns, although it's the unpredictability that wears you down rather than the lack of hours. If only babies came with a schedule.
That would be a lifesaver. I wish I could say I'd refuse out of pride, but the truth is I'd cry with gratitude. On the other hand, would you really want to spend your visit changing diapers?
It wasn't until you stood in my doorway today that I realized how much I'd missed you too. I wish we hadn't let so much time slip by, but at least we're making up for it now.
Deal. The more you cook, the more I'll like having you here, and I won't say no to the walk either, in case the baby finally decides to fall asleep in the stroller.

scenarios.scenario: Returning to a hometown to visit a friend who stayed behind
scenarios.context: After fifteen years in the city, a woman visits an old friend who still runs the family bakery in their hometown.

speakerA.en: I can't believe the old bakery is still standing. Had it not been for your emails, I'd have assumed the place had closed years ago, since everything else on this street looks different.

It's lovely, although I miss the old wooden one. Then again, I'm bound to feel nostalgic, whereas you have to live with the practicalities. How do you manage when the big supermarket chain keeps undercutting you?
That makes sense. I'd say it's the smartest strategy for a small business. Were I in your position, I'd probably have given in and moved to the city, so I admire your stubbornness.
That's the part I find hardest to explain to my colleagues in the city. People there tend to keep their distance, whereas here everyone seems to know your story. Do you ever find that suffocating?
I can see why. Had I known how much I'd miss this place, I'd have visited much more often. Would you mind if I stayed a couple of days, provided I'm not in the way?
You're on. Had you told me that years ago, I might have moved back already. I'll bring my bags in, and then perhaps you can show me what's changed besides the counter.

speakerB.en: It nearly did, to be honest. Were it not for the regulars, I'd have sold up long ago. Come in, and tell me what you make of the new counter, because I've been agonizing over it for months.

Mostly by not competing on price. Customers tend to come for the quality, and whereas the supermarket sells bread, we sell the feeling of knowing the person who baked it. Had I tried to match their prices, I'd have gone under.

Stubbornness is one word for it. Had you stayed, you'd have laughed at how many times I nearly gave up. Still, people in a small town tend to look out for each other, so someone always turned up with an order just in time.

Sometimes, I won't deny it. Were it not for my sister living nearby, I'd probably feel more isolated than supported. On the other hand, I wouldn't swap this for anonymity, not even for a bigger income.

You'd be most welcome, and the spare room is yours for as long as you like. Were you to stay longer, I'd even put you to work behind the counter, since I could do with a second pair of hands on weekends.
Gladly. Give me ten minutes to close up, and we'll walk around the old square. Were it not for the rain, I'd show you the river as well, but it can wait until tomorrow.

scenarios.scenario: Visiting a friend who has traded city life for a remote village
scenarios.context: A city-dweller visits an old friend who left a high-powered career to live in a remote mountain village.

speakerA.en: Tomas, this place is extraordinary! The last stretch of road was terrifying, but what strikes me is the silence. Rarely have I heard so little noise, and I'm not sure whether I find it soothing or unnerving.

Apart from the goats on the road, yes. Honestly, I still can't picture you without a suit and a deadline. What I'd like to know is what made you leave, since you never explained it properly in your letters.

I do, though I assumed it was simply the job. In hindsight, I should've asked more questions. Not only did you stop answering my calls, but you also stopped laughing, which worried me more. Do you ever miss that world?
That's a strong statement. If I'd made your choice, I'd probably be bored by now. Mind you, I envy the clarity you seem to have. Is it lonely, though? Not many neighbors, I imagine.
Strangely, yes, although I'd never admit it in the city. Little did I expect to feel envious, but here I am. What is it that you do all day, apart from chopping wood? I'm genuinely curious.
Very much. Whatever else happens this weekend, I'd like to understand how you made this life work. Come to think of it, perhaps I could return in the summer, for longer, if that's convenient.

speakerB.en: Both, at first, and then it becomes soothing. It took me about six months to stop reaching for my phone. Had you told me, ten years ago, that I'd live like this, I'd have laughed. Did the journey go smoothly otherwise?

It wasn't one decision so much as a slow accumulation of doubts. The more successful I became, the less I recognized my own life. Were it not for a minor illness, I might never have stopped. Do you remember how exhausted I looked?

Occasionally, mostly the conversations. By and large, though, I don't miss the pace. What I do miss is spontaneity, since everything here requires planning, from buying bread to charging the battery. Whatever the drawbacks, I'd never go back.

Eleven households, to be precise, and we all know one another's business. Lonely is not quite the word. It's closer to being exposed, in the sense that nobody lets you hide. Needless to say, it takes some getting used to. Do you find that appealing?

I teach the village children three mornings a week, and I'm restoring the old mill with a neighbor. Not only is the work satisfying, but it also gives me a reason to talk to people. Would you like to see it?
You'd be most welcome, and I'd enjoy it. All things considered, I think you've made the right decision to come. Let's drop your bags, and I'll show you the mill before the light fades.

scenarios.scenario: Seeing an old friend whose career has far outstripped your own
scenarios.context: Two old friends meet for dinner, and the one who stayed in a quiet profession feels mixed emotions about the other's fame.

speakerA.en: Ben, it's been far too long! I know it's my fault, since I've been traveling constantly. Seldom have I had a free evening this year, so I'm delighted you could meet. How have you been?

You could've said anything. What I've missed is being able to talk to someone who knew me before all this. Had it not been for old friends, I think I'd have lost my sense of perspective. Are you still teaching?

Funny, because I often envy your stability. What I find exhausting about success is that everyone wants something. Were it not for my assistant, I wouldn't see my own family. Do you honestly regret not following the same path?

Indeed, but it's worth more than people admit. Mind you, I suspect we both have a distorted picture of each other's lives. Little did I think, at university, that I'd be the one who needed reminding what a quiet evening looks like.

Absolutely. I'd suggest a standing dinner, once a month, wherever I happen to be. Not only would it keep us in touch, but it would also keep me honest. Whatever my schedule says, I'll honor it. Would you agree?

Yes, and let's make this the first of many. For what it's worth, you were always the better writer among us, and I've never forgotten it. Come to think of it, you should send me something. I'd love to read it.

speakerB.en: Well enough, Naomi, and thanks for making the time. I've followed your career with great interest, naturally. Not that you'd know it, since I never wrote. To be honest, I wasn't sure what to say.

Yes, and I still enjoy it, though the pay is modest. Granted, I sometimes compare myself with you, which is unfair on both of us. Such was our ambition at twenty, I suppose, that neither of us expected to end up here.
Some days, I do. The more I read about your work, the more I wonder what I might have done differently. By and large, though, I'm content. Not that contentment is the same as ambition, as you know.
That's rather touching. What worries me, to be candid, is that our friendship might have drifted for good. Had we been more diligent, we'd have kept in touch. Is there any way we can repair that?

Gladly, as long as you let me choose the restaurant occasionally. I'd hate to be known as the friend who always accepts. All things considered, I'm glad you suggested it first. Shall we begin with dessert?
That's very generous, and I'll take you at your word. Not that I expect you to publish it, of course. Seldom have I felt so at ease in a restaurant like this, and that's thanks to you.

scenarios.scenario: Asking about origin and background
scenarios.context: People ask each other about nationality, city, etc.

speakerA.en: Hi! Where are you from?
I'm from Spain. Which city are you from?
I know it! It's beautiful. Do you live here now?
How long have you lived here?
Great. Welcome to our country!
Which city are you from?
speakerA.fa: از کدام شهر هستید؟

speakerA.en: Are you originally from here?
speakerA.fa: اصلأ اهل اینجا هستید؟

speakerA.en: What is your nationality?
speakerA.fa: ملیت شما چیست؟

speakerA.en: How long have you lived in this city?
Do you miss your hometown?

speakerB.en: I'm from Brazil. And you?
I'm from Rio de Janeiro. It's a big city.
Yes, I live here with my sister.
For two years. I like it.
Thank you very much!
I'm from Tehran, the capital.
speakerB.fa: اهل تهران، پایتخت هستم.

speakerB.en: No, I moved here five years ago.
speakerB.fa: نه، پنج سال پیش به اینجا نقل مکان کردم.

speakerB.en: My nationality is Italian.
speakerB.fa: ملیت من ایتالیایی است.

speakerB.en: I moved here three years ago.
Yes, a lot. I visit my family every summer.

scenarios.scenario: Asking about job and study
scenarios.context: People ask about occupation or education.

speakerA.en: What do you do?
I'm a student. I study computers.
Yes, but it's difficult. Where do you work?
Do you like your job?
That's a very good job.
What do you do for a living?
speakerA.fa: چه شغلی دارید؟

speakerA.en: Are you a student or working?
speakerA.fa: دانشجو هستید یا شاغل؟

speakerA.en: What do you study?
speakerA.fa: چه رشته‌ای تحصیل می‌کنید؟

speakerA.en: What's your profession?
speakerA.fa: حرفه شما چیست؟

speakerA.en: Do you enjoy working at the bank?

speakerB.en: I'm a nurse. What about you?
That's interesting. Do you like it?
I work at a hospital near here.
Yes, I do. I like helping people.
Thanks. Good luck with your studies!
I study business administration.
speakerB.fa: مدیریت بازرگانی می‌خوانم.

speakerB.en: I'm a software engineer.
speakerB.fa: مهندس نرم‌افزار هستم.

speakerB.en: I work in a bank downtown.
speakerB.fa: در یک بانک در مرکز شهر کار می‌کنم.

speakerB.en: I'm in my second year. I want to become an accountant.
Yes, I do. My colleagues are very kind.

scenarios.scenario: Family and hobbies
scenarios.context: Asking about family, interests, free time.

speakerA.en: Do you have a big family?
Nice! What do they do?
What do you do in your free time?
I like tennis too. Let's play on Sunday!
Do you have any children?
speakerA.fa: بچه دارید؟

speakerA.en: What are your hobbies?
speakerA.fa: سرگرمی‌های شما چیست؟

speakerA.en: How do you spend your free time?
speakerA.fa: وقت آزادتان را چطور می‌گذرانید؟

speakerA.en: Do you like to read or watch movies?
speakerA.fa: کتاب خواندن یا فیلم دیدن را دوست دارید؟

speakerA.en: Which do you enjoy more, books or films?
How old are your children?
How often do you go hiking?

speakerB.en: No, it's small. I have two brothers.
One is a student. The other is a driver.
I read books and play tennis.
Great idea! See you then.
I'm married with two kids.
speakerB.fa: متاهل هستم و دو تا بچه دارم.

speakerB.en: I enjoy hiking and photography.
speakerB.fa: کوهنوردی و عکاسی را دوست دارم.

speakerB.en: In my free time, I like to cook and travel.
speakerB.fa: در وقت آزادم آشپزی و سفر را دوست دارم.

speakerB.en: I also enjoy long walks on the weekend.
I love both! I read novels and watch documentaries.
speakerB.fa: هر دو را دوست دارم! رمان می‌خوانم و مستند می‌بینم.

speakerB.en: My son is seven and my daughter is four.
Almost every weekend, if the weather is good.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for name and age
scenarios.context: Two people meet and ask for basic details like name, spelling and age.

speakerA.en: What's your name, please?
How do you spell it?
Thank you, Hana. How old are you?
I'm thirty. Nice to meet you.
Excuse me, what's your full name?
Could you spell your last name for me?
How old are you, if you don't mind?
I'm thirty-two. When is your birthday?

speakerB.en: My name is Hana.
H-A-N-A.
I'm twenty-five. And you?
Nice to meet you too.
My name is Karim Rahimi.
R-A-H-I-M-I.
I'm twenty-eight. And you?
It's on the fifteenth of May.

scenarios.scenario: Giving contact details
scenarios.context: A receptionist asks a new customer for contact details.

speakerA.en: Welcome! Can I have your name, please?
Thank you. What's your phone number?
And your email address?
Great. Thank you, Mr. Brown.
Could I have your phone number, please?
Could you give me your email address, too?
And what is your home address?
Thank you. Is there a better time to call you?

speakerB.en: Yes. It's Daniel Brown.
It's daniel at mail dot com.
You're welcome. Goodbye!
Yes, it's anna.lee@example.com.
I live at 24 Oak Street, apartment 5.
Yes, after five o'clock is best.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about where you live
scenarios.context: Two neighbors talk about their homes and who they live with.

speakerA.en: Do you live in this building?
Oh, I live on the third floor. Do you live alone?
Is your apartment big?
Good. Do you like the area?
Is your home a house or an apartment?
Who do you live with?
How many rooms do you have?
Do you like your neighborhood?

speakerB.en: Yes, I live on the second floor.
No, I live with my parents.
It's small, but it's very nice.
Yes, it's quiet and clean.
I live in a small apartment near the park.
I live with my sister and our cat.
We have three rooms and a small balcony.
Yes, it's quiet and the neighbors are friendly.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about languages
scenarios.context: Two classmates ask which languages they speak.

speakerA.en: Which languages do you speak?
Really? I speak Spanish and a little English.
Thank you. Is English difficult for you?
Me too. Let's practice together!
Which languages do you speak?
How long have you studied English?
Do you find English difficult?
Would you like to practice together?

speakerB.en: I speak Persian and English.
Your English is good!
A little, but I practice every day.
Good idea. Let's start now.
I speak Spanish and a little English.
For about two years.
Speaking is hard, but I can read well.
Yes, that's a great idea. Let's meet after class.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about likes and favorites
scenarios.context: Two new friends talk about things they like.

speakerA.en: What's your favorite food?
I like pasta. What's your favorite color?
Mine is green. Do you like music?
Me too! Who is your favorite singer?
What kind of music do you like?
What's your favorite food?
Do you prefer summer or winter?
What do you usually do on Sundays?

speakerB.en: I love pizza. What about you?
It's blue. And yours?
Yes, I like pop music.
I like Adele. Her songs are beautiful.
I like pop and sometimes jazz.
I love pizza, especially with mushrooms.
Summer. I like swimming at the beach.
I usually relax at home and watch movies.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about hobbies and interests
scenarios.context: Two new acquaintances discuss what they do in their free time.

speakerA.en: What do you usually do when you're not working? Do you have any hobbies?
That's great! How long have you been practicing?
I used to play the piano when I was younger, but I stopped after I moved here.
Maybe I will. Have you ever thought about playing in front of other people?

speakerB.en: I've recently started learning the guitar, although I'm not very good yet.
For about six months. I try to play for at least half an hour every evening.
You should start again. Learning something new is a good way to relax after a long day.
Not yet, but my teacher says I'll be ready for a small concert next year.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing where you grew up
scenarios.context: Two people at a party talk about their hometowns and childhoods.

speakerA.en: Where did you grow up? Your accent sounds a little different.
That must have been a big change. Did you find it difficult to adapt?
I had a similar experience when I moved abroad for university.
Every now and then, especially during the holidays. How about you?

speakerB.en: I was born in a small village in the north, but we moved to the capital when I was twelve.
At first, yes. Everything was so fast and crowded compared with the village.
Then you understand how strange it feels. Do you ever miss your hometown?
All the time. I go back every summer to visit my grandparents.

scenarios.scenario: Asking about work and career plans
scenarios.context: Two people who have just met talk about their jobs and future goals.

speakerA.en: So what do you do for a living, if you don't mind me asking?
That sounds creative. Is it what you always wanted to do?
Do you see yourself staying with the same company for a long time?
That's an ambitious plan. I'm sure you'll be successful if you keep working hard.

speakerB.en: I'm a graphic designer. I work for a company that makes mobile games.
More or less. I studied art, and then I discovered that I love working with technology too.
Probably not. I'd like to start my own studio in a few years, if everything goes well.
Thank you. I'm saving some money now, so I'll be ready when the opportunity comes.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing life goals and values
scenarios.context: Two new friends talk about what matters to them in life.

speakerA.en: If you could change one thing about your life right now, what would it be?
I can relate to that. I tend to overthink every decision, which isn't exactly relaxing.
Probably freedom, although I've learned that it often comes at the expense of stability.
That took courage. Do you ever regret it, especially during the difficult months?

speakerB.en: That's a tough question. I suppose I'd spend less time worrying about things I can't control.
What do you value most when you make those decisions, security or freedom?
That's a trade-off I've struggled with too. I left a stable job to start my own business.
Occasionally, but I'd rather regret trying than wonder what might have been.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about cultural background and identity
scenarios.context: Two colleagues discuss growing up between two cultures.

speakerA.en: You mentioned you grew up in two countries. How did that shape the way you see things?
That's interesting. Do you feel more attached to one culture than the other?
I imagine that gives you a useful perspective, especially when working with international clients.
I envy that, to be honest. I've lived in the same town my entire life, and my horizons feel narrow.

speakerB.en: It made me more adaptable, but also left me feeling slightly out of place everywhere.
It depends on the situation. At home I'm completely at ease, but professionally I lean towards the local norms.
It does, although I sometimes have to explain jokes or customs that nobody else finds puzzling.
It's never too late to broaden them. Travel, or even a good conversation, can change the way you think.

scenarios.scenario: Learning about someone's daily routine
scenarios.context: Two neighbors compare how they structure their days.

speakerA.en: You always seem so well organized. What does a typical day look like for you?
Five o'clock is far too early for me. I'm hopeless until I've had at least two cups of coffee.
Do you manage to keep that up at the weekends, or do you allow yourself a sleep-in?
I admire your discipline. My schedule tends to fall apart the moment something unexpected happens.

speakerB.en: I get up at five and go for a run before the traffic builds up. It clears my head.
I used to be the same, but I found that mornings are the only time I'm truly productive.
Generally I stick to the routine, although I make an exception when I've been out late.
That's perfectly normal. Flexibility is just as valuable as routine, provided you don't take it too far.

scenarios.scenario: Tracing a career path
scenarios.context: Two guests at an industry dinner compare how they arrived at their current professions.

speakerA.en: I'm curious how you ended up in urban planning. It isn't the sort of career people usually stumble into.
That's a significant distinction. Did the change of direction cost you much, professionally speaking?
Not at all. I began in journalism, drifted into policy research, and eventually realized I preferred shaping decisions to reporting on them.
Constantly. I still catch myself interrogating people in meetings, though my colleagues seem to find it oddly endearing.

speakerB.en: Quite by accident, really. I trained as an architect, but one municipal project convinced me I cared more about how people use a space than how it looks.
A few years of seniority, certainly, but I've never regretted it. Your own path strikes me as rather unconventional, if you don't mind my saying so.
That makes sense. Did you find it difficult to shed the habits of a reporter once you were on the other side?
I'd call it an asset. Asking the right question is half the battle in this field.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing formative influences
scenarios.context: Two new friends talk about the people and experiences that shaped who they are.

speakerA.en: You mentioned you were raised mostly by your grandmother. How did that shape the person you've become?
That's a remarkable foundation. I suspect that kind of upbringing leaves one with a rather different set of priorities.
My secondary school music teacher, oddly enough. She was the first adult who took my ambitions seriously, which gave me the confidence to pursue them.
Precisely, which is why I mentor young people whenever I can. It feels like settling a debt I can never fully repay.

speakerB.en: Profoundly. She had very little money but an extraordinary sense of dignity, and she taught me that how you treat people matters more than what you own.
It does, and it occasionally puts me at odds with colleagues who equate success with status. Was there anyone who played a similar role for you?
It's striking how often a single person's belief can alter the course of a life.
That's a lovely way to put it. Perhaps that's how kindness is meant to travel, from one generation to the next.

scenarios.scenario: Handling an overly personal question
scenarios.context: A guest politely deflects an intrusive question at a social gathering, and the conversation moves on.

speakerA.en: If you don't mind my asking, why did you leave such a prestigious firm? Most people would have clung to that position.
Of course, I didn't mean to pry. I only ask because I've been weighing a similar decision myself.
That's easier said than done when you have a mortgage and a family to consider.
I appreciate your candor. It has given me a good deal to think about.

speakerB.en: I'd rather not go into the details, if it's all the same to you. Let's just say it was time for a change.
In that case, I'm happy to share what I can. The short version is that I wanted work I could believe in, even if it meant a smaller salary.
It is, and I won't pretend the adjustment was painless. Careful planning made it possible, and so did a very patient spouse.
Take your time with it. A decision like that is worth making deliberately rather than in a rush.

scenarios.scenario: Learning about a new colleague's unconventional career path
scenarios.context: Two colleagues talk over lunch about how one of them ended up in the profession.

speakerA.en: I've been curious about something since you joined. Your CV reads like three separate careers rather than a single trajectory.
How does one accidentally become a data analyst? I'd have thought it required a certain deliberate intent.
There's a lesson in that, though I'm not sure it's one I'm brave enough to apply to my own career.
I like that. I might start describing my own muddled choices as a deliberately eclectic portfolio.

speakerB.en: That's a fair assessment. I started in marine biology, drifted into journalism, and eventually landed in data analysis almost by accident.
Not if you keep volunteering to fix the spreadsheet nobody else understands. Competence has a way of becoming a vocation.
Most of my decisions seemed reckless at the time. It's only in hindsight that they acquire the dignity of a plan.
Do. Confidence is half the battle, and the other half is persuading people not to ask too many follow-up questions.

scenarios.scenario: Asking tactful questions about someone's background
scenarios.context: A person gets to know a new acquaintance without prying into sensitive areas.

speakerA.en: You mentioned you'd moved here recently. I hope you won't think me nosy, but what drew you to this part of the country?
That I can appreciate. Do you still have family back where you came from, or have you cut the ties altogether?
I understand entirely. If I may ask, what do you miss most, apart from them?
Then you must cook for us sometime. I'd be a most appreciative and very uncritical guest.

speakerB.en: Not nosy at all. It was partly work, but mostly a wish to be somewhere with more sky and fewer people.
My parents are still there, and we speak weekly. It's complicated, but in the gentle way that most families are.
Oddly enough, the food. No one here seems to know how to make a proper stew, and I've had to learn the hard way.
Careful, I may take you up on that. I've been waiting for an excuse to show off.

scenarios.scenario: Getting to know a prospective flatmate
scenarios.context: Two people discuss lifestyle, habits and expectations before sharing a home.

speakerA.en: Before we go any further, I think it's only fair that we're candid about our habits. I'd hate us to discover incompatibilities after you've signed the lease.
I'm more of a night owl, though I'm generally considerate with headphones. What about guests?
That suits me well. As for the washing-up, I'm told I'm tolerable but not exemplary.
Then I think we'll get along splendidly. Shall we put the principal terms in writing, just to avoid any misunderstanding?

speakerB.en: Agreed. I'll confess at the outset that I'm a chronic early riser, which isn't always a virtue when one shares a thin wall.
Occasionally, with some notice. I'm not hostile to company, but I do value a calm evening at home.
Honesty is a refreshing quality in a flatmate. I'll do my best not to leave judgmental notes on the fridge.
Sensible. A friendly agreement now is worth a hundred diplomatic incidents later.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about your job and a typical day
scenarios.context: Two new acquaintances ask each other about work.

speakerA.en: So, what do you do for a living?
I'm an accountant for a small company. Is your job difficult?
I can imagine. Do you work night shifts?
I admire that. My job is much quieter, honestly.

speakerB.en: I work as a nurse in a children's hospital. What about you?
It can be tiring, but it's rewarding when the children get better.
A few times a month. It was hard at first, but I've got used to it.
Quiet jobs have their advantages too. You get to go home on time.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing hometowns and life changes
scenarios.context: Two people discuss where they grew up and why they moved.

speakerA.en: Where did you grow up? I can hear a slight accent.
Did you find it difficult to adjust to the big city?
And now? Would you ever go back?
I was born here, but I'd love to live abroad for a few years.

speakerB.en: I'm from a small town in the north. I moved here for university.
At first, yes. Everything was faster, noisier and more expensive.
Maybe one day, when I want a quieter life. And you?
That's a great idea. You should do it while you're young.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about hobbies and daily routines
scenarios.context: Two new colleagues get to know each other during a lunch break.

speakerA.en: So, how long have you been working here? I'm still new, and I'm trying to get to know everybody.
That's quite a long time. What do you usually do after work? I can never decide whether to go home or join a club.
I've always wanted to try that. Have you been doing it for long, and is it difficult for beginners?
That doesn't sound too bad. I used to play tennis when I was younger, but I haven't touched a racket for years.
I'd love to come along sometime, as long as you don't mind a complete beginner on the team.
Great. It'd be nice to meet new people, and it's a good way to relax after a long day at the office.

speakerB.en: I've been here for about six years. I started in the sales department and moved to the planning team two years ago.
Most days I go swimming at the sports center near the station. It helps me forget about work, and it keeps me in shape.
I've been swimming since I was a child, so it feels natural. If you're a beginner, there's a group that meets on Tuesdays.
That's a pity. Some of us play tennis on Saturday mornings at the park. We're not very good, but we have a lot of fun.
Of course not. Everybody is welcome, and we change partners after every game, so you'll get to talk to everyone.
Exactly. Just bring comfortable shoes and a bottle of water. I'll send you the details by message this afternoon.

scenarios.scenario: Getting to know a new roommate
scenarios.context: Two people who will share an apartment talk about their lifestyles and habits.

speakerA.en: Hi, I'm Tom. I'm really glad we finally have the chance to meet before I move in next week.
I'm a graduate student, so I spend most of the day at the university, and I usually study at the library in the evenings.
I'm quite tidy, although I'm not a fanatic. I try to wash the dishes straight away, and I don't mind sharing the cleaning schedule.
I rarely have guests, but occasionally friends come over on weekends. I'll always tell you in advance, of course.
Good point. I usually go to bed around eleven, but I'll make sure to keep the noise down if I come home late.
That sounds fair. I think we'll get along well. Is there anything else I should know before I bring my things?

speakerB.en: Nice to meet you, Tom. I'm Jack. I've been looking for someone reliable for a while, so I'm happy that you're interested.
That sounds good. I work from home three days a week, so I need a quiet apartment during the day if possible.
That's what I was hoping to hear. My last roommate never did the dishes, and it drove me crazy by the end.
That's absolutely fine with me, as long as it doesn't happen too often, and nobody stays up too late during the week.
I'm an early bird, so I usually wake up at six. I'll try not to make noise in the morning, but the walls are quite thin.
Just one thing: the heating is expensive in winter, so we agreed to share the costs equally. Does that work for you?

scenarios.scenario: Discussing life goals on a first meeting
scenarios.context: Two people at a language exchange talk about their ambitions and what they value.

speakerA.en: So, what brought you to this language exchange? Were you hoping to improve for work, or is it more of a personal interest?
That's a great motivation. I'm learning English because I'd like to study abroad, but I'm not sure which country to choose, or what to study yet.
I've been considering something in environmental science, as I've always been fascinated by the relationship between human activity and nature. What about you?
That sounds like a rewarding path. Do you ever worry that choosing a career based on passion rather than salary might be a mistake?
I take your point. I suppose the ideal situation would be to find something that combines both, although that isn't always possible.
I'd like that. Let's try speaking only in English for the next fifteen minutes and see how long we can last without switching.

speakerB.en: I'm learning for professional reasons, mainly. I work in international sales, and my company is opening offices abroad, so being able to communicate fluently is essential.
I can imagine that it isn't an easy decision. Have you thought about what subject you'd like to specialize in, or are you still exploring different possibilities?

That's a worthwhile field, particularly with all the attention that climate change is receiving. I studied economics, but I've sometimes wondered whether I should have chosen something more meaningful.
It's a question that I ask myself regularly. I've noticed that people who follow their interests tend to be more resilient, even though they may earn less in the beginning.
Exactly. Having said that, the more I learn about different careers, the more I think that the ideal job is one that you create for yourself over time.
Good idea. If I make a mistake, please correct me. I'd rather be corrected than continue repeating the same errors for years.

scenarios.scenario: Exploring cultural identity with a new neighbor
scenarios.context: Two new neighbors discuss growing up in different countries and what home means.

speakerA.en: You mentioned that you grew up in several countries. That must have given you quite a different perspective from people who stayed in one place.
I imagine it does. I've lived in the same town all my life, so I sometimes wonder whether I've missed something by not experiencing other cultures.
That's an interesting way of putting it. Do you ever feel that you belong somewhere in particular, or is the idea of a single home too limiting?
I suppose that's why the idea of home is so personal. For some people it's a place, and for others it's a feeling that comes from the people around them.
It sounds as though your experiences have made you quite adaptable. Do you find it easy to make friends when you arrive in a new place?
I'll certainly bear that in mind. Perhaps you could teach me a few phrases from the languages you've picked up along the way.

speakerB.en: That's true. My father worked for an international company, so by the age of fifteen, I had lived on three continents and attended five different schools.
I wouldn't say that you've missed out. Staying in one place gives you roots, which is something that I've often envied, because I've never had a hometown in the usual sense.
I've stopped asking myself that question. I feel at home wherever I can find a sense of routine and a few close friends, regardless of the country.
Exactly. When people ask me where I'm from, I often don't know how to answer, since my accent, my habits, and my tastes come from so many different places.
Over time, I've learned to be proactive about it. I say yes to invitations, even when I'm tired, because the first few weeks are crucial for building connections.
With pleasure. I'd be happy to, as long as you promise to teach me what's special about this town, which I'm only beginning to discover.

scenarios.scenario: Interviewing a prospective flatmate
scenarios.context: Two people discuss lifestyles and expectations to see whether they would be compatible as flatmates.

speakerA.en: Thanks for coming to see the flat. Before we go any further, I'd like to ask you a few questions about what you're looking for, and tell you a little about how I live.
I work from home about three days a week, so it's quite important to me that the flat is quiet during the day, and that I have somewhere to work without being disturbed.

I'm fairly tidy, but I'm not obsessive. I'd expect the shared areas to be kept reasonably clean, and I'd suggest a rota for the main tasks, so that nobody feels that they're doing more than their share.
As for guests, I don't mind occasional visitors, provided that I'm told in advance, and that it doesn't turn into a regular habit. What about you?
That sounds compatible, so far. One last thing: what would you do if we disagreed about something, such as bills or household rules? I find that it helps to know in advance.
I appreciate your honesty. Why don't we both think about it overnight, and then let each other know tomorrow? It's an important decision for both of us.

speakerB.en: Thank you for showing me around. It's a lovely flat, and the location is perfect for me. I'm happy to answer anything you'd like to know, and I'd also like to ask a few questions.
That shouldn't be a problem. I'm a nurse, and I work irregular shifts, so I'm often out during the day, and sometimes I sleep in the morning. A quiet flat would suit me, too.
That sounds fair. I'm quite organized, and I'd have no objection to a rota. In my last flat, we used a shared spreadsheet, which worked very well, and nobody ever had to remind anybody.
I rarely have people over, but my sister visits about once a month, and she sometimes stays the night. I'd obviously tell you in advance, and she'd sleep on the sofa bed.
I'd prefer to talk things through as soon as they come up, rather than letting them build into a larger problem. I think that's the most important rule for living with other people.
That's a good idea. I'd like to think about it too, but I can say honestly that I'd be happy to move in, and I think we'd get along.

scenarios.scenario: Meeting a mentor for the first time
scenarios.context: A new employee meets a senior colleague assigned as a mentor and discusses expectations.

speakerA.en: It's a pleasure to meet you. I was told that you'd be my mentor for the first six months, and I'm honestly very grateful. I've heard a lot about your work from other people in the team.
I'm hoping to learn as much as I can about how the department works, and I'd also like to develop my skills in managing projects, since that's the area in which I feel least confident.
I studied economics, and I worked for three years in a small consultancy, where I did a bit of everything. It was an excellent training, but I never had the chance to specialize.
That would be very useful. In terms of how often we should meet, would every two weeks be reasonable, or would you prefer a different arrangement, depending on your schedule?
I'll do that. And if I may ask, what would you say is the most important lesson that you've learned during your career? I'd be interested to know what shaped you.
Thank you for such honest advice. I'll make sure to come to our next meeting with a few specific goals, so that we can use the time efficiently.

speakerB.en: The pleasure is mine. I've been looking forward to this, since I remember how valuable it was when somebody took the time to guide me at the start of my career. Tell me a little about yourself.

That's a very sensible goal. Project management is a skill that's best learned by doing, so I'll try to involve you in a couple of live projects, where you can observe and then take on small responsibilities.
That's a good background. A broad experience gives you flexibility, and it will help you to see how different parts of a business connect, which many specialists tend to overlook.

Every two weeks sounds fine. I'd suggest that we keep the first half hour for specific questions, and then use the rest for broader topics, such as career development or dealing with difficult situations.
That's a good question. I'd say that it's the importance of listening. Early on, I was so eager to prove myself that I often spoke before I'd really understood the problem, and it cost me.
I'm glad to hear it. Remember that mentoring is a two-way street. I'll learn from you, as well, since you'll have a fresh perspective that I may no longer have.

scenarios.scenario: Getting to know a colleague on a business trip
scenarios.context: Two colleagues from different departments talk on a long train ride to a client meeting.

speakerA.en: I realize we've worked in the same building for a year without actually talking, so if you don't mind my asking, how did you end up in logistics? It doesn't strike me as an obvious path for someone with a degree in philosophy.
I'd like to hear how you work that out. To me, arguing about ethics seems miles away from rerouting a delayed shipment, although I suppose both involve weighing competing priorities.

That's a nice link. I'd say my own route was less logical. I drifted into marketing after dropping out of an engineering course, and what I regret isn't the change but not having made it sooner. Do you ever wonder how things might have turned out otherwise?
What made you turn it down, if you don't mind my asking? You strike me as someone who's rather adventurous.
