Yes. Is Tuesday at ten o'clock okay?
What is your name, please?
See you on Tuesday.

scenarios.scenario: Following the doctor's advice after a check-up
scenarios.context: A patient discusses his test results with the doctor.

speakerA.en: Your results are mostly good, but your cholesterol is a little high.
It's not serious yet, but you should change a few habits.
Eat less fried food, exercise three times a week and come back in two months.
Not for now. We'll decide after the next test.

speakerB.en: Is that serious? I've never had any problems before.
What exactly do you recommend?
I'll try. Do I need to take any medication?
Thank you, Doctor. I'll start walking every day this week.

scenarios.scenario: Calling in sick and explaining symptoms
scenarios.context: An employee calls his manager because he is ill.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'm afraid I can't come in today. I've had a high temperature since last night.
Not yet, but I have an appointment this afternoon.
I will. Could you tell the team that I'll miss tomorrow's meeting as well?
Thank you for understanding. I'll check my emails if I feel better.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry to hear that. Have you seen a doctor?
Good. Please let me know what the doctor says.
Don't worry. I'll ask Anna to take notes for you.
Please don't. Just rest and get well soon.

scenarios.scenario: Explaining a week of symptoms to a doctor
scenarios.context: A patient explains symptoms and receives advice from a doctor.

speakerA.en: Good morning, doctor. I've been feeling unwell for about a week, and it doesn't seem to be getting better.
I have a sore throat and a cough, and I've been very tired. Yesterday I also had a slight fever.
No, I haven't taken anything yet. I wasn't sure whether it was safe to take painkillers without asking someone first.
I see. Should I stay at home and rest, or is it all right to go to work if I wear a mask?
That makes sense. If the symptoms haven't improved after a few days, should I come back for another check-up?
Thank you, doctor. I'll follow your advice and make sure I drink plenty of fluids and get enough sleep.

speakerB.en: Good morning. Please sit down and tell me what's been bothering you. How long have you been feeling like this?
Let me take a look. Open your mouth, please. Yes, your throat is quite red. Have you taken any medicine for it?
You were right to ask. I'd recommend paracetamol for the fever, and a throat spray might also relieve the pain.
I'd advise you to stay home for at least two days. If you go back too soon, you might infect your colleagues.
Yes. If your fever lasts longer than three days or gets worse, come back and we'll do some blood tests.
Good. Rest is the best medicine in this case. Here's a note for your employer, and I hope you feel better soon.

scenarios.scenario: Picking up medicine at the pharmacy
scenarios.context: A customer asks a pharmacist about a prescription and how to take the medicine.

speakerA.en: Hello. I have a prescription from my doctor, and I'd like to pick up the medicine, please.
Thank you. Could you explain how often I should take it? The doctor said something, but I didn't understand everything.
Is it better to take it before or after meals? Last time, a different medicine made my stomach hurt.
I also take vitamins every morning. Is it safe to take them together with this medicine?
Good to know. What should I do if I forget to take a tablet? I'm worried that I might miss one.
That's very clear. Thank you for explaining everything so carefully. I feel much more confident now.

speakerB.en: Of course. May I have your name and date of birth? I'll check whether it's been prepared yet.
Certainly. You should take one tablet three times a day, with a glass of water, and finish the whole box, even if you feel better.
It's best to take it after eating, since that reduces the risk of stomach problems. Avoid drinking alcohol while you're on this medicine.
Vitamins are generally fine, but if you take any iron supplements, leave at least two hours between them and these tablets.
If you forget, take the next one as soon as you remember, unless it's almost time for the next dose. Never take a double dose.
You're welcome. If you notice any strange side effects, such as a rash, stop taking it and contact your doctor immediately.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about living a healthier lifestyle
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss their habits and how they would like to improve them.

speakerA.en: I've decided to start taking better care of myself. I've been sitting at a desk for far too long.
I want to start walking after work, and maybe cook at home more often instead of eating out.
That's what I'm afraid of. When I'm tired, I usually order food, and my good intentions disappear.
That's a smart idea. Did you find that you felt different after you stopped drinking so much coffee?
I'll try that. If I could sleep better, I think I would have more energy to exercise as well.
Thanks for the advice. Let's check in with each other in a month and see how we're doing.

speakerB.en: That's a good decision. I felt the same way last year, and I've made a few changes since then.
Those are good habits to start with. The key is to keep it simple, because big plans are harder to follow.
I used to do that too. Now I prepare meals on Sundays so that I don't have to think about it during the week.
Definitely. I sleep much better now, and I'm less tired in the afternoon, which helps me stay active.
Sleep is important. Try to go to bed at the same time every night, and avoid looking at your phone for an hour before.
Good idea. If we encourage each other, it'll be easier to keep going, even when we don't feel like it.

scenarios.scenario: Making a doctor's appointment by phone
scenarios.context: A patient phones a clinic and tries to get an appointment as soon as possible.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'd like to make an appointment to see a doctor, please. It's fairly urgent, if possible.
I've had a pain in my back for about two weeks, and it's getting worse. Yesterday I could hardly get out of bed.
I'm free at any time tomorrow, but I have to be at work on Wednesday. Is there anything available in the afternoon?
That's perfect. Do I need to bring anything with me, such as my insurance card or previous test results?
Alright. And what should I do if the pain becomes unbearable before then? Should I go to the hospital?
Thank you very much. I'll see you tomorrow at three, and I'll make sure to arrive a little early.

speakerB.en: Good morning, and thank you for calling the clinic. Is this your first visit, or have you been here before?
I'm sorry to hear that. Because it's getting worse, I'd recommend seeing a doctor as soon as possible. When are you available?
Let me check the calendar. Dr. Weber has a cancellation tomorrow at three, which would give you the earliest possible appointment.
Yes, please bring your insurance card and any documents related to your back. If you've taken any medication, make a note of it.
If you have severe pain, numbness, or difficulty moving your legs, don't wait. Go to the emergency room straight away.
You're welcome. I've booked the appointment under your name. Please call us if you need to change it. Take care.

scenarios.scenario: Having a check-up at the dentist
scenarios.context: A patient talks to a dentist during and after a routine check-up.

speakerA.en: Good afternoon. I haven't been to the dentist for almost two years, so I'm a little nervous.
Actually, one of my teeth has been sensitive when I drink something cold. It started a few weeks ago.
Is it serious? I've been brushing my teeth twice a day, but I don't always use dental floss.
I see. Will the treatment be painful, and how long will it take to finish everything?
That doesn't sound too bad. Is there anything I should avoid eating or drinking afterwards?
Thank you for explaining everything so clearly. I'll make the next appointment at the reception desk.

speakerB.en: Good afternoon. Don't worry. Most people feel the same way, and I'll make sure that you're comfortable. Do you have any problems at the moment?
Let me have a look. Open wide, please. Yes, I can see a small cavity on the lower left side. It's not too deep yet.
It isn't serious if we deal with it now. If you had waited longer, you might have needed a more complicated treatment. Flossing every day would help a lot.
I'll give you a local anesthetic, so you won't feel any pain. The filling itself will take around thirty minutes.
Try not to eat or drink anything hot for a couple of hours, and avoid chewing on that side until the numbness has gone.
You're welcome. I'd like to see you again in six months, so that we can make sure everything stays healthy.

scenarios.scenario: Recovering from an injury with a physiotherapist
scenarios.context: A patient discusses exercises and progress with a physiotherapist after a knee injury.

speakerA.en: Hello. It's my third session, and I'd like to know whether I'm making any progress with my knee.
It's much better than before. I can walk without a stick now, but I still feel pain when I go up the stairs.
I've been doing the exercises you gave me, although I missed a few days last week because I was traveling.
I'd like to start running again as soon as possible. I've been training for a marathon, and I've already missed so much.
That's disappointing, but I understand. Is there any form of exercise I can do in the meantime without damaging my knee?
Thanks. I'll try swimming this weekend, and I'll be more disciplined with my daily exercises.

speakerB.en: Hello. Let me look at your knee. How have you been feeling since our last session?
That's quite normal at this stage. Stairs put a lot of pressure on the joint, so it'll take a little more time to heal completely.
It's important to do them regularly. If you skip too many days, the muscles around the knee become weak again, and recovery slows down.
I'm afraid that running is out of the question for at least another six weeks. If you started too soon, you could injure yourself again.
Swimming and cycling on a stationary bike are both excellent. They keep you fit without putting too much stress on your knee.
Good. If you keep going like this, I'm confident that you'll be back on your feet, and maybe even running, by the end of next month.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the pros and cons of private healthcare
scenarios.context: Two friends debate public versus private healthcare systems.

speakerA.en: My brother had to wait nearly eight months for a routine operation, and now he's considering paying for a private clinic, even though it will cost him his savings.
I understand why he's tempted, but it concerns me that people with more money can jump the queue, while others simply have to endure the pain.
That's a valid argument, but you could say that private care reduces the pressure on the public system, since those who pay don't use up public resources.
In theory, perhaps. But in practice, doctors who work in both sectors may spend less time in public hospitals, which can make waiting lists even longer.
I'd say the real solution is to invest more in public services, so that nobody has to choose between their health and their financial security.
We can at least agree that no one should suffer unnecessarily. I hope your brother's situation is resolved quickly, whichever route he chooses.

speakerB.en: That's awful. Long waiting times are one of the biggest weaknesses of public systems, and they can have a serious impact on people's quality of life.
It's a difficult issue. Supporters of private healthcare argue that competition improves efficiency, whereas critics say that it creates two classes of patients.
Sometimes it does work like that, but the evidence is mixed. Countries with strong private sectors often show greater inequality in access to treatment.
That's one of the concerns, yes. Not to mention that many private clinics don't have emergency facilities, so complicated cases are transferred to public hospitals anyway.
I tend to agree, although I recognize that governments face limited budgets, and healthcare costs are rising faster than the economy in most countries.
Thanks. He's been in a lot of pain, so I hope that he'll be able to have the operation before the end of the year.

scenarios.scenario: Consulting a doctor about long-term stress
scenarios.context: A patient describes ongoing stress and asks for medical advice.

speakerA.en: Thank you for seeing me. I've been feeling constantly exhausted for several months, and I have trouble concentrating, even though I sleep for eight hours.
It started after a reorganization at work. I'm now doing the job of two people, and I find it almost impossible to switch off in the evenings.
I've also noticed frequent headaches and tension in my shoulders. A friend suggested that it might be linked to stress, but I wanted to hear a professional opinion.
I've tried to cut down on coffee, and I take short walks, but it doesn't seem to make a significant difference. Would you recommend any kind of treatment?
I'm not keen on taking medication, unless it's absolutely necessary. Do you think counseling might be more appropriate in my situation?
That sounds sensible. I'll make an appointment, and I'll also talk to my manager about reducing my workload, if that's possible.

speakerB.en: Of course. I'm sorry to hear that you've been struggling. Can you tell me when the symptoms began, and whether anything in your life has changed recently?
That could certainly be a factor. Chronic stress affects both the body and the mind, and it often leads to the kind of fatigue and poor concentration that you describe.
Your friend may well be right. Headaches and muscle tension are common physical reactions. Still, I'd like to run a few blood tests to rule out other causes, such as anemia.
Those are good habits, but they may not be enough if the source of the stress remains unchanged. We should consider a combination of lifestyle changes and, if needed, therapy.
I'd say that's a perfectly reasonable preference. Talking therapy has been shown to be highly effective, and I can refer you to someone who specializes in work-related stress.
I'd encourage you to do both. If you hadn't come in today, the symptoms might have continued for months. Let's review your progress in a month's time.

scenarios.scenario: Explaining test results and treatment options
scenarios.context: A doctor explains results to a patient and discusses what to do next.

speakerA.en: Hello, doctor. I came as soon as I received your message. I must admit that I've been quite anxious since I heard that the results had arrived.
I'd prefer that you were direct with me. If there's a problem, I'd rather know exactly what it is and what the options are.
I see. Is it something that could have been prevented if I had come earlier, or is it more or less unrelated to my lifestyle?
What would the treatment involve, and how long would it take before I notice an improvement? I'm worried about missing work.
I'd like to think about it and discuss it with my family before deciding. Would it be all right if I gave you my answer at the end of the week?
Thank you for being so clear and patient. It's a relief to understand what's happening, even though it's not the news that I was hoping for.

speakerB.en: Hello, and thank you for coming in so promptly. Please sit down. I'll explain everything as clearly as I can, and you can ask questions at any point.
Certainly. Your blood tests show that your cholesterol is considerably higher than it should be, and there are also signs of mild high blood pressure.
It's difficult to say with certainty. Genetics play an important role, but diet and lack of exercise certainly contribute. The good news is that we've caught it at an early stage.
In the first instance, I'd suggest changes to your diet and a regular exercise program. If there's no improvement after three months, we might consider medication.
Of course. There's no need to rush. It's your decision, and it's important that you feel comfortable with the plan. I'll give you some written information to take home.
You're very welcome. I'm optimistic that, with some changes, you'll make a full recovery. Don't hesitate to contact the clinic if you have any concerns.

scenarios.scenario: Following up on test results and insurance
scenarios.context: A patient calls the clinic about test results and what the insurance will cover.

speakerA.en: Hello. I'm calling about the results of the blood tests that I had last week. The receptionist said that the doctor would call me, but I haven't heard anything yet.
My name is Anna Fischer, and I'm registered with Dr. Morris. I'm a little anxious, because I was told the results would be available within three days, and it's now been eight.
I see. In that case, could you ask the doctor to call me this afternoon? If there's something that I need to be aware of, I'd rather know as soon as possible.
Thank you. I'd also like to ask about the cost. I've heard that my insurance may not cover the second set of tests that were recommended, and I'd like to know what I'll have to pay.
That would be very helpful. If I'd known about the possible costs in advance, I might have asked whether the tests were strictly necessary, but I'd still like to get them done.
Thank you for your help. I'll wait for the call, and I'll bring my insurance details with me to the appointment on Monday.

speakerB.en: Good morning, and thank you for calling. Let me find your file. Yes, I can see that the results were received on Tuesday, but they haven't yet been reviewed by the doctor.
I apologize for the delay. The laboratory sent them late, and the doctor has been seeing patients all week. I'll make sure that she looks at them today, and that she calls you.
I'll put a note on your file marked as a priority. She finishes her consultations at four, so you should hear from her between four and five. Is this the best number to reach you?

I can check that for you. For the second set of tests, the insurance usually covers eighty percent, provided that there's a referral from the doctor. The remaining twenty percent is paid by the patient.
Based on the price list, that would be around forty euros. Of course, if the doctor decides that the tests aren't needed, you won't have to pay anything, so it's worth discussing it with her.
You're welcome. Please don't hesitate to call again if you haven't heard anything by five, and I'll follow it up personally.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing persistent headaches and daily habits with a doctor
scenarios.context: A patient who has had headaches for weeks explains his symptoms and daily habits to the doctor.

speakerA.en: Good morning. Please take a seat. What seems to be the problem? You mentioned on the phone that you've been feeling unwell, so I'd like to hear exactly what's been going on.
How long have you been experiencing the headaches, and have they been getting worse? I'd also like to know whether you've been taking anything for them, since that can sometimes make matters worse.

That could well be a factor. I'd recommend that you cut back on painkillers, as they can cause rebound headaches if you've been taking them daily. Have you been drinking enough water and eating regularly?
I see. Let me check your blood pressure and your eyes, as a precaution. I'd recommend that you have your eyesight tested as well, since eye strain is a common cause of this kind of headache.

Your blood pressure is slightly high, but nothing alarming. I'd say it's most likely stress, provided the symptoms improve once you've changed your habits. I'd recommend that you take regular breaks and walk outside every day.

If they haven't improved within two weeks, come back, and we'll arrange some tests. In case you notice any vision changes or severe pain, go to the emergency room immediately. Otherwise, I'm confident you'll feel better soon.

speakerB.en: Good morning, doctor. I've been having headaches for about three weeks, and I've been waking up exhausted, no matter how early I go to bed. To be honest, it's starting to affect my work.

They've been getting steadily worse, and I've been taking painkillers every day, which I suspect isn't helping. I've also been staring at a screen for ten hours a day, since I've been working on a deadline.
Not really. I've been skipping lunch, and I've been drinking far too much coffee. On the other hand, I've been trying to improve my sleep, although it hasn't been working so far.
I haven't had my eyes checked in years. Is there anything serious I should be worried about, or is it more likely to be stress and tiredness? I'd rather know the worst than keep guessing.
That sounds manageable. What if the headaches don't improve? Should I come back, or would it be better to see a specialist, in case it's something else entirely?
Thank you, doctor. That's very reassuring. I'll book an eye test this week and try to take proper breaks, and I'll come back in two weeks if I'm still having trouble.

scenarios.scenario: Getting advice from a pharmacist about a new prescription
scenarios.context: A customer picks up an antibiotic and asks the pharmacist how to take it safely.

speakerA.en: Good afternoon. Is that a new prescription? Let me take a look. It's an antibiotic, and it's important that you understand how to take it properly, so I'll go through the instructions with you.
Of course. You'll need to take one tablet three times a day, preferably with food, and it's essential that you finish the whole course, even if you feel better after a few days.

It really is important. If you stop too soon, the infection can return, and the bacteria may become resistant. You should also avoid drinking alcohol, since it can interfere with the medication and make the side effects worse.

Some people experience nausea or mild stomach upset, which is why taking it with food helps. Should you develop a rash or difficulty breathing, however, stop taking it immediately and contact a doctor.

The vitamins are fine, but be sure to leave a gap of two hours between the supplement and the tablet, since some minerals reduce absorption. The antihistamine is generally safe, but I'd suggest that you check with your doctor to be certain.

Avoid too much direct sun, as the medication can make your skin more sensitive. Beyond that, drink plenty of water and get some rest. If you've got any further questions, don't hesitate to come back or phone us.

speakerB.en: Yes, the doctor prescribed it this morning for a throat infection. To be honest, I wasn't paying much attention in the office, since I had a fever, so I'd be grateful for a clear explanation.
I've always been tempted to stop early, once the symptoms disappear. Is it really that important to complete it, or is it just a precaution, as people sometimes say?
I'll make sure to do that. Are there any side effects I should be aware of? I tend to have a sensitive stomach, so I'd hate for this to make it worse.
That's useful to know. On the other hand, I've been taking a daily vitamin supplement and occasionally an antihistamine for hay fever. Is it all right to take them together with the antibiotic?
I'll do that. It's good to have someone explain this in detail. Is there anything else I should be careful about, such as sunlight or certain foods, while I'm on the course?
Thank you very much. You've been extremely helpful. I'll start this evening with dinner, finish the whole course, and avoid alcohol, as you suggested. I hope I'll be feeling better by the weekend.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a doctor about alternatives and a second opinion before surgery
scenarios.context: A patient who has been advised to have knee surgery asks her doctor about the alternatives and whether she should seek a second opinion.

speakerA.en: Doctor, thank you for seeing me. I've been thinking about the surgery you recommended, and to be honest, I'm still unsure. I'd rather understand every option before I decide. Could you explain why surgery is better than continuing physiotherapy?

Mainly the recovery. I work as a teacher, so I'd rather not be off for months. Were I to go ahead, how long would I realistically be away from work? And regardless of the result, would I need further operations later?

It's actually better than I feared. On the other hand, I'm wondering whether I should get a second opinion. I'd rather you didn't take it personally, since it's a big decision, and as far as I'm concerned, it's better to be sure.

I'd appreciate the referral, thank you. In the meantime, is there anything I should avoid? I'd rather not make it worse while I wait, since the pain gets sharper when I climb stairs. Is it safe to keep exercising?
Dull most of the time, but sharp when I twist. I'd say it's worse in the evenings. Whether or not that's a bad sign, I thought I should mention it. Could it mean the damage is spreading?

None that I know of. Thank you for being so patient, Doctor. I feel much calmer now. Regardless of the second opinion, I'm glad I asked, because I'd rather make this decision with all the facts than rush into it.

speakerB.en: Of course, and you're right to ask. Since the cartilage damage hasn't improved after six months of treatment, I'd say surgery gives you the best chance of walking without pain. That said, it's your decision. Which part of the procedure worries you most?

Most patients return to light work within four to six weeks, although you'd need crutches at first. As for further operations, it's unlikely, provided that you follow the rehabilitation plan. Were you to skip it, the risk would rise. Does that match what you expected?

I wouldn't take it personally at all. In fact, I'd encourage it, whether or not the second doctor agrees with me. If you like, I can send your scans to a colleague at the university hospital. Would you prefer that, or would you rather choose someone yourself?

Light swimming and cycling are fine, but I'd advise against running or deep squats. Regardless of what you decide, strengthening the surrounding muscles will help. Were the pain to become severe or the knee to swell, please call us immediately. How would you describe it at the moment?

It's not necessarily a sign of spreading, but it's worth monitoring, since swelling often builds up by evening. I'd say we should check it again in two weeks. In the meantime, I'll prescribe an anti-inflammatory gel. Do you have any allergies I should know about?

That's exactly the right approach. I'll have the referral ready at reception by this afternoon. Were you to decide on surgery, we'd book it within a month. Take care, and don't hesitate to call if anything changes.

scenarios.scenario: Persuading a relative to see a doctor about a persistent cough
scenarios.context: A son gently tries to persuade his father, who dislikes hospitals, to see a doctor about a cough that has lasted for weeks.

speakerA.en: Dad, I couldn't help noticing that you've been coughing for almost a month. To be honest, I'm worried. It's high time you saw a doctor, don't you think? I'd say it's better to check than to keep guessing.

It might have started as a cold, but a cough this long can't be ignored. However busy you are, it's high time you looked after yourself. Is there a reason you're avoiding the doctor, or is it simply that you dislike waiting rooms?

You might have, although it could be something else, and that's exactly why I'd feel better if a professional looked at it. However reasonable your explanation sounds, it's only a guess. What if I booked an early appointment, so that you wouldn't have to wait long?

I'll call tomorrow and ask for Wednesday at nine. It's about time we sorted this out, and I'll come with you, as long as that's fine with you. I can drive, and we can have breakfast afterwards, whatever the result.

Absolutely. Anything that has changed recently could be relevant, however small it seems. Mum said you've lost your appetite too, so you'd better tell the doctor everything. It's much easier for them to help when they have the full picture.

Exactly, so please give yourself the same advice. Even if the news is good, you'll feel better knowing. And if it isn't, it's high time we found out, since the earlier it's treated, the better the outcome. I'll pick you up on Wednesday at eight-thirty.

speakerB.en: I'm fine, really. It's just a cold that hasn't gone away. You know I've never liked hospitals, and as far as I'm concerned, it's a waste of everyone's time. Besides, the weather has been terrible lately, so it can't be anything serious.

A bit of both, I suppose. The last time I went, I waited three hours and was told to rest. On the other hand, I do get tired climbing the stairs, which is unusual for me. I must have caught something at the office, mustn't I?
You'd do that for me? Well, I'd rather go on a weekday morning, since the clinic is quieter then. Even if it turns out to be nothing, I suppose it would put your mind at rest. When would you suggest?
That's kind of you, though I don't want to be a burden. I'd better write down my symptoms, in case I forget something. Do you think I should mention that I've been sleeping badly as well?
Your mother talks too much! But she's right, I suppose. I can't remember when I last had a proper check-up, which is probably a mistake. If it were anyone else, I'd have told them to go weeks ago.
All right, you win. Thank you for pushing me, even though I grumbled. I'd better get an early night so that I'm in a good mood. And as far as I'm concerned, breakfast afterwards is on me.

scenarios.scenario: Finding a specific place on foot or by car
scenarios.context: A person is lost and asks a stranger for directions.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Where is the bank?
Is it far from here?
Which way, please?
Thank you very much.
How do I get to the National Museum from here?
speakerA.fa: چطور از اینجا به موزه ملی برسم؟

speakerA.en: Is this the right way to the train station?
speakerA.fa: آیا این راه درست برای رسیدن به ایستگاه قطاره؟

speakerA.en: Could you tell me where the nearest subway station is?
speakerA.fa: میشه بگید نزدیک‌ترین ایستگاه مترو کجاست؟

speakerA.en: I'm looking for 5th Avenue. Am I anywhere close?
speakerA.fa: دنبال خیابان پنجم می‌گردم. آیا نزدیکم؟

speakerA.en: Is there a pharmacy around here that's open 24 hours?
speakerA.fa: آیا این حوالی داروخانه‌ای هست که ۲۴ ساعته باز باشه؟

speakerA.en: Could you please mark it on my map? I'm terrible with directions.
speakerA.fa: میشه لطفاً روی نقشه‌ام علامت بزنید؟ من جهت‌یابی رو بلد نیستم.

speakerA.en: How long does it take to walk there?
Thank you. Is there a bank near the museum?

speakerB.en: It's next to the post office.
No, it's near. Five minutes on foot.
Go straight, then turn left.
You're welcome.
Go straight ahead for two blocks, then turn left. You can't miss it.
speakerB.fa: دو بلوک برید مستقیم، بعد بپیچید چپ. پیداش می‌کنید.

speakerB.en: Actually, you're going the wrong way. You need to turn around.
speakerB.fa: در واقع دارید اشتباه می‌رید. باید برگردید.

speakerB.en: Take the first right, then the second left. It's across from the bank.
speakerB.fa: اولین خیابان رو برید راست، بعد دومی رو چپ. روبروی بانکه.

speakerB.en: You are quite close. It's about a 5-minute walk from here.
speakerB.fa: نسبتاً نزدیکید. حدود ۵ دقیقه پیاده‌روی از اینجا فاصله داره.

speakerB.en: Yes, there's one on the corner of 2nd and Maple. It's always open.
speakerB.fa: بله، یکی در گوشه خیابان دوم و میپل هست. همیشه بازه.

speakerB.en: Sure, let me draw the route for you. Go straight until you see a big fountain.
speakerB.fa: حتماً، بذارید مسیر رو براتون بکشم. مستقیم برید تا یه فواره بزرگ ببینید.

speakerB.en: About ten minutes. It's next to the big park.
Yes, there's one across the street.

scenarios.scenario: Asking the way
scenarios.context: A tourist asks a stranger for the way.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Where is the park?
Is it far?
Do I turn left at the corner?
Thank you.
Excuse me, I'm a tourist. Could you help me?
I'm looking for the old castle.
Is it a long way from here?
Can I take a bus instead?

speakerB.en: Go straight.
No, it's near.
No, turn right.
You're welcome.
Of course. Where do you want to go?
It's on the hill. Take the second street on the right.
No, it's about a ten-minute walk.
Yes, bus number 5 stops right in front of it.

scenarios.scenario: Looking for the bus stop
scenarios.context: A person asks where the bus stop is.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Where is the bus stop?
Is it on this street?
How many minutes?
Thank you very much.
Excuse me, where is the nearest bus stop?
Is that the stop for the airport bus?
How can I cross the road safely?
Thank you very much for your help.

speakerB.en: It's in front of the school.
Yes, it is. Go straight.
About two minutes.
No problem.
It's next to the post office, on Green Street.
No, you need the stop across the road.
Use the crossing near the traffic lights.
You're welcome. Have a good trip!

scenarios.scenario: Finding a restaurant
scenarios.context: A person asks for a restaurant nearby.

speakerA.en: Is there a restaurant near here?
Which way?
Is it open now?
Great. Thanks!
Excuse me, is there a good restaurant near here?
Is it expensive?
Which way should I go?
Is it open for lunch?

speakerB.en: Yes, there is one next to the bank.
Turn left, then go straight.
Yes, it is open until ten.
Enjoy your meal!
Yes, there's an Italian place on the next corner.
Not really. A meal costs about fifteen dollars.
Walk down this street and turn right at the pharmacy.
Yes, it opens at eleven thirty.

scenarios.scenario: Going to the train station
scenarios.context: A person asks how to get to the train station.

speakerA.en: Where is the train station?
Can I walk there?
Is there a bus?
Thank you. Goodbye.
Excuse me, how do I get to the train station?
Where is the subway entrance?
Can I walk there instead?
OK. I'll take the subway. Thanks!

speakerB.en: It's behind the big hotel.
Yes, it's ten minutes on foot.
Yes. Take bus number five.
Goodbye. Have a nice trip!
Take the subway, line two. It's only three stops.
It's in front of that big supermarket.
You can, but it takes about forty minutes.
No problem. Have a safe journey!

scenarios.scenario: Places on a street
scenarios.context: Two people talk about the buildings on a street.

speakerA.en: What is that building?
What is across from the library?
Where is the supermarket?
I see it. Thank you.
What's that building on the corner?
And what's next to it?
Is there a pharmacy on this street?
Where is the post office?

speakerB.en: It's the library.
It's a small coffee shop.
It's between the bank and the school.
You're welcome.
That's the town library. It's very old.
A bakery. They make the best bread in town.
Yes, it's opposite the bank, near the traffic lights.
It's behind the bank, at the end of the street.

scenarios.scenario: Lost in the city
scenarios.context: A lost person asks a police officer for help.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, officer. I'm lost.
I want to go to the hotel.
It's the Sun Hotel.
Thank you for your help.
Excuse me, officer. I'm lost. Can you help me?
I'm looking for the Grand Hotel on Oak Avenue.
I don't have much money. Is there a bus?
Could you write the name of the stop for me?

speakerB.en: Where do you want to go?
What's the name of the hotel?
Go straight and turn left at the corner.
You're welcome. Be careful!
Of course. Where are you trying to go?
That's quite far from here. You can take a taxi.
Yes, take bus number 12 from the corner.
Sure. Get off at Oak Avenue. It's the fifth stop.

scenarios.scenario: Finding a place using landmarks
scenarios.context: A tourist asks a local how to reach a museum.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the City Art Museum?
And after the fountain? I'm afraid I get lost easily.
Is the museum right next to the church, or is it further on?
Thank you so much. Roughly how long will it take on foot?

speakerB.en: Sure. Go straight down this street until you reach the big fountain in the square.
Turn left at the fountain, and you'll see a tall church on your right.
It's just behind it. You can't miss the red building with the large columns.
About fifteen minutes. If you reach the river, you've gone too far.

scenarios.scenario: Getting lost and asking for help
scenarios.context: A driver stops to ask a pedestrian for directions.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I think I'm lost. I'm trying to find the highway to the airport.
My navigation app stopped working, and the road signs are confusing.
Do I take the first or the second exit at the roundabout?
That sounds simple enough. How far is it from here?

speakerB.en: You're going in the wrong direction. You need to turn around and go back to the traffic lights.
At the lights, turn right and follow the signs. Keep going until you pass a gas station.
The second one. After that, you'll see signs for the airport almost immediately.
About twenty minutes if there's no traffic. Have a safe trip!

scenarios.scenario: Giving directions to a visitor
scenarios.context: A resident explains to a friend how to reach his new apartment.

speakerA.en: Hi, I'm at the train station now. How do I get to your apartment?
Got it. Do I walk past the supermarket or turn there?
And then? Is your building next to the park?
Which floor are you on? I don't want to ring the wrong bell.

speakerB.en: Take the main exit and cross the street. You'll see a supermarket on the corner.
Walk past it and keep going for about two blocks, until you see a small park.
It's across from it. It's the yellow building with a blue door.
The third floor, apartment number 9. I'll watch for you from the window.

scenarios.scenario: Navigating with unclear instructions
scenarios.context: A traveler gets conflicting directions and asks for clarification.

speakerA.en: I was told the conference center is a ten-minute walk from here, but I seem to have gone in circles.
I turned left at the cathedral and followed the canal until it split into two.
And once I'm across, is the building immediately visible, or do I need to look out for something?
Thank you. I'd have wandered around for another hour if you hadn't stopped to help.

speakerB.en: It's easy to get confused around here. Which way did you set off from the station?
That's where people go wrong. You need to take the right-hand branch and cross the second bridge.
You'll see a modern glass structure with a large clock on the front. It's hard to miss.
No trouble at all. If you reach a bakery on your left, you've gone a little too far.

scenarios.scenario: Giving directions in a foreign language
scenarios.context: A local struggles to explain the way to a visitor.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, do you speak English? I'm trying to find the railway museum.
Your English is fine. I'm simply grateful for any help at all.
Is it a long way, or can I walk there?
That's clear enough. Would it be quicker to take a tram, perhaps?

speakerB.en: A little. I will try to explain, but my English is not very good.
You go... how do you say... straight, until the big supermarket. Then you turn to the left side.
You can walk. Maybe twenty minutes. The museum is behind the park, near the old factory.
The tram is slower because of the road work. I would walk, and the park is pleasant at this time of day.

scenarios.scenario: Finding a specific address in an unfamiliar area
scenarios.context: A courier asks a resident for help locating an address.

speakerA.en: I'm trying to deliver a parcel to number forty-two, but the numbers on this street don't seem to follow any logic.
So where would I find forty-two? I've already walked from one end to the other.
That would explain it. Do you happen to know who lives there? The name on the label is Mr. Alvarez.
That's extremely helpful. I would never have found it on my own.

speakerB.en: That's a common problem here. The street was extended in the nineties, and they numbered the new section separately.
You need to go back to the roundabout and enter the street from the other side.
I know the family. They live in a white house with a green gate, just beyond the pharmacy.
Don't mention it. If nobody answers, you can leave it with the neighbor next door, as they usually take parcels in.

scenarios.scenario: Navigating a complex public transport route
scenarios.context: A tourist asks a local for a route that involves a transfer.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I'm trying to reach the botanical gardens, but my map app keeps rerouting me. Could you suggest the simplest way?
How many changes would that involve? I have a heavy bag, so I'd prefer to keep them to a minimum.
And how do I know which stop to get off at? I don't want to end up miles past it.
That's wonderfully clear. Is it worth buying a day pass, given that I'll be returning the same way?

speakerB.en: The simplest isn't necessarily the quickest. You could take the metro to Central Station, but the gardens are better served by the tram from there.
Just one. Take the red line three stops, change at Central, and board the number twelve tram toward the harbor.
It's the fifth stop, named after the university. You'll see the glass greenhouse on your left as the tram pulls in.
Absolutely. A day pass covers the metro and trams, and it works out cheaper than two single journeys.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for directions on a rural road
scenarios.context: A driver without a GPS signal asks a local for directions on a country road.

speakerA.en: Sorry to trouble you. My GPS lost its signal a few miles back, and I'm not entirely sure I'm still on the right road for Millbrook.
I recall passing a chapel, though I didn't notice a crossroads. Was it the one with the broken signpost?
That's easy to miss. How far is it from there to Millbrook?
I'll bear that in mind. Thank you so much. You've saved me from wandering around all afternoon.

speakerB.en: You're a little off course, I'm afraid. You'll need to turn around and go back to the crossroads by the old chapel.
That's the one. Take the left fork there, which looks like a farm track but is actually the main road to the village.
About six miles, though the road is narrow and winding, so allow twenty minutes. Watch out for tractors around the bends.
Not at all. It happens to everyone around here. Safe travels.

scenarios.scenario: Guiding a visitor through a large complex
scenarios.context: A receptionist directs a patient to a department in a sprawling hospital campus.

speakerA.en: I have an appointment in the cardiology department at half past two, but I've been wandering around for ten minutes and can't find it.
So I'll need to go outside? I had hoped there would be an internal corridor.
And once I'm across, will it be obvious where to go?
Thank you. That's far clearer than the signage, which seems designed to confuse.

speakerB.en: I'm not surprised. The campus is a labyrinth. Cardiology is in the east wing, which isn't connected to this building at ground level.
There is, but it's on the second floor. Take the elevator up, follow the yellow line past the pharmacy, and cross the glass bridge.
Yes, you'll see the cardiology reception directly ahead. If you get lost, any member of staff in blue scrubs will point you the right way.
You're not the first to say so. We've been promising to improve it for years.

scenarios.scenario: Navigating with imprecise directions in a rural area
scenarios.context: A driver gets lost and asks a local for help in a place with few signs.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I seem to have lost my bearings. I'm looking for the old mill, which I was told is somewhere near the village.
The crooked oak? Is that a formal landmark, or are we relying on a slightly poetic description?
And after the telephone box? I'd rather not wander the lanes of the countryside indefinitely.
Unmarked tracks make me nervous, but I'll trust you. Is there anywhere to turn around if I overshoot?

speakerB.en: You're nearer than you think, though the signposts around here are notoriously unreliable. Follow this road until you reach the crooked oak.
Both, I suppose. You can't miss it; it leans at an angle that defies physics. Turn left there, and continue past the telephone box.
Carry on for about half a mile, and you'll see a track on your right, unmarked. The mill sits at the end of it.
There's a wide verge just beyond the track. Failing that, ring the farmhouse; they'll set you straight.

scenarios.scenario: Giving clear directions to a visitor in a complex city center
scenarios.context: A local describes a route involving several turns, landmarks and a shortcut.

speakerA.en: I'm trying to reach the national archive, but my map seems to be sending me in circles. Could you point me in the right direction?
The cathedral on my left, understood. And then?
Goodness, I would never have noticed that. Is it a safe route, or is it one of those shortcuts that tourists regret?
That's wonderfully clear. I'm grateful, and I'll try not to feel quite so out of my depth in future.

speakerB.en: Gladly. The streets here are confusing, but the route is simple once you know it. Head down to the cathedral, and keep it on your left.
Cross the square, and take the narrow alley beside the bookshop. It looks like a dead end, but it opens onto a quiet street.
Perfectly safe, and it saves you ten minutes. At the end, turn right, and the archive is the grey building with the large doors.
Don't be hard on yourself. Even locals get lost here, and we simply pretend we meant to.

scenarios.scenario: Confirming a meeting point over the phone
scenarios.context: Two people struggle to agree on an unambiguous place to meet in a busy station.

speakerA.en: I'm at the main entrance, beneath the large clock. Are you anywhere near? I can't see you in the crowd.
No, mine faces the departure board. There seem to be two, which explains a great deal about our difficulty.
I do. I'm standing roughly ten meters from it, beside a man selling newspapers.
Splendid. I'm wearing a navy coat and carrying a red umbrella, in case you're still unsure.

speakerB.en: I'm by the clock, but I think we may be at different ones. Is yours the one facing the taxi rank?
Let's use a more reliable landmark. Do you see the coffee kiosk with the green awning?
Then we are on opposite sides. I'll walk toward the kiosk, and you do the same; we should meet in the middle.
I can see you now. You were right in front of me all along, which I find rather embarrassing.

scenarios.scenario: Asking where the restroom is
scenarios.context: A person asks a stranger for the restroom.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Where is the restroom?
Is there an elevator?
Thank you. Is it free?
That's great. Thanks for your help.

speakerB.en: It's on the second floor.
Yes, it's next to the café.
Yes, it is. It's free for everyone.
You're welcome.

scenarios.scenario: Finding the nearest pharmacy
scenarios.context: A person asks a stranger where the nearest pharmacy is.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Is there a pharmacy near here?
Is it far?
Do I go straight?
Thank you very much.

speakerB.en: Yes, there is one on Main Street.
No, it's five minutes on foot.
Yes, then turn left at the bank.
No problem. Have a nice day!

scenarios.scenario: Giving directions to a tourist
scenarios.context: A local person explains the way to a tourist.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, how can I get to the museum?
Two blocks, and then?
Is the museum near the church?
Thank you. Is it far on foot?

speakerB.en: Go straight along this street for two blocks.
Turn right at the traffic lights. You'll see a big church.
Yes, it's opposite the church, next to a small café.
No, about ten minutes. You can't miss it.

scenarios.scenario: Explaining how to get to your house
scenarios.context: A man explains the way to his house on the phone.

speakerA.en: Hi, I'm at the bus station. How do I get to your house?
How many stops is that?
What do I do after the park?
Okay, I understand. See you soon.

speakerB.en: Take bus number twelve and get off at the park.
Five stops. It takes about fifteen minutes.
Walk past the bakery. My house is the green one on the left.
Call me if you can't find it.

scenarios.scenario: Getting lost and calling for help
scenarios.context: A tourist phones a friend because he is lost.

speakerA.en: Hi, I think I'm lost. I've been walking in circles for twenty minutes.
There's a big supermarket on my left and a petrol station across the road.
And then? Is it a long way from there?
Got it. I'll send you a message when I find it.

speakerB.en: Don't worry. Can you see any landmark near you?
Okay, that's the Green Street. Walk past the petrol station and turn right.
Not at all. You'll see a bridge, and the café is just after it.
Perfect. If you have any trouble, I'll come and meet you.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for the best route to the airport
scenarios.context: A visitor asks a hotel receptionist about getting to the airport.

speakerA.en: Could you tell me the best way to get to the airport tomorrow?
Which one is quicker?
My flight is at nine, so I need to leave early. Is the bus running at that time?
I think I'll take the taxi to be safe. Could you order one for me?

speakerB.en: You have two options: a taxi or the airport bus from the main square.
A taxi takes about thirty minutes, while the bus takes closer to fifty.
The first bus leaves at five thirty, which should be early enough.
Certainly. Shall I arrange it for half past five?

scenarios.scenario: Locating a restaurant by landmarks
scenarios.context: A visitor asks a passer-by how to find a restaurant in an unfamiliar neighborhood.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I'm looking for a restaurant called The Blue Door. I've been walking around for twenty minutes, and I can't find it.
I think it's somewhere near the old post office, but my phone's map isn't working properly in this area.
Left at the bank, and then straight on. How far is it from there? I don't want to walk too long, because I'm wearing new shoes.
Got it. And if I reach the fountain, does that mean I've gone too far?
That's very clear. By the way, do you happen to know if the restaurant is open on Mondays?
Thanks a lot. I would never have found it without your help, and I really appreciate it.

speakerB.en: Let me think. The Blue Door... yes, I know it. It's not far from here, but it's easy to miss because the entrance is small.
You're quite close, actually. Go back along this street until you see the bank on the corner, and then turn left.
It's only about five minutes on foot. Walk past the pharmacy and the bookshop, and you'll see a small square with a fountain.
Yes, exactly. If you reach the fountain, you've gone a little too far. The restaurant is on the right, just before the square, with a blue door.
I believe it's open every day from noon, but you could call to make sure. It's usually busy in the evenings, so it's worth booking.
You're welcome! Enjoy your meal. The fish soup is excellent, if you like seafood.

scenarios.scenario: Getting directions to a hospital
scenarios.context: A driver asks for directions to the hospital and learns about parking and entrances.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the city hospital? I'm visiting a relative, and I'm not familiar with this part of town.
I came by car, so I'd like to know where I can park. I've heard that the parking area in front of the main entrance is always full.
That's useful. And which entrance should I use for visitors? I was told that the main gate is closed for renovation.
How long does it take to walk from the car park to the ward? My relative is on the fourth floor, and I'm carrying a heavy bag.
I see. Then I'll take the lift to the fourth floor. Do I need to register at the reception desk first?
Thank you very much. You've been extremely helpful, and I appreciate your time.

speakerB.en: Of course. Go straight ahead for about two kilometers, until you reach a large roundabout. Take the second exit, towards the river.
You're right, it's often full. There's a bigger car park behind the building, on Park Street, which is usually less crowded.
Use the side entrance on the north side, next to the pharmacy. There's a sign saying 'Visitors', and you can't miss it.
It's about five minutes on foot. There's also a free shuttle that runs every ten minutes, if you'd rather not walk.
Yes, visitors have to sign in at the desk and show some identification. Visiting hours are between two and seven in the afternoon.
You're welcome. I hope your relative gets better soon. Take care, and drive carefully on the roundabout.

scenarios.scenario: Navigating an unfamiliar city with a local
scenarios.context: A traveler asks a local resident to explain a complicated route.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I'm trying to find the Museum of Modern Art, but my phone has run out of battery, and I'm afraid that I've completely lost my sense of direction.
I see. So I'd have to cross the bridge, take the second left after the cathedral, and then continue until I reach a square with a fountain. Have I understood correctly?
Is it easier to go by tram, or would you recommend walking? I'm not in a hurry, and I'd rather see something of the city, as long as it's a pleasant route.
That sounds lovely. And if I wanted to return to the central station afterwards, would it be simpler to take the same route, or is there a more direct way?
Thank you. That's extremely helpful. I would never have found the market street without your advice, and I'm looking forward to the walk.
I'll certainly do that. You've been wonderfully patient, and I really appreciate you taking the time to explain.

speakerB.en: Of course. It's a bit complicated from here, because the streets in the old town aren't laid out in a regular pattern. Let me explain it as clearly as I can.
Nearly. After the bridge, you turn left, not right, and then you walk past the covered market. The square with the fountain comes about five minutes after the cathedral, on your right-hand side.
If you have the time, I'd suggest walking. The route through the market street is much more interesting, and it takes about twenty minutes. The tram is faster, but you'd see very little.
There's a direct bus from the museum to the station, which runs every ten minutes, but I'd recommend walking back along the river, where it's quieter, and you'll pass some beautiful old buildings.
My pleasure. Be careful on the stone streets, which can be slippery after rain. And if you get lost again, don't hesitate to ask somebody. People here are usually glad to help.
It was no trouble at all. Enjoy the exhibition, and the view from the top floor is well worth the climb.

scenarios.scenario: Giving precise directions to a remote location
scenarios.context: A host explains how to reach a countryside house to a visitor on the phone.

speakerA.en: Hello, I think I'm lost. I've been following the navigation system, but it keeps telling me to turn onto a road that doesn't seem to exist. Where exactly should I be going?
I've just passed a petrol station and a small chapel, and I'm now at a crossroads with a red barn on the left. Does that sound right, or have I gone the wrong way?
Understood. So I should take the narrow road past the barn, go down the hill, and then look for a gate with a white mailbox. Is that the entrance to your property?
And what about the dog? I was told that you have a rather large one, and I'd prefer to know whether it's friendly before I get out of the car.
That's a relief. I should be there in about ten minutes, unless I run into more problems. Thank you for guiding me so patiently.
I'll see you in a few minutes. I'm looking forward to a hot cup of tea after this adventure.

speakerB.en: Don't worry, it happens to most visitors. Our house isn't on any map, and the navigation system often sends people in the wrong direction. Where are you now?
You're almost there. You've come the right way. The red barn is the last landmark before the turn. Take the narrow road to the left, and keep going for about two kilometers.
That's it exactly. The road is rough in places, so drive slowly. You'll see a small stream at the bottom of the hill, which you cross by a little bridge.
Oh, you needn't worry about Max. He's enormous, but he's as gentle as a lamb. He'll probably greet you at the gate and demand attention.
Perfect. I'll put the kettle on now. If you can't see the house from the gate, just follow the gravel path through the trees, and you'll find us at the end.
Safe driving. And if you lose your way again, phone me right away, and I'll come out to meet you.

scenarios.scenario: Guiding a driver by phone through roadworks
scenarios.context: A friend gives phone directions to a driver who is lost because of a diversion.

speakerA.en: Hi, I'm nearly there, but there's a diversion on the main road, and the navigation system keeps trying to send me back through the roadworks. Where should I turn?
I've just passed the supermarket with the big red sign, and now there are cones across the road. There's a sign pointing right, but it doesn't say where it leads.
Okay, I'm on the narrow road now. There's a church on my left and a row of houses on my right. Should I keep going straight, or is there another turning?
I can see a small roundabout ahead, with a statue in the middle. Which exit do I take? I don't want to end up back on the highway.
Right, I've taken the second exit, and I'm going uphill. I can see a bakery on the corner, with a blue awning. Is that the one you mentioned?
I can see your building now, and there's a parking space opposite. Thank you so much. I'd never have found it without your help.

speakerB.en: Don't worry, it's confusing at the moment. The diversion was put in last week, and nobody seems to have updated the maps. Where exactly are you now?
That's the right place. Follow the sign to the right, and then continue along that road for about a kilometer. You'll pass a school and a petrol station. Tell me when you see them.
Good, you're on the right track. Keep going straight, past the church, and ignore any turnings on the right. After about five hundred meters, you'll reach a small roundabout.
Take the second exit, the one that leads uphill, away from the highway. After that, you'll see a bakery on the corner, and you should turn left immediately after it.
That's it. Now carry on for another two hundred meters, and my building will be on your right, a tall one with a green door. I'll wait for you outside, so you can't miss me.
Perfect. I'll come down and help you with the bags. You've done really well, considering the circumstances. Come up and have a cup of tea.

scenarios.scenario: Finding the right platform and exit in a large station
scenarios.context: A traveler asks a station employee how to reach a connecting service in a large, complex station.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I've just arrived on platform nine, and I'm trying to get to the regional train to Freiburg. Could you tell me which platform it leaves from, and how to get there?
I only have twelve minutes before it leaves, and I have a large suitcase. Is there a lift or an escalator, or will I have to carry it up the stairs?
I see. And is it signposted clearly? I was here once before, and I remember getting lost, because the signs seemed to point in all directions.
Thank you. If I miss it, what's the next train, and would my ticket still be valid on that one, since it's a different service?
That's reassuring. One more question: is there somewhere I can buy a quick sandwich on the way? I haven't eaten anything since this morning.
Thanks a lot. You've been very helpful, and I'll make sure that I follow your instructions exactly.

speakerB.en: Of course. The regional train to Freiburg leaves from platform fourteen, which is on the other side of the station. You'll need to go down to the main concourse, and then up again.
There's a lift just behind you, next to the information desk. Take it to the ground floor, and then follow the yellow signs for platforms ten to fifteen. It should take about five minutes.

It's much better than it used to be. Look out for the large screens that show the next departures, and follow the number fourteen. If you're unsure, there are staff in orange jackets near each entrance.
The next one leaves at a quarter past the hour, so you'd only lose thirty minutes. Your ticket is valid for any train on that route during the day, so you wouldn't have to pay anything extra.
There's a small kiosk on the concourse, right by the stairs to platform fourteen. They sell fresh sandwiches and drinks, but if you're short of time, I'd suggest that you buy something on the train.
You're welcome. Don't run, you've got plenty of time. Have a pleasant journey, and I hope you arrive on schedule.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a local for directions to the cathedral
scenarios.context: A tourist whose phone has died asks a passer-by how to reach the old cathedral and where to eat nearby.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I'm afraid I'm a little lost. I'm trying to get to the old cathedral, but my phone has run out of battery, and none of these street names are on the map I've got.
That sounds straightforward. Would it be quicker to take a taxi, or is it better to walk? I'm in no hurry, but my feet are killing me, since I've been sightseeing since this morning.
The tram sounds ideal. Should I buy a ticket on board, or do I need one beforehand? I wouldn't want to get fined, in case there's an inspector, as I've heard happens quite often.

That's a good tip. On the other hand, I'm also looking for a decent restaurant nearby, preferably something local. Could you recommend somewhere near the cathedral, in case I'm hungry when I get there?
Thank you, that's extremely helpful. One more question, if you don't mind. In case I get lost on the way back, is there a landmark I should look out for, to help me find the hotel?
That's perfect, I'm just a few minutes from the station. Thank you so much for your time. I was starting to panic, but you've been wonderfully clear. Have a lovely afternoon.

speakerB.en: No problem at all. The cathedral's about fifteen minutes from here on foot. Keep going down this road until you reach the large square with the fountain, and then turn left. You can't miss it.

It might be quicker to take the tram, to be honest. It runs from the stop just around the corner, and it takes you right past the cathedral. You'd need to get off at the third stop, and you can't miss it.
You'd better buy one from the machine at the stop, since drivers don't sell them. It might be worth getting a day pass, as long as you're planning to travel around the city this afternoon.
There's a lovely little place just behind the cathedral, on the corner of Rose Street. Keep walking until you see a blue awning, and you can't miss it. It might be busy, so book a table if you can.
Where are you staying? If it's near the station, you can see the clock tower from almost anywhere in the center. Walk toward it until you reach the main road, and you can't miss it.
My pleasure. Enjoy the cathedral, and if you've got time, climb the tower for the view. It might be a bit of a climb, but it's worth every step. Have a wonderful visit.

scenarios.scenario: Guiding a friend to your house over the phone
scenarios.context: A driver who has just left the highway phones a friend, who guides him street by street to her house.

speakerA.en: Hi, I've just come off the highway, and I'm not sure which way to go. Your directions said to take the second exit, but the roundabout has four exits, and I can't tell which is which.
I can see a gas station, but it's on my left. I wonder if I've gone around the wrong way. To be honest, I didn't realize roundabouts worked in different directions here, as I'm used to the opposite.
Right, I've done that, and I can see the river now, along with the supermarket. What next? Should I turn left or right at the lights, or is it straight on until I reach the bridge?
Understood. On the other hand, I'm a little worried about parking, since I've got a rather large car. Is there somewhere close by, or should I find a parking lot nearby and walk the rest of the way?
That's a relief. I can see the boathouse now, so I think I'm almost there. Is your building the one with the green door, or the tall one next to it? I'd hate to ring the wrong bell.
Perfect, I'm turning onto Orchard Lane now. I can see you waving from the window. I'll park right here and be up in two minutes, so put the kettle on.

speakerB.en: Don't worry, it's confusing. Which exit are you looking at? Once you've gone around, you should see a gas station on your right. If you pass the gas station, you've gone too far.
That's the problem. Make sure you go around clockwise, and take the second exit. Once you've done that, you'll be heading toward the river. If you see a large supermarket, you've gone the right way.

Straight on, until you reach the bridge, but be careful not to cross it. Once you've reached the bridge, turn right immediately, and follow the road along the river. If you pass the boathouse, you've gone too far.

There's a small lot behind the pub, but make sure you don't use it, because it's for customers only. Once you've turned onto Orchard Lane, you'll find free street parking on the left, which is much better.

It's the one with the green door, number fourteen. Make sure you ring the top bell, since the others belong to the neighbors. Once you've parked, I'll come down and meet you, in case you can't find the entrance.
Brilliant, I'll do that. Well done for finding it in the end. Be careful not to slam the car door, as the neighbor is sleeping, and I'll see you in a moment.

scenarios.scenario: Helping a lost visitor find a hidden museum in the old town
scenarios.context: A local resident helps a visitor who has wandered into the old town and is looking for a small museum tucked away behind the market.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I'm afraid I'm completely lost. I've been looking for the Folk Art Museum for half an hour, and my map doesn't seem to match the streets. To be honest, the old town is far more confusing than I expected. Could you point me in the right direction?
From the cathedral. I followed the main street until I reached a fountain, and then I turned left. Is that wrong? I'd say I went the right way, although it's possible I took one turn too many.

I think I remember the market hall, but it was closed when I passed. Will I be able to walk through it, or should I go around? I'd rather not get lost again. As far as I'm concerned, one afternoon of being lost is enough.

Not really, but the museum closes at five, and I'm told the textile collection is the highlight. Provided I get there by half past four, I'll have enough time. Is it worth the entrance fee, in your opinion?
That's reassuring, thank you. Is there anywhere nearby for a coffee afterwards? I'd like to sit down for a while, as long as it isn't too touristy. Somewhere local would be ideal.

Wonderful, that settles it. Fountain, turn right, through the market hall, and then the courtyard. Thank you so much for your help, you've saved my afternoon. I'll make sure to try the cake, since you recommend it so strongly.

speakerB.en: Of course. You're actually very close. It's easy to miss, since the museum is tucked away behind the market, in a courtyard whose entrance looks like a private house. Where did you come from, the station or the cathedral?

Close, but not quite. Go back to the fountain, the one in front of which you'll see a small café with blue chairs. Turn right there, not left, and you'll find a narrow lane at the end of which stands the market hall. Does that sound familiar?

Unless it's a holiday, the side passage is open, so you can walk straight through. If you were to go around, you'd lose ten minutes. On the other hand, the outside route is prettier, which is why many visitors prefer it. Are you in a hurry?

Absolutely, it's one of the best small museums in the country. The textile room, in which the older tapestries hang, is stunning. Provided you ask for the audio guide, you'll learn a great deal. Were you to visit only one place in the old town, I'd say this should be it.

There's a small bakery next to the museum, whose owner makes the best almond cake in town. Unless you've already eaten, you should try a slice. To be honest, the cafés on the main square are overpriced, so I'd avoid those.
You've got it exactly right. Enjoy the museum, and if you get lost again, ask anyone for 'the blue-door courtyard'. Everyone here knows it. Have a lovely afternoon, and welcome to our town.

scenarios.scenario: Choosing a route when the GPS fails on a road trip
scenarios.context: Two friends driving through the countryside lose their GPS signal and weigh up a scenic coastal road against a longer highway route.

speakerA.en: The GPS has lost the signal again, and we're in the middle of nowhere. To be honest, I'd say we should have printed a map. If it hadn't been for that road sign a while ago, I wouldn't even know which valley we're in. What now?

The coastal road is nowhere near as quick, but it's far more beautiful. We aren't in a hurry, so I'd sooner enjoy the view than save half an hour. On the other hand, it's only half as wide, and the weather is closing in.

About three hours, although we stopped twice. It's nowhere near as long as it feels. If it hadn't rained, I'd have suggested it without hesitation. Whichever we choose, we'll need fuel, and the tank is nearly empty.

It does, a little. I'd sooner arrive late than be stranded on an empty road. Still, I hate giving up the coast. Could we take the highway there, and then drive back along the coast tomorrow, when it's sunny?

Then it's settled. Let's find the junction first, and I'll watch for road signs while you drive. If we were to miss the turning, we'd lose another half an hour. Is the sun going to be a problem, by the way, at this time of day?

Found it, folded up with an old receipt! Honestly, I'd rather have a paper map than rely on a signal. Whichever route you take tomorrow, I'll navigate. Had I known it was there, we could have saved ourselves ten minutes of arguing.

speakerB.en: Don't panic. According to the sign, the highway is twenty kilometers east, and the coastal road is about the same distance to the west. I'd rather take the highway than the coastal road, since it's much faster. Which would you prefer?

That's exactly my concern. Had we left an hour earlier, we'd have had better light for the coast, but it's already four o'clock. As far as I'm concerned, the highway is the safer option. Do you remember how long the coastal road took last time?

Good point. The map at the last junction showed a petrol station about ten kilometers along the highway. I'd rather fill up there than risk running dry on a coastal road with no villages. Does that change your mind?

That's a clever compromise. If it hadn't been for your idea, we'd have argued all evening. Tomorrow's forecast is twice as good as today's, so we'd see the cliffs properly. Whichever way we look at it, the plan is sound.

A little, since we're heading east, but it's nowhere near as bad as at noon. I'll put the visor down. Actually, could you check the glove compartment? I'm fairly sure there's a paper map in there from our last trip.
Don't blame yourself, it's more fun this way. To be honest, I'd sooner have an adventure than a perfect journey. Let's go, and let's hope the petrol station is as close as the map says.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing weekend plans and hobbies
scenarios.context: Talking about what to do in free time or upcoming events.

speakerA.en: What are you doing this weekend?
What do you do in your free time?
I like football, too.
Great idea! See you then.
Do you have any plans for the holiday?
speakerA.fa: برای تعطیلات برنامه‌ای داری؟

speakerA.en: I'm thinking of going to the cinema. Would you like to join?
speakerA.fa: دارم به سینما رفتن فکر می‌کنم. دوست داری بیای؟

speakerA.en: I usually play football with my friends on Saturdays.
speakerA.fa: معمولاً شنبه‌ها با دوستام فوتبال بازی می‌کنم.

speakerA.en: I've taken up painting as a new hobby. It's quite relaxing.
speakerA.fa: تازه نقاشی رو به عنوان یه سرگرمی شروع کردم. خیلی آرامش‌بخشه.

speakerA.en: Let's catch up over a coffee sometime. When are you free?
speakerA.fa: یه وقتایی بریم یه قهوه بخوریم و گپ بزنیم. کی آزادی؟

speakerA.en: A new comedy. It starts at eight on Friday.
In front of the cinema at seven thirty.

speakerB.en: I don't know yet. Maybe I'll stay home.
I read books and play football.
Really? Let's play together on Saturday.
See you on Saturday!
I'm going to visit my parents. It's been a while.
speakerB.fa: می‌رم به دیدار پدر و مادرم. مدتی هست که نرفتم.

speakerB.en: That sounds fun! What movie are you going to see?
speakerB.fa: خوش می‌گذره! چه فیلمی می‌خواین ببینید؟

speakerB.en: That's great. I prefer hiking myself. Do you like nature?
speakerB.fa: عالیه. من خودم پیاده‌روی تو کوه رو ترجیح می‌دم. طبیعت رو دوست داری؟

speakerB.en: Really? That's interesting. I've always wanted to learn how to paint.
speakerB.fa: واقعاً؟ جالبه. من همیشه می‌خواستم نقاشی یاد بگیرم.

speakerB.en: I'm free on Wednesday after 4 PM. Let's meet at that new café downtown.
speakerB.fa: چهارشنبه بعد از ۴ عصر آزادم. بیا همون کافه جدید مرکز شهر.

speakerB.en: I'd love to come. Where shall we meet?
Perfect. I'll buy the popcorn.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about hobbies
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about their hobbies.

speakerA.en: What's your hobby?
Do you play the guitar?
Is it hard?
I like drawing.
What do you like doing when you have free time?
How long have you played the guitar?
Do you have any other hobbies?
That sounds great. Can I come and try your food?

speakerB.en: I like music.
Yes, I do. I play every day.
No, it's fun.
That's nice!
I play the guitar and I paint a little.
For about three years. I take lessons every week.
I also like cooking. I try a new recipe every Sunday.
Of course! Come next Sunday.

scenarios.scenario: Weekend plans
scenarios.context: Two friends make plans for the weekend.

speakerA.en: Are you free on Saturday?
Let's go to the park.
At ten o'clock.
Bring some water.
Do you have anything planned for this weekend?
That sounds boring. Do you want to go hiking?
There's a nice trail near the river.
At eight, so we can come back before dark.

speakerB.en: Yes, I am.
Good idea. What time?
OK. See you at ten.
OK. I will.
I'm going to clean the house and then relax.
Good idea. Where do you want to go?
OK. What time shall we start?
Fine. I'll bring snacks and water.

scenarios.scenario: Going to the cinema
scenarios.context: Two friends plan to see a movie.

speakerA.en: Do you want to see a movie?
It's a funny movie.
The movie starts at seven.
I'll buy the tickets.
Let's see a movie tonight. What do you want to see?
I like action movies, but I also like comedies.
OK. What time does it start?
The seven o'clock show is better for me.

speakerB.en: Yes, I do. Which movie?
I like funny movies.
OK. Let's meet at six thirty.
Thank you. I'll buy the popcorn.
I don't mind. What kinds of movies do you like?
Then let's see the new comedy. It has good reviews.
There's a show at seven and another at nine thirty.
Great. I'll book two tickets online.

scenarios.scenario: Playing sports
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about playing football.

speakerA.en: Do you like football?
Can you play on Sunday?
Where do you play?
Can I play with you?
Do you play football?
Where do you play your games?
Can I join your team?
What should I bring?

speakerB.en: Yes, I love it.
Yes, I can.
I play at the school field.
Of course. Come at nine.
Yes, I play with my friends every Saturday.
At the sports center near the station.
Sure. We need one more player.
Bring sports shoes and a bottle of water.

scenarios.scenario: Staying at home
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about what they do at home.

speakerA.en: What do you do at home?
Do you cook?
What do you cook?
Can I come to your house?
Are you going out tonight?
What are you going to do?
Which series are you watching?
Can you tell me the name? I need something to watch.

speakerB.en: I read books.
Yes. I cook with my mother.
I cook rice and chicken.
Yes, you can. Come for dinner.
No, I'm staying home. I'm tired.
I'm going to watch a series and order pizza.
It's a detective story. It's very exciting.
Sure. I'll send you the title.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a picnic
scenarios.context: Two friends plan a picnic.

speakerA.en: Let's have a picnic.
What can we bring?
Is it going to rain?
Let's go on Sunday.
Let's have a picnic on Saturday.
How about the lake? It's quiet and there's a lot of shade.
I'll bring sandwiches and fruit.
Don't forget a blanket and some plates.

speakerB.en: That's a nice idea.
Bread, fruit and juice.
No, it's sunny.
OK. I'm happy.
Great idea! Where shall we go?
Perfect. What food should we bring?
I'll make a salad and bring drinks.
I won't. I'll also bring a ball for games.

scenarios.scenario: Deciding what to do on the weekend
scenarios.context: Two friends make plans for their free time.

speakerA.en: Do you have any plans for the weekend? I'm bored of staying at home.
That sounds great. We could rent a boat or just have a picnic.
Deal. Should we invite a few more people, or keep it small?
Good idea. I'll text them tonight and let you know what they say.

speakerB.en: Not yet. I was thinking about going to the lake if the weather is nice.
A picnic sounds more relaxing. I'll bring sandwiches if you bring the drinks.
Let's ask Mia and Tom. They've been looking for something to do as well.
Perfect. If it rains, we can go bowling instead.

scenarios.scenario: Taking up a new hobby
scenarios.context: A woman tells her friend about a new hobby she has started.

speakerA.en: I've started a pottery class on Wednesday evenings, and I'm really enjoying it.
At first, yes. My first bowl looked terrible, but it's getting better every week.
It helps me forget about work. I concentrate so hard that I don't think about anything else.
Yes, a new one starts next month. You could try one lesson before you decide.

speakerB.en: Really? I always thought it would be difficult. Is it hard to learn?
What do you like most about it?
That sounds wonderful. Do they have any beginners' courses?
I might do that. Send me the information, and I'll think about it.

scenarios.scenario: Joining a sports or hobby club
scenarios.context: A newcomer asks a club member about joining a local club.

speakerA.en: Hi, I'm interested in joining the photography club. How does it work?
I'm not a professional. Is that a problem?
Do I need any special equipment, or can I use my phone camera?
How much does membership cost?

speakerB.en: Welcome! We meet every second Thursday, and we usually go on a photo walk once a month.
Not at all. We have members of all levels, and we like to share tips with one another.
A phone is fine for now. Many of us started that way before buying a proper camera.
Twenty dollars a year. You can come to the next meeting for free and see if you like it.

scenarios.scenario: Balancing hobbies and responsibilities
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about finding time for personal interests.

speakerA.en: I used to paint every weekend, but since the new job, I haven't picked up a brush in months.
In theory, yes, but by Saturday I'm so exhausted that I can't muster the energy.
You may have a point. I let it slip because I felt I needed to be productive all the time.
I'll try to reserve Sunday mornings for painting, and treat it as a firm appointment.

speakerB.en: That's a pity. Don't you think it's important to make time for something that gives you pleasure?
Perhaps you could set aside even an hour a week. A little regularly is better than nothing.
