A hobby is meant to be an escape from precisely that kind of pressure.
Good idea. And if you need an incentive, I'd love to see what you create.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing an extreme sport
scenarios.context: A thrill-seeker tells a skeptical friend about his new pastime.

speakerA.en: I've taken up rock climbing, and I can't tell you how much I'm enjoying it.
It sounds more daunting than it is. We train indoors first, with ropes and helmets.
There's some risk, as with any sport, but you learn to manage it. Safety checks are almost obsessive.
You'd surprise yourself. Come along to a beginners' session, and if you hate it, I'll never mention it again.

speakerB.en: Rather you than me. I get dizzy on the top step of a ladder.
Even so, surely there's a risk involved? One careless move, and it's all over.
I admire your courage, although I'd have to be dragged up a wall kicking and screaming.
All right, I'll give it one try, but I make no promises about keeping my eyes open.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a creative project together
scenarios.context: Two friends plan to start a podcast.

speakerA.en: I've been toying with the idea of starting a podcast about local history. What do you think?
By focusing on stories no one else is telling, such as the forgotten characters of our own town.
We could interview older residents. Their memories are a goldmine that will vanish with time.
I can handle that part. Let's record a pilot episode and see whether it holds together.

speakerB.en: It's an appealing idea, but there's no shortage of podcasts. How would yours stand out?
That could work, provided we do thorough research and don't just retell what's on the internet.
I like that. I have some basic recording equipment, though I'm hopeless at editing.
Agreed. If it goes well, we might even apply for a small grant from the council.

scenarios.scenario: Turning a hobby into a business
scenarios.context: A woman asks a friend for advice about turning her pottery into a small business.

speakerA.en: I've been toying with the idea of turning my pottery into a proper business. Friends keep telling me I should.
That's what worries me. At the moment, it's the one thing I do purely for pleasure, with no deadlines or expectations.
That's a sensible approach. It would let me test demand without giving up my day job.
You make it sound so straightforward. I suppose the hardest part is simply taking the first step.

speakerB.en: That's exciting, but I'd be cautious. Turning a hobby into a livelihood can sometimes drain the enjoyment out of it.
Then perhaps start small. Sell a few pieces at a local market and see how you feel about the pressure.
Precisely. And if it takes off, you'll have evidence rather than just enthusiasm to base the decision on.
It usually is. I'll be your first customer, provided you give me a friend's discount.

scenarios.scenario: Debating gaming versus outdoor activities
scenarios.context: Two friends disagree about how best to spend their free time.

speakerA.en: You spend every weekend gaming, and I can't help feeling you're missing out. Wouldn't a hike do you more good?
I don't doubt the skill involved, but there's something irreplaceable about fresh air and physical exertion.
Perhaps that's the very reason to go. Exercise tends to give you energy rather than take it away.
That's a deal, though I reserve the right to say I told you so when you come home glowing.

speakerB.en: I'd contest that. Gaming isn't passive for me; I play with friends across the world, and it demands real strategy and teamwork.
I won't deny it. My problem is that by Friday I'm so drained that a strenuous outing sounds like a punishment.
You may have a point. Suppose we compromise: one weekend outdoors, one at the console, and see how I feel.
Fair enough, but I'll expect you to try the game afterwards. It's only fair that the exchange goes both ways.

scenarios.scenario: Organizing a charity run
scenarios.context: Two volunteers plan a community fun run to raise money for a local charity.

speakerA.en: If we want the charity run to succeed, we need to settle the route soon. The council requires our application a month in advance.
Sensible, though we'd need to close part of the road. Do you think we'll get permission, given the traffic it will cause?
That's a real coup. If they cover the water, we can direct more of the entry fees toward the charity.
Ambitious, but achievable if we publicize it properly. I'll draft a social media plan this weekend.

speakerB.en: Agreed. I'd suggest a loop around the lake, which is scenic and flat, so it will appeal to beginners and experienced runners alike.
It's likelier on a Sunday morning. I've also spoken to a local sports shop about sponsoring the water stations.
That was my thinking. We should aim for at least three hundred participants, which would raise a respectable amount.
Excellent. I'll finalize the route and submit the application on Monday.

scenarios.scenario: Taking up a demanding hobby later in life
scenarios.context: A person discusses beginning a challenging pursuit and the obstacles it presents.

speakerA.en: I've decided to learn the cello, which at my age is either admirably ambitious or frankly delusional.
Humility is certainly what I'm receiving. My first lesson produced sounds that resembled a distressed animal.
My teacher says I'll need at least a year before anything resembling music emerges. I fear my neighbors may not survive it.
Excellent advice. I find that the process, however clumsy, is rather more satisfying than I'd anticipated.

speakerB.en: I'd say it's neither. It's simply an exercise in humility, and those are in surprisingly short supply nowadays.
Every cellist has endured that stage. The remarkable thing is that the instrument rewards patience in a way few things do.
Then I'd suggest practicing with a mute and a generous supply of apologetic baked goods.
That's the secret. Those who persevere are usually the ones who learn to enjoy being bad at something first.

scenarios.scenario: Debating the merits of solitary versus group pursuits
scenarios.context: Two friends compare how they spend leisure time and what they gain from it.

speakerA.en: I've never understood your enthusiasm for team sports. I prefer pursuits where success or failure rests with me alone.
Or an unnecessary vulnerability. I'd rather not have my enjoyment depend on somebody else's mediocre performance.
I concede that. My long walks are marvelous for clearing the head, but they rarely produce friendships.
A sensible compromise. I might try joining a walking group, provided nobody expects me to chat incessantly.

speakerB.en: That's precisely what appeals to me about them. A team forces you to rely on others, which is a valuable discipline.
There's something to be said for independence, but I find that camaraderie deepens the experience in a way solitude can't replicate.
Quite. Perhaps the ideal arrangement is a blend of both, a solitary routine and a communal pursuit to balance it.
A walking group is the perfect middle ground. You can be sociable without ever being obliged to speak.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a long-awaited weekend away
scenarios.context: Two friends devise a getaway that balances relaxation and adventure.

speakerA.en: We've been promising ourselves a weekend away for over a year. I propose we stop deliberating and simply commit.
Guilty as charged, but I'm prepared to compromise. What if we hike in the morning and devote the afternoons to doing absolutely nothing?
Naturally. I've found a small inn near the coast with a reputation for superb seafood and an indifference to mobile signal.
The weekend after next, if your calendar permits. I'll book the rooms tonight before one of us loses our nerve.

speakerB.en: Agreed. The difficulty is that I'd like to relax, whereas you're likely to propose a punishing mountain trail.
That's a more civilized proposal. I'd add that the evenings must be reserved for a proper dinner and a bottle of something decent.
The absence of a signal is the most persuasive argument you've made so far. When shall we go?
Do. If we wait any longer, our free time will be consumed by the very obligations we're trying to escape.

scenarios.scenario: Organizing a weekend hiking trip
scenarios.context: Two friends organize a day trip to the mountains.

speakerA.en: Would you like to go hiking on Saturday? The weather should be perfect.
There's a trail near the lake that takes about four hours. It's not too difficult.
Let's meet at eight so we can avoid the crowds. Could you bring some sandwiches?
Great. I'll check the map tonight and make sure we know the way.

speakerB.en: That sounds fantastic. I haven't been outdoors for weeks. Where were you thinking of going?
Four hours is fine with me, as long as we can take a break halfway for lunch.
No problem. I'll also pack water and some fruit. Should I bring my camera as well?
Perfect. Don't forget to charge your phone, just in case we need to call someone.

scenarios.scenario: Choosing between a movie and a game night
scenarios.context: Two roommates decide how to spend a free Friday evening.

speakerA.en: I've been working all week and I have no energy. What should we do tonight?
I'd rather stay in, to be honest. We could order pizza and play that board game.
Fine, but if I win again, you have to wash the dishes tomorrow.
Then it's settled. I'll order the pizza while you set up the table.

speakerB.en: Same here. We could go to the cinema, or we could just relax at home.
That's a good idea, though last time you took the game much too seriously.
You're on. But I've been practicing, so don't be surprised if I finally beat you.
Sounds good. Let's get one with mushrooms this time, since it's your turn to choose.

scenarios.scenario: Starting a new creative hobby
scenarios.context: A person tells a friend about their plan to learn painting.

speakerA.en: I've decided to try something new this year. I'm going to take a painting course on Wednesday evenings.
I've never painted before, but I've always wanted to. When I was younger, my teacher told me that I had no talent for art.
That's true. I've realized that life is too short to avoid things just because other people have discouraged you.
The course lasts ten weeks, and everything is included, so I don't have to buy any materials. At the end, there's even an exhibition.
I'd love that. It would be nice to have a friend there. Are you free next Wednesday to come and see?
Brilliant. I'll ask if you can join one lesson for free, and you can decide whether you'd like to enroll.

speakerB.en: That's wonderful! What made you choose painting? I thought you were more interested in photography.
Don't listen to that. Talent is much less important than practice, and it's a great way to relax after a stressful week.
I completely agree. Someone once told me that I couldn't sing, but now I'm in a choir, and I've never been happier.
That's a great opportunity. I might come to the exhibition. Do you think there'll be a chance to buy any of the pictures?
I'd be curious to try it, actually. I've always been better at looking at art than creating it, but who knows?
That would be really kind of you. It would be fun to do something creative together for a change.

scenarios.scenario: Joining a volunteer group in free time
scenarios.context: Two acquaintances talk about volunteering on weekends.

speakerA.en: I've been wondering what to do with my weekends lately. I'm tired of sitting at home, watching series all day.
I've been thinking about volunteering, but I don't know where to start. What kind of work do you do?
That sounds rewarding. Do you need any special qualifications, or can anyone join the group?
I'd be happy to give it a try. How much time would I have to spend each week, though?
That's not too much, and it's a good way to meet new people. When is the next meeting?
I'll be there. Thanks for the invitation. It's exactly the push that I needed.

speakerB.en: That's a common problem. You might enjoy volunteering, actually. I've been helping at an animal shelter for the past two years.
I walk the dogs, clean the cages, and sometimes help with the paperwork. It's tiring, but it makes me feel useful.
Anyone can join. All you need is a bit of free time and a willingness to learn. Most of the training happens on the job.
Just a few hours on Saturday mornings. If you can't come one week, you simply tell the coordinator, and nobody minds.
It's this Saturday at ten. Come along, and have a look around before deciding. I'll introduce you to the manager.
Great. Wear old clothes, because you'll probably get a little dirty. The dogs will love you, I'm sure.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the value of hobbies in a busy life
scenarios.context: Two colleagues debate whether hobbies are essential for wellbeing.

speakerA.en: I've been wondering whether having a hobby is really as important as people say. Between work and family, I hardly have a moment to myself.
I see your point, but isn't there a risk that hobbies become one more obligation? I know people who feel guilty if they don't practice their instrument every day.
That's a good distinction. I suppose the aim is to do something without being judged on the result, which is a rare thing in modern life, where everything is measured.
I used to paint when I was younger, but I stopped because I felt that I wasn't good enough. I wonder now whether that was a mistake.
You may be right. I might try again, even if it's only for half an hour a week, and see how I feel after a month or two.
Thanks for the encouragement. If I hadn't had this conversation, I'd probably have kept postponing it for years.

speakerB.en: Personally, I think it's crucial. A hobby gives you a space where you're not defined by your job or your family role, and that can be a powerful way of recharging.
That's true, and it's why I'd say the best hobbies are those that you do for the pleasure of it, not to achieve anything. Once it becomes a duty, it loses its purpose.
Exactly. Studies show that activities that make you lose track of time tend to reduce stress, partly because they give the mind a break from constant planning.
That's a pity, because enjoyment isn't about skill. If you had continued, you might have found that your standards changed as you developed, and the pleasure grew with them.
I'd encourage you to do it. It doesn't need to be impressive. Even a few quick sketches would be a good start, and you might find that your hands remember more than you think.
That's what conversations are for. Let me know how it goes, and perhaps we could visit an exhibition together to get inspired.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a long weekend with competing preferences
scenarios.context: Two partners negotiate how to spend a free weekend.

speakerA.en: We finally have a free weekend, and I'd like to make the most of it. I've been dreaming about a trip to the coast, even if it's only for two days.
I know you'd prefer to stay at home, but we've been working so hard lately that I think a change of scenery would do us both good, and we wouldn't have to spend much.
That's a fair compromise. We could leave on Saturday morning and come back on Sunday afternoon, which would give you the rest of the evening to relax before the new week begins.
I'd also like to include something active, such as a walk along the cliffs. If the weather turns bad, we could visit a museum or just read in a café.
You're right. We should avoid over-planning, because the point is to relax, not to follow a schedule. Let's decide once we're there, depending on how we feel.
Great. I'll look for a small guesthouse near the sea, and I'll make sure that it has a cancellation option, in case the forecast changes.

speakerB.en: That does sound tempting, but I was hoping to catch up on sleep and do absolutely nothing. I haven't had a quiet weekend in almost two months.
You may have a point. We've both been so busy that we haven't spent any real time together. I'm just worried that traveling will be more tiring than staying home.
I could agree to that, as long as we don't have to rush. If we take it slowly and don't set an alarm, I'd actually enjoy it. And Sunday evening at home sounds good.
Walking on the cliffs would be wonderful, provided it isn't too windy. Last time we went, I nearly lost my hat. Maybe I'll bring a scarf instead.
That's the best approach. I always find that the best moments on trips are the ones that nobody planned, like discovering a little restaurant by accident.
Good idea. Choose somewhere that allows breakfast to be served late. That's non-negotiable, if I'm to be persuaded to go away at all.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating weekend plans with a group
scenarios.context: A group of friends tries to agree on what to do on Saturday.

speakerA.en: So, what are we doing on Saturday? I've been looking forward to it all week, but we still haven't decided anything, and we're running out of time.
I'd suggest going to the lake, since the weather's supposed to be fine. We could rent a few boats, and have a picnic on the shore, which wouldn't cost much.
That's a fair point. I suppose it depends on how many people want to come. If we had a group of eight or more, it might be cheaper to hire a minibus than to take several cars.
I'd be happy with either option, as long as we decide soon. If we can't agree by this evening, I think we should just flip a coin, and stop arguing about it.
Okay, so we've got a majority for the lake. Let's meet at the station at ten, and bring food to share. Does anyone have a speaker for music?
Great, then it's settled. I'll send a message to the group with the details, and I'll ask everyone to confirm by tonight.

speakerB.en: I know, we keep going around in circles. Some of us want something active, while others would rather relax, and it's difficult to find something that suits everybody.
That sounds nice, but it might be a bit tame for those who'd like to do some sports. Could we combine it with something, like volleyball, or a short walk around the lake?
Good idea. I hadn't thought of that. If eight people are coming, it might even be cheaper than taking public transport. I could ask my cousin whether we could borrow his van.
I'm in favor of the lake, though I'd prefer not to rent a boat, because it's quite expensive. We could just swim, if the water's warm enough, and bring a few games for the shore.
I've got a small speaker that works well. And I'll bring a frisbee as well, in case anyone wants to play. What about food? Shall we each bring something, or organize it centrally?
Sounds good. I'll make a salad, and I'll bring some fruit. Please remind everybody to bring sun cream. Last time, half the group came home looking like lobsters.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a first camping trip
scenarios.context: Two inexperienced friends plan a camping weekend and discuss what to bring.

speakerA.en: I've never been camping before, but I've been wanting to try it for years. Do you think we could manage a weekend on our own, or should we go with someone who knows what they're doing?
That's a relief. What do we need to take with us? I'm worried that I'll forget something important and we'll end up spending the night cold and hungry.
A tent and sleeping bags, obviously. I know that someone in my family has an old tent, but I'm not sure whether it's waterproof. Should I buy a new one, to be on the safe side?
Good point. And what about the campsite? Should we book in advance, or can we just turn up and find a place? I'd hate to arrive and discover that it's full.
That seems wise. In that case, I'll reserve a pitch tonight. Do you think that we should also plan some activities, or just spend the weekend relaxing by the fire?
Perfect. Let's make a checklist tomorrow, and go through it together before we leave, so that we're sure we've got everything.

speakerB.en: I think that we'd be fine, as long as we choose a good campsite and keep it simple. We don't need to go into the wilderness. A site with toilets and showers is a safe place to start.

Make a checklist. Tent, sleeping bags, mats, a torch, a stove, a cooking pot, matches, water bottles, warm clothes, a first aid kit, and plenty of insect repellent. If you pack carefully, you won't forget anything.
Test it first. Put it up in the garden, and spray it with a hose, to see whether it leaks. If it does, borrow or hire one, since camping in the rain with a wet tent is miserable.
Always book in advance during the summer. Popular campsites fill up weeks beforehand, especially at weekends, and it's frustrating to be turned away after a long drive.
A short hike and a campfire would be plenty. Bring a book and a deck of cards, too. It's surprising how quickly the time goes when you're outdoors without a screen.
Agreed. And we'll cook something simple, like pasta and sausages. It will taste better than anything you've had at a restaurant, believe me.

scenarios.scenario: Convincing a friend to try rock climbing
scenarios.context: An enthusiastic climber tries to persuade a stressed, hesitant friend to join her at an indoor climbing gym.

speakerA.en: I've been rock climbing at the indoor gym ever since I moved here, and I keep thinking you'd love it. It's not that it's easy, it's just that it's far more rewarding than I ever expected.

I know what you mean, but you'd be surprised. Beginners tend to start on the low walls, where you can't fall far, and the instructors have been teaching newcomers for years. I'd say it's more about technique than strength.

That's exactly why you should try it. I've been going on Tuesday evenings, and I tend to forget about work completely, because you have to concentrate so hard on each move. Is that something you'd find useful?

Nobody pays any attention to anyone else, I promise. Most people tend to be extremely friendly, and they've been giving me tips ever since my first week. It's not that they're being polite, it's just that climbers love to share.

You can rent everything for the first month, shoes and harness included, so there's no need to buy anything. I'd say it's best to wait until you've been a few times before investing, as most people tend to do.
Take your time, but let me know by Monday, so that I can book you a slot with the beginner instructor. I've been looking forward to having someone to go with, ever since I started.

speakerB.en: I'm sure it is, but it's not really my thing. It's not that I'm afraid of heights, it's just that I tend to hurt myself whenever I try something athletic, and I've been avoiding sports ever since that ankle injury.

That's reassuring, although I'd still rather watch first. I've been meaning to try something new ever since work got so stressful, but it's not that I lack ideas, it's just that I never find the time.

Honestly, it would be. I tend to take my worries home, and I've been waking up at night thinking about emails. On the other hand, I'd feel self-conscious in front of experienced climbers, to be honest.
All right, you've half convinced me. What would I need to bring? I've been told that the shoes are rather expensive, and I'd prefer not to spend a fortune before I know whether I enjoy it.

That's sensible. Let me think about Tuesday. I've been trying to leave work on time, ever since my manager started encouraging it, so it might actually be possible. It's not that I'm making excuses, it's just that I want to be sure.
Fine, put me down. It's not that I'm confident, it's just that I'd regret saying no. I'll meet you there at six, and I tend to arrive early when I'm nervous, so don't be surprised.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a weekend around different interests
scenarios.context: Two partners with different energy levels and interests work out a weekend plan that includes hiking, pottery and a family dinner.

speakerA.en: I've been trying to plan the weekend, and I'm struggling to fit everything in. I'd rather we didn't spend both days at home, so that we can make the most of the good weather, but I know you're tired.

That could work, supposing we set off by one. I'd rather we avoided the main trail, though, since it's always packed on Saturdays. There's a quieter route along the ridge, which is said to have wonderful views.

Good point. Supposing the weather turns, we could visit the pottery workshop I mentioned, in order to try something different. I'd rather you came along than stayed at home, but I'll leave it up to you.

Sunday would suit me better too, in order to leave Saturday free for the hike. I'd rather we kept the evenings relaxed, so that we're not exhausted by Monday morning. Supposing we cooked at home, would that be all right?
I'd love that. I'd rather she came on Saturday, so that we've got Sunday to ourselves. Supposing she brought dessert, I'd happily make the main course, in order to share the work.
That sounds ideal. I'd rather end the weekend feeling rested than rushed, so that I can start Monday with some energy. Supposing everything goes to plan, it should be a wonderful two days.

speakerB.en: I am, to be honest, and I'd rather we kept Saturday morning free, so that I can sleep in. Supposing we went hiking in the afternoon instead, would that suit you, or would it be too late to start?
I'd prefer the quieter one too. Suppose it rains, though, what then? I'd rather we had a plan B, so that we don't end up arguing about what to do instead.
Pottery sounds fun, actually. I'd rather we booked in advance, so that we're guaranteed a place. On the other hand, would Sunday be better for it, since the workshop might be quieter?

That's perfect. I'd rather cook than eat out after a long day outdoors. Suppose we invited my sister for dinner on Saturday, though, so that she doesn't feel left out again? She's been asking for weeks.
I'll ask her tonight. To be honest, I'd rather we didn't plan too much, so that there's room for spontaneity. Suppose we leave Sunday afternoon open, in case we feel like doing nothing?
Agreed. I'll make a rough list tonight, in order to avoid forgetting anything. I'd rather you didn't mention it to anyone else yet, so that we don't get dragged into other plans.

scenarios.scenario: Explaining why you took up a demanding hobby late in life
scenarios.context: A colleague asks why a forty-five-year-old has started learning the violin, and the conversation turns to the rewards and frustrations of learning something new.

speakerA.en: I heard you've started learning the violin, which surprised me, to be honest. Isn't it supposed to be a hobby for children? I'd say you've set yourself quite a challenge. What made you decide to take it up at forty-five?

I tried the piano at school, but I gave up after a year. I can't stand practicing scales, and my teacher wasn't patient. Honestly, I'd say it's hard to keep going when progress is so slow. How do you cope with the frustration?

Perhaps, although I wish I had more free time. Between work and the children, there's hardly a spare hour. Is it difficult to find time for practice, or do you simply make it a habit? I'd be curious to know how you organize your week.

It does, actually. On the other hand, I'd worry about looking foolish in front of a teacher half my age. Do you ever feel self-conscious? If I were in your position, I'd probably hate being a beginner again, since I'm used to being good at my job.

That's a lovely way to see it. As far as I'm concerned, learning something new at any age is impressive. I wish I had your courage. Is there any piece you're hoping to play eventually, or are you simply enjoying the process?

I'm sure you'll manage. Would you let me hear it when it's ready? I wouldn't miss it for anything, and I might even think about starting the piano again. It's never too late, is it? Thank you for the inspiration.

speakerB.en: You're not the first to say so! The thing is, I've always loved the sound of it, and I couldn't help feeling that if I didn't try now, I never would. I wish I'd started as a child, but there's no point in regretting that. Have you ever played an instrument yourself?

Some days I can't, to be honest. The first three months sounded like a cat in distress, and my neighbors were far from pleased. But it's well worth sticking with it, since the small improvements feel wonderful. I look forward to my lessons every Thursday. Do you think you'd ever go back to music?

I practice for twenty minutes every morning before breakfast. It's no use waiting for a free evening, because something always comes up. What I've learned is that short, regular sessions beat long, rare ones. I can't help feeling that it's also made me calmer at work. Does that sound plausible?

At first, yes, very much so. But my teacher is wonderful, and she says adults have an advantage, since we understand why we're practicing. It's worth remembering that nobody is watching as closely as you imagine. And I find that being a beginner keeps me humble, which is no bad thing.

Both, really. There's a slow Bach melody I can't help humming all day, and I'd love to play it for my mother's birthday in March. There's no point in rushing, though. If I can manage it by then, I'll be delighted. And if not, I'll simply play something easier.

I'd be honored, and you must come to the birthday! Honestly, there's no point in waiting for the perfect time. Just start, and see what happens. I can't help thinking you'd be better at it than you believe.

scenarios.scenario: Deciding whether to turn a hobby into a small business
scenarios.context: A woman who makes ceramics in her free time discusses with a friend whether to start selling her work online.

speakerA.en: Can I ask your opinion about something? Several people have told me my ceramics are good enough to sell, and I've been wondering whether to start an online shop. To be honest, I'm torn, since pottery has always been my escape from work. What would you do?

I suppose it's a bit of both. What I'm afraid of is that I'd stop enjoying it. Suppose I had orders to fill every week, it might start to feel like a second job. On the other hand, I'm running out of shelf space, and I can't keep giving mugs away to friends!

Twenty would be fine, but I'd need photographs, a website and packaging. I've never done any of that, so I'm not sure where to start. I could have my brother take the photos, since he's a decent photographer, and I'd get the site built by a freelancer. Is that realistic?

Not properly. A friend said I should charge about forty euros per mug, which seems a lot, although each one takes hours. As far as I'm concerned, pricing is the hardest part. If I charge too little, I'll feel exploited, and if I charge too much, nobody will buy.

That's a brilliant idea. I could get a small stall at the weekend market and see how people react. What matters most is that I'd get honest feedback face to face. If nobody bought anything, at least I'd know before spending money on a website.

Put like that, almost nothing. I feel much clearer now, thank you. The point is that I don't have to decide everything today. I'll book a stall for next month, and if it goes well, I'll bring you a mug as a thank-you.

speakerB.en: That's exciting! I'd say the first thing to ask yourself is why you want to sell. Is it the money, or is it that you'd like people to enjoy your work? And what is it exactly that worries you about turning a hobby into a business?

That's a very real risk, I'd say. But the point is that you don't have to go all in. What matters is that you start small, so that selling doesn't take over your life. Were you to sell just twenty pieces a month, would that already feel like pressure?

Very realistic, and sensible too. The fact that you're thinking about delegating the parts you're weaker at shows good judgment. Supposing the site costs around three hundred, would your first few sales cover it? And have you thought about pricing yet?

Forty is fair for a handmade piece, provided that the quality is consistent. The point is that people buying handmade goods expect to pay more, and they value the story behind it. Would you consider having your first batch tested at a local market before going online?

Exactly, and you'd learn what colors and shapes sell best. Supposing it went well, you could have your logo designed and move online in spring. And if it didn't, you'd simply keep the hobby as it is, with nothing lost. What's the worst that could happen?

I'd love that, although I'd insist on paying full price to support a local artist! Seriously, I'm proud of you for even considering it. Whatever you decide, keep making things, because that's what matters most.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about jobs and daily work routine
scenarios.context: Colleagues or friends discuss their work and responsibilities.

speakerA.en: Where do you work these days?
What do you do?
Do you like your job?
What time do you start work?
How many hours do you work a day?
speakerA.fa: روزی چند ساعت کار می‌کنی؟

speakerA.en: Do you enjoy your job?
speakerA.fa: از شغلت لذت می‌بری؟

speakerA.en: I've got a new project at work. It's really challenging.
speakerA.fa: یه پروژه جدید سر کار گرفتم. واقعاً چالش‌برانگیزه.

speakerA.en: My boss is very understanding and supportive.
speakerA.fa: رئیسم خیلی فهمیده و حامی است.

speakerA.en: I'm thinking about changing careers. I need a fresh start.
speakerA.fa: به تغییر شغل فکر می‌کنم. یه شروع تازه نیاز دارم.

speakerA.en: What does a normal day look like for you?
Do you ever work from home?

speakerB.en: I work at a school.
I'm a teacher.
Yes, I do. It's good.
I start at nine o'clock.
Usually around 8 hours, sometimes more.
speakerB.fa: معمولاً حدود ۸ ساعت، بعضی وقتا بیشتر.

speakerB.en: Yes, I love it. It keeps me busy and I learn a lot.
speakerB.fa: بله، عاشقشم. منو سرگرم می‌کنه و کلی یاد می‌گیرم.

speakerB.en: That sounds interesting! What's it about?
speakerB.fa: به نظر جالب میاد! درباره‌ش چیه؟

speakerB.en: You're lucky. Mine is quite strict and demanding.
speakerB.fa: خوش‌شانسی. مال من خیلی سخت‌گیر و پرتوقع است.

speakerB.en: That's a big decision. What field are you considering?
speakerB.fa: تصمیم بزرگیه. به چه زمینه‌ای فکر می‌کنی؟

speakerB.en: I answer emails in the morning and have meetings after lunch.
Yes, twice a week. It saves me a lot of time.

scenarios.scenario: Meeting colleagues or work-related questions
scenarios.context: In a meeting or office environment, asking about tasks and schedules.

speakerA.en: Good morning. Is Mr. Brown here?
Where is the meeting?
Can I use your phone, please?
Thank you for your help.
Are you busy right now? Can I talk to you?
speakerA.fa: الان مشغولی؟ می‌تونم باهات صحبت کنم؟

speakerA.en: What's on your to-do list for today?
speakerA.fa: امروز چه کارهایی داری انجام بدی؟

speakerA.en: Could you help me with this report? I'm stuck on the third page.
speakerA.fa: میشه تو این گزارش کمکم کنی؟ توی صفحه سوم گیر کردم.

speakerA.en: When is the deadline for this project?
speakerA.fa: ددلاین این پروژه کیه؟

speakerA.en: I'm going to be late for work today. My car broke down.
speakerA.fa: امروز سر کار دیر می‌رسیم. ماشینم خراب شده.

speakerA.en: Let's schedule a meeting for next Tuesday to go over the details.
speakerA.fa: یه جلسه برای سه‌شنبه آینده بذاریم تا جزئیات رو مرور کنیم.

speakerA.en: Can we move the meeting to Thursday morning?
I'll send you the report before then.

speakerB.en: Yes, he's in his office.
It's in room two.
Yes, of course. Here you are.
You're welcome.
Sure, come in. I have a few minutes.
speakerB.fa: حتماً، بیا داخل. چند دقیقه وقت دارم.

speakerB.en: I have to finish the sales report and call some clients.
speakerB.fa: باید گزارش فروش رو تموم کنم و به چندتا مشتری زنگ بزنم.

speakerB.en: Let me take a look. I think you missed a formula here.
speakerB.fa: بذارید نگاه کنم. فکر کنم یه فرمول اینجا جا گذاشتید.

speakerB.en: The deadline is this Friday at 5 PM.
speakerB.fa: ددلاین جمعه این هفته ساعت ۵ عصر است.

speakerB.en: No problem. Just let the team know so we can adjust.
speakerB.fa: اشکالی نداره. به تیم خبر بده تا تنظیم کنیم.

speakerB.en: Perfect. I'll send out the invites shortly.
speakerB.fa: عالیه. دعوت‌نامه‌ها رو به زودی می‌فرستم.

speakerB.en: Yes, ten o'clock works for me.
Thanks. Please include the sales numbers.

scenarios.scenario: A new job
scenarios.context: A person talks about a new job.

speakerA.en: I have a new job.
It's at a hospital.
I'm a nurse.
I start on Monday.
I have some good news. I got a new job!
I'll be a sales assistant at a big company.
I start next Monday. I'm a little nervous.
Thanks. Do you have any advice?

speakerB.en: That's great! Where?
What do you do there?
That's a good job.
Good luck!
Congratulations! What will you do there?
That sounds exciting. When do you start?
Don't worry. You'll do great.
Ask questions and be friendly with everyone.

scenarios.scenario: First day at work
scenarios.context: A new worker meets a colleague on the first day.

speakerA.en: Hello. I'm the new worker.
Where is my desk?
Where is the kitchen?
Thank you for your help.
Hi. I'm new here. Today is my first day.
Thank you. Where can I put my things?
What time is the lunch break?
Who should I ask if I have a problem?

speakerB.en: Welcome! My name is Sara.
It's over there, by the window.
It's down the hall.
No problem. Ask me anytime.
Welcome! I'm Daniel. Let me show you around.
You can use the desk by the window.
We usually eat at one o'clock in the canteen.
You can ask me or your manager, Ms. Clark.

scenarios.scenario: Working hours
scenarios.context: Two colleagues talk about their work schedule.

speakerA.en: What time do you finish work?
Do you work on Saturday?
Do you have lunch at work?
Let's have lunch together.
What time do you start work in the morning?
Do you have a break for lunch?
Do you ever work on weekends?
I work late on Thursdays. It's very tiring.

speakerB.en: I finish at five o'clock.
No, I don't.
Yes. I have lunch at noon.
Good idea. See you at noon.
I start at nine and finish at five.
Yes, we have an hour. Sometimes I eat at my desk.
Not often, only when we have a big project.
I understand. Maybe you can leave early on Friday.

scenarios.scenario: A phone call at the office
scenarios.context: An employee answers a work phone call.

speakerA.en: Hello. Mr. Smith's office.
Sorry, he's in a meeting.
Call after two o'clock.
You're welcome. Goodbye.
Good morning. Blue Sky Company. How can I help you?
May I ask who's calling?
I'm sorry. Mr. Hill is in a meeting right now.
Of course. Could I have your number?

speakerB.en: Hello. Can I speak to Mr. Smith?
When can I call again?
OK. Thank you.
Goodbye.
Hello. I'd like to speak to Mr. Hill, please.
This is Ms. Brown from Delta Print.
Could you ask him to call me back?

scenarios.scenario: Asking for help at work
scenarios.context: A worker asks a colleague for help with a computer.

speakerA.en: Can you help me, please?
I can't open this file.
Oh, I see. It works now!
Thank you very much.
Excuse me. Do you have a minute? My computer isn't working.
The screen is black and I can't open my files.
Yes, I restarted it twice, but nothing happened.
Oh, I feel silly. Thank you so much!

speakerB.en: Yes, of course. What do you need?
Let me see. Click here.
Good.
You're welcome.
Sure. What's the problem?
Did you restart it?
Let me check the cable. Ah, it's not plugged in.
No problem. It happens to everyone.

scenarios.scenario: Asking the boss for a day off
scenarios.context: An employee asks his manager for time off.

speakerA.en: Do you have a minute? I wanted to ask whether I could take Friday off.
Yes, my sister is getting married, and I need to travel on Thursday night.
I'll complete the report before I leave, and I can check my email in the evening if necessary.
I'll write a short summary for my colleagues and send it tomorrow.

speakerB.en: Is it for something important? We have a deadline next week.
Congratulations to her! I think that should be fine as long as your tasks are finished.
That won't be necessary. Just make sure someone knows where the files are.
Great. Enjoy the wedding, and give my regards to your family.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing a problem with a coworker
scenarios.context: Two colleagues talk about a project that is behind schedule.

speakerA.en: Have you looked at the project plan? I think we're falling behind.
Should we talk to the manager and ask for a few more days?
Agreed. Could you prepare a list of what has already been completed?
That will make the conversation easier. When would you like to meet with her?

speakerB.en: I know. The client changed the requirements twice, so we had to redo a lot of work.
I think so. It's better to be honest than to hand in something unfinished.
Sure. I'll also write down what's still missing and how long it will take.
Tomorrow morning, before the other meetings start.

scenarios.scenario: Having a job interview
scenarios.context: A candidate answers questions in a job interview.

speakerA.en: Thank you for coming in today. Could you tell us a little about your previous experience?
What was the biggest challenge you faced in that role?
That sounds practical. Why do you want to work for our company?
Do you have any questions for us before we finish?

speakerB.en: Of course. I've worked as a project coordinator for four years, mainly in the construction industry.
Managing several teams with different schedules. I solved it by introducing a shared calendar.
I admire your focus on sustainability, and I'd like to use my skills to help with that.
Yes. What would a typical day look like, and how big is the team?

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating a salary increase
scenarios.context: An employee discusses a raise with his manager.

speakerA.en: Thank you for making time for me. I'd like to discuss my compensation, if I may.
It does. Over the past year, I've taken on additional responsibilities, including managing two junior colleagues.
In light of that, I'd like to propose an increase of around ten percent.
I'd be more comfortable with seven, particularly given the scope of my current duties.

speakerB.en: Of course. I assume this relates to the performance review we had last month.
That hasn't gone unnoticed. Your contribution has been valuable, and the client feedback has been positive.
I appreciate your directness, but the budget is tight this year. I could probably manage five.
Let me discuss it with HR. I can't promise anything, but I'll make a strong case on your behalf.

scenarios.scenario: Handling workplace conflict
scenarios.context: A team leader mediates a disagreement between two coworkers.

speakerA.en: I'd like to hear from both of you about what's been happening, without any interruptions.
That's not fair. I only challenge them when I think they're impractical, and I always give reasons.
I wasn't aware it came across like that. It certainly wasn't my intention to belittle anyone.
I'm willing to do that, as long as I'm given the chance to explain my thinking fully.

speakerB.en: Frankly, I feel that my ideas are consistently dismissed in meetings, and it's affecting my motivation.
It doesn't feel that way. The tone is often condescending, and others notice it too.
Then perhaps this is a case of miscommunication. Could you try raising concerns more constructively?
That seems reasonable on both sides. Let's review how it's going in a couple of weeks.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing work-life balance and remote work
scenarios.context: Two colleagues compare the pros and cons of working from home.

speakerA.en: Now that remote work is permitted two days a week, I find I'm far more productive at home.
That's a fair point. I notice I'm sometimes answering emails at ten at night.
I've started shutting my laptop at six, regardless of what's pending, and it has helped enormously.
Initially, yes, but I turn off notifications on my phone, which removes most of the pressure.

speakerB.en: I'm not so sure. I miss the spontaneity of the office, and the boundary between work and leisure has blurred.
Exactly. Without a clear cut-off point, work tends to creep into every corner of one's life.
I should try something similar. Do you find it hard to resist the temptation to check your messages?
I'll experiment with that. Whatever the arrangement, I think flexibility is what really counts.

scenarios.scenario: Presenting a proposal to senior management
scenarios.context: An employee pitches a restructuring initiative to a skeptical director.

speakerA.en: Thank you for giving me the time. I'd like to propose consolidating our three regional support teams into a single unit, which I believe would cut costs by around twenty percent.
The figures rest on shared tooling and a reduction in duplicated management layers. Quality should improve, as customers would no longer be passed between teams.
I share that concern, which is why I'm proposing a phased transition over twelve months, with retention incentives for key personnel.
Certainly. I'll have a draft to you by the end of next week, including contingency measures.

speakerB.en: That's an ambitious claim. What assumptions are you basing it on, and what would happen to service quality in the process?
In theory, yes. In practice, mergers of this kind tend to trigger resignations, and we can't afford to lose experienced staff.
That's a more thoughtful plan than I expected. Can you put together a risk assessment for the board meeting next month?
Good. I'm not promising approval, but you've given me something worth taking seriously.

scenarios.scenario: Giving constructive feedback in a performance review
scenarios.context: A manager gives a team member candid feedback during an annual review.

speakerA.en: I'd like to start by saying that your analytical work has been outstanding this year. The market report you produced was among the best we've had.
There is, though it's more of a development point. In meetings, you tend to hold back, and your ideas don't always reach the people who matter.
Exactly. Data rarely persuades on its own; people need to hear the story behind it. I'd like to see you present more often.
Yes, we run a workshop next quarter, and I'd be happy to coach you in the meantime. I think you'll surprise yourself.

speakerB.en: Thank you, that's good to hear. I sense there's a "but" coming.
That's fair. I've always preferred to let the data speak for itself, but I realize that doesn't always get noticed.
I'm willing to try, though public speaking doesn't come naturally to me. Would there be any training available?
Then I'll sign up. I'd rather be pushed out of my comfort zone than stay quietly overlooked.

scenarios.scenario: Resigning from a position gracefully
scenarios.context: An employee tells her manager she is leaving for another company.

speakerA.en: I'd like to speak to you in private. I've accepted an offer elsewhere, and I wanted you to hear it from me first.
Honestly, no. The role offers a level of responsibility that I couldn't have reached here for several years. It was a difficult decision.
I appreciate that, but my mind is made up. I'm happy to work out my notice and ensure a smooth handover.
Of course. I'll prepare a full handover file by the end of next week, and I'll train whoever takes over.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry to hear that, though I can't say I'm entirely surprised. Was it something we could have changed?
I understand. You've been a valued member of this team, and I'd have liked the chance to make a counteroffer.
That's professional of you. Could you document your current projects, so that your successor isn't starting from scratch?
Thank you. I'll be sorry to lose you, but I wish you every success. Our door will always be open.

scenarios.scenario: Making the case for a raise after expanded duties
scenarios.context: An employee presents a case for a raise to a manager who has budget constraints.

speakerA.en: Thank you for seeing me. I'd like to discuss my compensation in light of the responsibilities I've taken on over the past year.
I'd like to propose an adjustment of fifteen percent, which I believe reflects both my expanded remit and the market rate for comparable positions.
I understand the constraints, and I've prepared a summary of the results I've delivered, including the revenue from the new accounts.
I'd be open to that, provided the review is formally scheduled and tied to clear objectives rather than left to goodwill.

speakerB.en: Of course. I'm aware you've been doing more than your role originally entailed, and I appreciate it. What did you have in mind?
That's a considerable request. I'll be candid: the budget is tight this year, and I'd need to justify it to senior management.
That's helpful. If I couldn't secure the full amount, would you consider a smaller increase now, with a review in six months?
Fair enough. Let me take your figures to the director, and I'll aim to have an answer for you by the end of next week.

scenarios.scenario: Mediating a dispute between two team members
scenarios.context: A manager navigates a delicate conflict over credit and responsibility.

speakerA.en: I'd like us to be candid about what's happened. Both of you have concerns, and I want to understand them before any decisions are made.
I can see why that would be frustrating. Let me hear the other perspective before I draw any conclusions.
Generosity is admirable, but it must not come at the expense of clear attribution. I think we can agree that was an oversight rather than an affront.
Then let's agree on a protocol: credit will be assigned explicitly in every future submission, and I'll circulate a note correcting the record.

speakerB.en: My concern is simple. I conceived the proposal and did most of the groundwork, yet it was presented as a collaborative effort without my name.
In fairness, I did incorporate her ideas, and I believed that acknowledging the team as a whole was the more generous approach.
I'll accept that, provided it doesn't happen again. I'm not seeking a grand apology, only that my contribution be recognized.
That's perfectly acceptable. And I apologize, genuinely, if I was careless; it wasn't my intention to diminish anyone.

scenarios.scenario: Delivering a candid performance review
scenarios.context: A manager balances honesty with encouragement when addressing a staff member's shortcomings.

speakerA.en: I'd like to begin by saying that your analytical skills are among the best on the team, and that's not something I say lightly.
Fair enough. The difficulty is communication. Your reports are rigorous, but they're often impenetrable to anyone outside your field.
It's an important one, though a report that no one understands accomplishes little. I'd like you to practice distilling your findings into plain language.
An excellent suggestion. I'll arrange it, and we can revisit your progress in a couple of months.

speakerB.en: Thank you. I sense there's a 'but' approaching, so I'd prefer that you simply come to it.
I hadn't appreciated that. I suppose I've always assumed that precision was the highest virtue.
That's a fair criticism, and I'd welcome guidance. Perhaps I could have my drafts reviewed by someone outside the technical group.
Thank you for being forthright. It's far more useful than the vague praise I've received in the past.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for a day off
scenarios.context: An employee asks the manager for a day of leave.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, do you have a minute?
I'd like to ask for a day off next Friday.
Yes, I have to go to my sister's wedding.
Of course. Thank you very much.

speakerB.en: Sure. What can I do for you?
Is there a special reason?
That's fine. Please finish your report before you go.
Congratulations to your sister. Enjoy the wedding.

scenarios.scenario: Talking to the manager about work hours
scenarios.context: An employee asks the manager about changing his working hours.

speakerA.en: Could I talk to you about my schedule?
I live far away, and the traffic is terrible in the morning.
Could I start at ten and finish at six?
That would help me a lot. Thank you.

speakerB.en: Yes, of course. What's the problem?
I see. What would you like to change?
I think that's possible. Let's try it for a month.
No problem. Let me know if there are any difficulties.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing a deadline with a colleague
scenarios.context: Two colleagues talk about a project that is running late.

speakerA.en: Have you seen the latest schedule? The client wants the report by Thursday.
Could you send me what you have so far? I can help with the charts.
Do you think we should ask our manager for an extension?
You're right. Let's work through lunch and meet again at four.

speakerB.en: Yes, and I'm worried. We still haven't finished the data analysis.
That would be a relief. I'll send the file within an hour.
I'd rather try to finish on time. We've asked for extra time twice already.
Agreed. I'll bring some sandwiches so we don't lose time.

scenarios.scenario: Introducing an idea in a team meeting
scenarios.context: An employee suggests a new idea to improve the team's work.

speakerA.en: Before we finish, I'd like to suggest something about our weekly meetings.
I think they take too long. We often discuss the same topics twice.
We could send a short summary by email and only meet for urgent matters.
Should we try it for a month and see how it goes?

speakerB.en: Of course. Go ahead. We're listening.
That's true. What do you suggest we do instead?
That's an interesting idea. It would save a lot of time.
Yes, let's do that. Could you prepare a template for the summary?

scenarios.scenario: Asking for a day off and arranging cover
scenarios.context: An employee asks a manager for time off and explains how the work will be covered.

speakerA.en: Do you have a moment? I wanted to ask whether I could take next Friday off, if that's possible.
I have a family event that I can't miss. I would have asked earlier, but the date was only confirmed yesterday.
I've already spoken to Sara, and she's agreed to take over my clients as long as I do the same for her next month.
I'll finish the report before I leave, so that nothing will be left unfinished. I've also prepared a list of all my current tasks.
That's a relief. Should I send the list to you or directly to Sara so she can start preparing?
Thank you so much. I'll make sure everything is in order, and I'll be reachable by phone in case of an emergency.

speakerB.en: Of course. Let me check the schedule first. Is there a particular reason, or is it something personal?
I understand. The problem is that we have an important client visiting on that day, so I need to know who will be dealing with them.
That sounds reasonable. As long as the arrangement is clear, I don't see a problem with it.
Good. I appreciate that you've planned ahead. Few people think about the consequences before they ask for time off.
Send it to both of us, please. If any questions come up, Sara can contact me directly while you're away.
There's no need to be reachable unless it's urgent. Enjoy your day, and I'll see you on Monday.

scenarios.scenario: Receiving feedback after a project
scenarios.context: A manager gives feedback on a finished project, and the employee responds constructively.

speakerA.en: Thanks for meeting with me. I'd like to hear your honest opinion about how the project went.
I agree. I think I underestimated how long the testing phase would take, which made the final week very stressful.
That's useful to know. I've been trying to improve my presentations, but I still get nervous when there's a large audience.
I'll definitely try that. Would it be possible for me to lead a smaller meeting next month, so that I can practice?
That would be great. I'd also like to take a course in project management, if the company is willing to pay for it.
Thank you for your support. I'll send you some course options by the end of the week so that you can review them.

speakerB.en: Overall, I was impressed. The results were better than we expected, and the client was very pleased with the final report.
That's an honest assessment. In future, it would help if you shared problems earlier, so that we can adjust the schedule together.
Your slides were clear, but you spoke too quickly. If you slowed down and made more eye contact, people would follow you more easily.
That's a good idea. There's a team meeting on the fifteenth that you could lead, and I'll be there to support you.
I think that's reasonable. We have a training budget, and an investment like this would benefit the whole department.
Please do. You've worked hard this year, and I'd like to see you continue growing within the company.

scenarios.scenario: Answering questions at a job interview
scenarios.context: A candidate answers an interviewer's questions about experience and goals.

speakerA.en: Good morning. Thank you for inviting me. I've been looking forward to learning more about the position.
I've worked in customer service for four years, during which I've dealt with complaints, managed schedules, and trained new staff.
One of my strengths is communication. When a customer was upset last year, I listened carefully, and we found a solution that satisfied everyone.
I'd say my weakness is that I sometimes take on too much work. I'm learning to ask for help before things become overwhelming.
In five years, I hope to have moved into a leadership role, ideally managing a small team and helping others develop their skills.
Yes, I do. Could you tell me what the team is like, and what opportunities there are for training?

speakerB.en: Good morning, and welcome. Please have a seat. I'd like to start by asking about your work experience.
That's quite a lot of experience. Which of those responsibilities did you enjoy the most, and why?
That's a great example. And what would you say is your biggest weakness? Please be honest.
It's good that you recognize that. Many employees struggle with that problem, and it's something that can be improved with experience.
Those are ambitious but realistic goals. Our company often promotes people from within, provided they show initiative.
Of course. The team is friendly and supportive, and we offer a training program every quarter. We'll contact you by Friday.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating a deadline with a colleague
scenarios.context: Two colleagues discuss a deadline that seems too tight and try to find a compromise.

speakerA.en: Do you have a minute? I've been looking at the schedule for the new campaign, and I'm worried that we won't finish on time.
The problem is that the designs weren't sent to us until Monday, so we've lost almost a week that we had planned to use for testing.
I could work faster, but I wouldn't want to send something to the client that hasn't been checked properly.
That might work, although it depends on whether the client agrees to receive the final version a few days later.
I'll write to them this afternoon. If they say yes, we'll have enough time to correct any mistakes.
Thanks for being so understanding. I'll keep you informed as soon as I hear anything.

speakerB.en: Of course. I had the same feeling. Which part of the project do you think is the most likely to cause delays?
I know, and that's not fair on us. Could we ask the design team to send the remaining files by tomorrow morning?
I agree. A rushed job could damage our reputation, and it would take longer to fix the problems afterwards.
Perhaps we could deliver the first part on the original date, and promise the rest by the end of the following week.
That sounds sensible. In the meantime, I'll start on the parts that don't depend on the designs, so that we save as much time as possible.
No problem. We're in this together, and I'm sure we'll find a solution that works for everyone.

scenarios.scenario: Meeting the team on your first week
scenarios.context: A new employee talks to a colleague about the company and how things work.

speakerA.en: Hi, I'm Daniel. I started on Monday, and I'm still trying to learn how everything works around here.
I'll be working in the marketing team. I used to work for a smaller company, so this place feels huge.
Not yet. Everyone has been friendly, but I'm afraid I've already forgotten most of the names I was told.
That would be great. Is there anything about the company that I should know, like unwritten rules or habits?
Good to know. And where do people usually have lunch? I've been eating at my desk because I didn't want to ask.
I'd love to. Thank you for being so welcoming. It makes the first week much less stressful.

speakerB.en: Nice to meet you, Daniel. I'm Lisa. I've been here for three years, so feel free to ask me anything.
You'll get used to it quickly. People here are very helpful, and the atmosphere is more relaxed than you'd expect from a big company.
Don't worry, that's completely normal. If you like, I can introduce you to some of the people in the other departments.
Well, meetings usually start on time, but nobody minds if you ask questions. And the manager prefers to be called by her first name.
Most of us go to the cafeteria on the second floor, or to the small park nearby when the weather is nice.
Why don't you join us tomorrow? We go at half past twelve, and you can meet the rest of the team.

scenarios.scenario: Settling a disagreement about responsibilities
scenarios.context: Two coworkers discuss who should be responsible for a task that has been neglected.

speakerA.en: I'd like to talk about the monthly reports. It seems that we both thought the other person was dealing with them.
I understand, but I was told by our manager that the sales department would collect the data and send it to you.
That may be true, but it isn't the first time that this has happened, and it's affecting the quality of our work.
I agree. It would be better if each task had a name next to it, so that nobody has to guess.
Fine. I'll take the reports from now on if you're willing to prepare the presentations, since you're better at that than I am.
Good. Let's tell our manager about the new arrangement, so that everybody is aware of it.

speakerB.en: I was wondering about that too. I thought you had prepared them, because you did last month.
That wasn't clear to me. I never received any data, and nobody told me that I'd have to ask for it.
You're right. We've both been busy, and the lack of communication has caused unnecessary stress for everyone.
That's a good idea. We could create a shared document that lists every task, who is responsible, and when it must be finished.
That seems fair, and it would make better use of our skills. I'm happy to prepare the presentations if the deadlines are realistic.
I'll write a short email this afternoon, and we can discuss the details at the next team meeting.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing a promotion with a manager
scenarios.context: An employee asks about career progression and responds to feedback in a performance review.

speakerA.en: Thank you for taking the time to meet with me. I'd like to discuss my development within the company and where I might go from here.
Over the past year, I've taken on additional responsibilities, including leading the onboarding of new staff, and I believe that I've made a real contribution to the team.
I appreciate your honesty. If I had been aware earlier that presenting to senior management was an expectation, I would have asked for training long before now.
I'd be very keen to do that. Could you explain what criteria will be used when the next promotion decisions are made?
That's helpful. Would it be possible to set specific goals over the next six months, so that we both know what I'm working towards?
Thank you. I'll draft a proposal and send it to you by the end of the week, so that we can review it together.

speakerB.en: Of course. I'm glad you asked. You've performed very well this year, and I've received positive feedback from several colleagues, particularly about your reliability.
That's true, and it hasn't gone unnoticed. However, being considered for a more senior role would require a stronger presence in meetings with clients and directors.
I should have communicated that more clearly, and I apologize. There's a leadership program starting in January, and I'd happily recommend you for it.
Decisions are based on performance, initiative, and the ability to manage others. Technical skills alone, however strong, don't usually suffice at that level.
That's an excellent suggestion. We could agree on three or four measurable objectives, and review them together every two months to see how things are progressing.
Please do. I'm confident that, provided you continue as you have, a promotion within eighteen months is a realistic prospect.

scenarios.scenario: Debating the four-day work week
scenarios.context: Two colleagues discuss the advantages and disadvantages of a shorter work week.

speakerA.en: Have you heard that some companies are experimenting with a four-day work week without reducing salaries? I can hardly believe it works.
According to the trials, productivity stayed the same or even improved, because employees were more focused and wasted less time in unnecessary meetings.
That's what the supporters say, but I'm skeptical. In sectors like healthcare or customer service, you can't simply compress the work into fewer days.
True, although there might be ways of organizing shifts that would allow people to work fewer days while the service remains available.
I'd argue that the benefits go beyond productivity. Employees who have more time to rest are less likely to burn out and take sick leave.
Perhaps the best approach would be to let each company try it on a small scale first, and then decide on the basis of real results.

speakerB.en: I've read about it. Several trials in Europe reported that employees were happier and healthier, and that very few of them wanted to return to a five-day week.
That makes sense, up to a point. If people know they have an extra day off, they tend to concentrate harder in order to finish everything on time.
That's a fair objection, and the researchers admit that the results are less clear in jobs that depend on constant availability. It isn't a universal solution.
Some hospitals have already experimented with longer shifts over fewer days, although critics say that this can lead to exhaustion, which defeats the purpose.
That's a strong argument. The costs of stress-related illness are enormous for both employers and governments, so even a small reduction could save a great deal of money.
I think that's a sensible compromise. Evidence should guide policy, and it would be a pity to reject a promising idea simply because it sounds unfamiliar.

scenarios.scenario: Handling a conflict within a team
scenarios.context: A team leader speaks with a team member about a tense working relationship.

speakerA.en: Thanks for agreeing to meet. I wanted to speak with you privately, since I've noticed some tension between you and Mark in recent meetings.
I don't want to take sides, but if the situation continues, it could affect the entire team. Could you tell me how you see things?
I understand that. It's difficult when you feel that your efforts haven't been acknowledged. Has Mark been made aware of how you feel?
I think it would be worth having a direct and calm conversation with him. I could be present, if you'd feel more comfortable that way.
Good. Perhaps you could prepare a few specific examples, rather than general complaints, so that the discussion remains constructive.
I appreciate your openness. Let's arrange a meeting for Thursday, and I'm confident that we can find a way forward.

speakerB.en: Thank you for raising it. I'd rather clear the air, because the atmosphere has been uncomfortable for weeks, and I'm not sure how to improve it.
Honestly, I feel that Mark often takes credit for work that we've done together, and when I mention it, he dismisses my concerns as being oversensitive.
I haven't brought it up with him directly, mainly because I'm afraid it might turn into an argument, and I don't want to make things worse.
That would be a relief. I'd probably find it easier to speak openly if someone else were there to keep the conversation balanced.
That's a good point. I can think of at least three occasions when my contribution wasn't mentioned in the final presentation, even though I had written most of it.
Thank you. I feel better already, simply having said it out loud. I hope that we can resolve it without damaging the working relationship.

scenarios.scenario: Presenting a project update and answering tough questions
scenarios.context: A project manager gives a progress report and responds to concerns from senior management.

speakerA.en: Thank you all for coming. I'd like to give you a brief overview of where the project stands, and then I'll be happy to answer any questions.

Overall, we're about ten percent behind schedule, largely because of delays in receiving data from the supplier. However, we've adjusted the plan, and I'm confident that we'll catch up by the end of next month.

That's a fair question. If the supplier fails to deliver by the fifteenth, we'd have to use the backup source, which would cost around twelve thousand euros more, but wouldn't affect the final deadline.
I understand your concern about the budget. We've already identified some savings in other areas, which should offset most of the additional expense, and I'll send you the detailed figures by Friday.
That's a good point, and I should have mentioned it earlier. The team is stretched, so I'd like to propose bringing in one temporary specialist for six weeks, to reduce the risk of burnout.
Thank you for your questions. I'll circulate a written summary this afternoon, and I'll update you again in two weeks, or sooner if anything significant changes.

speakerB.en: Thank you, Maria. Before you continue, could you tell us exactly how serious the delay is? Last month, we were told that everything was on track.
I see. And what happens if the supplier misses the deadline again? We can't afford a repeat of what happened on the last project, where the problems only came to light at the final stage.
That's an additional cost that we hadn't anticipated. Is there any possibility of renegotiating the contract with the supplier, so that they bear some responsibility for the delay?
Please do. I'd also like to know whether the team has the capacity to absorb these changes, because I've heard that morale has dropped recently, and I'd like to avoid losing key people.
That sounds reasonable, provided that the specialist is fully briefed. I'll talk to the finance director about approving the additional expense, and I'll let you know by tomorrow.
Thank you. I appreciate your openness. It's better to hear about difficulties early than to be surprised later, and I think the board will see it the same way.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating a flexible work arrangement with a manager
scenarios.context: An employee asks her manager to approve two remote-working days per week and offers something in return.

speakerA.en: Thank you for making time. I'd like to propose a flexible arrangement, in which I work from home two days a week, since my commute has become increasingly exhausting and I believe I'd be more productive.

I understand that. In return for the flexibility, I'd be willing to be available for calls during core hours, and I'd be expected to attend all team meetings in person on the other three days. Would that address your concern?

Absolutely. I'd be happy to submit a weekly summary, and I'd expect to be held accountable for my targets. Having said that, I'd like the arrangement to be reviewed after three months rather than fixed indefinitely.

I've thought about that. On the other hand, on the days I'm in the office, I'd be expected to handle collaborative tasks, whereas the focused work would be done at home. In return, I'd cover for colleagues' urgent requests on the remote days.

That would be very helpful, thank you. To be honest, I hadn't expected such a positive response. In return for your support, I'd be happy to mentor the new recruits, which I know you've been looking for someone to do.
Of course. I'll send a draft by Thursday, in which I set out the schedule, the reporting arrangements, and the review date. Having said that, please let me know if anything needs to be changed.

speakerB.en: I appreciate you raising it directly. That said, I need to understand how it would work in practice. Our clients are expected to have access to the full team, and I'd be required to justify any change to the director.

It would go a long way. That said, some colleagues might feel it's unfair, and I'd be required to treat everyone consistently. In return, would you be prepared to document your output so that we can review it?

That's a sensible suggestion. A trial period would make it easier to get approval, and I'd be required to report the results anyway. That said, I'd want to hear whether the team's workload would be affected.

Good, I like that you've thought it through. That said, there might be technical requirements, and you'd be expected to use the company's secure connection. In return, I could arrange a second monitor for your home office.
That's a useful offer. That said, I can't promise anything until I've spoken to the director. I'd be required to submit a formal proposal, so could you write down the details we've discussed today?
Perfect. I'll present it at Monday's meeting, and I'd expect an answer within a week. In return for your flexibility on the details, I'll do my best to make this work.

scenarios.scenario: Resolving a disagreement over a tight deadline
scenarios.context: Two colleagues discuss an unrealistic deadline that one of them agreed with a client, and work out a compromise.

speakerA.en: Do you have a minute? I wanted to talk about the Henderson report. I see where you're coming from about the deadline, but I don't think two days is realistic, which is why I wanted to raise it before it's too late.
I appreciate that. You ought to have asked, since I'm the one doing most of the analysis. I should have spoken up earlier too, which is why I'm bringing it up now rather than on Thursday night.
That's true. I'd say the appendix could be shortened, since the client hardly reads it. On the other hand, the data section really needs the full treatment, which is why I'd rather not rush it.
That might work, provided the client agrees. I ought to have suggested it sooner, which is why I'm glad we're talking now. Would you be willing to call them, or should I do it?

I think that's wise. To be honest, I was worried you'd be defensive, but you've been very reasonable. You ought to have heard how nervous I was rehearsing this conversation, which is why I'm so relieved.
That would help a great deal. I'll draft the summary tonight, so that you have something to send on Friday. I ought to thank you for listening, which is more than I expected.

speakerB.en: Of course. I see where you're coming from, but the client has been very clear about Friday, which is why I committed to it. I should have consulted you before agreeing, though, and I apologize for that.
Fair enough. I see where you're coming from, but could we cut something to make it work? We ought to have scoped the project more carefully, which is probably why we're in this position now.
Agreed. We should have allowed more time for it from the start. I see where you're coming from, so what if we sent the main findings on Friday and the appendix on Monday, with a note explaining why?
I should be the one to call, since I made the commitment. I'd rather not damage the relationship, which is why I'll be honest about what's realistic. I should have done that from the beginning.
I see where you're coming from, and I'd have felt the same. We should have communicated better, which is why I'd like us to have a short check-in every Monday from now on, to avoid surprises.
Thank you for raising it. I should have noticed the pressure you were under, which is why I'll ask how you're doing more often. Let's talk to the client first thing tomorrow.

scenarios.scenario: Explaining why you cannot accept a promotion that requires relocation
scenarios.context: An employee has been offered a promotion abroad and explains to her manager why she is hesitant, asking whether other options exist.

speakerA.en: Thank you for seeing me. I wanted to speak to you about the promotion to the Singapore office. Grateful as I am for the offer, I have some reservations, and to be honest, I haven't slept well since you mentioned it. Could we talk it through?

The relocation, I'd say. Much as I'd love the responsibility, my daughter starts secondary school this autumn, and my husband's job can't be moved. But for the family situation, I'd have accepted immediately. As far as I'm concerned, the role is exactly what I've been working toward.

I'd love to be more flexible, but a permanent move isn't possible. On the other hand, I'd be willing to spend three months there, provided the company covered the travel. Would a temporary assignment be an option, or does the role need someone permanently on site?

Challenging as that would be with the time difference, I'd be willing to try. Provided I had a strong deputy on site, I think it could work. I'd also want the title and salary to reflect the full role, rather than a reduced version of it.

Certainly. I'll outline the structure, the travel schedule and the support I'd need. Convinced as I am that it can work, I'd rather be realistic about the risks. If it doesn't work after six months, we should be able to review it honestly, don't you think?

Only your support with the board. Thank you for listening, since I was dreading this conversation. I'm relieved, although I realize it isn't settled yet, so I'll send the proposal by Monday. I'd rather have you as an ally than an obstacle.

speakerB.en: Of course, and please be frank. Tempting as the role may be, I'd rather you made the right choice than a quick one. Which part is giving you the most doubt, the work itself or the relocation?

I appreciate your honesty, and I understand. Difficult as it must be to turn down a major opportunity, it's better to say so now than after you've moved. Were it not for the deadline in January, I'd say take your time. How flexible could you be?

That's a fair question. Honestly, the team in Singapore would prefer a permanent leader, since they've had several changes. But for your track record, I wouldn't even consider alternatives. Could you manage the team remotely, with visits every quarter?

That's reasonable, and I'd say you've earned it. Impressive as your results have been this year, I'll need to convince the board, who may prefer someone local. Would you put your proposal in writing, so I can present it next week?

Absolutely, and I'd suggest a formal review after six months. I'm impressed by how well you've thought this through, though I shouldn't be, given your record. But for your frankness today, I might have assumed a refusal. Is there anything else you'd need from me?
You have me as an ally. Send it by Monday, and I'll argue your case as strongly as I can. Whatever the board decides, you've handled this with maturity, and I'm proud to have you on my team.

scenarios.scenario: Giving constructive feedback to a colleague after a client presentation
scenarios.context: An experienced team member offers a colleague honest but supportive feedback after a presentation to an important client.
