speakerA.en: Do you have a few minutes? I wanted to talk about this morning's client presentation. On the whole, I'd say it went well, but there are a couple of things I noticed that might help next time. Would you be open to some feedback?

That's actually one of my points. You appear to have spent too long on the background and then rushed the recommendations, which are what the client cares about most. If anything, I'd shorten the introduction rather than the conclusion. Does that make sense?

I'd give them a short summary, in two minutes at most, and let them ask questions. That way, they feel involved rather than lectured. By and large, clients prefer a conversation to a monologue. What's more, it gives you more time to talk about the results.

Honestly, I'm not always relaxed! I've learned to rehearse out loud, rather than just reading slides in my head. If anything, rehearsing three times matters more than perfecting the slides. And as far as I'm concerned, one confident sentence beats five nervous ones.

Plenty, and I'm glad you asked. Your charts were clear, and you answered the difficult question about pricing calmly, which impressed me. You appear to have prepared the numbers thoroughly. What's more, your tone was warm, and the client seemed to relax.

I'd be glad to, and we could run through them together, rather than just by email. On the whole, I think you're stronger than you realize, and a few small changes will make a big difference. Shall we schedule an hour on Thursday?

speakerB.en: Of course, I'd welcome it. To be honest, I felt it went well, but I was nervous, and I seem to have rushed through the final slides. What did you notice?
It does, although I wanted to show that we understood their situation. On the other hand, I can see that I may have lost their attention. What would you do instead of explaining everything in detail?

That's a good point. I tend to read from my notes rather than looking at the audience, which probably made it worse. It seems to be a habit I've developed under pressure. How do you manage to stay so relaxed?
I'll try that. Rehearsing out loud sounds uncomfortable, but it seems to have worked for you. Was there anything I did well? I'd like to know what to keep doing, rather than only what to change.

That's encouraging, thank you. I spent a lot of time on the pricing figures, so it's good to know it showed. Would it help if I sent you the slides before the next presentation, so you can review them beforehand?

Thursday works perfectly, thank you. I really appreciate your honesty, as it can't be easy to give feedback like this. If anything, I wish more colleagues would do the same. See you then, and thanks again for taking the time.

scenarios.scenario: Asking and telling the time and making appointments
scenarios.context: People ask about time, set up meetings or get-togethers.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, what time is it?
Thank you. What time is the class?
Am I late?
Great. Thanks for your help.
When should we meet?
speakerA.fa: کی باید همدیگر را ببینیم؟

speakerA.en: What time does the movie start?
speakerA.fa: فیلم چه ساعتی شروع می‌شه؟

speakerA.en: Can we postpone our meeting to 3 PM? I'm running late.
speakerA.fa: میشه جلسه‌مون رو به ساعت ۳ موکول کنیم؟ دارم دیر می‌شم.

speakerA.en: Let's confirm the date: Are we meeting on the 15th or the 16th?
speakerA.fa: بیا تاریخ رو تأیید کنیم: جلسه ما پانزدهمه یا شانزدهم؟

speakerA.en: I'm free anytime after 4 PM. What suits you best?
speakerA.fa: بعد از ۴ عصر هر وقتی آزادم. چه زمانی برات بهتره؟

speakerA.en: Where shall we meet? At your place or at the cinema?
OK. I'll arrive ten minutes early.

speakerB.en: The class is at eleven o'clock.
No, you have thirty minutes.
You're welcome.
How about 6 o'clock in the evening?
speakerB.fa: ساعت ۶ عصر چطوره؟

speakerB.en: It starts at 7 PM. We should leave at 6.
speakerB.fa: ساعت ۷ شب شروع می‌شه. باید ساعت ۶ حرکت کنیم.

speakerB.en: Sure, 3 PM is fine. I'll adjust my schedule.
speakerB.fa: حتماً، ساعت ۳ خوبه. برنامه‌ام رو تنظیم می‌کنم.

speakerB.en: I believe it's the 15th. Let me double-check my calendar.
speakerB.fa: فکر می‌کنم پانزدهم باشه. بذارید تقویمم رو دوباره چک کنم.

speakerB.en: 4 PM sounds perfect. I'll see you then.
speakerB.fa: ساعت ۴ عالی به نظر میاد. پس همون موقع می‌بینمت.

speakerB.en: Let's meet at the cinema entrance.
Good. I'll buy the tickets before you come.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about days and dates
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about the day and the date.

speakerA.en: What day is it today?
Is tomorrow Tuesday?
What is the date today?
When is your birthday?
Which day of the week is it today?
What is the date of your birthday?
What date is the meeting next week?
Thanks. I'll write it in my calendar.

speakerB.en: It's Monday.
Yes, it is.
It's May fifth.
My birthday is in June.
It's Wednesday, the fourteenth of June.
It's on the twenty-second of August.
It's on Tuesday, the twentieth.
Good idea. I always forget dates.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about a daily schedule
scenarios.context: A student asks a friend about a normal day.

speakerA.en: What time do you get up?
When do you have breakfast?
What time do you go to work?
When do you go to bed?
What time do you get up in the morning?
When do your classes start?
What do you do after school?
What time do you go to bed?

speakerB.en: I get up at six o'clock.
I have breakfast at seven.
I go to work at eight.
I go to bed at ten o'clock.
I get up at six thirty and have breakfast.
At eight forty-five. I take the bus at eight.
I do my homework and then I go to the gym.
Usually around eleven o'clock.

scenarios.scenario: Making a doctor's appointment
scenarios.context: A patient calls the doctor's office to make an appointment.

speakerA.en: Hello. I want an appointment, please.
Is Monday OK?
Yes, ten o'clock is fine.
My name is Sara Brown.
Good morning. I'd like to make an appointment, please.
Do you have anything on Tuesday?
I work until four. Do you have a later time?
Five fifteen is perfect. Thank you.

speakerB.en: Yes. What day is good for you?
Yes, Monday at ten o'clock is free.
What is your name, please?
OK, Ms. Brown. See you on Monday.
Of course. What day would you prefer?
Let me see. Yes, at three thirty in the afternoon.
I have a free time at five fifteen.
You're welcome. Please arrive ten minutes early.

scenarios.scenario: Planning to meet a friend
scenarios.context: Two friends decide when and where to meet.

speakerA.en: Are you free on Saturday?
Let's meet at the café.
Is two o'clock OK?
OK. See you on Saturday!
Are you free on Saturday afternoon?
Let's go for a coffee at three o'clock.
At the café opposite the bookstore.
If you're late, please call me.

speakerB.en: Yes, I am free in the afternoon.
Good idea. What time?
Yes, two o'clock is good.
See you! Bye!
Yes, I am. What do you have in mind?
OK. Where shall we meet?
I know it. I'll see you there at three.
I will. I'll leave home early.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing for being late
scenarios.context: A person arrives late to a meeting.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry I'm late.
The bus was late.
Yes. What time is the meeting?
I'm only five minutes late.
I'm so sorry I'm late.
The bus was stuck in traffic.
How long have you been waiting?
Next time I'll leave earlier.

speakerB.en: That's OK. Don't worry.
Is everything fine?
It starts at ten fifteen.
Yes. Please sit down.
That's OK. We just started.
Don't worry. It happens.
Only about fifteen minutes.
Good idea. Let's order something now.

scenarios.scenario: Asking about opening hours
scenarios.context: A customer asks about the opening hours of a shop.

speakerA.en: What time does the shop open?
What time does it close?
Is it open on Sunday?
Thank you. I'll come on Monday.
Excuse me, what time do you open?
And what time do you close?
Are you open on Sundays?
Great. I'll come on Saturday then.

speakerB.en: It opens at nine o'clock.
It closes at six o'clock.
No, it is closed on Sunday.
You're welcome.
We open at nine in the morning.
We close at six, except on Fridays.
Only from ten to two.
OK. I'll see you then!

scenarios.scenario: Booking a haircut appointment
scenarios.context: A customer calls a salon to make an appointment.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'd like to book a haircut for this Saturday, if you have any free times.
That's a little late for me. Is there anything in the morning?
That's fine, as long as it doesn't take more than an hour.
It's Julia Reed, and my number is 555-0178. Do you send reminders?

speakerB.en: Let me check. We're quite busy on Saturdays. Would eleven thirty be possible?
There's a slot at nine fifteen, but only with a junior stylist.
A basic cut takes about forty-five minutes. Can I have your name and number?
Yes, we'll send a text message the day before. See you on Saturday!

scenarios.scenario: Running late for a meeting
scenarios.context: A person calls to say he will be late for a meeting.

speakerA.en: Hi, it's me. I'm sorry, but I'm going to be late for our meeting.
There was an accident on the highway, and traffic is barely moving.
Probably thirty minutes, maybe more. Could you start without me?
Thanks for understanding. I'll try to find a faster route.

speakerB.en: What happened? Everyone has already arrived.
How late do you think you'll be?
Of course. I'll go through the first part of the agenda, and we'll save the rest for when you arrive.
No problem. Drive carefully, and don't worry about us.

scenarios.scenario: Rescheduling a meeting
scenarios.context: Two colleagues change the time of a planned meeting.

speakerA.en: I'm afraid I can't make our meeting at three tomorrow. Something urgent has come up.
I'm free on Thursday morning, or any time on Friday afternoon.
That's perfect. Should we keep it online, or would you prefer to meet in person?
Thanks. I'll prepare the figures in advance so we don't waste any time.

speakerB.en: That's all right. Do you have any other time in mind?
Thursday is difficult for me. Would Friday at two work for you?
Online is more convenient. I'll update the calendar invitation now.
Great. If anything changes, let me know as early as you can.

scenarios.scenario: Managing a tight schedule
scenarios.context: Two colleagues try to coordinate a busy week.

speakerA.en: My calendar is almost impossible this week. Would it be feasible to postpone our review until Monday?
I'd prefer not to, as I have a family commitment, but I could carve out half an hour at lunch.
In that case, would you mind sending me the figures beforehand, so I can prepare in advance?
I'll block out the time and decline anything that tries to creep into the slot.

speakerB.en: That's cutting it fine, given that the report is due on Tuesday. Could we do it on Friday evening instead?
Half an hour won't do it justice. There's a lot to cover, particularly the budget forecasts.
That's a sensible compromise. I'll email them tonight, and we can use the half hour to go through only the problem areas.
Excellent. Let's hope nothing urgent comes up in the meantime.

scenarios.scenario: Dealing with a double-booked appointment
scenarios.context: A client and a receptionist sort out a scheduling error.

speakerA.en: I have an appointment with Mr. Wilson at two, but your assistant seems to think I'm not on the schedule.
That's most inconvenient. I've traveled over an hour to be here.
I can wait, but only until half past. I have a train to catch this evening.
That's kind, thank you. For the future, though, I'd appreciate a confirmation email the day before.

speakerB.en: I do apologize. It appears there's been a double booking, and another client has just gone in.
I understand, and I'm truly sorry. Mr. Wilson should be free in about twenty minutes, if you could bear to wait.
I'll make sure he knows that. In the meantime, may I offer you a coffee as a gesture of goodwill?
Absolutely. I'll flag it on your file so it doesn't happen again.

scenarios.scenario: Reflecting on time management habits
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss why they never seem to have enough time.

speakerA.en: I'm always running behind, however early I start the day. Where does the time go?
You're right. I probably lose a couple of hours a day that way without noticing.
Doesn't that make people think you're being unresponsive?
That's reassuring. I might try it for a week and see whether my stress levels drop.

speakerB.en: I think a lot of it vanishes into small distractions, like checking my phone or answering messages as they arrive.
I've started batching tasks, so I deal with emails only twice a day, and it's made a tangible difference.
Initially, but I explained my approach, and no one seems to mind. Genuine emergencies are phoned through anyway.
Do. Also, plan your most demanding work for the hours when you're sharpest.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating a deadline extension
scenarios.context: A freelance designer asks a client for more time after the project scope changed.

speakerA.en: I wanted to raise something before we get too close to the deadline. The scope has grown considerably since the original brief, and I'm concerned about delivering to the standard we both want.
The additional animations and the second language version weren't part of the initial agreement, and together they add roughly two weeks of work.
I could prioritize the core deliverables and hand over the extras in a second phase, which would keep the launch on track.
The main interface and the English version. The animations and translation could follow within ten days of launch.

speakerB.en: I appreciate the early warning. What exactly has changed, in your view?
I see. The launch date is fixed, though, so I'm reluctant to move the deadline. Is there any way of compressing the schedule?
That's a workable compromise. Which elements would you consider essential for day one?
Agreed, as long as you confirm the revised plan in writing. I'd rather have a clear arrangement than an optimistic one.

scenarios.scenario: Coordinating a meeting across time zones
scenarios.context: Two colleagues in different countries search for a meeting slot that works for both teams.

speakerA.en: Finding a time that suits both offices is proving to be a puzzle. Our morning is your late evening, and I don't want to impose on your families.
Thursday at seven works for me, though I'd have to ask a couple of the team to join from home. Would that be acceptable on your end?
Sensible. I'll circulate an agenda in advance so we spend the time on decisions rather than updates.
That should help. And if it overruns, we can pick up the remaining points by email rather than extend the call.

speakerB.en: I appreciate that. Evenings are tolerable for a one-off, but I'd rather not make it a habit. What about early on Thursday your time?
It would be midday for us, which is ideal. Shall we cap the call at an hour, given the early start?
Excellent. I'll also ask the team to submit their questions beforehand, which should keep the discussion focused.
Agreed. I'll send the invitation now, with the time shown in both zones to avoid any confusion.

scenarios.scenario: Prioritizing a crowded calendar
scenarios.context: A director and her assistant decide which commitments to keep after a week of conflicting meetings.

speakerA.en: My calendar for Tuesday is, frankly, absurd. Three meetings overlap, and I can't be in all of them. Where would you suggest I cut?
Which of the remaining two is more critical? I'd rather not disappoint either, but I have to be realistic.
That's a reasonable solution. Could you arrange a fifteen-minute briefing with her tomorrow afternoon?
Please do, and apologize on my behalf. I'd rather postpone gracefully than turn up distracted.

speakerB.en: The budget review is the only one that can't be moved, since the finance team has already traveled in. The other two have more flexibility.
The supplier negotiation carries higher stakes, though your deputy could attend in your place if you briefed her beforehand.
I'll book it now. And for the third meeting, I could propose a short call on Wednesday instead, if you'd like.
Understood. I'll also block out an hour in your calendar on Tuesday so that you can breathe between commitments.

scenarios.scenario: Rescheduling a critical meeting at short notice
scenarios.context: An assistant tries to find a new slot for several busy executives.

speakerA.en: I'm afraid the board meeting scheduled for Thursday can't proceed as planned. The chair has been called away unexpectedly.
I appreciate that, and I wouldn't have asked if there were an alternative. Would Monday morning be feasible for you?
Two o'clock would suit the chair. Let me confirm with the others, and I'll circulate a revised agenda by this evening.
A good point. I'll arrange for a connection and send the details once the time is confirmed.

speakerB.en: That's awkward. Half of the board has already rearranged their diaries, and several are traveling from overseas.
Monday is difficult, as I'm committed until noon. I could manage the afternoon, though not before two.
Please do. I'd also suggest that we keep the video link open for those who can't attend in person.
Thank you for handling it so gracefully. Rearranging a meeting of this size is never a thankless task if done with tact.

scenarios.scenario: Arguing for more notice before a deadline shift
scenarios.context: A team member challenges an unrealistic timetable diplomatically.

speakerA.en: I've seen the revised deadline, and I must register some concern. Moving it forward by a week leaves us with very little margin for error.
I appreciate your position. However, rushing the final stage risks compromising quality, which would reflect worse on us than a short delay.
I'd propose delivering a functional first version on the new date, with the refinements to follow a few days later.
Exactly. I'll prepare a brief outline of what each delivery would contain, so the expectations are clear from the start.

speakerB.en: I understand, but the client has been insistent, and I'm under pressure to accommodate them.
What would you suggest, then? I can't simply refuse the client outright.
That might satisfy them. They'd see progress, and we'd retain the time to do things properly.
Do that, and I'll present it to the client tomorrow. It's far better to negotiate openly than to promise something we can't deliver.

scenarios.scenario: Managing a packed schedule without sacrificing priorities
scenarios.context: Two colleagues discuss how to protect time for essential work amid constant demands.

speakerA.en: I've realized that my calendar is controlled by everyone but me. By the end of each day, I've accomplished none of what I intended.
That sounds sensible, though I'm not sure how to decline requests without appearing uncooperative.
That leaves the door open without conceding my time. I rather like it.
I'll try that. I suspect my colleagues will protest initially, but they'll adjust if I'm consistent.

speakerB.en: A familiar predicament. The trick is to treat your own priorities as appointments and defend them as you would a client meeting.
I find that a polite deferral works better than an outright refusal. Something like, 'I can help, but not before Thursday.'
I also reserve the first hour each morning for deep work and treat it as inviolable. The world rarely ends before ten.
They will. People respect boundaries once they realize they're serious rather than negotiable.

scenarios.scenario: Rescheduling a meeting at work
scenarios.context: Two colleagues find a new time for a meeting.

speakerA.en: I'm afraid I can't make our meeting tomorrow at two. Something urgent has come up.
Would Thursday morning be an option? Any time before noon is fine.
That's perfect. Should I book the same meeting room?
Good idea. I'll send an updated invitation to everyone.

speakerB.en: That's okay. When would suit you better?
Let me check my calendar. I'm free at ten thirty.
Yes, and I'll invite Tom as well, since he's involved.
Thanks. See you on Thursday, then.

scenarios.scenario: Making a dentist appointment
scenarios.context: A patient arranges a dentist appointment by phone.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'd like to make an appointment for a check-up, please.
Yes, about a year ago. My name is Reza Mohammadi.
Unfortunately, I'm at work until five. Is there anything later or earlier?
Wednesday at eight is perfect. Should I bring anything?

speakerB.en: Certainly. Have you been to our clinic before?
Thank you. We have an opening next Tuesday at a quarter past four.
Let me see. There's a slot on Wednesday at eight in the morning.
Just your insurance card, and please arrive ten minutes early.

scenarios.scenario: Rescheduling a doctor's appointment
scenarios.context: A patient phones a clinic to change an appointment because of a conflict.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I have an appointment with Dr. Brown tomorrow at ten, but I'm afraid I won't be able to come.
Something unexpected came up at work, and I have to attend an important meeting at exactly the same time.
I'd prefer to come as soon as possible. Do you have anything available later this week, perhaps on Thursday or Friday?
Thursday afternoon would be perfect. I finish work at three, so any time after four would be fine.
That's great. Will I receive a reminder, or do I need to write it down myself so that I don't forget?
Thank you for your flexibility. I'm sorry for the inconvenience, and I'll be there on time on Thursday.

speakerB.en: Good morning. May I have your name and date of birth, so that I can find your appointment on the system?
Thank you. I see that you're booked for tomorrow at ten. That's no problem, but we ask patients to give us at least a day's notice.
Let me check the calendar. Dr. Brown is fully booked on Thursday morning, but there's a free slot at four fifteen in the afternoon.
Then I'll put you down for Thursday at four fifteen. Please arrive about ten minutes early to fill in a short form.
You'll get a text message the evening before, but it's always a good idea to make a note yourself, just in case.
That's no trouble at all. We'll see you on Thursday. Have a good day, and take care.

scenarios.scenario: Arranging a meeting across time zones
scenarios.context: Two colleagues in different countries try to find a time for a video call.

speakerA.en: Hi, thanks for replying so quickly. I'd like to arrange a video call to discuss the project timeline.
I'm in London, and you're in New York, so there's a five-hour difference. That makes it a bit tricky to find a good time.
Mornings are usually best for me, but I could stay a bit later if necessary. What time would suit you?
That would be eleven o'clock in the morning for me, which is fine. I'll block out an hour in my calendar.
Would you mind sending me the agenda beforehand, so that I can prepare my questions and check the figures?
Great. If anything changes, let me know as early as possible, and we'll find another slot.

speakerB.en: Of course. I'm available most days next week, although Tuesday and Wednesday are quite full for me.
That's right. Since I'm five hours behind, nine in the morning for me is two in the afternoon for you, so it might be a good compromise.
Thursday at nine my time would work well. I could also do Friday, but I have a doctor's appointment in the afternoon.
Perfect. Let's confirm Thursday at nine, then. I'll send you the link as soon as I've set up the call.
I'll do that tonight, and I'll include the latest report as well, so that we can go through it together.
Will do. Thanks for being so flexible. Working across time zones isn't always easy, but it's good to see that it can be done.

scenarios.scenario: Managing time and priorities as a student
scenarios.context: Two students discuss how to balance studying, work, and social life.

speakerA.en: I don't know how you manage it. You study full-time, work twice a week, and still seem to find time to go out with friends. I can barely keep up with my assignments.
That sounds like a lot of planning. Do you really write down everything in advance, or do you adjust your plans according to how you feel each day?
I tend to leave tasks until the last minute, and then I regret it. Do you have any advice on how to avoid procrastinating, especially when there's something more attractive to do?
That seems reasonable. Perhaps I'm being too ambitious, trying to do everything perfectly. If I were more realistic about what's possible, I might feel less overwhelmed.
I'll try your method for a week and see whether it works. If I'd known about it at the beginning of the semester, I could have saved myself a lot of stress.
Thanks. Maybe next time we could study together on Sundays. It would be good to have some accountability.

speakerB.en: Honestly, it's mostly organization. Every Sunday evening, I plan the week in detail, and I include free time too, otherwise I'd burn out within a month.
Both, really. I have a basic structure, but I leave room for flexibility. If something unexpected comes up, I shift tasks to another day rather than abandoning them.
What works for me is breaking big tasks into small steps and setting deadlines for each part. It's much less intimidating than facing a whole essay on the last night.
That's a common mistake. Aiming for perfection can paralyze you, whereas accepting that a first draft will be imperfect lets you start, and starting is usually the hardest part.
It took me a couple of years to figure it out, so don't be too hard on yourself. The important thing is that you're thinking about how to improve.
That's a great idea. I find that working alongside someone else makes it much easier to stay focused, as long as we don't spend the whole time chatting.

scenarios.scenario: Coordinating a complicated schedule for a family event
scenarios.context: Two siblings negotiate dates and tasks for organizing their parents' anniversary.

speakerA.en: We need to settle on a date for Mum and Dad's anniversary party. I've looked at the calendar, and the only weekend when most of the family is free is the third of November.
I know it's a bit close to the exams for the cousins, but if we hold it on Saturday afternoon, they'll still have the rest of the weekend to study.
In that case, I'll book the venue tomorrow. Could you take care of the invitations? Please make sure that they go out by the end of this week, since many people need to arrange travel.
Also, I haven't decided who's going to give the speech. I'd rather not do it myself, since I get nervous in front of large groups, and you're much better at it.
Thank you. I'll prepare a short slideshow with pictures from over the years. Dad will pretend that he hates it, but I know he'll be moved.
Perfect. Let's talk again on Wednesday evening and check that everything is on schedule.

speakerB.en: That's good to know. I'd been worried about the clash with Aunt Maria's trip, but if she's back by then, it should work. How many people are we expecting?
That's a fair point. Do you think that three o'clock would be too early, or would it give us enough time to prepare the food in the morning without being stressed?
I'll do that tonight. I'll also ask everyone to confirm by the fifteenth, so that we can give the caterer an accurate number, and avoid wasting food.
All right, I'll do it, but only if you promise to help me with the content. I don't want it to be too sentimental, but I don't want it to be dry either.
That's a lovely idea. Perhaps we could ask the relatives to send photographs of their own, which would make it a more collective gift for them.
Agreed. And if anything goes wrong, we'll stay calm. The most important thing is that they have a day that they'll always remember.

scenarios.scenario: Rescheduling a business meeting
scenarios.context: A manager phones a client to change the time of an important meeting.

speakerA.en: Good morning, Mr. Clarke. This is Sandra from Linton Partners. I'm calling about our meeting scheduled for Thursday at two, and unfortunately, I have to ask whether we could reschedule it.
A client of ours has requested an urgent session at the same time, and I'm afraid that it can't be postponed. I'm very sorry for the short notice, and I wouldn't ask unless it were really necessary.
I'd be happy to come to your office on Friday morning, if that suits you. Alternatively, we could meet on Monday, although I appreciate that that would delay the decision for several days.
Thank you for being so flexible. Would ten o'clock on Friday be convenient, or would you prefer a different time? I'm free until noon, so I can adapt to your schedule.
Excellent. In that case, I'll send you an updated invitation, along with the agenda, so that you can see what we'll cover. It should take no more than ninety minutes.
Thank you again for your understanding. I'll see you on Friday at ten, and I'll make sure that we use the time efficiently.

speakerB.en: Good morning, Sandra. Thank you for letting me know. I'd been looking forward to Thursday, but I understand that these things happen. What do you suggest?
That's quite all right. Clients' demands can't always be predicted, and I'd rather have your full attention than a rushed discussion. Is it a matter of days, or could we meet later today?
Friday morning could work, but I have another appointment at eleven. If we started at ten, I'd have to leave by ten fifty, which might not be enough time to cover everything.
Let me check my diary. How about nine thirty? That would give us a full ninety minutes, and I'd still be able to reach my next meeting comfortably. Does that fit with your schedule?
That would be helpful. Please also include the figures for the second quarter, so that I can look at them before we meet. It would make the discussion more productive.
Excellent. I'll see you on Friday at nine thirty, then. Thank you for calling, and for being so considerate about it.

scenarios.scenario: Booking several appointments with a clinic receptionist
scenarios.context: A patient arranges multiple medical appointments and tries to fit them around work.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I need to make three appointments, if possible: a dental check-up, an eye test, and a follow-up with my regular doctor. I'd like to schedule them all in the same week, to save time.
I work until five on weekdays, so evenings or early mornings would be best. I could also come on Saturday morning, if the clinic is open then.
The dental appointment on Tuesday at seven thirty would be perfect. I'd have to make sure that I can leave work on time, but I think it's manageable.
And for the eye test, would it be possible to have it on the same day as the doctor's visit? It would be much more convenient than making two separate trips.
That sounds good. How long should I allow for each appointment? I need to tell my manager how much time I'll need, and I'd like to be accurate.
Thank you. Could you send me a confirmation, listing all three appointments, with dates and times? It's easy to get confused when you're trying to remember everything.

speakerB.en: Good morning. Of course, I'll do my best to accommodate you. Let me see what's available. The clinic is open until eight on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and on Saturday mornings from nine until twelve.
For the dental check-up, there's a free slot on Tuesday at seven thirty in the morning, and another on Thursday evening at six. Which would you prefer, given your work schedule?
That's fine. I'll book you in for Tuesday. The eye test is carried out by a specialist who works on Thursdays and Saturdays, so we could combine it with the doctor's visit on Saturday at ten.
Yes, that's possible. Dr. Lewis will see you at ten, and the eye test will take place at eleven. It means you'll be here for about an hour and a half altogether, but you can leave in between.
The dental check-up takes about thirty minutes, the doctor's appointment about twenty, and the eye test around forty. Please arrive ten minutes early for the first one, to complete the paperwork.
Certainly. I'll email you the confirmation within the hour, and we'll also send a text message the day before each appointment, as a reminder.

scenarios.scenario: Rescheduling a meeting that clashes with another commitment
scenarios.context: Two professionals try to find a new time for a meeting because one of them has a conflict on Thursday morning.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'm calling about our meeting on Thursday at ten. I'm afraid something has come up that clashes with it, and it would suit me better if we could move it to later in the week.

The afternoon is difficult, since I won't be free until three, and I'd have to leave no later than four to catch my train. Would a short meeting between three and four work, or would that be too tight?
One o'clock is possible, as long as I can finish my other meeting by twelve-thirty, which I won't know until Wednesday evening. Would you mind if I confirmed no later than Wednesday at five?

Thank you, I appreciate your flexibility. On the other hand, if I can't make it at one, would you be able to do Tuesday of the following week? I wouldn't be available until the afternoon, but it's open.
Forty-five minutes should be enough, provided we send the documents beforehand. I'd say it's best to circulate them no later than Monday, so that everyone has time to read them before we meet.
Of course. I'll send you the draft on Thursday morning, and I'll confirm the one o'clock slot no later than Wednesday. Thank you for being so accommodating. I realize it's a nuisance, and I'm sorry.

speakerB.en: Thank you for letting me know. It would suit me better if we kept to Thursday, since I'm traveling on Friday and won't be back until the following Wednesday. Could you possibly manage the afternoon instead?
That would be tight, as I wouldn't be able to finish the presentation until Thursday morning anyway. It would suit me better if we met at one, as I'm not due at the airport until six.
That's fine. I wouldn't be able to book the meeting room until you've confirmed, so it would suit me better if you could let me know earlier, but I understand. I'll hold the slot until then.

Tuesday afternoon would work, although I wouldn't be able to give you a full hour until I've cleared my calendar. It would suit me better if we could keep it to forty-five minutes, no later than a quarter to five.

That makes sense. I won't be able to review them until I've seen the final figures, which should arrive by Friday. It would suit me better if you could send me a draft before it goes out to the others.
Not at all, these things happen. I'll make a note of both options and wait for your confirmation. It will suit me either way, as long as we've got the time to discuss the figures properly.

scenarios.scenario: Booking a dental appointment and joining a cancellation list
scenarios.context: A patient with a sensitive tooth phones a dental office and tries to get an appointment sooner than the first available date.

speakerA.en: Good afternoon, Greenfield Dental. How can I help you? Please bear in mind that we're fairly busy this month, so I may not be able to offer you your first choice of date.

I see. The earliest I can offer is the twenty-sixth, at half past nine, though please bear in mind that it's a fairly short slot. Would you prefer to wait for a longer appointment, which wouldn't be until December?

There is, and I'll put you on it. Bear in mind that cancellations are usually announced at short notice, sometimes the same morning, so you'd need to be able to arrive within an hour. Is that something you could manage?

Certainly, or I can send a text message, whichever you'd find more convenient. Please bear in mind that we can only hold the slot for fifteen minutes, so you'd need to reply quickly once we get in touch.

That's a sensible precaution. Bear in mind that if the pain becomes severe, or if you notice any swelling, you should call us immediately, whichever day it is, and we'll try to see you as an emergency.

Yes, please bring your insurance card and a form of identification. Bear in mind that if you arrive more than ten minutes late, we might have to reschedule, so do try to be on time, whichever route you take.

speakerB.en: Good afternoon. I'd like to book a check-up, and I'd also like to have a tooth looked at, since it's been sensitive for about a week. Is there anything available soon? Whichever day suits you is fine.
I'd rather not wait, since the tooth is bothering me. I was wondering whether there's a cancellation list, in case something opens up sooner. Whichever time you call, I'll do my best to come in.

I work nearby, so I should be able to manage it, as long as my manager doesn't object. On the other hand, I'm not sure whether I'll be able to take a call during meetings. Could you leave a voicemail instead?

A text would be better, then. I was wondering whether I should do anything before the appointment, such as stop eating certain things? I've been avoiding cold drinks, which seems to make the sensitivity worse.
Thank you, that's reassuring. I'll book the twenty-sixth at half past nine, then, and stay on the cancellation list. I was wondering whether I need to bring anything, such as my insurance details?
I'll make sure of it. Thanks for your help. I was wondering whether I could also have a reminder the day before, since I tend to forget appointments when I'm busy at work.

scenarios.scenario: Resolving a double-booked appointment at a clinic
scenarios.context: A patient arrives to find that her appointment has been double-booked, and the receptionist tries to find a fair solution.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I have an appointment with Dr. Patel at ten, but the doctor's assistant says another patient is already inside. To be honest, I took the morning off work specially, so I'd appreciate an explanation. What exactly has happened?

It's a follow-up on my blood pressure, so it's not an emergency. Still, at no point did anyone call to warn me, and I'd say that's the real problem. Since I've already arranged cover at work, I'd rather be seen today than come back next week.

Twenty minutes would be fine, provided the doctor has my latest test results. On the other hand, if she's rushed, I'd prefer a proper appointment. As far as I'm concerned, quality matters more than speed when it comes to health. Could you check which days she has free?

Friday works, although I'd still like to be seen today if possible. Rarely do I take a morning off, so it feels a pity to leave empty-handed. Is there any chance somebody might cancel before noon, since people often do?

That's kind, thank you. While I'm here, could I also ask for a printed copy of my previous results? At no point have I received them by email, and I'd like to read them before I see the doctor, in case I have questions.

Yes, please, otherwise the visit would be pointless. Thank you for dealing with this so calmly. Should I be called in, I'll take the short consultation, provided the results are there. If not, I'll gladly book Friday.

speakerB.en: I'm very sorry, Ms. Clarke. It seems your slot was booked twice, once by phone and once online. Rarely do we make this mistake, but I can see it has happened today. May I ask how urgent your problem is, and whether you could wait?

That's completely fair. Should a space open up, I'll put you first on the list. Otherwise, the doctor finishes at noon, and I could squeeze you in during her lunch break, as long as you don't mind a shorter consultation. Would twenty minutes be enough?

Certainly. She has a full day on Thursday, but at no time on Friday afternoon is she booked, so you'd have a longer slot. Should you choose Friday, I'll send a reminder text the day before. Would that suit your schedule?

There is, and I'll keep an eye on the screen. Should anyone cancel, I'll call you straight away, so please keep your phone nearby. In the meantime, may I offer you a coffee while you wait? It's the least we can do.

Of course. I'll print them now. Seldom do patients ask for them, which is a shame, since they're entitled to see everything. Let me check that the file is complete. Ah, it seems the latest test isn't uploaded yet. Shall I ask the lab to send it?

That sounds sensible. I'll chase the lab right now, and I'll call you within the hour either way. Again, our apologies for the confusion. At no point should a patient be left feeling unimportant, and I'll make sure it's addressed with the team.

scenarios.scenario: Defending a realistic project timeline to a senior stakeholder
scenarios.context: A project manager explains to a senior stakeholder why a product launch cannot safely be brought forward by a month.

speakerA.en: I'll be direct. The board would like the product launch brought forward by a month, and I'd like to know whether that's realistic. To be honest, the competition is moving so fast that waiting until March could cost us the market. What's your view?

Please do. I understand the risks, but the board is anxious, and as far as I'm concerned, a delay is also a risk. What specifically would need to be cut, and how much time would you really save by cutting it?
Neither, honestly. On the other hand, could you add people to the team? Since we have budget left, I'd happily approve two more developers if that brought the date forward. Would that work?

I'd like that, because I'll need evidence for the board. Meanwhile, what can you promise? Would a phased release, with the main features first, be possible? I'd say that might satisfy everyone, although it must not damage the brand.

They can, as long as I give them two weeks' notice. I'd also want weekly progress reports, since the board will ask. To be honest, I'd rather present a safe plan than an exciting one that fails. What would a report need to include?

Please do. Thank you for standing your ground, because I'd rather hear honest numbers than comfortable promises. I'll tell the board we're aiming for a phased launch, provided your first report looks healthy. Does that seem fair?

speakerB.en: Thank you for being straightforward. I'd say a month is too ambitious, since we're only two thirds through testing. Were we to launch early, we'd risk such serious bugs that customers would lose confidence. May I explain where the biggest risks lie?

Only by dropping the payment feature could we gain two weeks, and that's the part customers value most. Were we to shorten testing instead, we'd save more, but the product could fail at launch. Which option do you think the board would accept?

Unfortunately, it's not so simple, as new developers need weeks to understand the code. Only after they'd learned the system could they help, and by then the deadline would have passed. It's such a common mistake that it has its own name in our industry. Would you like me to show you the data?

That's an interesting compromise. Were we to release the core features in February, we could add payments in March, provided testing goes well. The risk would be so small that I'd feel comfortable signing off. Could the marketing team adjust their campaign accordingly?

Only with clear indicators can we reassure them, so I'd propose three: bugs fixed, tests completed and risks remaining. The report would be so brief that it takes five minutes to read. Shall I draft the first one by Friday?

It does, and I appreciate your trust. Only if something unexpected happens would I ask to revise it, and I'd tell you at once. Were we to hit February with the core features, it would be a real achievement for the team.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing views on different topics
scenarios.context: Two people discuss a movie, food, or event and give their opinion.

speakerA.en: Do you like this movie?
I think the actors are very good.
Do you like the music?
I agree. Let's go for pizza after the movie.
What do you think about this movie?
speakerA.fa: نظرت درباره این فیلم چیه؟

speakerA.en: I really liked the food at that restaurant.
speakerA.fa: من واقعاً غذاهای اون رستوران رو دوست داشتم.

speakerA.en: In my opinion, traveling is the best way to learn new cultures.
speakerA.fa: به نظر من، سفر بهترین راه برای یادگیری فرهنگ‌های جدید است.

speakerA.en: I feel that we should focus more on our environment.
speakerA.fa: احساس می‌کنم باید بیشتر روی محیط‌زیست تمرکز کنیم.

speakerA.en: To be honest, I'm not a big fan of horror movies. They scare me too much.
speakerA.fa: راستش، من زیاد طرفدار فیلم‌های ترسناک نیستم. بیش از حد می‌ترسوننم.

speakerA.en: From my perspective, this decision will benefit the whole team.
speakerA.fa: از دیدگاه من، این تصمیم به نفع کل تیم خواهد بود.

speakerA.en: I thought the music was great.
Would you watch it again?

speakerB.en: Yes, I like it a lot.
Me too. They are funny.
No, I don't. It's too loud.
Good idea. I love pizza!
It was okay. I liked the ending.
speakerB.fa: بد نبود. از پایانش خوشم اومد.

speakerB.en: Me too! The pasta was delicious.
speakerB.fa: منم همینطور! پاستاش عالی بود.

speakerB.en: I agree. You get to see how other people really live.
speakerB.fa: موافقم. می‌بینی که مردم دیگه واقعاً چطور زندگی می‌کنن.

speakerB.en: That's true, but we also need to balance it with economic growth.
speakerB.fa: درسته، اما باید با رشد اقتصادی هم تعادلش کنیم.

speakerB.en: I know what you mean. I prefer comedies; they lift my mood.
speakerB.fa: می‌دونم منظورت چیه. من کمدی رو ترجیح می‌دم؛ روحیه‌م رو عالی می‌کنن.

speakerB.en: I see your point, but we should consider the risks involved as well.
speakerB.fa: متوجه منظورت می‌شم، اما باید ریسک‌های مربوطه رو هم در نظر بگیریم.

speakerB.en: I agree. The songs fit the story well.
Maybe. I'd like to see it with my brother.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about food
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about what they like to eat.

speakerA.en: Do you like pizza?
I don't like fish.
What is your favorite food?
This soup is very good.
What kind of food do you like?
Do you like spicy food?
Which food do you really not like?
Can you cook?

speakerB.en: Yes, I love pizza.
Really? I like fish.
My favorite food is rice.
I agree. It's delicious.
I like Italian food, especially pizza.
A little, but not too hot.
I don't like mushrooms. They taste strange.
A little. I make pasta and omelets.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about feelings
scenarios.context: A person asks a friend how they feel.

speakerA.en: How do you feel today?
Why are you sad?
Are you tired?
I'm sorry. Can I help?
You look happy today. What's going on?
That's wonderful! How do you feel?
Were you nervous before the exam?
Let's celebrate with ice cream.

speakerB.en: I feel sad.
I miss my family.
Yes, I am very tired.
Thank you. You are kind.
I got a good grade on my exam.
I feel proud, but also very tired.
Yes, I was very nervous yesterday.
Great idea. I'd love that.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about hobbies
scenarios.context: Two classmates share what they like to do.

speakerA.en: Do you like sports?
I love reading books.
Do you like music?
Dancing is fun.
What do you like to do after school?
I enjoy playing basketball. Do you like sports?
Which hobby is more fun for you?
Can I see your pictures sometime?

speakerB.en: Yes, I like football.
Me too. Books are great.
Yes, I do. I like pop music.
I think so too.
I like drawing and listening to music.
Not really. I prefer quiet activities.
Drawing. I can do it for hours.
Sure. I'll bring my notebook tomorrow.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about a place
scenarios.context: Two people talk about their city.

speakerA.en: Do you like this city?
I think it is too big.
Is the park nice?
I like the people here.
What do you think about your city?
Is it a good place for young people?
What is the problem with your city?
Would you like to live somewhere else?

speakerB.en: Yes, it is beautiful.
Yes, but it is very nice.
Yes, I love the park.
They are very friendly.
I like it. It's clean and friendly.
Yes, there are many cafés and parks.
The traffic is terrible in the morning.
Maybe, but I would miss my friends.

scenarios.scenario: Agreeing and disagreeing
scenarios.context: Two friends agree or disagree about simple things.

speakerA.en: This coffee is great.
Summer is the best season.
Math is easy.
English is fun!
I think summer is the best season.
Why? Summer is warm and sunny.
Cats are better than dogs, in my opinion.
We have different opinions, but that's fine.

speakerB.en: Yes, I agree.
No, I like winter.
I don't think so. It's hard.
Yes, I think so too.
I don't agree. I prefer autumn.
It's too hot for me. I like cool weather.
I see your point, but I love dogs.
Yes, it's more interesting that way.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about a school day
scenarios.context: A student talks about school.

speakerA.en: Do you like your school?
I like my teacher.
The class is boring today.
I'm happy it's Friday!
How was school today?
What was your favorite class?
Did you have any homework?
Do you want help with your homework?

speakerB.en: Yes, I like it.
Me too. She is very nice.
Really? I think it's interesting.
Me too. I love the weekend.
It was a long day, but I enjoyed it.
Art. We painted a picture of the sea.
Yes, a lot of math problems.
Yes, please. Math isn't easy for me.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing a movie after watching it
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about a movie they just saw.

speakerA.en: So what did you think of the movie? I wasn't sure about the ending.
I see what you mean, but I thought the acting was fantastic.
Maybe we expected too much because of the great reviews.
You may be right. Still, I wouldn't say it was a waste of time.

speakerB.en: Honestly, I found it a little disappointing. The story started well, but then it lost its way.
That's true. The main actor was convincing, but the plot didn't make much sense to me.
Probably. I think I would have enjoyed it more if it had been shorter.
No, I'm glad we went. Next time, let's choose something more light-hearted.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing feelings about a big change
scenarios.context: A man talks to a friend about moving to another city.

speakerA.en: I've decided to accept the job in Berlin. I'm excited, but also a little scared.
Leaving my family and friends behind. I'm not sure I'll make new friends so easily.
Thanks. I just hope I'm not making a mistake.
You're right. I keep telling myself that, but it helps to hear it from someone else.

speakerB.en: That's completely understandable. It's a big step. What worries you the most?
I think you will. You're open and friendly, and people like you.
Every big decision involves some risk, but you'll regret it more if you don't try.
I'm proud of you. And you know you can always call me when you feel lonely.

scenarios.scenario: Disagreeing politely at a meeting
scenarios.context: Two coworkers disagree about a business idea.

speakerA.en: I understand your point, but I'm not convinced that this is the best approach.
In the short term, perhaps. But I'm worried about the quality of the final product.
I think we should test the idea on a small scale before making a final decision.
Exactly. We could review the results after a month and then decide.

speakerB.en: Why not? I believe it would save us a lot of time and money.
That's a fair concern. What would you suggest instead?
That's reasonable. It would take longer, but it would reduce the risk.
All right, I'm willing to try that. Let's present it to the team together.

scenarios.scenario: Debating a social issue
scenarios.context: Two friends exchange views on a controversial topic.

speakerA.en: I read that the city plans to ban cars from the center altogether. What's your take?
I see the benefits, but I worry about those who depend on their vehicles, such as the elderly or people with disabilities.
Even so, local shops might suffer if customers can't park nearby. I've seen it happen in other towns.
Perhaps, but I'd want to see proper figures before drawing conclusions.

speakerB.en: On balance, I'm in favor. The air quality would improve, and the streets would be much safer.
That's a legitimate concern, and I assume there would have to be exemptions for those groups.
The evidence is mixed. In some places, footfall actually increased once the streets became pedestrian-friendly.
Fair enough. It's a complicated question, and I doubt it has a perfect answer.

scenarios.scenario: Expressing disappointment
scenarios.context: A person tells a friend how let down she felt after a promotion went to someone else.

speakerA.en: I didn't get the promotion. They gave it to someone who has been at the company for half as long as I have.
It does, and what upsets me most is that no one had the courtesy to explain the decision.
I have, but I'm afraid I'd say something I'd regret. Right now, I'm too angry to be diplomatic.
You're probably right. I just wish I didn't feel so undervalued.

speakerB.en: I'm so sorry. After everything you've put into that job, it must feel like a slap in the face.
Have you thought about asking for a meeting with your manager to find out what went wrong?
Then wait a few days until you've cooled down. You'll make your point more effectively.
Your worth isn't determined by one decision. If this company doesn't see it, another one will.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing excitement and gratitude
scenarios.context: A woman tells a friend she has been accepted onto a program she had dreamed of.

speakerA.en: You'll never guess what has happened. I've been accepted into the graduate program in Edinburgh!
I still can't quite believe it. I was convinced they'd turn me down after the interview.
I owe much of it to you. If you hadn't encouraged me to apply, I would have talked myself out of it.
Whatever the case, I'm grateful. Let me take you out for dinner to celebrate.

speakerB.en: That's absolutely wonderful! I'm thrilled for you. You've worked so hard for this.
You were always more capable than you imagined. I never doubted you for a moment.
I merely nudged you. The real credit goes to your determination.
I accept, on the condition that you tell me every detail of what the program involves.

scenarios.scenario: Debating artificial intelligence in everyday life
scenarios.context: Two colleagues disagree about how much we should rely on AI tools at work.

speakerA.en: I'll admit I'm uneasy about how quickly everyone has started relying on AI tools. People seem to have stopped questioning what they produce.
A calculator doesn't pretend to understand context, though. These systems can sound completely authoritative while being quite wrong.
In principle, yes. My fear is that juniors will skip the drudgery that taught us the fundamentals in the first place.
I'd support that. I simply don't want convenience to erode the skills it was meant to supplement.

speakerB.en: I understand the concern, but I'd argue the tools are simply the latest in a long line of aids. Nobody laments the calculator anymore.
That's a fair distinction, and it's why verification matters. Used with judgment, they free us from drudgery and leave more time for real thinking.
That's a legitimate worry, and one that employers should take seriously. Perhaps training needs to deliberately preserve some of that groundwork.
On that, we're in complete agreement. The tool should sharpen our judgment, not replace it.

scenarios.scenario: Expressing mixed feelings about a success
scenarios.context: A woman tells a friend that her promotion has left her feeling conflicted.

speakerA.en: I should be thrilled about the promotion, and yet I keep feeling oddly flat. Does that make any sense?
Partly, but mostly it's that my closest colleague applied for the same role. We've barely spoken since the announcement.
Exactly. I keep wondering whether I deserved it or simply benefited from circumstances.
Perhaps I should reach out to her honestly instead of letting the silence harden.

speakerB.en: More than you'd think. Is it the new responsibility that's weighing on you, or something else?
That's painful. Success can feel strangely hollow when it comes at a friend's expense, even though you've done nothing wrong.
You earned it, and I think you know that. But it's perfectly natural to grieve what the competition cost you.
I think that would mean a great deal. Whatever she says, at least you'll know you tried.

scenarios.scenario: Defending an unpopular viewpoint respectfully
scenarios.context: A guest at a dinner party defends a controversial opinion while remaining courteous.

speakerA.en: I realize this is an unpopular position, but I genuinely believe cars should be banned from the city center altogether.
Those are the objections I'd expect, and they deserve a serious answer. Cities that have tried it report higher foot traffic and better air quality, provided public transport is improved in tandem.
True, and I wouldn't advocate it everywhere. But I find the status quo hard to defend when it prioritizes parked cars over people.
Skepticism is healthy. I'd rather be challenged by someone thoughtful than agreed with by someone indifferent.

speakerB.en: That's bold. Surely it would cripple businesses and leave elderly and disabled residents stranded?
"In tandem" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Not every city has the resources, or the political will, to make that happen.
I'll concede that the framing is persuasive, even if I remain skeptical about the practicalities.
Well, you'll certainly get no indifference from me. Pass the wine, and let's continue this over dessert.

scenarios.scenario: Disagreeing with a respected colleague in a meeting
scenarios.context: A professional dissents politely without undermining the other person's authority.

speakerA.en: I have the utmost respect for your experience, but I find myself unable to endorse this approach. May I explain why?
My concern is that it relies on assumptions that haven't been tested. If they prove wrong, the cost of correcting course will be considerable.
I agree that delay has its price. Perhaps a small pilot would allow us to test the assumptions without committing fully.
I'm grateful for your open-mindedness. I'd have hated for this to become a contest rather than a joint inquiry.

speakerB.en: By all means. I'd rather hear a reasoned objection than discover it after the fact.
That's a fair point, though I'd argue that waiting for certainty is itself a form of risk. Time isn't on our side.
That's a constructive compromise. It would address your concern while preserving momentum.
As would I. The best decisions usually emerge from friction, provided it's conducted with good grace.

scenarios.scenario: Conveying disappointment without causing resentment
scenarios.context: A friend explains how a broken commitment made them feel, avoiding accusation.

speakerA.en: There's something I'd like to raise, and I hope you'll take it in the spirit in which it's offered. I was disappointed that you weren't there on Saturday.
I don't want you to feel guilty, only to understand that it mattered. I'd been counting on your presence, and it left me feeling rather exposed.
I appreciate that. I suppose what I'm really asking is that you let me know when things come up, rather than leaving me to wonder.
Thank you. I feel considerably better for having said it, and I hope it hasn't made things awkward.

speakerB.en: I know, and I'm sorry. I should have called, and I've been feeling guilty about it ever since.
That's entirely fair. I let other pressures crowd out something that deserved my attention, and I'd like to make amends.
I will. Honesty would have cost me far less than silence, and I regret that I didn't see it at the time.
Quite the opposite. It's a relief to be told plainly, and I value the trust that it implies.

scenarios.scenario: Expressing ambivalence about a major life decision
scenarios.context: Two close friends talk through mixed feelings about a significant change.

speakerA.en: I've been offered the position in Lisbon, and I should be thrilled. Instead, I find myself oddly paralyzed.
What troubles me is that I can't tell whether I want the job or simply the idea of being someone who takes it.
I have, and it's surprisingly appealing. I can picture the commute, the tiny café, the unfamiliar language slowly becoming familiar.
That's uncomfortably accurate. I suppose I've been mistaking fear for doubt.

speakerB.en: That's understandable. Ambition and apprehension often arrive together, and neither is easily dismissed.
A perceptive distinction. Have you tried imagining an ordinary Tuesday there, rather than the romantic version?
Then perhaps your hesitation isn't about the place at all. It might be the fear of leaving behind a life you've worked hard to build.
It's a common confusion. The question is whether you'd rather live with the uncertainty of going or the regret of staying.

scenarios.scenario: Giving an opinion on a new restaurant
scenarios.context: Two friends share what they thought of a restaurant they just visited.

speakerA.en: So, what did you think of the place? Honestly, I was a little disappointed.
The food was fine, but the service was very slow, and it was far too noisy.
I suppose so. Still, I wouldn't go back unless they improved the atmosphere.
Maybe you're right. I'm happy to give it another chance if you want to.

speakerB.en: Really? I actually enjoyed it. The pasta was excellent, and the prices were reasonable.
That's true, we did wait a long time. But I think they were short of staff that night.
Perhaps, but the dessert alone was worth the visit. I'd recommend it for a special occasion.
Let's try it on a weekday, when it's quieter. I'm sure it will feel different.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about feeling stressed at work
scenarios.context: A coworker tells a friend how stressed she has felt lately.

speakerA.en: Do you have a minute? I've been feeling really stressed about work lately.
I have too many projects, and my manager expects everything to be finished by Friday.
I'm afraid I'll make mistakes if I rush. Do you think I should tell her?
You're right. Thanks for listening. I already feel a bit lighter.

speakerB.en: Of course. You look tired. What's been going on?
That sounds like a lot of pressure. Have you tried explaining how busy you are?
I think so. Most managers prefer an honest conversation to a late or careless report.
Anytime. And remember to take a proper break. A short walk at lunch really helps.

scenarios.scenario: Debating whether to work from home
scenarios.context: Two colleagues exchange views on remote work.

speakerA.en: What do you think about working from home? Our company is considering letting us do it two days a week.
Personally, I'd love it. I spend almost two hours commuting every day, and I could use that time more productively.
That's a fair point, but I find that I can concentrate better at home, away from the noise and the constant interruptions.
I agree that it's important to see colleagues, though. Maybe a mixture of both would be the best solution for most people.
Exactly. As long as the company is flexible, I think everyone could find a rhythm that works for them.
I hope so. I'll mention it at the next team meeting and see what other people think.

speakerB.en: I'm not so sure. I think it's good to have a change of scenery, but I miss the contact with other people when I work alone.
That's true, and the commute is a waste of time for everybody. But I find it difficult to switch off when my office is in my living room.
Maybe, but I worry that we'd lose the team spirit. Some of my best ideas have come from casual conversations at lunch.
That sounds reasonable. If everyone could choose, some people would be at the office every day, and others would hardly come at all.
I'd also like to know how the company plans to measure our results, because some managers don't trust employees who aren't in the office.
That's a good idea. It's better to discuss it openly, rather than assuming that everybody agrees.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing feelings about moving to a new city
scenarios.context: A person tells a friend about mixed feelings regarding a move.

speakerA.en: I have some news. I've been offered a job in another city, and I have to give an answer by Friday.
It's a great opportunity, and the salary is much higher than I'm earning now. But it means leaving everything behind.
That's what worries me most. I've lived here all my life, and my family and friends are nearby. I'd miss them terribly.
I know, but I'm not sure whether I'm brave enough. What if I move and then I hate it?
I hadn't thought of it that way. I could always come back if it doesn't work out, and I'd have gained experience anyway.
Thank you for listening. I feel much clearer now, and I think I know what I'm going to do.

speakerB.en: Wow, that's big news! Congratulations. How do you feel about it? You don't look as happy as I expected.
I can understand that. It's exciting, but also frightening. Change is never easy, even when it's something we want.
You'd miss them, of course, but you could visit often, and you can talk to them every day online. Distance doesn't mean the end of a friendship.
Nobody can be sure. But if you never take a risk, you'll always wonder what might have happened if you'd said yes.
Exactly. In my opinion, you'll regret not trying more than you'll regret trying and failing.
Whatever you decide, I'll support you. And if you move, I'll be your first visitor, I promise.

scenarios.scenario: Arguing for and against social media regulation
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss whether governments should regulate social media more strictly.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking about whether governments should do more to regulate social media. The amount of misinformation spreading online is genuinely worrying.
I'd argue that platforms have far too much influence over what people see and believe, and they've shown very little willingness to regulate themselves.

That's a valid concern, and I wouldn't want governments to decide what people are allowed to say. But there's a difference between censorship and requiring platforms to be transparent about their algorithms.
I also think that it's unrealistic to assume that individuals can always recognize false information, especially when it's designed to be emotionally persuasive.
Perhaps the best approach would be to combine regulation with education, so that people learn how to evaluate sources critically, regardless of what the laws say.
Well said. It's reassuring that we can disagree on some points and still reach a reasonable conclusion.

speakerB.en: I share your concern, but I'm cautious about the solutions. Once governments start deciding what counts as false, there's a serious risk that the power will be misused.
That's true, but private companies deciding on their own isn't ideal either. They're motivated by profit, which isn't necessarily in the interest of the public.
I agree with that distinction. Requiring openness about how content is selected would give researchers and journalists a chance to identify problems, without limiting free expression.
That's a good point, and it's why education is so important. Even a well-regulated system can't protect people who have never learned to question what they read.
I think that's the sensible middle ground. Neither pure freedom nor strict control works, and the details of how the rules are applied are what really matter.
Exactly. Perhaps the most important thing is that we continue to discuss it openly, instead of leaving the decision to the people who profit.

scenarios.scenario: Expressing disappointment and disagreement at work
scenarios.context: An employee explains her disappointment to a manager and proposes an alternative.

speakerA.en: Thank you for meeting with me. I'd like to be honest about how I feel regarding yesterday's decision, since I think it's important that you understand my perspective.
I was surprised and rather disappointed that the project was handed to another team, especially after I'd spent three months developing the initial proposal.
I appreciate the reasoning, but I'd argue that changing leadership midway makes it likely that we'll lose time, since someone new will have to learn everything from scratch.
I'm not saying that I should have complete control. All I'm asking is that I be involved in the transition, and that my contribution be recognized.
That would be acceptable. I'd also like to discuss what other projects I could be considered for, since I want to continue to develop within the company.
Thank you for listening. I feel better knowing that my opinion has been heard, even if the decision itself hasn't changed.

speakerB.en: Thank you for being direct. I'd much rather hear your concerns now than have them develop into resentment. Please go ahead and tell me what's on your mind.
I understand that. Your work was excellent, and I should have discussed the change with you before announcing it. That was a mistake on my part, and I apologize.
That's a fair criticism. The decision was based on resource constraints, rather than on your performance, and I'm aware that it isn't the most efficient solution.
I think that's entirely reasonable. I'll ask the new project leader to work with you during the first month, so that your knowledge is passed on properly.
There's a new initiative starting in January, which will need someone with your skills. I'd like to recommend you for the position, if you're interested.
I'm glad you raised it. Honest feedback is the only way for me to improve as a manager, and I value your trust.

scenarios.scenario: Voicing an opinion at a residents' meeting
scenarios.context: A resident expresses a view on a proposed change and responds to counterarguments.

speakerA.en: Thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak. I'd like to share my views on the proposal to convert the courtyard into a parking area, because I have serious reservations about it.

I understand that parking is a problem, and I sympathize with those who struggle to find a space. However, the courtyard is the only green area that the children have, and losing it would affect the quality of life for everybody.
I'm not saying that nothing should be done. I'm merely suggesting that we should look at alternatives first, such as renting spaces in the nearby car park, or encouraging car sharing among residents.
That's a fair point, and I accept that renting spaces would cost money. But if we compare it with the cost of constructing a new parking area, I think it would actually be cheaper in the long run.
I'd propose that we hold a vote only after an independent study has compared the options. If the results show that the courtyard is the only solution, I'd accept it, though not gladly.
Thank you. I appreciate that everyone here wants what's best for the building, and I hope we can reach a decision that respects all the different interests.

speakerB.en: Thank you, and I'd like to respond briefly. I understand your concern about the children, but we must also consider the elderly residents, for whom walking from a distant car park isn't realistic.
That's true, but the current situation can't continue. Cars are parked on the pavements, and last month an ambulance had difficulty getting through. We have a safety issue that can't be ignored.
Renting spaces in the next street is a good idea in theory, but those places have long waiting lists, and the cost would be passed on to the residents, which not everyone can afford.
I doubt that figures would support that conclusion, but I'm willing to look at them. What I'd like to avoid is a discussion that goes on for months without leading to any decision.
I think that's a reasonable proposal. Perhaps we could set a deadline of six weeks for the study, and then vote at the next meeting. Does everyone agree with that timeline?
Thank you for your contribution. It's much more helpful to hear different opinions expressed respectfully than to have a discussion in which only the loudest voice is heard.

scenarios.scenario: Disagreeing tactfully with a plan at work
scenarios.context: An employee voices concerns about a proposed strategy without being confrontational.

speakerA.en: Thank you for explaining the plan. I can see the thinking behind it, and I'd like to share a few reservations, if I may, because I believe it's important that we examine all the angles.

My main concern is the timeline. Launching the product in just six weeks seems to me very ambitious, considering that we haven't yet completed the final testing, and any problems would reflect badly on us.
I'm not suggesting that we abandon the idea. On the contrary, I think it's a strong concept. I simply feel that a slightly later launch, perhaps in ten weeks, would reduce the risks substantially.
I take your point about the competitor. But if we release something that doesn't work properly, we'd lose credibility, whereas a short delay might be forgiven, and the final result could be better.
Could we perhaps agree on a compromise? We could release a limited version to a small group of customers first, and gather feedback, before the full launch takes place.
I'm glad that you're open to that. Thank you for listening, and I'll prepare a short proposal for how we might implement it.

speakerB.en: Thank you for being so frank. It's useful to hear your perspective, because sometimes I get so absorbed in the schedule that I overlook the practical difficulties. What worries you most?
I understand. The timing was driven by the fact that our main competitor is releasing a similar product next month, and I'm afraid that we'd lose market share if we waited too long.
That's a valid concern. A delay of four weeks isn't impossible, but it would have to be justified to the board, and they'd want to see concrete evidence that the extra time would improve the outcome.
You make a good argument. Releasing something imperfect can do more harm than being late. But I'm not sure that the customers would be patient, particularly since we've been promoting the launch.
That's an interesting idea. A pilot release would allow us to meet the competitor's date in a limited way, while still giving us time to correct the faults before the main release.
Please do. I'd like to see the details, including the cost implications, before presenting it to the board. And thank you for raising your concerns so constructively.

scenarios.scenario: Reacting to a friend's plan to leave a secure job
scenarios.context: A friend announces that she is leaving a well-paid job to start a small business, and the other person responds with honest but supportive reservations.

speakerA.en: I've finally made up my mind: I'm handing in my notice at the bank next month to start a small furniture business. I wish I'd done it years ago, although I know it sounds reckless to a lot of people.
It's not so much the money as the feeling that I'm wasting my best years behind a desk. If only I'd had the nerve earlier, I'd have a workshop by now, and I wouldn't be dreading every Monday morning.

I've saved enough to cover about eighteen months, as long as I keep my expenses low. It's not so much a gamble as a calculated risk, since I've already had three orders from people who saw my work online.

It might, although I'm not sure I could work for someone else again. It's not so much that I dislike being managed as that I want my own name on what I make. If only the rent on a workshop weren't so high.

I hadn't thought of that, but it makes sense. I wish I'd spoken to you sooner, since you always see the practical side. Sharing would cut the costs in half, and it's not so much a compromise as a smart way to start.

That's sound advice, and I'll follow it. If only everyone were as direct as you are, I'd have fewer sleepless nights. Do you think I should tell my manager now, or wait until the first orders are confirmed?

speakerB.en: To be honest, I'm surprised, but I can see how much this means to you. Much as I'd like to cheer you on without reservations, I'd say it's worth asking what's driving the decision. What exactly made you decide now?

I understand that, and I do admire your honesty. Much as I'd like to say it's an easy choice, you'd be giving up a steady salary, and the business could take a long time to pay for itself. How long can you manage?

Three orders is encouraging, I'll give you that. On the other hand, I wish you'd told me earlier, because I could have introduced you to my cousin, who runs a workshop and might have taken you on part-time first. Would that interest you?

Fair enough, and I'd say that's a perfectly good reason. Much as I'd like to reassure you, though, the rent worries me too. Have you looked at sharing a space with other makers, in case you can't afford your own at first?

Then I'd say that's your best option, as long as you agree the terms in writing from the beginning. Much as I'd like to stay neutral, I think you should also keep some savings aside in case a big order falls through.

To be honest, I'd wait until the contracts are signed, since you don't want to burn bridges too early. It's not so much about secrecy as about timing. Whatever you decide, I'm on your side, and I'll help with the website.

scenarios.scenario: Voicing disappointment after a long-awaited concert
scenarios.context: Two friends compare their reactions after a highly anticipated concert that did not live up to their expectations.

speakerA.en: Well, that was a letdown, wasn't it? Had I known the sound would be so muddy, I'd have saved my money. To be honest, I spent the whole evening wishing I'd stayed at home with a good book.

It's hard to say, since both were disappointing. Had I known they would skip half their best-known songs, I wouldn't have paid so much for the tickets. As far as I'm concerned, a band owes its fans a proper set.

Not really, because tiredness is no excuse when people have waited months. On the other hand, I admit the singer looked exhausted. Had I known that, I might have been more patient, but nobody warned us.
I did, and I almost joined them. Had I known the venue was so badly designed, I'd have chosen a different date. Still, the guitarist's solo in the middle was brilliant, so it wasn't a complete waste.
As far as I'm concerned, it's worth a try, although I doubt they'll agree. Had I known that refunds were even possible, I'd have asked at the door. What reason should we give if they ask?
Agreed. Let's write it tomorrow, once we've both calmed down. To be honest, I'd still go and see them again, but only in a smaller place. Had I known that, I'd have booked the club show instead.

speakerB.en: I'd say it wasn't quite that bad, although I agree the first half dragged. If it weren't for the encores, I'd have left early. What bothered you most, the sound or the song choices?

That's a fair point, although they've been touring for almost a year, so I suppose they're tired. If it weren't for the long schedule, they might have played with more energy. Doesn't that make it a bit more forgivable?

To be honest, I'd say the organizers were more to blame than the band. If it weren't for the poor acoustics in that hall, the evening would have been far better. Did you notice how many people left early?
I'd say that solo made the whole evening worthwhile. If it weren't for that, I'd be a lot more critical. Do you think we should write to the organizers and ask for a partial refund?

I'd say we simply describe the poor sound and the missing songs, since those are facts rather than opinions. If it weren't for the sound, I wouldn't bother at all, but that really did spoil the evening.
Same here, and I'd say that's the real lesson. If it weren't for how much I like their older albums, I wouldn't have gone at all. Shall we check the dates for the smaller venues before we write?
