scenarios.scenario: Telling a close friend that you feel taken for granted
scenarios.context: A woman tells a close friend that she feels she is always the one who makes the effort in their friendship.

speakerA.en: Can we talk for a minute? There's something that's been bothering me for a while, and I'd rather say it than let it grow. To be honest, I've been feeling a bit taken for granted lately. Is this a good moment?
It's not that I mind helping you. It's just that I'm always the one who calls first and makes the plans. What I'd like is a bit more balance. I wish you'd suggest something once in a while.

Well, you forgot my birthday dinner, and what hurt most was that you didn't even text. If only you'd said something, I'd have understood. Much as I'd like to think it's about work, I'm not sure it is.

It's not about a gift. What matters is that you make a little effort, since friendships need it from both sides. I'd say a simple call every week would mean a lot. On the other hand, I don't want it to feel forced.

It would, and thank you for not getting defensive. Much as I dreaded this talk, I feel lighter already. I should say, though, that it's not that I want to keep score. I just want us to look after each other.
I'd love that. And in case I forget to say it, I'm grateful you listened. To be honest, I was afraid you'd be angry. It's not that I doubted you, but I did doubt myself for speaking up.

speakerB.en: Of course, I'm glad you told me. I had no idea. What's been on your mind? And please be honest, because I'd hate to think I'd upset you without realizing it.

I see, and you're right, I know. It's not that I don't care. It's that work has been so overwhelming that I've barely had energy for anything. Still, as far as I'm concerned, that's no excuse. Did I miss something important recently?
That was a terrible oversight, and I'm genuinely sorry. It wasn't that I forgot you, but that I lost track of the date completely. I wish I could undo it. What could I do to make it up to you?

It won't, I promise. What I'll do is put a reminder in my calendar so that I call you every Sunday. If only I'd done that earlier, we wouldn't be having this conversation. Would that feel like enough to you?
I know, and I'd want the same. What I value most about you is that you tell me the truth, even when it's uncomfortable. I wish more people did that. Shall we meet for dinner this weekend, my treat?
You were right to speak up, and I'm glad you did. What would have been worse is silence, since it would have slowly damaged us. See you on Saturday at seven, and I'll book the table myself.

scenarios.scenario: Debating whether social media does more harm than good
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss an article claiming that social media does more harm than good and weigh up their own experience.

speakerA.en: I read an article this morning claiming that social media does far more harm than good. To be honest, I'd say it's partly true, since people are said to spend almost three hours a day scrolling. What's your view?

To some extent, yes. However, the more time people spend online, the less they seem to talk face to face. Teenagers in particular are said to feel lonelier than ever, no matter how many followers they have. Isn't that worrying?

Honestly, yes. The more I look at other people's holidays, the worse I feel about my own life. It's said that most posts show only the best moments, and I know that, but it still affects me. Do you ever feel that way?

That's a fair point. I could unfollow accounts that make me feel bad. Still, the more I think about it, the more I believe companies design these apps to be addictive. They're widely known to use tricks that keep us scrolling. Should they be regulated?

Maybe one hour a day, no matter how tempting. It's reported that some countries are testing exactly that for teenagers. To be honest, I'm not sure I could manage it myself, although I'd like to. Would you try it with me?

Let's start with the one that wastes the most time. I'm glad we talked, since it's more balanced than the article. As far as I'm concerned, the answer is neither all good nor all bad. It's about how we choose to use it.

speakerB.en: I'd say that's a bit exaggerated. Social media is widely believed to cause anxiety, but far from being useless, it also helps people stay in touch. As far as I'm concerned, the harm depends on how you use it. Don't you think so?

It is worrying, but the research isn't clear. Far from proving a direct link, many studies suggest that other factors, like sleep and family life, matter more. On the other hand, I agree that comparison with others can hurt. Do you feel that yourself?

Sometimes, although I try to remind myself that no matter how perfect something looks, it's usually edited. Far from making me envious, my feed usually gives me ideas for trips. Perhaps it's about choosing whom you follow, in case that helps?

I'd say so, at least when it comes to children. As long as the rules are clear, I don't see why not. On the other hand, adults should take responsibility, since nobody forces us to open the app. What limit would you set?

Why not? The more people join in, the easier it becomes. Let's try one week and compare our moods. Far from being a punishment, it might even be a relief. Should we also delete one app from our phones, just for the experiment?
Well said. And whatever happens during our week, we'll have learned something about our habits. I'll text you tomorrow evening to see how it's going, as long as I manage to stay off my phone!

scenarios.scenario: Requesting assistance or repetition
scenarios.context: In daily life, asking someone for help or to repeat something.

speakerA.en: Could you please help me with this bag? It's too heavy.
Thank you. Sorry, what time is the bus?
Sorry, can you say that again?
Please speak slowly.
I'm sorry, I didn't understand. Could you repeat that?
speakerA.fa: ببخشید، متوجه نشدم. میشه دوباره بگید؟

speakerA.en: Could you speak a little more slowly, please?
speakerA.fa: میشه لطفاً کمی آهسته‌تر صحبت کنید؟

speakerA.en: Would you mind helping me with this math problem?
speakerA.fa: میشه کمکم کنید این مسئله ریاضی رو حل کنم؟

speakerA.en: I'm looking for the post office. Could you show me on the map?
speakerA.fa: دنبال اداره پست می‌گردم. میشه روی نقشه نشونم بدید؟

speakerA.en: Do you have any idea how to get this application to work?
speakerA.fa: نظری ندارید چطور این برنامه رو راه بندازم؟

speakerA.en: I hate to bother you, but could you lend me a pen for a moment?
speakerA.fa: از اینکه مزاحم می‌شم خجالت می‌کشم، اما میشه یه لحظه خودکارتون رو قرض بگیرم؟

speakerB.en: Sure, let me give you a hand.
It's at five o'clock.
Sure. The bus is at five.
OK. The bus is at five o'clock. Is this better?
Of course. I said we need to finish the report by Friday.
speakerB.fa: حتماً. گفتم باید گزارش رو تا جمعه تموم کنیم.

speakerB.en: Yes, sorry. I'll try to speak more clearly.
speakerB.fa: بله، ببخشید. سعی می‌کنم واضح‌تر صحبت کنم.

speakerB.en: I can try, but it's been a while since I did math.
speakerB.fa: می‌تونم امتحان کنم، اما مدتی هست ریاضی کار نکردم.

speakerB.en: Sure, it's right here. See this red marker?
speakerB.fa: حتماً، اینجاست. این علامت قرمز رو می‌بینید؟

speakerB.en: Actually, you need to restart the computer first.
speakerB.fa: در واقع، اول باید کامپیوتر رو ری‌استارت کنید.

speakerB.en: Not at all. Here you go.
speakerB.fa: خواهش می‌کنم. بفرمایید.

scenarios.scenario: Not understanding a word
scenarios.context: A student does not know a word and asks for help.

speakerA.en: I don't understand.
What does this word mean?
How do you spell it?
Can you write it, please?
Sorry, I didn't catch that word. Could you repeat it?
What's the difference between 'borrow' and 'lend'?
Could you give me an example sentence?
Is there another way to say it?

speakerB.en: Let me explain again.
It means 'big'.
It's B-I-G.
Sure. Here you go.
Of course. The word is 'borrow', B-O-R-R-O-W.
You borrow from someone, and you lend to someone.
Sure. Can I borrow your pen? I'll give it back soon.
Yes, you can say 'use something for a short time'.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for help in a shop
scenarios.context: A customer asks a shop assistant for help.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, can you help me?
I need a blue shirt.
How much is it?
Thank you for your help.
Excuse me, I'm looking for a black jacket in a medium size.
Do you have this one in a different color?
Could you tell me where the fitting rooms are?
Can I return it if it doesn't fit?

speakerB.en: Yes. What are you looking for?
They are over here.
It's twenty dollars.
You're welcome.
Let me check. We have two styles in that size.
Yes, it also comes in grey and dark blue.
They're at the back of the shop, on your left.
Yes, within fourteen days, if you keep the receipt.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a classmate for help
scenarios.context: A student asks a classmate for help with homework.

speakerA.en: Can you help me with my homework?
Page ten, number three.
Can I use your pen?
Thank you. You are very kind.
I missed the lesson yesterday. Could you tell me what we did?
Could you explain this exercise? I don't understand the instructions.
Can I take a photo of your notes?
Could we do the homework together this evening?

speakerB.en: Yes, sure. Which page?
This one is easy. Look.
Yes, here you are.
No problem.
Sure. We studied the past simple and did some exercises.
You have to choose the correct verb form. Look at the first example.
Sure, go ahead. My handwriting isn't very clear, though.
Good idea. Let's meet in the library at six.

scenarios.scenario: Getting help with a phone
scenarios.context: A person asks a friend to help with a phone problem.

speakerA.en: Can you help me with my phone?
I can't call my mother.
Oh, it works now!
No, thank you. You are so kind.
My phone is very slow today. What should I do?
I don't know how to connect to the Wi-Fi.
It asks for a password. Do you know it?
My storage is almost full. Can I delete some photos?

speakerB.en: Yes. What is the problem?
Let me see. Press this button.
Good. Do you need anything else?
You're welcome.
Try closing the apps you aren't using.
Go to Settings, tap Wi-Fi, and choose your network.
Yes, it's on the back of the router. I'll show you.
Yes, but back them up first so you don't lose them.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for help at the library
scenarios.context: A visitor asks the librarian for help.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I need a book.
It's a book about animals.
Where are the stairs?
Thank you very much.
Excuse me, how can I join the library?
How many books can I borrow at one time?
What happens if I return a book late?
Can I renew the book online?

speakerB.en: What book do you need?
It's on the second floor.
They are next to the door.
You're welcome. Enjoy your book.
You need an ID card and proof of address. It takes about five minutes.
You can borrow up to five books for three weeks.
There's a small fee of fifty cents for each day.
Yes, log in to your account and click 'Renew'.

scenarios.scenario: Offering help
scenarios.context: One person offers help to another.

speakerA.en: Do you need help?
Let me open it for you. Is your bag heavy?
Let me carry your bags.
I can help you to the car.
You look busy. Would you like some help with those boxes?
Where do you want me to put them?
Is there anything else I can do?
Let me know if you need anything else.

speakerB.en: Yes, please. I can't open this door.
Yes, a little.
Thank you. You are kind.
Thanks a lot.
That would be great. They're heavier than I thought.
Please take them to the room at the end of the hall.
Yes, could you hold the door while I carry this?
I will. Thanks for your help. I really appreciate it.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a colleague to explain a task
scenarios.context: A new employee asks a coworker to clarify instructions.

speakerA.en: Sorry to bother you, but I'm not sure I understood the instructions for this report.
I don't know which figures I should include, the monthly ones or the yearly totals.
Could you show me an example, so I can see how it should look?
That would help a lot. What should I do if I get stuck again?

speakerB.en: No problem. Which part is confusing you?
You need the monthly ones, and then a short summary of the yearly trend at the end.
Sure. I'll send you last month's report. You can use it as a model.
Just ask me. It's always better to check than to redo the whole thing.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a stranger for help with a machine
scenarios.context: A woman asks a stranger for help at a ticket machine.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, could you help me for a moment? I can't work out how this machine works.
To the airport, but the screen keeps asking me to choose a zone, and I have no idea which one.
It says my card has been declined. Do you know what I should do?
That worked! Thank you so much. I would have missed my train without you.

speakerB.en: Of course. Where do you want to go?
You need zone three. Then press the green button and select the number of tickets.
Try inserting it the other way around. Sometimes the machine has trouble reading the chip.
Don't mention it. Have a good trip.

scenarios.scenario: Asking someone to repeat and explain
scenarios.context: A student asks a teacher to clarify something during a lesson.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, could you go over the last part again? I didn't quite catch it.
The rule. I don't understand when to use the past perfect instead of the past simple.
So in 'I had finished when she arrived,' finishing came first?
Yes, please. I think it will help me remember it.

speakerB.en: Certainly. Which part do you mean, the grammar rule or the example?
We use the past perfect for something that happened before another event in the past.
Exactly. Would you like to try writing a sentence of your own?
Good. Write it down, and I'll check it with you after the lesson.

scenarios.scenario: Seeking clarification on ambiguous instructions
scenarios.context: An employee asks a supervisor to clarify a vague request.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry to take up your time, but I'm not entirely sure what you expect from me on this report.
Mainly the scope. Do you want a detailed analysis of every region, or just a summary of the overall trends?
That helps. And is there a particular format the board prefers, or can I use my own judgment?
Understood. If I run into any difficulties with the data, would it be all right to consult you again?

speakerB.en: Of course. Which aspects are unclear? I may have been too brief in my email.
The overall picture, with a closer look at the two regions where sales dropped.
Keep it to two pages, and put the key figures in a table. The directors rarely read beyond that.
By all means. It's far better to ask than to spend days heading in the wrong direction.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for help with a complicated form
scenarios.context: A resident asks an official for assistance with paperwork.

speakerA.en: I've been trying to fill in this tax form for an hour, and I'm afraid I'm completely stuck.
Section four, where it asks me to declare income from abroad. I'm not sure whether my freelance work counts.
I have most of them, but a few clients paid in cash, and I never kept records.
I see. Is there a risk of a penalty if my estimates turn out to be slightly off?

speakerB.en: These forms can be quite confusing. Which section is giving you trouble?
It does, provided the payments were made to you personally. Do you have the invoices?
In that case, you'll need to estimate as accurately as you can, and be prepared to justify your figures.
Not if you've acted in good faith. I'd recommend keeping a note of how you arrived at the numbers.

scenarios.scenario: Admitting you don't understand a technical explanation
scenarios.context: A client asks an engineer to simplify a complex explanation.

speakerA.en: I'm afraid you've lost me. Could you explain the problem in less technical terms?
So it's rather like a pipe that's too narrow for the volume of water passing through it?
And which of those options would be more cost-effective in the long run?
I'd like to hear the figures before I make a decision. Could you put them in writing?

speakerB.en: Certainly. In short, the software is struggling to cope with the amount of data it's being fed.
Exactly. We either need to widen the pipe or reduce the flow.
Upgrading the system costs more initially, but it would save you from recurring problems.
I'll send you a proposal tomorrow, with a plain-language summary at the top.

scenarios.scenario: Seeking a mentor's guidance on a dilemma
scenarios.context: A young professional asks a senior colleague for advice on a difficult career decision.

speakerA.en: I wondered whether I could borrow half an hour of your time. I'm facing a decision, and I value your perspective.
I've been offered a role abroad that would accelerate my career, but it would mean leaving my family and the team I've built here.
That's precisely the difficulty. My instinct seems to change by the hour, which is why I came to you.
That's a helpful way of framing it. I hadn't thought about it in terms of regret.

speakerB.en: Of course. Come in and sit down. What's on your mind?
That's no small thing. What does your instinct tell you, setting aside what you think you ought to want?
Then perhaps the question isn't which option is better, but what you'd regret not having tried in ten years' time.
Take a few days with it. And if it helps, I'm happy to talk it through again whenever you wish.

scenarios.scenario: Clarifying a clause in a contract
scenarios.context: An employee asks the HR manager to explain an unclear clause in a new employment contract.

speakerA.en: Thank you for sending the contract. There's one clause I'd like to clarify before I sign, if you have a moment.
Section eight, regarding intellectual property. It states that anything I create "in connection with the company's business" belongs to the company. That seems very broad.
That's reassuring, but the wording doesn't actually say so. Would it be possible to amend it to reflect that distinction?
Thank you. I'd rather resolve the ambiguity now than discover a dispute later.

speakerB.en: Certainly. Which clause is it?
I can see why it caught your eye. In practice, it applies to work done in your role, not to unrelated projects you pursue in your own time.
I'd have to consult our legal team, but I don't see why not. It's a reasonable request, and others have raised it before.
Quite right. I'll send you a revised version by Friday, and you're welcome to have your own lawyer review it.

scenarios.scenario: Asking about etiquette before a formal business dinner
scenarios.context: A newcomer asks an experienced colleague how to behave at a formal dinner with overseas partners.

speakerA.en: I've been invited to a dinner with our partners from Tokyo next week, and I'm anxious about committing some terrible faux pas. Could you give me a few pointers?
Noted. What about exchanging business cards? I've heard there's a particular way of doing it.
That's more ceremony than I'm used to. Is there anything I should avoid doing at the table?
I'll bear that in mind. Thank you; I feel considerably less nervous already.

speakerB.en: Happily. The key is to show respect rather than perfection. Arrive a few minutes early, and wait to be shown to your seat.
Present and receive cards with both hands, and take a moment to read the card rather than pocketing it. It signals respect.
Don't pour your own drink; pour for others, and they'll do the same for you. And never stand your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice.
Don't worry about it. They'll appreciate the effort far more than any slip you might make.

scenarios.scenario: Requesting clarification on ambiguous instructions from a superior
scenarios.context: An employee seeks to resolve uncertainty without appearing incompetent.

speakerA.en: I want to be sure I've understood the brief correctly, because I can interpret it in two quite different ways. Might I clarify a couple of points?
When you say the report should be 'comprehensive but concise,' do you favor completeness or brevity if the two come into conflict?
That helps considerably. And regarding the audience, is it primarily the executive team, or will the technical staff also read it?
Understood. I'll draft an outline and send it to you tomorrow, so we can agree on the structure before I proceed.

speakerB.en: Please do. Ambiguity at this stage is far preferable to a misunderstanding discovered at delivery.
A fair challenge. In this case, I'd lean toward brevity, with appendices for anything that doesn't fit within the main text.
Both, in fact, which is why I'd suggest a short summary followed by a more detailed section for the specialists.
Excellent. That kind of diligence will save us both a great deal of effort later on.

scenarios.scenario: Asking an expert for assistance with an unfamiliar problem
scenarios.context: A professional humbly seeks guidance from a more experienced colleague.

speakerA.en: I'm out of my depth with this contract, and I'd rather admit it than blunder through. Could you spare a few minutes?
The indemnity clause in particular baffles me. It seems to shift an enormous amount of liability onto us, but I can't pinpoint the mechanism.
That's what I suspected, but I wasn't confident enough to challenge it. How would you handle it?
Thank you. I'll draft the amendment and send it to you for review before it goes out.

speakerB.en: Of course. There's no dishonor in asking, and frankly, the people who don't are the ones who worry me.
Let me look. Ah, there it is. The wording is deceptively broad; it covers indirect losses, which is highly unusual.
I'd propose limiting the clause to direct damages and capping the liability at the contract value. It's a standard request.
Do, and don't hesitate to ask again. I'd much rather clarify a clause than clean up after a mistake.

scenarios.scenario: Seeking help when facing a language barrier abroad
scenarios.context: A traveler asks for assistance in a country where communication is difficult.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I'm sorry to interrupt, but my command of the language is woefully inadequate. Would you mind helping me with something?
I need to find a pharmacy that's open this evening. I've developed a rather troublesome headache, and I've run out of tablets.
That's very kind. Might I trouble you to write the name down, in case I mispronounce it?
You're extremely generous. I'm afraid I can offer nothing in return but my profound gratitude.

speakerB.en: I'll do my best. My English is not perfect, but we can try to understand each other.
There is a pharmacy that stays open late, near the station. It is not far, perhaps ten minutes on foot.
Of course. I will write it, and also the street, so you can show anyone if you become lost.
That is enough. Someone once helped me in a foreign country, so I am happy to repay it.

scenarios.scenario: Asking someone to speak slowly
scenarios.context: A visitor asks a local person to speak more slowly.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, could you say that again, please?
My English is not very good. Could you speak more slowly?
Yes, much better. What does 'platform' mean?
Oh, I understand now. Thank you for your patience.

speakerB.en: Of course. I'm sorry, I spoke too fast.
Yes, no problem. Is this better?
It's the place where you wait for the train.
You're welcome. Please ask me if you need anything else.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for help to fill in a form
scenarios.context: A person asks a clerk for help with a form.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I don't understand this form. Can you help me?
What should I write in this box?
And here, what does 'date of birth' mean?
Thank you. I think I can finish the rest.

speakerB.en: Of course. Which part is difficult?
That's for your full name, as it is in your passport.
It means the day, month and year you were born.
Good. Please bring it back to me when you finish.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a neighbor to help carry furniture
scenarios.context: A person asks a neighbor for help moving a heavy piece of furniture.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, are you busy right now? I need a hand with something.
I just bought a bookshelf, and it's too heavy for me to carry upstairs alone.
That would be wonderful. It's in the hallway downstairs. I think it's about forty kilos.
Thank you so much. Let me at least offer you a cup of tea afterwards.

speakerB.en: Not really. I was just about to make some coffee. What do you need?
That sounds tricky on your own. I'd be happy to help you carry it.
No problem. We can take it in two steps and rest on the landing if necessary.
That would be lovely, but really, there's no need. That's what neighbors are for.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a teacher to explain homework
scenarios.context: A student asks the teacher for clarification after class.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, could I ask you something about the homework before I leave?
I don't understand the second exercise. What exactly do we have to write?
I see. So should we use the examples from the book, or can we choose our own?
That's very clear now. Thank you for taking the time to explain.

speakerB.en: Of course. What part is confusing you? I'm happy to go through it again.
You need to write a short paragraph describing your daily routine, using at least five new words.
You can choose your own, as long as the sentences are correct and make sense.
You're welcome. If you have any other questions, come and see me tomorrow morning.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a stranger to explain a ticket machine
scenarios.context: A traveler asks someone for help using a ticket machine at a station.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I'm sorry to bother you, but could you help me with this machine? I can't figure out how it works.
I want to buy a day ticket for the whole city, but the screen keeps asking me to choose a zone, and I don't know which one.
I'm staying near the cathedral, and I plan to visit the museums and the botanical garden. Is one zone enough for that?
Thanks. And what if I want to pay by card? Nothing seems to happen when I insert it.
I see, I had to tap it instead of inserting it. That makes sense. Does the ticket have to be stamped afterwards?
You've saved me a lot of time. Thank you so much, and I hope you didn't miss your train because of me.

speakerB.en: Of course. I use it every day. What are you trying to buy? Let me see if I can walk you through it.
The zones are marked on the map next to the machine. Where exactly are you staying, and where do you want to go?
In that case, the central zone is enough. Choose the option that says 'Zone 1', and then press the button for a day ticket.
Hold the card against the sign on the right, instead of putting it in. This machine is a bit confusing for newcomers.
Not for this kind of ticket. It's already valid when you buy it, but keep it with you, because inspectors check them often.
Not at all, the next one comes in five minutes. Enjoy your stay, and don't hesitate to ask if you need anything else.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a colleague to clarify instructions
scenarios.context: An employee asks a coworker to explain an unclear email from a manager.

speakerA.en: Do you have a minute? I received an email from Mr. Harris this morning, and I'm not sure what he wants me to do.
He says that I should prepare the figures for the quarterly report, but he doesn't mention which department he means.
I assumed that, but I was afraid of making a mistake. Could you tell me what format is normally used for these reports?
That's very helpful. Is there a template that I can use, or do I have to create the document from scratch?
Great, I'll look for it. When do you think I should send it to him? He didn't give a deadline in the email.
Thanks for your help. I'll ask him directly if I have any other questions, and I'll let you know how it goes.

speakerB.en: Sure. Let me have a look. Hmm, I see what you mean. His emails are often short, and he expects people to understand.
I'm fairly sure that he means the sales department, because we've sent them the same request every quarter for the last two years.
Normally, we use a spreadsheet, with one page for each month and a summary chart at the end. It's not complicated once you've seen an example.
There's a template in the shared folder under 'Reports'. If you can't find it, I'll forward you the one that I used last time.
I'd aim to send it by Thursday, to be on the safe side. If you ask him, he'll probably say that he needs it before the weekend.
No problem. It's better to ask than to guess. If you're still unsure, call me, and we'll go through it together.

scenarios.scenario: Requesting clarification on a complex contract
scenarios.context: A client asks a lawyer's assistant to explain unclear terms in an agreement.

speakerA.en: Thank you for seeing me. I've read through the contract several times, but there are a few clauses that I find rather ambiguous, and I'd like to be certain before I sign.
The first is clause seven, which states that either party may terminate the agreement with 'reasonable notice'. Could you clarify what is meant by reasonable in this context?
I see. And what about the penalty mentioned in clause eleven? As far as I can tell, it applies even if the delay is caused by circumstances beyond my control.
That's precisely what concerns me. Is it possible to ask for an amendment, or is the document considered final once it has been sent to me?
In that case, I'll ask for these two changes in writing. Would you be able to help me phrase the request so that it doesn't sound confrontational?
Thank you. It's reassuring to know that I'm not obliged to accept everything. I'd never have noticed these problems had I not asked.

speakerB.en: Of course. It's always wise to ask questions before signing, and it's my job to make sure that you understand every point. Let's go through them one by one.

In legal terms, it usually means a period that would be considered fair, given the circumstances. In practice, it's often interpreted as thirty days, but without a specific number, it can lead to disputes.

You're quite right. As the clause is currently worded, you'd be liable whatever the reason for the delay, which seems unbalanced. I'd recommend negotiating an exception for events outside your control.
Contracts are rarely final at this stage. The other party will probably expect some negotiation, and it's perfectly normal to propose changes before both sides agree.
Certainly. I'll draft a short message that explains your concerns politely and suggests specific alternative wording, so that the discussion remains constructive.
That's exactly why I'm here. If anything else seems unclear before you sign, don't hesitate to contact me, even if it seems minor.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a supervisor for guidance on a research problem
scenarios.context: A graduate student asks a professor for help with a difficult stage of a thesis.

speakerA.en: Thank you for making time for me, Professor. I wanted to ask for your advice, because I've reached a point in my research where I'm not sure how to proceed.
The data from the second experiment doesn't support my original hypothesis, and I'm unsure whether to treat it as a failure or as a possible indication that the premise itself needs rethinking.
That's reassuring, but I'm worried that the deadline for the next chapter is approaching, and I wouldn't want to change direction completely at this stage.
I hadn't considered that. So you're suggesting that I should present the unexpected result as a finding in its own right, instead of hiding it or trying to explain it away?
Would you be kind enough to recommend any literature that deals with similar results? I'd like to see how other researchers have handled this kind of problem.
Thank you. This conversation has given me a lot to think about, and I feel much more confident about the next steps.

speakerB.en: Of course, come in. I'm glad you asked. Many students keep their doubts to themselves until it's too late. Tell me about the data and what you've found so far.

In science, results that contradict expectations are often more interesting than those that confirm them. Before drawing conclusions, though, you should check that the method and the sample were sound.
I understand, but I wouldn't advise you to rush. A thesis that explains an unexpected finding honestly will be judged more favorably than one that forces the data to fit a theory.
Exactly. Examiners value intellectual honesty. If you show that you've considered alternative explanations and discussed the limitations, it demonstrates maturity as a researcher.
Certainly. I'll send you two articles this afternoon, one of which examines a very similar situation. I'd also suggest talking to Dr. Hale, who ran a comparable study last year.
You're welcome. Come back next week with a revised outline, and we'll review it together. And remember that setbacks are part of the process.

scenarios.scenario: Asking IT support to fix a recurring problem
scenarios.context: An employee describes an ongoing computer issue and asks for a lasting solution.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'm calling about a problem that I've reported twice already, and which keeps coming back. My computer freezes several times a day, and I lose whatever I'm working on.

It usually happens when I have several programs open at once, especially the spreadsheet and the video conferencing software. After about a minute, everything starts working again, but sometimes it doesn't.
The last time, someone from your team restarted the computer remotely, and it seemed to improve for a few days. But the same thing happened again yesterday, in the middle of an important call.
I'd prefer a permanent solution, rather than another temporary fix. Is it possible that the computer is simply too old for the programs that we're using nowadays?
That would make sense. In the meantime, is there anything that I can do to reduce the risk, such as closing certain programs or adjusting some settings?
Thank you. I'll wait for your technician. Please let me know the time, so that I can make sure to back up my files first.

speakerB.en: Good morning, IT support. I'm sorry that you've had trouble. Let me look at the tickets you've opened. I can see two previous reports, both closed after remote restarts, which wasn't really adequate.
Thank you for the details. That sounds like a memory issue. Running a spreadsheet, a video call, and probably a browser with several tabs at the same time can overload an older machine.
I agree that restarting only treats the symptom. I'll escalate this to a technician, who can check the hardware, and see whether the memory or the hard drive is failing.

It's quite possible. How old is the computer? Yours is about five years old, according to our records, which means it's due for a replacement under our normal cycle, if the diagnostic confirms the problem.
I'd suggest closing any programs you aren't using, and avoiding having more than five browser tabs open. Also, saving your work frequently will limit the damage if it freezes again.
A technician will come to your desk tomorrow morning at nine. He'll run the diagnostics, and if the computer needs replacing, we'll arrange a new one within a week.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a landlord about repair responsibilities
scenarios.context: A tenant asks a landlord to clarify who is responsible for repairs under the lease.

speakerA.en: Thank you for meeting me. I'd like to clarify a few points about the lease, because there's been a misunderstanding about who is responsible for certain repairs, and I'd like to avoid any disputes.
The washing machine broke down last week. When I contacted the agency, they told me that I'd have to pay for the repair, but I thought that appliances were included in the rent.
I've read the contract again, and it says that the landlord is responsible for 'major equipment', but it doesn't define what that means. Would a washing machine be considered major equipment?
That seems reasonable, but I'd like it in writing, so that there's no confusion in the future. Could we add a short clause to the agreement that lists exactly which items are covered?
I'd also like to ask about smaller problems, like a dripping tap or a loose door handle. I'm happy to deal with those myself, but I want to be sure that I won't be blamed for something later.
Thank you. This conversation has cleared up a lot, and I feel more comfortable now that we've agreed on what each of us is responsible for.

speakerB.en: Of course. I'm glad you asked, because it's better to settle these things at the start. What exactly did the agency tell you? I'm afraid that they're sometimes a bit rigid in their interpretation.
I see. That's not how I understood it, either. The washing machine was part of the inventory when you moved in, and I'd consider it my responsibility, unless it was damaged through misuse.
Good question. In my view, major equipment includes the boiler, the cooker, the washing machine, and the refrigerator. I'll include a list in an addendum, so that we both have a clear reference.
That's an excellent idea. I'll draft it this week, and we can both sign it. I'd prefer that things are clear from the beginning, since it saves a lot of unpleasantness later on.
For minor repairs, such as the ones you mention, the tenant is generally responsible, as long as the cost is under fifty euros. Anything above that, you should tell me before doing anything.
I'm pleased that we've cleared that up. Please let me know if anything else comes up, and I'll arrange for someone to repair the washing machine by the end of the week.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a former professor to clarify feedback on a thesis chapter
scenarios.context: A graduate student visits a former professor to understand vague comments on a draft chapter and to ask for guidance on revising it.

speakerA.en: Thank you for seeing me at such short notice, Professor. I'd appreciate it if you could help me understand your comments on chapter three, since I'm not sure what you mean by saying the argument lacks a clear thread.

The second half, I think, where I move from the literature review to my own data. I'd appreciate it if you could show me where the connection breaks down, because to me it seemed logical when I wrote it.
Yes, I do now. I'd appreciate it if you could tell me whether I should cut that section entirely or rewrite it, since it took me weeks to collect the material and I'd hate to lose it.

That's very generous of you. I'd appreciate it if you could also look at my methodology, because one reviewer said it wasn't clear how I selected the participants. Should I explain that in the main text or in a footnote?
Thirty-two, though four dropped out halfway through. I'd appreciate it if you could advise me on how to report that, since I don't want it to look as if I'm hiding anything.

That's a very helpful suggestion. I'll revise the chapter and send it back in two weeks. I'd appreciate it if you could let me know whether that's too ambitious, given that I'm also teaching this term.

speakerB.en: Of course. Once you've read the chapter again with fresh eyes, you'll probably see what I mean, but let me explain. Should you find the structure confusing yourself, that's a good sign we're on the same page. Which section troubles you most?

The problem is the transition. Once you've stated your research question, every paragraph should relate to it, and in the second half several don't. Should you need an example, look at page forty, where the focus shifts quite suddenly. Do you see it?

I wouldn't cut it, although I'd move it to an appendix. Once you've decided which findings really support your argument, the rest can go in the notes. Should you be unsure about a particular passage, send it to me, and I'll tell you honestly.

In the main text, definitely. Once you've explained the selection criteria clearly, readers won't have to guess. Should anyone challenge the sample size later, you'll be able to point to that paragraph and defend your choices. How many participants did you have?

Report it openly. Once you've mentioned the dropouts and the reasons, it actually strengthens your credibility. Should the committee ask about it, you'll have an answer ready. I'd also suggest a short table, so that the numbers are easy to follow.

Two weeks is realistic, as long as you set aside regular time. Once you've sent it, I'll give you comments within a few days. Should anything come up in the meantime, just email me, and don't wait for our next meeting.

scenarios.scenario: Asking an administrator to clarify an unfamiliar permit procedure
scenarios.context: A newly arrived resident visits a municipal office to understand a confusing residence-permit procedure after receiving contradictory information.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'd appreciate it if you could clarify something for me. Two different offices have given me contradictory information about the documents I need for my residence permit, and I'd rather not make the journey twice.

I was told to bring a rental contract, a bank statement, and a health insurance certificate. Had I known the rules had changed, I'd have checked the website first, but the old version was still online.

That's good to know. I'd appreciate it if you could tell me whether a certified translation is needed, since my rental contract is in two languages and my insurance certificate is only in my own language.

I'd appreciate it if you could give me that list. Had I known about the translation requirement, I'd have arranged it earlier, because I understand these services can take a week or more. How long does the whole procedure take afterwards?
Is there a way to speed it up? I have a job offer that starts in a month, and I'd appreciate it if you could tell me whether an employer's letter might help.
Not yet, but I'll ask my employer this afternoon. Thank you for being so patient. I'd appreciate it if you could write down the list of documents, since I'm afraid I'll forget something again.

speakerB.en: Certainly. Should you have your passport and proof of address with you, I can check what's missing. If it weren't for the recent changes in the rules, this would be much simpler, but the requirements were updated last month. Which documents were you told to bring?

That's a common problem. Should you find the website confusing, I'd suggest phoning ahead. The bank statement is no longer required, as long as you can show a signed contract, but the insurance certificate must now be an original rather than a copy.

The insurance certificate does need a translation, although the contract doesn't, since it's already bilingual. If it weren't for that clause, you could have submitted everything today. Should you need a translator, we keep a list of approved ones at the desk.

Once the file is complete, it usually takes about three weeks. Should there be any delays, you'll receive a letter, and if it weren't for the backlog at the moment, it would be faster. You can also track the application online.

It could, yes. Should you attach a letter confirming your start date, we can mark the file as urgent. Had you mentioned that earlier, I'd have told you straight away, so I'm glad you asked now. Do you have a letter yet?

Of course, I'll print it for you now, along with the translator list. Should you have any further questions, my direct number is at the bottom. If it weren't for people asking in advance, we'd have far more problems here.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a bank officer to explain unfamiliar loan terms
scenarios.context: A customer asks a bank officer to explain unfamiliar terms in a loan agreement before he signs it.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I received the loan agreement yesterday, and to be honest, some of the terms are quite unfamiliar. I was wondering whether you could walk me through the main points, so as not to sign anything I don't fully understand.

The repayment schedule, mainly. It mentions an 'early repayment charge', and I'd like to know what exactly that means. In the event that I pay off the loan sooner, would I be penalized? And how much would that be?

An example would help, since numbers are easier for me than definitions. On the other hand, I'd also like to know what 'default' means in the contract. Should I fail to make a payment, what exactly would happen?

That's clearer, thank you. Would you mind explaining the insurance clause? It says I must take out life insurance, and I wonder whether I have to buy it from the bank, or whether I can choose my own provider.

Yes, please. One more thing, I'd like to understand how the interest changes after five years. It says it's 'variable', but I'm unsure whether that's linked to the central bank or to your own policy. Could you clarify?

Thank you, that's exactly what I needed. Might I take the agreement home and read it again tonight? As far as I'm concerned, it's better to ask now than regret it later. I'll return it signed tomorrow, provided nothing else comes up.

speakerB.en: Of course, Mr. Rossi, that's very sensible. Let's begin with the interest rate, which is fixed at four percent for the first five years. Might I ask which part you found most confusing, the rate or the repayment schedule?

Good question. If you repay more than ten percent of the loan in a year, we charge two percent of the extra amount. In the event that you sell the house, the charge is waived. Does that make sense so far, or should I give an example?

Certainly. Suppose you borrow two hundred thousand and miss one payment. You'd have a grace period of fourteen days. Should you fail to pay by then, a late fee applies, and after three months we'd begin formal proceedings. I'd say that's quite fair.

You may choose any provider, as long as the policy covers the full loan. I'd suggest comparing three quotes, since prices differ widely. In the event that you find a cheaper one, just send us the certificate. Would you like a list of approved companies?

It's tied to the central bank's base rate, plus a margin of one point five percent. Should the base rate go up, your payments would rise, and the reverse is true if it falls. To be honest, many customers overlook this clause, so I'm glad you asked.
Please do. Here's my card, so you can call me directly with any questions. Should anything still seem unclear, I'd rather explain it twice than have you worry. We look forward to seeing you tomorrow.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a colleague to walk you through a new software system
scenarios.context: An employee asks an experienced colleague to explain the project software the company is about to introduce.

speakerA.en: Hi Dana, do you have a few minutes? I've just been told we're switching to the new project software next week, and to be honest, I find it quite overwhelming. Would it be possible for you to show me the basics?

The reports, I'd say. What I find hardest is understanding how the data gets in there. Do you happen to know whether it's updated automatically, or whether we have to enter it manually, in case I've missed something?
Yes, that would help. Could you also explain how I assign a task to someone? What I don't understand is why some names appear in grey, since I assumed they'd all be available.
It does, thank you. On the other hand, I'm worried about making mistakes, such as deleting something important. Would it be possible to undo an action if I click the wrong button?
Please. I'd like to take notes, so I'll write down the steps. Do you mind if I ask you again later, in case I forget anything? I'd rather ask twice than make a mess of the project.

Ten is perfect. Thank you so much, Dana, you've made it far less intimidating. As far as I'm concerned, this is the best way to learn, since it's much clearer than reading the manual alone. I owe you a coffee.

speakerB.en: Of course, I'd be happy to. I struggled with it myself at first, so I know how you feel. What I'd suggest is starting with the dashboard. Which part worries you most, the task lists or the reports?

Mostly automatically, as long as everyone logs their hours by Friday. The thing is, if someone forgets, the report looks incomplete. That's why I set a reminder every Thursday. Would you like me to show you how to do that?

Grey means the person is on leave or has a full workload. It's a good feature, because it stops you overloading anyone. Supposing you need that person urgently, you can still assign it, but they'll receive a warning. Does that answer your question?

Yes, there's an undo button for the last ten actions, and everything is saved for thirty days. So even if you delete something, I can restore it. To be honest, I'd say the biggest risk is renaming files, since that breaks links. Shall I show you a safe way?

Not at all, ask as often as you like. What also helps is the training video on the intranet, which takes about twenty minutes. I'd suggest watching it tonight, then we can meet tomorrow to go over anything unclear. How does ten o'clock sound?
Deal! And please don't hesitate to ask, whatever the question. We all started as beginners. By the end of next week you'll probably be teaching me a few tricks, I'd say.

scenarios.scenario: Giving compliments and responding politely
scenarios.context: People express appreciation or admiration towards others.

speakerA.en: You look nice today.
I like your bag.
Your English is good.
You are a good friend.
You look great today! Is that a new dress?
speakerA.fa: امروز عالی به نظر می‌رسی! این یه لباس جدید هست؟

speakerA.en: I love your hair. It really suits you.
speakerA.fa: موهات رو خیلی دوست دارم. خیلی بهت میاد.

speakerA.en: That was a really good presentation. You did a fantastic job!
speakerA.fa: ارائه واقعاً خوبی بود. کار عالی انجام دادی!

speakerA.en: I must say, your house is beautifully decorated.
speakerA.fa: باید بگم، خونه‌ات زیبا تزیین شده.

speakerA.en: You have a wonderful taste in music. This playlist is amazing.
speakerA.fa: سلیقه‌ات در موسیقی فوق‌العاده است. این پلی‌لیست عالیه.

speakerA.en: I appreciate you helping me out so quickly. You're a lifesaver!
speakerA.fa: ممنون که این سریع کمکم کردی. نجاتم دادی!

speakerB.en: Thank you. That's kind of you.
Thanks. It's a gift.
Thank you. I study every day.
Thank you. You are too.
Thanks! Yes, I got it last week.
speakerB.fa: ممنون! آره، هفته پیش خریدمش.

speakerB.en: Oh, really? Thank you! I just styled it differently today.
speakerB.fa: اوه، واقعاً؟ ممنون! امروز فقط یه جور دیگه حالتش دادم.

speakerB.en: Thank you so much! I was really nervous, so I'm glad it went well.
speakerB.fa: خیلی ممنون! خیلی عصبی بودم، پس خوشحالم که خوب پیش رفت.

speakerB.en: That's very kind of you to say. I did it all myself!
speakerB.fa: لطف دارید. خودم همه‌اش رو انجام دادم!

speakerB.en: Thank you! I'm glad you're enjoying it.
speakerB.fa: ممنون! خوشحالم که ازش لذت می‌برید.

speakerB.en: Anytime! That's what friends are for.
speakerB.fa: هر وقت! دوستان برای همین هستند.

scenarios.scenario: Saying please and thank you
scenarios.context: Two people use polite words in a café.

speakerA.en: A coffee, please.
Thank you very much.
Can I have some water, please?
Thanks a lot!
Could I have a cappuccino and a slice of cake, please?
To take away, please. How much is it?
Here you are. Could I have a receipt, please?
Thank you. Have a lovely day.

speakerB.en: Here you are.
You're welcome.
Of course. Here it is.
No problem.
Certainly. Would you like it here or to take away?
That's six dollars fifty, please.
Of course. Thank you very much.
Thanks, you too. See you next time.

scenarios.scenario: Saying excuse me and sorry
scenarios.context: People are polite in a busy place.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, is this seat free?
Sorry, I'm in your way.
Excuse me, can I pass?
I'm sorry. Is this your bag?
Excuse me, could you move your bag, please? I'd like to sit here.
Sorry to bother you. Do you know what time the next train is?
Excuse me, I think you dropped your ticket.
I'm sorry, I didn't mean to push you.

speakerB.en: Yes, please sit down.
That's OK. No problem.
Of course. Go ahead.
Yes, it is. Thank you.
Oh, sorry. Of course. I didn't notice.
No problem. It's at ten past five.
Oh, thank you! That's very kind of you.
That's all right. It's very crowded today.

scenarios.scenario: Complimenting a cook
scenarios.context: A guest compliments the food at dinner.

speakerA.en: The dinner is delicious.
You are a good cook.
Can I have some more rice?
Thank you for the nice meal.
This soup is amazing. What's in it?
It tastes wonderful. Did you make it yourself?
Could you give me the recipe?
Thank you for inviting us. It was a lovely evening.

speakerB.en: Thank you. I'm glad you like it.
That's kind of you.
Yes, of course. Please help yourself.
You're welcome. Come again.
Thank you! It's carrots, potatoes, and a little ginger.
Yes, it's my grandmother's recipe.
Of course. I'll write it down for you.
It was my pleasure. Please come again soon.

scenarios.scenario: Complimenting a classmate
scenarios.context: Two classmates say nice things to each other.

speakerA.en: Your drawing is beautiful.
You are very smart.
I like your new shoes.
You have a nice smile.
Your presentation was really good today.
You spoke clearly, and your pictures were great.
I really like your bag. Where did you buy it?
You always help everyone in our class.

speakerB.en: Thank you. I like drawing.
You are smart too.
Thanks. They are very comfortable.
Thank you. You're so kind.
Thank you! I practiced a lot at home.
That's nice to hear. I was a little nervous.
Thanks. My sister gave it to me for my birthday.
That's very kind of you to say.

scenarios.scenario: Being polite to a stranger
scenarios.context: A person helps a stranger with a door.

speakerA.en: Please, go first.
Can I open the door for you?
It's my pleasure. Have a nice day!
Excuse me, is anyone sitting here?
Thank you. Do you mind if I open the window?
Sorry, could you tell me the time, please?
Thanks a lot. I really appreciate your help.

speakerB.en: Thank you. That's very kind.
Yes, thank you.
You too. Thank you again.
No, please go ahead and sit down.
Not at all. It's quite warm in here.
Sure. It's a quarter to three.
You're welcome. Have a nice journey.

scenarios.scenario: Wishing someone well
scenarios.context: People say kind words on special days.

speakerA.en: Happy birthday!
Good luck with your test.
Congratulations!
Have a nice weekend.
Congratulations on your new job! I'm so happy for you.
I hope everything goes well. Good luck!
I heard you're not feeling well. Get well soon.
Have a safe trip, and enjoy your holiday!

speakerB.en: Thank you very much.
Thanks. I need it.
Thank you. I'm so happy.
You too. See you on Monday.
Thank you! I start next Monday.
Thanks. I'm a little nervous, but excited.
That's kind of you. I'll be back at work next week.
Thank you. I'll send you a postcard.

scenarios.scenario: Complimenting a colleague on a presentation
scenarios.context: A coworker congratulates another on a successful presentation.

speakerA.en: That was an excellent presentation. You explained everything so clearly.
You didn't look nervous at all. The charts you used made the results easy to understand.
It definitely paid off. Our manager looked very impressed.
I only made a few small suggestions. The hard work was all yours.

speakerB.en: Thank you so much. I was really nervous, so that's good to hear.
I spent most of the weekend working on them, so I'm glad they were useful.
I couldn't have done it without your feedback last week.
You're very generous. Let me buy you a coffee to say thank you.

scenarios.scenario: Thanking a host for dinner
scenarios.context: A guest thanks his hosts at the end of a dinner party.

speakerA.en: Thank you so much for having us. The meal was absolutely delicious.
It was the best I've had in a long time. Would you mind sharing the recipe?
Your home is lovely, too. You've decorated it with such good taste.
It shows. We'd love to return the favor and invite you to our place soon.

speakerB.en: We're so glad you enjoyed it. Did you like the dessert?
Of course. It's simpler than it looks, and I'll write it down for you.
That's very kind of you. We've worked on it for years.
We'd be delighted. Just tell us the date, and we'll be there.

scenarios.scenario: Politely asking for a favor
scenarios.context: A person asks a neighbor for a favor in a polite way.

speakerA.en: I hope I'm not disturbing you. I was wondering if I could ask you a small favor.
I'm going away for a week, and I'd really appreciate it if you could water my plants.
I can leave it with you today if that's convenient. I'll write down instructions too.
Only the big one in the living room. It needs a lot of water twice a week.

speakerB.en: Not at all. What can I do for you?
Of course, I'd be happy to. Where do you keep the key?
That would be perfect. Do any of them need special care?
No problem. Enjoy your trip, and don't worry about anything.

scenarios.scenario: Receiving praise graciously
scenarios.context: A colleague compliments another on handling a difficult situation.

speakerA.en: I wanted to say how impressed I was with the way you dealt with that client yesterday.
You wouldn't have known it. You stayed calm, even when he became quite rude.
It's a skill I wish I had. I tend to get defensive almost immediately.
Now you're flattering me. But I'll gladly take the compliment, and return it with interest.

speakerB.en: That's very kind of you to say, though I felt I was barely holding it together.
I've learned that responding to hostility with patience usually takes the wind out of its sails.
It takes practice. Honestly, I picked up most of it by watching you handle meetings.
Then we can consider ourselves even. Shall we celebrate with a coffee?

scenarios.scenario: Offering condolences
scenarios.context: A person expresses sympathy to a coworker who has lost a relative.

speakerA.en: I was very sorry to hear about your grandmother. Please accept my deepest condolences.
I can only imagine. If there's anything I can do, whether it's covering your work or simply listening, please say so.
She must have been a remarkable woman, judging by the way you've spoken about her.
She sounds like someone who left a lasting impression on everyone she met.

speakerB.en: Thank you. It was expected, but that doesn't make it any easier.
That's incredibly thoughtful. Right now, it helps just to know people care.
She was. She raised four children on her own and never complained once.
She did, and I'm grateful for the time we had. Thank you for taking the trouble to say this.

scenarios.scenario: Politely disagreeing while remaining respectful
scenarios.context: Two acquaintances disagree on a point but keep the conversation courteous.

speakerA.en: I appreciate your perspective, though I must admit I see the matter somewhat differently.
My concern is that the proposal overlooks the long-term costs, which could prove considerable.
Only rough estimates, but I'd be happy to share them if you'd like to look.
I'll send them over this afternoon. I hope I haven't come across as too critical.

speakerB.en: Please, I'd be interested to hear your view. I don't claim to have all the answers.
That's a valid point, and one I hadn't fully considered. Do you have figures to support it?
I'd appreciate that. It's always useful to have someone question my assumptions.
Not at all. Healthy debate is how good ideas get better.

scenarios.scenario: Congratulating someone on a hard-won achievement
scenarios.context: A colleague congratulates another on completing a doctorate after years of part-time study.

speakerA.en: I heard the news, and I wanted to congratulate you in person. Finishing a doctorate while working full-time is an extraordinary achievement.
It certainly shows in the result. Everyone who has read your thesis speaks of it with real admiration.
You deserve the recognition regardless. It takes a rare combination of discipline and humility to see something like that through.
We should celebrate properly. Allow me to take you to lunch, and I won't hear any objections.

speakerB.en: That's very kind of you. There were many nights when I doubted I'd ever see the end of it.
You're generous. I couldn't have done it without the patience of my family and the flexibility this team gave me.
I'm not sure about the humility, but I'll gladly accept the compliment. It means a great deal coming from you.
In that case, I accept with pleasure. I can't think of a better way to mark the occasion.

scenarios.scenario: Declining a generous offer graciously
scenarios.context: A guest politely declines the host's insistence on paying for an expensive dinner.

speakerA.en: Please, put your wallet away. Tonight is entirely on me, and I won't hear otherwise.
It's the least I can do after everything you did for us last year. Consider it a long-overdue thank you.
I admire your stubbornness, but I'm afraid I'm just as stubborn. How about a compromise? I'll pay tonight, and you can host the next one.
Then it's settled. And I'll warn you that I have expensive tastes.

speakerB.en: That's incredibly generous of you, but I really can't let you do that. You've been so hospitable already.
I appreciate the sentiment more than I can say. Still, I'd feel much more comfortable if we split it, or at least let me cover the wine.
Now that's a deal I can accept with a clear conscience. I'll hold you to your word on the venue, though.
I'll happily rise to the challenge. Thank you again, truly, for such a memorable evening.

scenarios.scenario: Responding gracefully to a backhanded compliment
scenarios.context: A woman handles a patronizing remark at a reunion without losing her composure.

speakerA.en: You look wonderful. I must say, I'm surprised. I'd have expected the years to be less kind after everything you've been through.
Oh, I didn't mean anything by it. I just meant that you've done remarkably well, considering.
Well, you know, the career change and all that. Not everyone would have had the courage.
I'm glad to hear it. Perhaps I've underestimated you.

speakerB.en: That's an interesting way of putting it. I'll take it as a compliment, even if it arrived slightly sideways.
Considering what, exactly? I'm always curious about the standard I'm being measured against.
Courage is generous, though I'd call it necessity. In truth, it has been the best decision I've made.
It happens. But I'm here to enjoy the evening, not to settle old scores. Shall we find something to drink?

scenarios.scenario: Receiving a compliment gracefully
scenarios.context: A person responds modestly to praise without deflecting it entirely.

speakerA.en: I must say, your presentation was outstanding. You had the audience in the palm of your hand from the first minute.
Not at all. The clarity of your argument was remarkable, and your handling of the questions was masterful.
Credit where it's due, but the delivery was entirely yours. Few people can make a technical subject feel so engaging.
You flatter me, though I shan't argue. Perhaps we could collaborate on something in the future.

speakerB.en: That's very generous of you. I'll admit I was nervous, so it's a relief to learn it didn't show.
I owe a great deal to the preparation, and to a colleague who rehearsed with me until I stopped fidgeting.
Thank you. Coming from you, whose talks I've admired for years, the praise means considerably more.
I'd be honored. I'll hold you to that, so consider yourself warned.

scenarios.scenario: Offering sincere condolences to a bereaved colleague
scenarios.context: A person expresses sympathy with sensitivity and restraint.

speakerA.en: I was so sorry to hear about your father. I don't have the right words, but I wanted you to know that I'm thinking of you.
Please don't feel obliged to discuss it. If you need time away from work, we'll manage perfectly well without you.
Of course, whatever helps. And if you ever wish to talk, or simply to sit in silence, my door is always open.
I'm sure of it. Please let me know if there's anything practical I can do, from meals to errands.

speakerB.en: Thank you. That means more than you might imagine. It's been a difficult week, and kind words are a genuine comfort.
I appreciate that, but I think I'd rather stay busy. Routine is something I can hold on to at the moment.
That's a kindness I won't forget. He spoke highly of this place, and I think he'd be glad I'm among friends.
I'll remember that. Thank you for being so thoughtful; it's a rare quality, and I'm grateful for it.

scenarios.scenario: Declining a request with tact and courtesy
scenarios.context: A person refuses a favor while preserving the relationship.

speakerA.en: I wonder if I might ask a rather large favor. I'm in a bind, and I'd like you to cover my shift on Saturday.
I understand entirely. I'd hoped, but I appreciate your candor, and I'd never wish to put you in an awkward position.
I hadn't thought of that. I'll approach him this afternoon, though I'm not optimistic.
That's more than generous, and I'm grateful even for the possibility. I'll do the same for you whenever you need it.

speakerB.en: I wish I could oblige, truly. Unfortunately, I've a prior commitment that I can't break, and I'd hate to promise something I couldn't deliver.
It's kind of you to say so. Have you tried asking Marcus? I believe he mentioned wanting extra hours.
Don't be disheartened. If he can't, let me know, and I'll see whether I can rearrange my own plans for a later date.
I'll hold you to it. Good luck, and I hope everything resolves without too much inconvenience.

scenarios.scenario: Complimenting a friend on a new haircut
scenarios.context: A person notices a friend's new look and gives a compliment.

speakerA.en: Wow, you've changed your hair! It really suits you. Did you go to a new salon?
Well, it looks great. It makes you look younger, and the color is very natural.
I might do that. I've been thinking about a change, but I'm a bit nervous.
Thanks for the advice. I'll give her a call this afternoon.

speakerB.en: Thank you! I wasn't sure about it at first, but I'm getting used to it. Yes, it's a salon near my office.
That's so kind of you to say. The hairdresser was fantastic. I can give you her number.
Don't be nervous. She listens carefully and doesn't cut more than you ask for.
Good luck! And tell her I sent you. She might give you a discount.

scenarios.scenario: Thanking a colleague for their help
scenarios.context: A worker thanks a colleague who helped finish an important report.

speakerA.en: I just wanted to thank you again for your help with the report yesterday.
I really mean it. Without your suggestions, I wouldn't have finished before the deadline.
I'd like to take you out for lunch as a thank-you. Are you free on Thursday?
Wonderful. I'll book a table and send you the details this afternoon.

speakerB.en: You're very welcome. I was glad to help. It was an interesting project.
I'm sure you would have managed, but I'm happy that it turned out well in the end.
That's really not necessary, but it's a lovely idea. Thursday works perfectly for me.
Great. I'm looking forward to it. Just let me know if I should bring anything.

scenarios.scenario: Thanking someone for a thoughtful gift
scenarios.context: A person thanks a friend for a birthday present and shows appreciation.

speakerA.en: I wanted to thank you again for the book. It was such a thoughtful present, and I started reading it the same night.
You really didn't have to go to so much trouble. How did you know that I'd been looking for this particular edition?
That's incredibly kind of you. I'd mentioned it only once, and I'm amazed that you remembered.
I'd love to say that I'm a good listener, but you're the one who deserves the credit. Is there anything I can do for you in return?
In that case, let me take you out to dinner next week. I know a quiet place, and the food is excellent.
Wonderful. I'll make a reservation and let you know the time. Thanks again for being such a good friend.

speakerB.en: I'm so glad that you liked it. I hesitated for a long time before choosing it, because I was afraid you might already have it.
It wasn't any trouble at all. I remembered that you talked about it when we visited the bookshop last spring.
I pay attention to the things that matter to my friends. It's more fun to give something that's been chosen carefully.
Please don't feel that you owe me anything. Seeing you happy is the best reward I could ask for.
That's a lovely idea, if you insist. I haven't been out for dinner in weeks, so it would be a nice change.
Perfect. I'm looking forward to it. And if you finish the book, tell me what you think about the ending.

scenarios.scenario: Offering a seat and making polite conversation
scenarios.context: A passenger offers a seat on the bus and chats with an older man.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, sir, would you like to sit down? I'm getting off at the next stop, so I don't mind standing.
It's no trouble at all. The bus is very crowded today, and you've been standing for quite some time.
I'm just on my way to work. I teach at the primary school near the park, and the journey takes about forty minutes.
That's wonderful. If you don't mind my saying so, you have a very kind face, and I'd love to hear more about your time as a teacher.
That must have been an amazing experience. Younger generations have so much to learn from people who have seen so many changes.
It was a pleasure talking to you. Please take care, and I hope you have a lovely day.

speakerB.en: That's very kind of you, young man. I would be grateful. My knees aren't what they used to be, I'm afraid.
Thank you. Not many people are so polite these days, so it's nice to meet someone who still has good manners.
A teacher! What a coincidence. I used to be a teacher myself for almost forty years before I retired.
That's very sweet of you. I taught history, and I can tell you that the children have changed, but they're just as curious as ever.
You're right. I've seen the world change so much, and I still love telling stories about it, whenever someone has time to listen.
Likewise, and thank you again for the seat. You've made my journey much more pleasant.

scenarios.scenario: Giving constructive criticism tactfully
scenarios.context: A colleague gives feedback on a presentation while keeping a considerate tone.

speakerA.en: I wanted to say that I really admired the way you handled the questions at the end of your presentation. You stayed calm even when the discussion became somewhat heated.
If I may offer one small suggestion, I think the introduction could have been shorter. By the time you reached the main argument, a few people seemed to be losing concentration.
Not at all. In fact, the content itself was excellent. I just feel that with a slightly sharper opening, the whole presentation would have had an even stronger impact.
I'm glad that you see it that way. Some people find criticism difficult to accept, so I always worry about how my comments will be received, however well-intentioned they may be.
That's very generous of you. Perhaps we could look at the slides together this week, and I could share some techniques that have worked for me in the past.
I'd be delighted. Honestly, I learned a great deal from watching you, so it feels good to give something back.

speakerB.en: Thank you, that's very kind of you to say. I was a little nervous, so I'm relieved that it came across as calm. Was there anything that you thought I could improve?
That's a helpful observation, and I suspected as much. I tend to over-explain the background because I'm afraid that people won't understand the argument otherwise.
I appreciate your saying so. It's encouraging to hear that the substance was good, because I put a lot of effort into the analysis. I'll definitely work on the structure next time.
Please don't worry. Feedback is only useful if it's honest, and you've expressed yours in a very respectful way. I'd much rather hear it from you than from a client.
That would be wonderful. I'd really welcome your advice, especially on how to make the opening more engaging without sacrificing the clarity of the message.
It's mutual, then. I'll bring a draft on Thursday. Thank you again for taking the time to give me such thoughtful comments.

scenarios.scenario: Handling a delicate request with courtesy
scenarios.context: A person asks a neighbor to reduce noise without causing offense.

speakerA.en: Good evening. I hope I'm not disturbing you. I wanted to have a quick word about something that's been on my mind, but I'd like to do it in a friendly way.
It's about the music in the evenings. I realize that you have every right to enjoy it in your own home, but the sound seems to carry through the wall, particularly after ten.
I'm so grateful for your understanding. I wouldn't normally mention it, but I've been struggling to sleep, because I have to get up very early for work.
That's very considerate of you. If there's anything that I can do in return, for instance, if you ever need someone to look after your plants while you're away, please just ask.
That would be much appreciated. I should say that I otherwise enjoy living next to you. You've always been a wonderful neighbor, and I wouldn't like this to affect that.
Thanks again. Good night, and please don't hesitate to tell me if there's anything that bothers you about me.

speakerB.en: Not at all, please come in. Is something wrong? You look as though you're trying to find the right words, and I'd rather you were completely open with me.
Oh dear, I'm so sorry. I had no idea that it was so loud. I've been using headphones less than I should have, because I thought the walls were thicker than they are.
I feel terrible that you've had trouble sleeping. Why didn't you say something sooner? I'd have turned it down immediately had I known how much it was affecting you.
That's very kind, but there's no need. It's simply a matter of being considerate. I'll make a point of keeping the volume low after nine, and I'll use headphones for late-night listening.
That's nice to hear, and I feel the same way. I'm glad that you spoke up, and I appreciate the polite way in which you did it. Many people would have simply complained to the landlord.
Good night. And please let me know if it ever happens again. I'd rather hear about it from you than be the cause of a problem.

scenarios.scenario: Declining food politely at a host's home
scenarios.context: A guest tactfully refuses a dish while showing appreciation to the host.

speakerA.en: This looks absolutely wonderful, and the smell is incredible. You must have spent hours in the kitchen, and I'm really touched by the effort you've gone to.
I wonder whether I might ask for a smaller portion of the meat. I'm afraid that I'm not very hungry, as I had a late lunch, and I wouldn't want to waste any of it.
It's not that I don't like it. On the contrary, it's delicious, and I'd be delighted to have a little more later. I just don't want to be uncomfortable before the dessert.
I must admit that I can't eat anything with nuts, so I'd better skip the sauce. I should have mentioned it earlier, and I apologize for not saying anything before you started cooking.
That's very thoughtful of you. I really appreciate it. I can see why your reputation as a cook is so well deserved, and I'd love to have the recipe, if you'd be willing to share it.
Thank you for such a lovely evening. I've enjoyed every moment, and the conversation has been as good as the food.

speakerB.en: Thank you, that's very kind of you. I'm so glad that you came. I hope you're hungry, because I've made far too much, as usual. Please, help yourself.
Of course, take as much or as little as you like. Please don't feel obliged to eat everything. I'd rather you enjoyed it than forced yourself to finish the plate.
That's perfectly fine. We can keep some warm for later, and you can have another helping if you feel like it. There's no hurry, and we have the whole evening ahead of us.
Oh, I'm so sorry. I should have asked in advance. I made a sauce without nuts for you, but I forgot to tell you. It's the one in the small jug on your left, so you can use that one.
I'd be happy to share it. It's my grandmother's recipe, and she never wrote it down, but I'll write it out for you before you leave. It's easier than it looks, as long as you're patient.
It's been a pleasure to have you. We should do this more often. And please, take some leftovers home with you. I insist.

scenarios.scenario: Turning down a colleague's request diplomatically
scenarios.context: An employee declines a colleague's request for a favor without causing offense.

speakerA.en: Hi, do you have a moment? I was hoping you could cover my shift on Saturday, because something has come up with my family, and I really don't know who else to ask.
I know it's a lot to ask at such short notice, and I'd completely understand if you can't. I just thought I'd try, since you've been so helpful in the past.
Of course. Please don't feel bad about it. I'm sure there's a good reason. Perhaps you could tell me which days you'd be available, in case I can arrange something with another colleague?
That's very kind of you. If you don't mind asking Peter, I'd be extremely grateful. I'd be glad to swap shifts with him for the following weekend, so he doesn't lose out.
Thanks. And please let me know if there's anything I can do for you in return. I don't want it to seem as though I'm only asking for favors when I need them.
Thanks again for being so understanding. I appreciate it more than you know.

speakerB.en: Hi. I'm sorry to hear that something has come up. I'd really like to help you, but I'm afraid that I can't this Saturday. I've already made arrangements, and it would be hard to cancel them.

Please don't apologize. It's a perfectly reasonable thing to ask, and I'd normally say yes without hesitation. It's just that this particular weekend is difficult for me, as I have a family commitment too.

I'm free next Saturday and the weekend after that, if that would be any help. For this weekend, though, you might want to ask someone who doesn't have plans, such as Peter, who's often available at short notice.
I'll mention it to him, and see what he says. If you like, I can send him a message on your behalf, and explain the situation, so that you don't have to go through it all again.
There's no need, really. We're a team, and that's what colleagues are for. But if you'd like to bring me a coffee on Monday, I won't say no.
Don't mention it. I hope that everything works out with your family, and that you manage to find a solution quickly.

scenarios.scenario: Thanking a mentor for unexpected support
scenarios.context: A young professional thanks a former manager who quietly helped her win a promotion, and they talk about how much the support meant.

speakerA.en: I wanted to thank you in person. If it weren't for your recommendation, I'd never have been considered for the team leader role. It's not so much that you gave me a chance as that you believed in me when I didn't.

Challenging, to be honest, but I'm learning quickly. If it weren't for the advice you gave me in my first year, I'd probably have given up. I wish I could repay you, although I know you'd never accept anything.

Mostly, although one colleague seems unhappy about my promotion. If it weren't for your example, I'd probably take it personally. It's not so much hostility as disappointment, since he applied for the same position. What would you do?
