That's a good idea. I wish I could have your calm in these situations, since I tend to get defensive. If it weren't for the training course you recommended, I wouldn't even know how to start the conversation.

Very. It's not so much the techniques as the way it made me think about listening. If it weren't for that course, I'd still be talking over people in meetings. I wish I'd taken it years earlier, honestly.

Next month, and I'd love you to come. If it weren't for your encouragement, I wouldn't have volunteered. It's not so much that I'm nervous as that I want to do it justice. I wish I could promise it'll go well.

speakerB.en: That's very kind, but I really didn't do much. It's not so much my recommendation as your own results that made the decision easy. I wish I could take credit, but you earned it. How are you finding the new role?

You'd be right, and there's no need. It's not so much about repayment as about passing it on. I wish I could say I always knew what I was doing, but someone helped me in the same way years ago. Does your team seem supportive?

I'd talk to him privately, and I'd ask for his advice on something specific. It's not so much a matter of winning him over as of showing respect. I wish I could promise it'll work, but it usually helps.

Calm is something you learn, not something you're born with. It's not so much about personality as about practice. I wish I could say I never lost my temper, but I certainly did when I was your age. Was the course useful?

Better late than never, as they say. It's not so much that you were slow as that you waited until you were ready, which is perfectly normal. I wish I could attend your first big presentation, though. When is it?
I'll be there, as long as my schedule allows. It's not so much a favor as a pleasure, so please don't thank me again. If it weren't for people like you, mentoring wouldn't be nearly so rewarding.

scenarios.scenario: Offering sincere praise to a colleague after a setback
scenarios.context: A colleague's project has just been turned down by the board, and a teammate tries to compliment her work sincerely without sounding patronizing.

speakerA.en: I just wanted to say how much I admired your presentation today. Much as I'd like to understand the board's decision, as far as I'm concerned, it was your best work yet, and the result doesn't change that.

I did, and I'd say you answered every difficult question with remarkable composure. Much as I'd like to blame someone, it's not so much your performance as the budget situation that decided things. Everyone in the room could tell.

Honestly, I'd say it was a minor moment. It's not so much that you didn't know the answer as that you admitted it openly, which showed integrity. Much as people like polished answers, they respect honesty even more.

Absolutely, provided you keep the core idea. Much as I'd like to promise a yes, I can tell you that several members said afterwards that they were impressed. It's not so much a rejection as a request for a stronger case.

Several people, including the finance director, who said it's not so much the concept as the cost estimate that needs work. I'd say if you revise the figures, you'll have a good chance. I'd be happy to review them with you.
It's not so much a favor as a pleasure, since I learn a lot from your work. Shall we sit down on Thursday morning and go through the figures together, before you start rewriting anything?

speakerB.en: That's very kind of you, though I'm not sure I deserve it. It's not so much the rejection that bothers me as the feeling that I let the team down. Did you really think the presentation went well?

I appreciate that, although I keep thinking about the question I couldn't answer. As far as I'm concerned, that's where I lost them. Much as I'd like to move on, I can't stop replaying it. Do you think they noticed?

That's a generous way of looking at it. As far as I'm concerned, the proposal was sound, but it's not so much the idea as the timing that was wrong. Would you say it's worth submitting again next year?
I hadn't heard that. As far as I'm concerned, that changes things. Much as I'd prefer an immediate yes, a promising maybe is far better than a flat no. Who told you that, if you don't mind my asking?

I'd really appreciate that. Much as I'd like to do it alone, I think a second pair of eyes would help. As far as I'm concerned, you've already done more than enough by telling me honestly what you thought.
Thursday sounds perfect. I feel much better already, to be honest. Much as I was dreading coming in today, I'm glad I did, and as far as I'm concerned, I couldn't ask for a better colleague.

scenarios.scenario: Complimenting a host while tactfully mentioning an allergy
scenarios.context: A guest at a dinner party praises the host's cooking while tactfully explaining that she cannot eat one of the dishes.

speakerA.en: Thank you so much for inviting us, Helen. Your home is lovely, and the smell from the kitchen is wonderful. It's so kind of you to go to such trouble. May I give you these flowers, and a small bottle of wine?

Actually, yes, and I'm so sorry to mention it so late. I'm allergic to shellfish, but lamb is perfect. Rarely have I looked forward to a meal so much. I didn't want to cause trouble, since you'd already planned the menu.

That's extremely thoughtful, thank you. Soup would be lovely, as long as it's not made with fish stock. On the other hand, I wouldn't dream of making extra work for you. It's very generous of you to adapt the menu.
Just water for now, thank you. Goodness, this soup is delicious, so rich that I could have it as a main course! Seldom have I tasted anything so well seasoned. May I ask what you put in it?

Medium, if that's all right. It looks wonderful. Honestly, it's so tender that I could eat it with a spoon. I can't tell you how much I appreciate this evening, particularly after such a long week at work.

Busy, but good. Thank you for asking, it's so nice of you to remember. Rarely have I felt so welcome in someone's home. As far as I'm concerned, this is the best dinner I've had all year, and I mean it.

speakerB.en: Oh, you shouldn't have, they're beautiful! Please, make yourselves comfortable. Dinner is almost ready. I've made a lamb stew with rosemary, my grandmother's recipe. Is there anything you don't eat, in case I forgot to ask?

Not at all, I'm glad you told me. There's no shellfish in the stew, but the starter has prawns, so let me bring you something else. Nothing would upset me more than your feeling unwell. Would some soup be all right instead?

It's no trouble at all. It's a vegetable soup, so it's perfectly safe. Seldom do guests warn me early enough, so I wasn't prepared, but I'm happy to improvise. Please sit here, next to the window. Would you like something to drink?

Roasted garlic and a little smoked paprika, nothing complicated. It's very kind of you to say so. Now, the stew should be ready. I hope you'll enjoy it, although I'd say it needs another minute. Do you take your meat well done?

I'm delighted, and it's lovely to have you here. Not for a moment did I think the evening would go so smoothly! Tell me, since you mentioned work, how is the new job going? I'd love to hear all about it.
You're far too kind, but I'll take the compliment gladly! Do come again soon, and next time I'll make sure the starter is safe for you. Now, who would like dessert? I've made an apple tart.

scenarios.scenario: Tactfully correcting a senior colleague's mistake in a meeting
scenarios.context: An analyst notices an error in a director's figures and raises it politely, first in the meeting and then in private conversation.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, Mr. Harrison, if I may interject. I hope you don't mind my asking, but I wonder whether the figure on slide six might be slightly different. If I'm not mistaken, last quarter's revenue was 4.2 million, not 4.8.

It comes from the finance report issued in October. It could well be that there are two versions, which would explain the difference. Might it be worth confirming with the finance team before we continue? I'd be inclined to check first.

I happened to have the October report open on my laptop, so the difference stood out. To be honest, I hesitated before speaking, because I didn't want to undermine you. Having said that, I thought accuracy mattered more.

One more, if I may. The growth percentage on slide eight seems to be calculated from a different baseline. It could be that I'm misreading it, but would it be fair to say that it compares two different periods?

Of course, I'd be happy to. If it helps, I could check the formulas this afternoon, so that we have time to fix anything. Might it also be worth adding a note explaining which report the data comes from?

Gladly. I'd be inclined to keep it short, since long checklists are rarely used. Thank you for taking the correction so well, I was a little nervous. It could well have gone differently with someone else.

speakerB.en: Hmm, let me check. You may well be right. I took those numbers from an older report, and I'd hate to present wrong data to the board. Could you tell me where your figure comes from?

Good thinking. Let's pause on that slide and return to it after the break. Thank you for raising it so tactfully, since it would have been embarrassing if the board had spotted it. How did you notice it?

You were right, and I appreciate it. As far as I'm concerned, I'd rather be corrected in the room than afterwards in the press. It seems to me that more people should speak up like that. Is there anything else you spotted?

Let me see. No, you're not misreading it, the baseline is wrong. That's two errors, which is embarrassing. I'm inclined to rebuild the whole table. Would you be willing to review the corrected version before it goes to the board?

Excellent idea, that would prevent confusion. I'd say it's a good habit anyway. And if I'm not mistaken, you're the one who suggested a data checklist last month. Perhaps it's time to adopt it. Would you draft one?

It could, but I'd much rather be right than comfortable. Let's resume after the break, and thank you again. As far as I'm concerned, you handled that with great professionalism, and I'll mention it to the director.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about past travels and experiences abroad
scenarios.context: People share stories and memories of their trips.

speakerA.en: Do you like traveling?
Where do you want to go?
Is it a big city?
Do you travel by plane?
Have you ever been to Italy?
speakerA.fa: تا حالا به ایتالیا رفته‌ای؟

speakerA.en: What's the best place you've ever visited?
speakerA.fa: بهترین جایی که تا حالا دیدی کجاست؟

speakerA.en: I went to Japan last year. It was an amazing experience!
speakerA.fa: پارسال به ژاپن رفتم. تجربه فوق‌العاده‌ای بود!

speakerA.en: The food in Thailand was incredibly tasty and diverse.
speakerA.fa: غذاهای تایلند فوق‌العاده خوشمزه و متنوع بود.

speakerA.en: I'd love to go hiking in the Alps someday. The scenery looks breathtaking.
speakerA.fa: دوست دارم یه روزی تو کوه‌های آلپ پیاده‌روی کنم. منظره‌اش نفس‌گیر به نظر میاد.

speakerA.en: How did you find the people and culture in Mexico?
speakerA.fa: مردم و فرهنگ مکزیک رو چطور دیدی؟

speakerB.en: Yes, I love traveling.
I want to go to Italy.
Yes, it is. It is very beautiful.
No, I travel by train.
No, but I've always wanted to go there.
speakerB.fa: نه، اما همیشه دوست داشتم برم اونجا.

speakerB.en: That's hard to choose! Maybe the beaches in Bali.
speakerB.fa: انتخابش سخته! شاید سواحل بالی.

speakerB.en: Wow, I've heard so much about Japan. What did you like most?
speakerB.fa: واو، کلی درباره ژاپن شنیدم. بیشتر از همه چی رو دوست داشتی؟

speakerB.en: I've been to Thailand too! The street food was my favorite.
speakerB.fa: منم به تایلند رفته‌م! غذای خیابونی بیشتر از همه دوست داشتم.

speakerB.en: I have to say, the Swiss Alps are unforgettable. You should definitely go!
speakerB.fa: باید بگم، آلپ سوئیس فراموش‌نشدنیه. حتماً باید بری!

speakerB.en: They were very friendly and welcoming. The food was a bit spicy for me though.
speakerB.fa: خیلی دوستانه و خونگرم بودن. غذاها برام یه کم تند بودن.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a trip
scenarios.context: Two friends plan a trip together.

speakerA.en: Let's go on a trip.
Let's go to the sea.
We can go in July.
It's five days.
Have you decided where we should stay?
Does the price include breakfast?
How are we going to get there?
Let's book the tickets today before the price goes up.

speakerB.en: Good idea! Where do we go?
Great. When do we go?
OK. How long is the trip?
That sounds nice.
I found a small hotel near the beach. It's not expensive.
Yes, and there's free Wi-Fi too.
We can take the train. It's faster and cheaper than driving.
Good idea. I'll do it online now.

scenarios.scenario: Packing a suitcase
scenarios.context: A traveler packs before a trip.

speakerA.en: Is your suitcase ready?
Do you have your passport?
Take a warm jacket.
It is a little cold at night.
What's the weather going to be like there?
Should I take an umbrella just in case?
Have you packed your charger and your tickets?
Don't forget to check the weight of your suitcase.

speakerB.en: Not yet. I need my shoes.
Yes, it's in my bag.
OK. Is it cold there?
Thanks. I'll take it.
It will be sunny during the day, but cool in the evening.
Yes, a small one. It could rain on Sunday.
Not yet. Thanks for reminding me.
Right. The airline only allows twenty kilos.

scenarios.scenario: At the airport
scenarios.context: A traveler checks in at the airport.

speakerA.en: Hello. Here is my ticket.
Here you are.
Yes, I have one bag.
Where is the gate?
Excuse me, which counter is for the flight to Madrid?
Could I have a window seat, please?
What time does boarding start?
Is the flight on time?

speakerB.en: Thank you. Your passport, please.
Do you have a bag?
Please put it here.
It's gate number five.
It's counter twelve, on the right.
Of course. Seat 14A is available.
It starts at 9:40. Please be at the gate by 9:30.
Yes, but please check the screens for any changes.

scenarios.scenario: Visiting a new place
scenarios.context: Two tourists look around a new town.

speakerA.en: This town is beautiful.
Look at that old church.
Are you hungry?
I like this trip.
Is it far to the old town from here?
Do you think we need a guide?
What time does the museum close?
Let's take a photo in front of the fountain.

speakerB.en: Yes, I love it.
It's very nice. Let's take a photo.
Yes, I am. Let's eat.
Me too. It's great.
No, it's about fifteen minutes on foot.
It might be a good idea. We can learn more about the history.
It closes at six, so we should hurry.
Great idea. Smile!

scenarios.scenario: Buying a souvenir
scenarios.context: A tourist buys a gift in a small shop.

speakerA.en: How much is this hat?
It's nice. I'll take it.
It's a gift for my mother.
Thank you. Goodbye!
Do you have anything cheaper than this?
I'll take two of them. Can you wrap them as gifts?
Do you accept credit cards?
Could I have a bag, please?

speakerB.en: It's ten dollars.
Thank you. Anything else?
She will like it.
Goodbye. Have a nice trip.
Yes, these magnets are only three dollars each.
Certainly. It will take a minute.
Yes, we do. Please enter your PIN.
Of course. Here's your receipt. Enjoy your stay!

scenarios.scenario: Sharing trip photos
scenarios.context: A person shows photos from a trip.

speakerA.en: Look at my photos.
It's a beach in Spain.
Yes, it was very hot.
Yes, every day!
Who's that next to you in this photo?
What was the best part of the trip?
Would you go there again?
Can you send me these photos?

speakerB.en: Wow! Where is this?
It's very nice. Was it hot?
Did you swim?
You had a great holiday.
That's our tour guide. He was very funny.
I loved the local food, especially the seafood.
Definitely. I'd like to stay longer next time.
Sure. I'll send them to you tonight.

scenarios.scenario: Telling a friend about a recent trip
scenarios.context: A woman describes her vacation to a friend.

speakerA.en: How was your trip to Portugal? You've been talking about it for months.
Where did you stay? Did you visit more than one city?
Was there anything you didn't like?
I'd love to go there. Would you recommend going in summer?

speakerB.en: It was even better than I expected. The food was incredible, and the people were so friendly.
We spent four days in Lisbon and three in Porto. Lisbon was busier, but Porto felt more relaxed.
The streets are very steep, so my legs hurt every night. But it was worth it for the views.
I'd go in spring or autumn instead. In July it was crowded and extremely hot.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a backpacking trip
scenarios.context: Two friends plan a long trip through Asia.

speakerA.en: I've been looking at flights to Bangkok. Prices are lower in the autumn.
I'd say about a month. That gives us enough time to visit Thailand, Vietnam, and Cambodia.
If we stay in hostels and eat local food, we can manage on about forty dollars a day.
I'd book only the first few nights and stay flexible after that.

speakerB.en: That's good to know. How long do you think we should stay in total?
It sounds amazing, but I'm worried about the budget. How much will we need?
That's reasonable. Should we book our accommodation in advance or just decide as we go?
Good idea. I'll check whether we need any vaccinations before we leave.

scenarios.scenario: Having trouble while traveling
scenarios.context: A traveler tells a friend about a problem during a trip.

speakerA.en: You won't believe what happened at the airport. My luggage didn't arrive.
I filled in a form at the lost luggage desk, and they promised to deliver it to my hotel.
Only clothes, but I had to buy a few things so I'd have something to wear.
Yes, two days later. The suitcase was fine, but one of the wheels was broken.

speakerB.en: Oh no! What did you do?
Did you have anything important in the suitcase?
That's annoying. Has it arrived yet?
At least you got it back. Did the airline offer any compensation?

scenarios.scenario: Recounting a cultural misunderstanding abroad
scenarios.context: A traveler tells a friend about an awkward moment on a trip.

speakerA.en: Did I ever tell you about the time I offended my host in Japan without realizing it?
I stuck my chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice, which apparently resembles a funeral ritual.
She was too polite to say anything, but I noticed the atmosphere change. Someone explained it afterwards.
Profusely, and she laughed it off, saying visitors couldn't be expected to know every custom.

speakerB.en: No, but I'm intrigued. What on earth did you do?
Oh dear. How did your host react? Was she very upset?
Did you apologize? I'd have been mortified.
That's a relief. It shows how much there is to learn when you step outside your own culture.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing up a risky travel destination
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss whether to visit a region with a travel advisory.

speakerA.en: I've always wanted to visit that region, but the government advises against nonessential travel.
True, but they tend to be cautious. Tourists go there every year without any trouble.
I hadn't considered that. It's a significant factor, especially if there were a medical emergency.
Possibly. I'd have to do more research to find an alternative that offers the same kind of landscape.

speakerB.en: I'd think carefully about it. Those warnings are usually issued for good reasons.
That may be so, but if something went wrong, your insurance might not cover you.
Couldn't you find somewhere similar that carries less risk, at least for your first trip?
Take your time. The place isn't going anywhere, and the situation might improve in a year or two.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing lessons learned from living abroad
scenarios.context: A returning expatriate reflects on a year overseas.

speakerA.en: Now that you're back, what would you say was the most valuable thing you gained from a year abroad?
Such as what? I'm curious which assumptions were challenged.
Did you find it difficult to readjust to the pace of life here?
I imagine it gave you a new appreciation for both ways of living.

speakerB.en: Probably a sense of perspective. Things I once took for granted turned out to be quite unusual.
The idea that everyone is in a hurry, for one. In the south, lunch can last two hours, and nobody frets about it.
At first, yes. I felt strangely impatient with the rush, and I still do.
It did, though I'd be lying if I said I didn't miss the long lunches.

scenarios.scenario: Replacing a lost passport abroad
scenarios.context: A traveler reports a lost passport at an embassy and asks about emergency documents.

speakerA.en: I'm afraid I've lost my passport, and my flight home leaves in three days. I'm told you can issue some kind of emergency document.
I did this morning. They gave me a form, though it's in the local language, and I'm not sure it will suffice.
I have a photocopy of my old passport and my flight confirmation. Would those be adequate?
That's all I need. How long will the process take, and what is the fee?

speakerB.en: We can. First, did you report the loss to the local police? We'll need a copy of the report.
That's fine; we'll accept it. You'll also need two passport photos, proof of citizenship, and details of your travel plans.
They'll help considerably. The emergency document is valid for a single journey, so it will only be good for your return home.
Usually two working days, and the fee is sixty dollars. I'll prioritize your application, given your departure date.

scenarios.scenario: Debating the impact of tourism on local communities
scenarios.context: Two travelers discuss whether mass tourism harms the places they love.

speakerA.en: Having seen how crowded the old town was, I can't help wondering whether we're destroying the very places we come to admire.
Depend on it, perhaps, but at a cost. Rents have soared, and long-standing residents are being priced out of their own neighborhoods.
I'm not suggesting a boycott, merely more responsible choices: staying in locally owned guesthouses, visiting off-season, and spreading our spending around.
Perhaps not alone, but regulation tends to follow changing attitudes. Someone has to go first.

speakerB.en: I share that unease, but local people depend on us. In many of these towns, tourism is the only thing keeping the economy afloat.
That's a serious problem, and I don't dismiss it. But boycotting those places would hurt precisely the people we're hoping to protect.
Those seem like practical steps. Whether individual choices can offset the scale of the problem, I'm less sure.
A fair point. I suppose I could start by not adding my own photo to the thousand taken at that fountain.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a sustainable, off-the-beaten-path trip
scenarios.context: A traveler asks an agent to design a low-impact trip away from the usual tourist routes.

speakerA.en: I'm looking for a trip that avoids the standard tourist circuit. I want to see something authentic without leaving a heavy footprint.
That sounds promising. How does the community model work in practice? I'd like to be sure the money really reaches the locals.
I'd appreciate that. What about getting around? I'd prefer to avoid domestic flights if at all possible.
Slow travel appeals to me. I'd rather arrive somewhere having earned it.

speakerB.en: That's increasingly common among our clients. Have you considered the highlands in the north? They're rarely visited, and several villages run community-based lodging.
Most of the income goes directly to the families hosting you, and a portion funds a village development scheme. I can share the details of how it's audited.
There's a scenic overnight train, followed by a short bus ride. It's slower, but it adds to the experience rather than detracting from it.
Then you'll enjoy this route. I'll put together a draft itinerary and send it over by the end of the week.

scenarios.scenario: Recounting a trip that didn't go to plan
scenarios.context: Two friends laugh about a journey full of mishaps that turned out memorable.

speakerA.en: I still can't decide whether our trip to Morocco was a disaster or the best holiday I've ever had. Probably both.
True, though I could have done without sleeping in a station because we'd misread the train timetable.
Remarkable how often the unplanned turns out to be the part worth remembering. I'd have missed all of it with a rigid schedule.
I'll drink to that. Where shall we get lost next time?

speakerB.en: It's the disasters that make the stories. Nobody has ever dined out on a flawless itinerary where nothing went wrong.
And yet that was where we met the old gentleman who shared his tea and taught us how to haggle properly.
That's what separates a traveler from a tourist, I suppose. One adapts to circumstance, and the other complains about it.
Let's pick somewhere without a guidebook and see what the place makes of us.

scenarios.scenario: Describing culture shock after relocating abroad
scenarios.context: A returning expatriate reflects on the disorientation of adapting to another way of life.

speakerA.en: The first few months were harder than I'd anticipated. It wasn't the language so much as the unspoken rules that tripped me up.
How close to stand, when to speak up in a meeting, whether a compliment is sincere or merely courtesy. Everything felt faintly miscalibrated.
Exactly. Eventually, I realized I'd stopped translating in my head and had begun simply to understand.
Profoundly. Things I'd taken for granted suddenly seemed arbitrary, and I could see my own habits as a visitor might.

speakerB.en: Such as?
That's the essence of culture shock. You lose the ability to read the room, and it's exhausting in a way that's hard to explain.
That's a rare milestone. Did you find that it changed how you saw your own culture on your return?
That's the unexpected gift of living abroad. You acquire a second pair of eyes you can never quite put away.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing ethical concerns about tourism's impact
scenarios.context: Two travelers discuss whether their trips harm the places they love.

speakerA.en: I've been wrestling with the ethics of travel lately. We cherish these places, yet our presence may be gradually eroding them.
Take that fishing village we visited. It was enchanting, but the locals now seem to live primarily for the benefit of visitors.
A fair rejoinder. I suppose the question is how to travel more responsibly, rather than whether to travel at all.
Modest steps, but better than complacency. I'll try to be a guest rather than a consumer.

speakerB.en: It's an uncomfortable paradox. The same attention that sustains local economies can also overwhelm fragile communities.
There's truth in that, though I'd hesitate to romanticize the alternative. Many of them are glad of the income, and they've chosen it.
Staying in locally owned guesthouses, avoiding peak seasons, and spending money where it genuinely reaches the community would be a start.
A distinction worth bearing in mind. The best travelers I know leave a place slightly better than they found it.

scenarios.scenario: Booking a hotel for a vacation
scenarios.context: A traveler books a hotel room for a holiday.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'd like to book a room for next month.
From the tenth to the fifteenth of June, for two people.
Is breakfast included in the price?
That sounds good. I'll take it.

speakerB.en: Certainly. For which dates?
We have a double room with a sea view. It's ninety dollars a night.
Yes, breakfast is served from seven to ten.
Great. Can I have your name and phone number, please?

scenarios.scenario: Passing through passport control
scenarios.context: A traveler answers questions at the airport border.

speakerA.en: Good morning. May I see your passport, please?
What is the purpose of your visit?
How long are you going to stay?
Thank you. Enjoy your stay.

speakerB.en: Here you are.
I'm here on holiday.
For ten days. I'm staying at a hotel in the city center.
Thanks. Where can I collect my luggage?

scenarios.scenario: Describing a trip that did not go as planned
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about a holiday that had unexpected problems.

speakerA.en: How was your trip to Greece? You said you'd send photos.
Oh no, what happened?
That sounds stressful. Did they find the luggage?
Well, at least the rest of the holiday went well.

speakerB.en: It was wonderful in the end, but the first two days were a disaster.
Our flight was cancelled, and the airline lost one of our suitcases.
Yes, it arrived two days later, so we had to buy a few things in the meantime.
It did. The beaches were amazing, and I'd go back tomorrow.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a road trip together
scenarios.context: Two friends plan a road trip along the coast.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking about a road trip along the coast this summer.
About a week. We could stop in a different town every night.
Good point. Who's going to do the driving?
Great. I'll make a list of places worth visiting.

speakerB.en: That sounds fantastic. How many days are you thinking about?
We should book the accommodation in advance, though. It gets busy in July.
We can take turns every two hours so nobody gets too tired.
And I'll check the budget, so we don't spend too much.

scenarios.scenario: Telling a friend about a trip you've just taken
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about a recent holiday that did not go exactly as planned.

speakerA.en: You're back! How was your trip to Portugal? I've been wondering about it all week.
That's great, but I heard that you had some problems with the weather. Was it really that bad?
Oh no. If I had been you, I think I would have stayed inside all day and just read a book.
At least the food made up for it. Did you manage to try the local dishes people keep recommending?
Now I'm hungry just thinking about it. Would you go back, or would you rather try somewhere new next year?
That sounds like a good plan. If you ever need a travel partner, you know where to find me.

speakerB.en: It was fantastic overall, although a few things went wrong. I've never walked so much in my life!
It rained for three days straight, so we couldn't visit the beaches, which were the main reason we'd gone there.
We did something like that, but by the third day we were bored, so we explored the old town in the rain.
Definitely. We ate grilled sardines at a tiny restaurant that had been recommended by our hotel owner, and it was the best meal of the trip.
I'd go back in summer, when the weather is better, but I'd also like to see Greece, which I've always wanted to visit.
I'll remember that. Maybe we can plan something together once we've both saved enough money.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a trip and comparing destinations
scenarios.context: Two friends compare two possible destinations for a holiday.

speakerA.en: I've been looking at flights for our trip. We could either go to Italy or spend the week in Turkey.
Italy is more expensive, but I've heard the museums and architecture are incredible. What do you think?
That's a good point. If we chose Turkey, we'd have more money left to spend on activities and food.
I'd prefer to stay in one city rather than travel around, because moving from place to place is exhausting.
Then let's choose Istanbul. Should we book the flights now, or wait until the prices drop?
You're right. Let's check the prices again on Friday, and if they haven't changed, we'll book straight away.

speakerB.en: Both sound great. Which one would you choose if money weren't an issue?
True, but Turkey has history and beautiful scenery too, and it's much cheaper, especially for accommodation and meals.
Exactly. We could even afford a boat trip along the coast, which I've always dreamed of doing.
I agree. We could spend four days in Istanbul and then take a short flight to the coast if we have time.
Prices usually go up as the date gets closer, so it might be risky to wait too long.
Good plan. In the meantime, I'll look for a hotel in the center, so that we can walk to most places.

scenarios.scenario: Dealing with a delayed flight and missing luggage
scenarios.context: A passenger speaks to an airline employee after a long delay and lost baggage.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, my flight was delayed for five hours, and now my suitcase hasn't arrived on the carousel.
It's a large black suitcase with a red ribbon on the handle. I've checked in at the desk, but nobody could find it.
I need my medication and some important documents that are inside it. Can you tell me how long it might take?
I'm staying at the Grand Hotel for a week. Will someone deliver the suitcase there when it's found?
I see. In the meantime, is there any compensation for the things I'll have to buy because of the delay?
Alright, I'll keep all my receipts. Thank you for your patience. I know it's not your fault personally.

speakerB.en: I'm very sorry about the inconvenience. Let me take down your details and see what I can find out.
Thank you. I've entered a report in the system, and your bag will be traced as soon as possible.
Normally, lost luggage is found within forty-eight hours. Since your suitcase contains medication, I'll mark it as urgent.
Yes, we'll deliver it free of charge to your hotel as soon as it arrives. We'll also call you to confirm the time.
Yes, if you keep your receipts, we can refund essential items up to a hundred euros. You'll need to fill out this form.
That's very understanding of you. Here's a reference number, and you can call this line at any time for updates.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a local for advice about hidden places
scenarios.context: A tourist asks a resident where to go to avoid the crowds.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, do you live here? I'm visiting for the first time, and I'm trying to find somewhere that isn't full of tourists.
I've already seen the cathedral and the main square, which were beautiful, but it was so crowded that I couldn't enjoy it.
That sounds perfect. How far is it from here, and is it easy to get there by public transport?
And what about food? I'd love to try something traditional, but I don't want to end up in a restaurant that's too expensive.
I'll go there tonight. Is there anything else that you think I shouldn't miss before I leave?
Thank you so much. You've been incredibly helpful, and I hope I'll have the chance to come back one day.

speakerB.en: Yes, I've lived here all my life. Welcome! Many visitors only see the center, but there's so much more to discover.
I know exactly what you mean. If you want a quieter experience, you should visit the old fishing village, which is only a few kilometers away.
You can take bus number nine, which leaves every twenty minutes from the station. The ride takes about half an hour.
There's a small family restaurant by the harbor, where the fish is caught the same morning. It's cheap, and the owner is very friendly.
Yes, go to the viewpoint behind the village at sunset. Most tourists don't know about it, but the view over the sea is breathtaking.
It was my pleasure. Enjoy the rest of your stay, and if you get lost, just ask anyone. People here are always happy to help.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing the best and worst travel experiences
scenarios.context: Two friends compare the best and worst moments from their travels.

speakerA.en: Have you ever had a trip that went completely wrong? I'm trying to decide whether my story is the worst one.
A few years ago, I was traveling through Thailand when my bag was stolen with my passport and wallet inside.
It was stressful, but strangely, it turned out to be a great experience. A family let me stay with them until my new documents arrived.
That's true. Since then, I've always believed that traveling teaches you more about people than about places. What about you?
That sounds like a dream. Did you ever get over the fear of heights, or did you only manage to do it once?
I'd love to try that someday. Maybe next year we could plan something adventurous together.

speakerB.en: Plenty of times! The worst one was when I was stuck in an airport for two days because of a snowstorm.
That's awful! What did you do? If it had happened to me, I think I would have panicked completely.
What a kind thing to do. People can surprise you when you need help the most, and those are the memories that last.
I agree. My best trip was hiking in Nepal, where I met a group of strangers who became close friends by the end of the week.
I'm still afraid of heights, but I've learned to deal with it. The view from the top made every difficult step worth it.
I'd be up for that. We should choose a place neither of us has been to before, so that we can discover it together.

scenarios.scenario: Booking a guided tour and asking about cancellation
scenarios.context: A traveler asks a tour agent about a day trip and the booking conditions.

speakerA.en: Hello. I saw your advertisement for the day trip to the mountains, and I'd like to know more about it.
How long does the tour last, and what's included in the price? I'd like to know whether lunch is provided.
That sounds reasonable. What happens if the weather is bad on the day? I wouldn't want to lose my money.
Good. And if I had to cancel for personal reasons, would I be able to get a refund, or only a voucher?
That seems fair. I'd like to book two places for Saturday, please. Do you need any information from me?
Thank you. I'll pay with my card now. Could you send me a confirmation, including the meeting point and the time?

speakerB.en: Hello, and thank you for your interest. The trip lasts about nine hours, and it includes transport, a guide, and a picnic lunch.
The price is sixty euros per person. Entrance to the national park is also included, but drinks and souvenirs are not.
If the weather is too dangerous, we'll cancel the tour, and you'll receive a full refund or the chance to choose another date.
If you cancel at least forty-eight hours in advance, you'll get a full refund. After that, we can only offer a voucher, I'm afraid.
I'll just need your name, phone number, and email address. Are you traveling alone, or will someone be joining you?
Of course. The confirmation will arrive within a few minutes. We'll meet in front of the tourist office at eight o'clock sharp.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the impact of mass tourism
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss the benefits and drawbacks of tourism for popular destinations.

speakerA.en: Have you read about the protests in Barcelona? Residents are complaining that tourism has pushed up rents and made the city unaffordable for local people.
I understand their frustration, but I'd say we shouldn't overlook the economic benefits, since millions of jobs depend on the industry in one way or another.
That's undeniable, though it's worth asking who actually benefits. Large hotel chains and platforms often take most of the profit, whereas ordinary residents bear the costs.
I suppose one solution would be to limit the number of visitors, as some places have already done, although that might simply make travel more expensive and exclusive.
Perhaps a better approach would be to encourage people to visit lesser-known areas, which would spread both the income and the pressure on local infrastructure.
I couldn't agree more. If we, as travelers, were more willing to stay a little longer and explore beyond the famous sights, we would probably enjoy the trip more as well.

speakerB.en: I did. It's a complicated issue, because the city has depended on tourism for decades, and yet many inhabitants feel that they've lost control over their own neighborhoods.
That's a valid argument. Entire regions, especially in the south, would struggle to survive without visitors, so a sudden reduction could have serious social consequences.
Precisely. The question is how to ensure that the profits are distributed more fairly, for example through taxes that are invested directly in housing and public services.
It's a delicate balance. In Venice, an entrance fee has been introduced for day visitors, and although it's controversial, it has encouraged some tourists to reconsider.
That's a promising idea, and some governments are already supporting it by promoting rural destinations. Not everyone wants to stand in a queue for three hours to see one painting.
Well said. Traveling responsibly isn't about giving up the pleasure of discovering new places, but about being more aware of the effect that we have on the places we visit.

scenarios.scenario: Recounting a culture-shock experience
scenarios.context: A person describes the surprises and difficulties of adapting to life in another country.

speakerA.en: When I first moved to Japan, I was completely unprepared for how different everyday life would be, even though I had read several books about the culture.
The language was the most obvious barrier, but what really caught me off guard were the unwritten rules, like not talking on the phone on the train.
I remember being told off by a stranger for something as trivial as blowing my nose in public, which I hadn't realized was considered impolite.
At first, I felt isolated, and I wondered whether I had made a mistake. If I had known how long the adjustment would take, I might have hesitated.
Gradually, though, I began to appreciate the politeness and the sense of consideration for others, which I now miss whenever I return to my own country.
I'd recommend it to anyone, as long as they're prepared to be patient with themselves. It changes the way you see your own culture, too.

speakerB.en: That must have been quite an adjustment. How long did it take before you started to feel comfortable, and what helped you the most?
That's fascinating. People often underestimate how much of a culture is made up of small, invisible habits that locals take for granted and never explain.
That sounds embarrassing, but it's also a good example of how perceptions of politeness vary. In many places, the same gesture would be perfectly normal.
That's understandable. Many expatriates describe a similar low point after the initial excitement fades, and it's often followed by a period of real growth.
It's interesting that you say that. Many people discover that living abroad makes them more critical of their own habits, but also more grateful for certain things at home.
Well, it sounds like it was a life-changing experience, and you've clearly become more open-minded as a result of everything you went through.

scenarios.scenario: Talking a travel agent through a complex itinerary
scenarios.context: A customer plans a multi-stop trip and asks about flexibility and insurance.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'm planning a three-week trip through South America, and I'd like some advice on how to organize the flights and accommodation.
I'd like to start in Peru, then travel to Bolivia and Chile, and finish in Argentina. I'm hoping to avoid backtracking, which would waste a lot of time.
That sounds sensible. However, I'd like to keep my schedule fairly flexible, because I'm not sure how long I'll want to stay in each place.
In that case, I'd rather book only the international flights now, and arrange the rest as I go. Would that cost significantly more in the long run?
I see. And what about insurance? I've been told that medical costs can be extremely high abroad, particularly if you need to be flown home.
Thank you, that's very helpful. I'll think it over this weekend, and I'll let you know my decision by Monday.

speakerB.en: Good morning, and welcome. That's an ambitious and wonderful itinerary. Do you already have specific dates in mind, or is the timing still open?
Your route makes sense geographically, and it follows the way most travelers choose to go. Flying between these cities can be expensive, so we should look at some overland options too.
Flexibility is certainly an advantage, but it can be costly if you book at the last minute, particularly during the high season, when buses and flights often sell out well in advance.
A mixed approach is quite common. You'd book the long-haul flights now, and leave a few connections open. Prices would vary, but you'd have the freedom you're looking for.
You're right to ask. I'd strongly recommend a comprehensive policy, covering medical treatment, evacuation, and trip cancellation. It's inexpensive compared with the risks involved.
Of course. Take your time. I'll put together a draft plan with approximate costs, so you can compare the options before you commit to anything.

scenarios.scenario: Replacing a lost passport at a consulate
scenarios.context: A traveler explains a lost passport to a consular officer and discusses the process.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I've lost my passport, and I need to travel home in four days. I'm hoping that you can tell me what the quickest way of getting a replacement is.
I realized it was missing yesterday, after I returned from a day trip. I've retraced my steps, and I've reported it to the local police, who gave me this report.
I do have a photocopy of the main page, which I keep on my phone, as well as my national ID card and my flight reservation. Will they be enough?
Four days is very tight. Is there any option for an emergency travel document, if the regular passport can't be issued in time?
That's a relief. How much does it cost, and do I need to bring new photographs, or can they be taken here at the consulate?
Thank you so much. I was starting to panic, but you've explained everything very clearly. I'll be back at two with the photographs.

speakerB.en: Good morning. I'm sorry to hear that, but don't worry. It happens more often than you'd think, and we have procedures for this. When did you last see it, and have you reported it?
That's good. The police report is essential, since it proves that you've informed the authorities. Do you have any other form of identification, such as a copy of the passport or an ID card?
Yes, those will help us to confirm your identity quickly. We'll also need to verify your details with the authorities at home, which usually takes a day or two.
Yes, we can issue an emergency travel document, which is valid only for a direct return journey. If everything goes smoothly, you could have it by Thursday afternoon.
The fee is fifty euros, payable by card. We can take your photographs on the premises for an extra five, so you won't need to find a studio.
You're welcome. Come back this afternoon with the completed form, and I'll make sure that your file is treated as a priority, given your departure date.

scenarios.scenario: Comparing a package holiday with independent travel
scenarios.context: Two colleagues planning a two-week trip debate whether to book an organized package or to travel independently.

speakerA.en: I'm torn between booking a package tour and planning everything myself. Much as I'd like the freedom of independent travel, I'm worried about the details. Had I known how complicated it would be, I might have asked a travel agent from the start.

Last time I traveled independently, and I wish I hadn't, since we missed a connection and lost a whole day. If only we'd booked a flexible ticket, we'd have saved a lot of money. On the other hand, we discovered a lovely village by accident.

I'd say that's the real question. If only I could be sure I'd stay calm, I'd go alone. Much as I trust myself, I'd hate to be stranded without a plan, especially in a country where I don't speak the language.
I haven't, but it's a good idea. If only more agencies advertised that option, I'd have found it sooner. Much as I'd like to save money, I'd pay extra for a guide who could handle the logistics.

Portugal and Morocco, although I'm leaning towards Morocco. If only I'd learned some Arabic or French, I'd feel more confident. Much as I enjoy a challenge, I think the language barrier might be too much without help.

Probably not, but I'd pay for a single room, as long as the price isn't ridiculous. If only I'd asked you sooner, I wouldn't have wasted a week going back and forth. Shall we look at some itineraries together tonight?

speakerB.en: I'd say it depends on what you want from the trip. If you prefer comfort, a package makes sense, although it can feel restrictive. What did you do on your last holiday, and what did you enjoy most about it?

That's the trade-off, isn't it? Much as I love surprises, I'd rather avoid the stress. Had I known how much time planning takes, I'd have joined an organized tour on my last trip. What would you do if something went wrong abroad?

Then perhaps a compromise would work, such as a package for the first week and independent travel for the second. Had I known that was possible, I'd have tried it years ago. Have you looked at companies that offer flexible itineraries?

I'd say the cost is rarely the problem; it's the lack of choice. On the other hand, a guide can take you to places you'd never find alone. Had I known that, I'd have booked one on my first trip abroad. Which countries are you considering?

In that case, I'd say a small group tour with a local guide is your best bet. Had I known how helpful guides are, I'd have used one on my first trip too. Would you be comfortable sharing a room with a stranger?

Gladly. Much as I'd like to say I'll be impartial, I'm already tempted to join you. Had I known you were considering Morocco, I'd have saved my leave days for the same dates. Let's compare notes this evening.

scenarios.scenario: Asking an innkeeper about a hike to a mountain village
scenarios.context: A traveler staying at a small inn asks the owner for directions and advice about a day hike to a nearby village.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'd appreciate it if you could tell me about the walk to the old village in the next valley. I've heard the views are stunning, but I'm not sure how long it takes or whether it's difficult.
A little, but never alone. I'd appreciate it if you could suggest what to bring, since the weather seems unpredictable. Should it rain heavily, is there somewhere to shelter along the way?
That's sensible advice. I'd appreciate it if you could also tell me whether the village has a café or somewhere to eat, as I'd prefer not to carry too much food with me.
Wonderful. I'd appreciate it if you could mark the route on this map for me, in case my phone loses signal. Should I leave early, or is it better to start after breakfast?
That's very helpful. I'd appreciate it if you could give me a rough idea of the return times for the bus, in case I'm too tired to walk back the whole way.
Perfect. I'd appreciate it if you could keep some dinner for me, should I be late. And thank you for taking the time to explain everything so patiently. I'm really looking forward to the walk.

speakerB.en: Good morning. It takes about four hours each way, and it isn't difficult, although the last stretch is steep. Once you've passed the stone bridge, you can't miss the path, because it's marked with red and white stripes. Have you hiked in the mountains before?

Yes, there's a small hut halfway up. Once you've reached the wooden cross at the top of the first hill, you can't miss it, because it stands right beside the path. Should the clouds come down, I'd turn back, though.

There's a small guesthouse that serves excellent soup. Once you've crossed the main square, you can't miss it, since it's the only building with a green door. Should it be closed, the bakery next door usually sells sandwiches.

I'd leave by eight, so you're back before dark. Should you start later, you'd have to hurry on the way down. Once you've left the village, the path follows the river, and you can't miss the signposts.

There's a bus at five and another at seven, although the later one doesn't run on Sundays. Should you take the five o'clock, you'll be back here by six. Once you've reached the bus stop, you can't miss the timetable on the wall.
Of course, I'll leave something warm on the stove. Should you need anything, just ring the bell. Once you've seen the view from the top, you'll understand why people come back every year. Enjoy it.

scenarios.scenario: Rebooking after a cancelled flight
scenarios.context: A business traveler asks an airline agent for help after his evening flight is cancelled and he must reach a meeting the next morning.

speakerA.en: Good evening. I've just been told that my flight to Lisbon has been cancelled, and to be honest, I'm quite shocked. I'd have thought that someone would have warned me earlier. What are my options?

Business. I have an important meeting at nine tomorrow morning, so I need to arrive tonight if possible. Had I known earlier, I'd have taken the train to another airport. Is there any alternative flight this evening?

The six-thirty would be too tight, since the meeting is at nine and I'd need to get through the city. I'd have thought you'd have a partner airline offering something earlier. Whichever option I take, can you guarantee a seat?

In that case, I'll take the eleven o'clock. However long the wait, I'd rather arrive tonight. What about compensation, though? I'd have thought that a last-minute cancellation entitles passengers to something.

That's helpful. Should I submit a form online, or is there a counter where I can do it? To be honest, I'd rather deal with it tonight than chase it for weeks. Whichever is quicker, I'm happy to follow it.

An aisle seat would be perfect, thank you. I must say, you've been very helpful, considering how stressful the evening must be for you. As far as I'm concerned, good service matters most in moments like this. Thank you.

speakerB.en: I'm very sorry, sir. The flight was cancelled due to a technical fault, and we've been trying to contact all passengers. May I see your booking reference, and may I ask whether you're traveling for business or leisure?

Let me check. There's a flight at eleven, which would land at one in the morning, but it's almost full. Had it been this afternoon, we'd have had far more choice. Alternatively, I can put you on the first flight tomorrow, at six-thirty.

I can guarantee the eleven o'clock, as long as you check in within the next twenty minutes. And you're entitled to a meal voucher, and to a hotel if you'd prefer to travel tomorrow. Should you choose the late flight, we'll also arrange transport at the other end.

Under the regulations, you're entitled to a refund or rebooking, and, since the cancellation happened with less than two weeks' notice, possibly compensation too. Had the cause been weather, that wouldn't apply, but a technical fault is different. I'll note it on your file.

The quickest is online, and I'll email you the link. Here is your new boarding pass, and a voucher for dinner at any restaurant in the terminal. Would you like me to reserve an aisle seat? I'd have thought you'd prefer one for a late flight.

That's kind of you to say. Please keep your boarding pass safe, and I do hope your meeting goes well. Had we known earlier, we'd have contacted you immediately. Have a pleasant flight, sir, and again, our apologies.

scenarios.scenario: Describing a memorable volunteering experience abroad
scenarios.context: A traveler who has just returned from volunteering in a mountain village tells a friend what the experience was like.

speakerA.en: I heard you've just come back from volunteering in Nepal. To be honest, I'd love to hear everything. What made you decide to go, and was it what you expected?
That sounds intense. What exactly did you do there? I'd imagine that living in a village without speaking the language must have been challenging, since you'd have struggled to communicate.
That must have been a relief. Did you ever feel lonely? I'd say being far from family for two months is hard, although the children must have kept you busy. How did you cope?

That's a lovely habit. On the other hand, did you ever question whether volunteering really makes a difference? I read that short visits can sometimes do more harm than good, so I'd like to know your view.
That's a mature way to see it. What was the most memorable moment, in your opinion? I'd imagine there were so many that it's hard to choose.
I'm getting emotional just listening. Would you do it again? Honestly, I'm tempted to try something similar myself, provided I could get time off work. What would you advise?

speakerB.en: Thanks for asking! Having felt stuck in my job for years, I wanted something completely different. It was a friend's story that first inspired me. Honestly, it was far tougher than I'd expected, although it turned out to be the best decision of my life.

I taught English at a small school. Not speaking Nepali at first, I relied on gestures and drawings. It was only after a month that I could follow simple conversations. What struck me most was how patient everyone was with my mistakes.

There were evenings when I felt homesick. Having shared a house with two other volunteers, though, I was never really alone. It was in those quiet evenings that we became close friends. What helped me was keeping a diary.

A fair worry, and I thought about it a lot. As far as I'm concerned, it matters that you work with a trustworthy organization. It was the local teacher who explained that our role was to support, not replace, local staff. Looking back, I think that's the key.

It was the last day. Having prepared a small show, the children sang a song they'd written about us. It was then that I realized how much it had all meant. Knowing I'd probably never see them again made it even more emotional.

Absolutely, I'd go back tomorrow. My advice is to choose a project that matches your skills, and to stay long enough, in case it takes time to settle in. It was the best way I could have changed my perspective. You should do it!

scenarios.scenario: Saying sorry and accepting apologies
scenarios.context: Someone makes a mistake and apologizes, the other responds.

speakerA.en: Hello. I'm sorry I'm late.
It's my mistake. I forgot the time.
I'm really sorry.
Please forgive me.
I'm so sorry! I didn't mean to step on your foot.
speakerA.fa: خیلی متأسفم! عمداً پات رو نگذاشتم.

speakerA.en: I apologize for being late. The traffic was terrible.
speakerA.fa: بابت دیر رسیدن عذرخواهی می‌کنم. ترافیک وحشتناک بود.

speakerA.en: I'm really sorry about the misunderstanding. It was my fault.
speakerA.fa: واقعاً بابت سوءتفاهم معذرت می‌خوام. تقصیر من بود.

speakerA.en: Please forgive me for forgetting your birthday. I feel awful.
speakerA.fa: ببخشید که تولدت رو فراموش کردم. حسابی شرمنده‌ام.

speakerA.en: I can't believe I broke your glass. I'll buy you a new one.
speakerA.fa: باورم نمیشه لیوانت رو شکستم. یه جدید برات می‌خرم.

speakerA.en: I must apologize for my behavior yesterday. I was under a lot of stress.
speakerA.fa: باید بابت رفتار دیروزم عذرخواهی کنم. خیلی تحت فشار بودم.

speakerB.en: That's OK. Come in.
It's fine. Everyone makes mistakes.
Don't worry about it.
Of course. It's OK.
Oh, no problem at all! It was my fault for standing too close.
speakerB.fa: اوه، اصلاً اشکالی نداره! تقصیر خودم بود که خیلی نزدیک ایستاده بودم.

speakerB.en: Don't worry about it. It happens to everyone.
speakerB.fa: نگران نباش. برای همه پیش میاد.

speakerB.en: It's okay. I understand that you didn't mean it.
speakerB.fa: اشکالی نداره. می‌دونم که عمدی نبود.

speakerB.en: Of course, I forgive you. Just don't do it again!
speakerB.fa: حتماً، می‌بخشم. فقط دیگه تکرار نکن!

speakerB.en: That's very thoughtful of you. Thank you.
speakerB.fa: خیلی با ملاحظه‌ای. ممنون.

speakerB.en: I appreciate the apology. Let's just move forward.
speakerB.fa: از عذرخواهیت قدردانی می‌کنم. بذارین جلو بریم.

scenarios.scenario: Stepping on someone's foot
scenarios.context: A person bumps into someone in a crowd.

speakerA.en: Oh, sorry! Are you OK?
I didn't see you.
Does your foot hurt?
I'm really sorry.
Oh, I'm so sorry. I wasn't looking where I was going.
Are you sure you're OK? Do you want to sit down?
Let me at least help you with your bag.
I'll be more careful next time.

speakerB.en: Yes, I'm fine. Thank you.
It's OK. It's very busy here.
No, it doesn't hurt.
Don't worry about it.
It's all right. It happens in crowds.
No, thanks. It only hurt for a second.
That's very kind of you, but I can manage.
Don't worry. No harm done.

scenarios.scenario: Forgetting something
scenarios.context: A person forgets a book for a friend.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry. I forgot your book.
I'll bring it on Monday.
Are you angry?
Thank you. You are kind.
I'm really sorry. I forgot to bring your book again.
I'll put it in my bag tonight so I don't forget.
I feel bad about it. I promised to bring it.
Thanks for being so patient with me.

speakerB.en: That's OK. Bring it tomorrow.
Good. I don't need it today.
No, I'm not angry.
You're welcome.
Don't worry. I don't need it until Friday.
That's a good idea. Maybe set a reminder on your phone.
It's not a big problem. Really.
No problem. We all forget things sometimes.

scenarios.scenario: Breaking something
scenarios.context: A guest breaks a cup at a friend's home.

speakerA.en: Oh no! I broke your cup.
I'm very sorry.
No, I'm fine. Where is the broom?
I'll buy you a new cup.
I'm so sorry. It slipped out of my hand.
I think it was a gift. I feel terrible.
Please let me pay for it.
Let me clean up the pieces.

speakerB.en: Don't worry. It's only a cup.
It's OK. Are you hurt?
It's in the kitchen.
You don't need to. Thanks.
Please don't worry. Accidents happen.
Yes, but it isn't important. I'm just glad you're not hurt.
No, really. It was old anyway.
Thank you. Be careful with the glass.

scenarios.scenario: Saying sorry to a friend
scenarios.context: Two friends talk after a small fight.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry about yesterday.
I was angry.
Are we still friends?
Thank you. Let's have tea.
I've been thinking about what I said, and I was wrong.
I shouldn't have shouted at you.
Our friendship is very important to me.
Let's not argue about small things again.

speakerB.en: It's OK. I'm sorry too.
I know. Let's forget it.
Yes, of course.
Good idea!
Thank you for saying that. I was upset too.
It's OK. Let's talk about it calmly now.
It's important to me too. I'm glad we talked.
Agreed. Let's forget it and move on.

scenarios.scenario: Missing a meeting
scenarios.context: A student apologizes to a teacher.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry, Mr. Green. I was sick.
Yes, I'm better today.
I missed the class yesterday.
Thank you very much.
I'm sorry I missed our meeting yesterday. I had a family emergency.
Yes, it's fine now. Could we arrange a new time?
Yes, that's perfect. I'll be there on time.
Thank you for being so understanding.

speakerB.en: That's OK. Are you better now?
Good. Please sit down.
I can give you the notes.
You're welcome.
I'm sorry to hear that. I hope everything is OK.
Of course. Are you free tomorrow at ten?
Good. Please bring your project so we can discuss it.
No problem. Just let me know next time if you can't come.

scenarios.scenario: Accepting an apology
scenarios.context: One person accepts a kind apology.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry I said that.
I didn't mean it.
Thank you for understanding.
I won't do it again.
Thank you for apologizing. It means a lot to me.
Everyone makes mistakes. Let's forget about it.
I was upset at first, but I understand now.
Let's move on and have a good day.

speakerB.en: It's all right.
I know. I forgive you.
No problem.
Good. Let's be happy.
I should have called you earlier. I really regret it.
Thank you for being so generous.
I'll try to be more careful in the future.
Sounds good. Thanks for giving me another chance.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing for forgetting a birthday
scenarios.context: A man apologizes to a friend for forgetting her birthday.

speakerA.en: I'm so sorry I forgot your birthday yesterday. I feel terrible about it.
That's no excuse. You'd never forget mine, and I should have set a reminder.
Let me make it up to you. Can I take you out for dinner tonight?
I want to. And this time, I'll put it in my calendar for next year.

speakerB.en: It's all right. I was a little hurt, but I know you've been busy lately.
Thank you for saying that. It really means a lot to me.
That would be lovely, but you really don't have to.
Fine, I forgive you. Just don't let it happen again.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing to a coworker after an argument
scenarios.context: Two coworkers make peace after a disagreement.

speakerA.en: Do you have a moment? I owe you an apology for the way I spoke to you in the meeting.
You're right. I was stressed about the deadline, and I took it out on you.
I agree. I'll try to stay calmer and listen to your side first.
Then let's forget about it and focus on finishing the project together.

speakerB.en: I appreciate that. I have to admit it upset me, because I thought it was unfair.
I understand, but next time I'd prefer that we talk about it privately.
Thank you. I could also have explained my point of view more clearly.
That sounds good to me. I'm glad we talked.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing for being late
scenarios.context: A person apologizes to a friend for arriving very late.

speakerA.en: I'm so sorry I'm late. I know I've kept you waiting for almost an hour.
My phone died, and then the bus broke down halfway here.
I will. I feel awful, especially because the movie has already started.
Thank you for being so patient. Let me buy the tickets and the popcorn.

speakerB.en: I was starting to worry. You could have called me.
That's unlucky. Next time, please let me know as soon as you can.
Don't worry about it. We can see the next showing in an hour.
Deal. Let's just enjoy the evening and forget about the delay.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing for a serious mistake at work
scenarios.context: An employee apologizes to a manager for a costly error.

speakerA.en: I need to take responsibility for the error in the invoice. It cost us a client, and I'm deeply sorry.
I was rushing to meet a deadline and neglected to double-check the figures. There's no excuse for that.
I'd like to contact the client personally, explain what went wrong, and offer to rectify the situation at no charge.
Thank you. I'll also set up a checklist so that it doesn't happen again.

speakerB.en: I appreciate you coming forward. May I ask how it happened?
Mistakes do happen, but what matters is how we respond. What do you propose to do about it?
That's a constructive approach. I'll accompany you on the call, as it reflects on the whole department.
Good. I'm willing to move on, provided we learn from it.

scenarios.scenario: Making amends after a long argument
scenarios.context: Two siblings reconcile after months of silence.

speakerA.en: I've wanted to call you for ages, but I didn't know how to begin. I'm sorry for the things I said.
I was angry, and I let my pride get in the way. It was foolish to lose touch over something so petty.
I know. I felt guilty every time she mentioned it. I'd like to put it behind us, if you're willing.
Then let's have dinner this weekend, with Mom, and clear the air once and for all.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry too. I said things I didn't mean, and I've regretted it ever since.
We both bear some responsibility. Mom has been miserable watching us avoid each other.
Of course I am. You're my brother, and no argument is worth losing that.
I'd like that very much. I'll cook, since it's the least I can do.

scenarios.scenario: Struggling to forgive a betrayal
scenarios.context: A woman confides in a friend about a breach of trust.

speakerA.en: I know I should forgive her, but I can't stop thinking about how she shared my secret with everyone.
She has apologized several times, yet it feels hollow, as if she's only sorry she was caught.
Perhaps. I'm just not sure I can ever be as open with her as I was before.
That's comforting. I was beginning to feel I was being petty and unforgiving.

speakerB.en: It's natural to feel hurt. Trust is hard to rebuild once it's been broken.
That could be true, but it might also be that she's genuinely ashamed and doesn't know how to make it right.
You don't have to forgive immediately, or fully. Forgiveness can happen in stages.
Not at all. Give yourself time, and see whether her actions match her words.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing to a client for a company error
scenarios.context: A manager phones a client to apologize after a data error exposed their information.

speakerA.en: I'm calling because I owe you a sincere apology. An error on our side meant that some of your account details were visible to other users for several hours.
It was caused by a configuration mistake during a system update, and the responsibility lies entirely with us. I won't offer excuses.
We've fixed the fault, notified the relevant authorities, and arranged a year of free credit monitoring for every affected client.
You'll have it within forty-eight hours. We take this very seriously, and I understand if your trust needs time to be rebuilt.

speakerB.en: That's deeply concerning. How could something like that happen? I trusted your firm with sensitive information.
I appreciate your candor, but an apology doesn't undo the exposure. What exactly are you doing about it?
That's a start. I'll also want a written account of what happened and the safeguards you're putting in place.
It will. Let's see how you handle the coming weeks, and then I'll decide whether we continue working together.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing without making excuses
scenarios.context: A man apologizes to his partner for missing an important family occasion.

speakerA.en: I owe you an apology for missing your sister's engagement party. I'm not going to hide behind work as an excuse.
You're right, and that's what I regret most. I should have called, and I'm sorry I put you in that position.
I know, and I've been avoiding that truth. I'd like to change it, rather than simply promise to.
I'll leave the office by six on weekdays, and I'll put family events in my calendar as non-negotiable. You can hold me to it.

speakerB.en: It wasn't just the party. It was the way you didn't even call. She asked where you were, and I had nothing to say.
It's the pattern that bothers me. This isn't the first time work has come before something that mattered to me.
Promises are easy. What are you proposing, concretely?
Then I'll give you the chance to prove it. But I'll be watching, and I hope you understand why.

scenarios.scenario: Accepting an apology while setting boundaries
scenarios.context: A woman accepts a colleague's apology for taking credit for her work, but makes her expectations clear.

speakerA.en: I wanted to apologize for what happened in the presentation. I presented your analysis as though it were mine, and there's no justification for that.
You'd have been within your rights. I let ambition cloud my judgment, and I'm genuinely ashamed of it.
That's completely fair. What would you like me to do to put it right?
I'll do both this week. And for what it's worth, I hope we can rebuild some trust.

speakerB.en: Thank you for saying so. I'll admit I was angry, and I considered raising it with our director.
I accept your apology, and I'd like to move on. But I need to be clear that I won't tolerate it happening again.
Correct the record with the director, and make sure my contribution is credited properly in the final report.
I hope so too. Trust takes time, but actions will speak louder than words.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing for a serious professional error
scenarios.context: A manager takes responsibility for a mistake that harmed a client.

speakerA.en: I asked to speak with you personally because I believe you deserve a direct apology. The error in your account was entirely ours.
You have every right to be. There's no excuse, and I won't offer one. What I can do is explain how it happened and how we'll prevent a recurrence.
A bit of both, frankly. A single check was bypassed under time pressure, and our process didn't force it to be repeated.
We'll reimburse the losses in full and introduce a second verification step. I'd welcome your scrutiny of the new procedure.

speakerB.en: I appreciate you coming forward. The mistake cost us a considerable sum, and I confess I'm still quite angry about it.
Go on. I'd like to hear whether the failure was one of carelessness or a systemic weakness.
I'm relieved you're candid about it. Evasiveness would have made me far more inclined to take my business elsewhere.
Very well. I'll accept that, though trust is easily lost and slowly regained. I'll be watching.

scenarios.scenario: Making amends after a long rift between siblings
scenarios.context: Two siblings attempt to repair a relationship damaged by an old grievance.

speakerA.en: I've rehearsed this conversation for years, and now that you're here, every prepared sentence has deserted me.
Honesty, then. I said things at the funeral that I've regretted every day since, and I allowed my grief to excuse my cruelty.
Silence was a poor substitute for a conversation. I wasted years when we might have supported each other.
I'd gladly accept that. I'd like to begin again, if you'll permit me, though I know trust must be rebuilt rather than assumed.

speakerB.en: Then perhaps we should abandon the script. I didn't come expecting eloquence, only honesty.
I wasn't blameless either. I responded in kind, and then I let the silence harden because it felt easier than backing down.
Which is why I'd like to stop apportioning blame. Neither of us was entirely right, and neither entirely wrong.
Then let's rebuild it. Start by telling me everything I've missed, and I'll do the same.

scenarios.scenario: Forgiving someone who has betrayed a confidence
scenarios.context: A person decides how to respond to a friend's breach of trust.

speakerA.en: I know I've forfeited the right to ask for anything, but I wanted to apologize in person for what I told her. It was unforgivable.
I wouldn't blame you if it didn't. I acted out of thoughtlessness and a desire to seem well-informed, which is a contemptible reason.
There's none to offer. All I can do is ask what I might do to begin repairing the damage.
That's more than fair. I'll prove through conduct, not promises, that your trust was not misplaced.

speakerB.en: It was a breach of something I'd entrusted to you alone. I've struggled to decide whether our friendship can survive it.
I appreciate that you haven't tried to justify it. Excuses would have been the final insult.
Time, mostly. I can forgive, but I can't forget on command, and I'll need to see consistency before I confide in you again.
Then we'll take it slowly. Forgiveness isn't an event, after all; it's a process that unfolds in small increments.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing for breaking something
scenarios.context: A guest apologizes for breaking a glass at a friend's house.

speakerA.en: I'm so sorry. I accidentally knocked over a glass, and it broke into pieces.
Please let me pay for it. I know it was part of a set, and I feel terrible.
Are you sure? I really don't want to spoil the evening because of my clumsiness.
Thank you for being so understanding. I'll be more careful from now on.

speakerB.en: Oh no, don't worry about it. Just be careful not to step on any pieces.
Please don't. It was an old glass, and honestly, I never liked it very much.
You haven't spoiled anything. Accidents happen to everyone. Let me get a brush and clean it up.
It's really fine. Now, come and sit down. Dinner is almost ready.

scenarios.scenario: Forgiving a friend who canceled plans
scenarios.context: Two friends talk after one of them canceled their plans at the last minute.

speakerA.en: I wanted to apologize for canceling on Saturday. It was very short notice.
My boss asked me to work, and I couldn't say no. I should have called you earlier.
I'd like to make it up to you. Could we go to that concert next month instead?
Thank you for understanding. I'll make sure nothing gets in the way this time.

speakerB.en: To be honest, I was a bit upset. I had been looking forward to seeing you all week.
I understand that work can be difficult, but a quick message would have helped.
That sounds like a good idea. I'm not angry anymore, and I appreciate your apology.
I know you will. Let's just forget about it and enjoy the evening when it comes.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing to a customer for a mistake
scenarios.context: An employee apologizes to a customer after a billing error.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'm calling about the bill I received yesterday. I believe I was charged twice for the same service.
That's what I thought. It's the second time this has happened this year, and I'm starting to lose patience with your company.
I appreciate your apology, but I'd like to know what you're going to do to make sure it doesn't happen again.
That sounds reasonable. How long will it take for the money to appear back in my account?
All right. I'll wait for the confirmation email. I'd also appreciate it if someone could check my account for any other mistakes.
Thank you. I'm willing to continue as a customer, but I hope that this will be the last time.

speakerB.en: Good morning, and thank you for calling. I'm very sorry to hear that. Let me look at your account right now.
You're right, and I sincerely apologize. There was an error in the system, and your payment was processed twice by mistake.
We're reviewing our billing process, and we've already reported the problem to the technical team, so it should be fixed within a week.
I've started the refund now. It usually takes three to five working days, and you'll receive a confirmation email shortly.
Of course. I'll go through your last six months of invoices myself, and if I find anything unusual, I'll contact you straight away.
Thank you for your patience and understanding. We truly value you as a customer, and we'll do everything to earn back your trust.

scenarios.scenario: Making up with a sibling after an argument
scenarios.context: Two siblings talk after a quarrel about a family matter.

speakerA.en: Hi. I wasn't sure whether you'd want to talk to me, but I wanted to say that I'm sorry about what I said last week.
I shouldn't have raised my voice, and I certainly shouldn't have criticized the way you look after Mum. You do far more than I do.
I've been feeling guilty ever since. I think I was stressed about work, and I took it out on you, which wasn't fair.
Thank you for saying that. I'd like us to share the responsibility more equally. Would you let me take care of her on weekends?
I'd love to. Maybe we could also have dinner together every Sunday, so that we can talk about things before they become problems.
Deal. I'm so relieved that we've sorted this out. I don't want to lose you over something so silly.

speakerB.en: I'm glad you called. To be honest, I was upset, but I've also been thinking about the argument all week.
I appreciate that. I know that I've been tired and short-tempered lately, and I probably overreacted as well.
We were both under pressure. The important thing is that we're talking now, instead of staying angry at each other.
That would be a big help. I've been feeling overwhelmed, and I didn't want to ask, because I thought you were too busy.
That sounds like a good idea. We never talk about important things until it's too late, and then we end up arguing.
Me neither. We're a family, and we'll always have differences, but we should never let them come between us.

scenarios.scenario: Taking responsibility for a serious professional mistake
scenarios.context: A team member admits an error that affected a client and discusses how to repair the damage.
