speakerA.en: I need to tell you something, and I'd like to do it before anyone else brings it to your attention. I made a mistake in the report that we sent to the client last week.
I used an outdated set of figures, and as a result, the projections were considerably too optimistic. I only noticed when I was reviewing the file yesterday evening.
I take full responsibility for this. I should have double-checked the source, but I was rushing to meet the deadline, and I didn't follow the usual verification process.
I've already prepared a corrected version, and I'd like to contact the client myself, to apologize and explain what happened, if you're happy for me to do so.
I understand. I'd also like to propose a new procedure whereby every report is reviewed by a second person before it's sent, so that this kind of error can't occur again.
Thank you for being so understanding. I'll make sure that I earn back your confidence, and that this never happens again.

speakerB.en: Thank you for coming to me directly. That took courage, and I appreciate your honesty. Please tell me exactly what happened, and how serious the consequences are.
That's a significant error, as the client may already have based decisions on those numbers. The sooner we inform them, the better the chances that we can limit the damage.
I appreciate that you're accepting responsibility, but it's also a lesson for the entire team. We shouldn't have allowed a situation in which one person's oversight could go unnoticed.
I think it would be best if we contacted them together. It will show that the company takes the problem seriously, and that you're willing to face it, which clients usually respect.
That's a constructive suggestion, and I'd like to put it into practice immediately. Mistakes will always happen, but it's how we deal with them that determines whether people trust us.
I'm sure you will. Everyone makes mistakes, but not everyone admits to them so promptly. That says a lot about your character.

scenarios.scenario: Rebuilding trust after a betrayal between friends
scenarios.context: Two friends talk after one shared a secret that was told in confidence.

speakerA.en: I don't know where to begin, but I owe you an explanation, and an apology. I told Julia about your plans to leave your job, and I know that I shouldn't have done it.
I didn't mean to cause any harm. It slipped out during a conversation, and I assumed she wouldn't mention it. That was naive and careless of me, and I'm deeply sorry.
I understand why you're upset. I'd be furious if the situation were reversed. What matters most to me is that you know that it wasn't done out of malice.
I'd like to make it right, if that's still possible. Is there anything I can do, such as speaking to Julia and asking her to keep it to herself until you're ready?
I'll go and talk to her this afternoon. And I promise that from now on, anything you tell me in confidence will remain between us, whatever happens.
Thank you for listening. I don't expect you to forgive me immediately, but I hope that in time we can put it behind us.

speakerB.en: I'm glad you came to talk to me, but I'll be honest, I'm still quite hurt. I told you because I trusted you, and I'd expected that it would stay private.
That's what bothers me the most. It wasn't a casual comment. It was something I hadn't even told my family, and now it may reach my manager before I've made a decision.
I do believe that you didn't mean to hurt me, but good intentions don't undo the consequences. Trust takes years to build, and a moment to damage.
It would help if you spoke to her, yes, but the damage might already be done. I'll have to decide whether to tell my manager myself before he hears it from someone else.
I'll try to believe that. Actions will speak louder than words, and I'd like to see how you handle things in the next few months. I'm not saying that the friendship is over.
Thank you for the apology. It means something to me that you didn't try to excuse yourself. Let's give it some time and see how it goes.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing for missing an important event
scenarios.context: A person apologizes to a friend for missing a significant occasion.

speakerA.en: I wanted to call you in person, because I couldn't bear to simply send a message. I'm so sorry that I missed your graduation ceremony, and I know how much it meant to you that I was there.
I won't make excuses. I'd promised to come, and I should have made it a priority. There was a problem at work, and I allowed it to take over, instead of keeping the promise that I'd made to you.
I understand that you're upset, and I'd feel the same way if I were in your position. I wish I could go back and change it, because I'd certainly make a different decision now.
I'd like to make it up to you, if you'll let me. I'm thinking of taking you out to dinner to celebrate properly, and I'd like to give you the present that I should have brought on the day.
I'll do whatever it takes to repair our friendship. I know that apologies can't undo what happened, but I hope that over time, you'll see that I truly regret it.
Thank you for listening. It means a great deal to me that you're willing to give me another chance.

speakerB.en: I appreciate that you called instead of sending a message. It shows that you do care, and I'm glad to hear your voice. But I'd be lying if I said that I wasn't hurt.
I looked around the hall during the ceremony, and every other person had someone there. I kept hoping that you'd appear at the last minute, but you never did. It was a difficult moment for me.
I know you didn't mean to hurt me, and I understand that work can be demanding. But it was a once-in-a-lifetime event, and a phone call or a message to explain would have meant a lot.
A dinner would be lovely, and I'd be glad to accept. It isn't about the present, though. What matters to me is knowing that I can count on you when something is important.
Actions matter more than words, and I'd like to see that you've learned from this. If you do, I'm sure we can put it behind us. Our friendship is too valuable to be damaged by one mistake.
Thank you for being honest and for apologizing sincerely. Let's go for that dinner next week. And you can tell me everything that I missed at work, as well.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing to customers for a delivery failure as a business owner
scenarios.context: A business owner apologizes to a customer for a missed delivery and explains the remedy.

speakerA.en: Good morning, Mrs. Taylor. I'm calling personally because I wanted to apologize for the failure to deliver your order yesterday. I'm aware that it was meant to arrive before your party, and I'm very sorry for the inconvenience.
What happened is that our delivery driver fell ill, and the replacement went to the wrong address. We should have contacted you immediately, and the fact that we didn't is entirely our fault.

I fully understand your frustration. Had the situation been reversed, I'd be equally annoyed, and I won't try to defend what happened. All I can do is make sure that we put it right as quickly as possible.
I'd like to offer a full refund for the order, and in addition, we'd be glad to give you a voucher for fifty euros towards your next purchase, as a gesture of goodwill.
Of course, if you'd still like the items, I can arrange for them to be delivered this afternoon, free of charge, and I'll bring them myself, if that would help.
Thank you for giving us another chance. I'll make sure that this kind of failure doesn't happen again, and I'll personally check your next order.

speakerB.en: Good morning. Thank you for calling. I must admit that I was quite angry yesterday. I'd spent weeks planning the party, and the cake and decorations were supposed to be the centerpiece.
I appreciate your honesty, though I wish that someone had told me earlier. If I'd known by noon, I could have found an alternative. As it was, I was waiting at home until nine in the evening.
I think it's good that you're willing to take responsibility. In my experience, many companies simply make excuses or ignore complaints, so the fact that you called yourself says a lot.
A refund is a fair solution, and the voucher is generous. I'd also like an assurance that the next order will arrive on time, because I'm planning another event in two months.
I'd appreciate that, but I don't need the items anymore, since I bought replacements at the last minute. Please just send the refund, and I'll consider placing another order for the next occasion.
I will. You've handled the situation very professionally, and I'm willing to give you another chance. But it needs to go smoothly next time.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing to a friend for revealing a secret
scenarios.context: A friend admits that she accidentally passed on a confidential piece of news, and the other person has to decide how to respond.

speakerA.en: I need to apologize for something, and it isn't easy. I mentioned your plans to move abroad to Clara last week, and she told several people. Had I known she'd pass it on, I would never have said a word.

It slipped out during a conversation about holidays. If only I'd thought before speaking, none of this would have happened. It's not so much that I wasn't careful as that I assumed she'd keep it to herself.
You're right, and I'm truly sorry. If only I could undo it, I would. Had I known how important it was to you, I'd have been much more careful. Is there anything I can do to make it right?
Of course, I'll call them today. Had I known they hadn't been told, I would have warned Clara straight away. If only she'd asked me first, instead of repeating it to everyone she knows.

That's fair, and I appreciate your patience. Had I known you'd react so calmly, I'd have been less afraid to tell you. It's not so much your anger I feared as losing your trust. Will you be able to forgive me?
Absolutely, and I'll prove it. Had I known how much it matters, I'd have kept every word to myself. From now on, I won't share anything personal, unless you tell me it's all right. I promise.

speakerB.en: To be honest, I'm quite upset. It's not so much that people know as that I wanted to tell my parents myself. Why did you mention it to her in the first place?

I understand it wasn't deliberate, but that's exactly why it hurts. Had I known you'd mention it, I wouldn't have told you at all. It's not so much a betrayal as a lack of thought, but the effect is the same.

I'd appreciate it if you could call my parents and explain that the news reached them before I could. It's not so much about punishing you as about reducing the damage. Would you be willing to do that?

Let's not blame Clara too much, since it was your slip that started it. It's not so much about who spread it as about how we handle it now. If only I'd told them earlier, we wouldn't be having this conversation.

Probably, although it will take a little while. It's not so much that I'm angry as that I feel exposed. If only I could be sure you'll keep my next secret, I'd tell you more freely. Can I count on that?
Thank you, that means a lot. It's not so much the apology as the way you've handled it that matters to me. If only everyone were so honest, there would be far fewer misunderstandings between friends.

scenarios.scenario: Accepting a colleague's apology after a public mistake
scenarios.context: A manager blamed a colleague in front of the team for a mistake that turned out to be someone else's, and now he apologizes to her in private.

speakerA.en: Do you have a minute? I owe you an apology for what I said in the meeting yesterday. I blamed you for the delay, and it turns out the error was in the supplier's data. If it weren't for the audit, I might never have found out.

I assumed it because the report carried your name, and I should have checked first. If it weren't for the pressure from the client, I'd have waited. That's no excuse, though, and I'd appreciate it if you could accept my sincere regret.

That's entirely reasonable. I'll send an email to everyone this afternoon and explain that the fault lay with the supplier. If it weren't for your careful records, we wouldn't have traced the problem so quickly. Would you like to see the draft first?

Fair enough. I'll make sure the tone is factual rather than defensive. If it weren't for your patience, this could have turned into a much bigger conflict, and I'm grateful that it didn't. Is there anything else I should do?

You have my word. If it weren't for this experience, I'd probably have gone on making snap judgments, so I'll treat it as a lesson. I'd appreciate it if you could tell me if I ever slip back into old habits.

Thank you, that's more generous than I deserve. I'd appreciate it if you could join me for lunch tomorrow, so that I can make it up to you properly. If it weren't for you, the project would have collapsed.

speakerB.en: Thank you for saying that. I'll admit that I was angry, since it happened in front of everyone. Much as I'd like to say it doesn't matter, it did affect how some colleagues looked at me. Why did you assume it was my mistake?

I do accept it, although I'd appreciate it if you could also correct the impression publicly. Much as I'd like to leave it behind, the team heard the accusation, and they should hear the correction too.

Yes, I'd appreciate it if you could send it to me before it goes out. Much as I trust your judgment, I'd like to be sure the wording is fair to everyone, including the supplier, who may not have known.

There is one thing. I'd appreciate it if you could ask for my views before drawing conclusions next time. Much as I understand the pressure you're under, a quick conversation would have prevented all this.
I will, and I'll do it kindly. Much as I'd hoped for an apology, I didn't expect one so thoughtful. If it weren't for your honesty, I'd still be resentful. Let's put it behind us, then.
Lunch sounds good, and I'd be glad to. Much as I'd like to forget the meeting, I think we both learned something from it. Shall we say one o'clock at the café across the street?

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing to a neighbor for a noisy party
scenarios.context: A resident knocks on a neighbor's door to apologize for a loud party the night before and offers to make amends.

speakerA.en: Good morning, Mrs. Novak. I hope I'm not disturbing you. I came to apologize for the noise last night. I can't tell you how embarrassed I am, since I know you have to get up early for work.

It was my sister's birthday, and the party simply got out of hand. I should have kept an eye on the time, and I shouldn't have let it go so late. Had I realized how loud it was, I'd have stopped it immediately.

You're absolutely right, and I should have told you. There's no excuse, to be honest. I'll see to it that it doesn't happen again. In future, I'll tell you a week in advance, in case you'd like to plan something.

Completely reasonable, and I'll see to it that the music is off by eleven-thirty. On the other hand, may I ask if there's anything else that bothers you? I'd rather know now than let resentment build.

I'm so sorry, I had no idea. I'll clean the hall myself right away, and I'll make sure my guests understand. Needless to say, I should have checked it earlier. Would it help if I brought you some coffee and pastries by way of apology?

I'll bring them right up. Thank you for being so understanding, Mrs. Novak. I'll see to it that next time everything's under control, and you're welcome to join us if you like, as long as you don't mind the music!

speakerB.en: Good morning. Well, I must admit I didn't sleep much. The music was still going at two in the morning. I wasn't going to say anything, but since you've come, I'll be honest. What happened?

I appreciate your honesty. I did consider knocking on your door, but I didn't want to cause a scene. What I'd have preferred is a warning beforehand, so that I could have gone to my sister's for the night.
That would be considerate. As long as it's occasional, I don't mind the odd party. What bothers me is the lateness, rather than the music itself. I'd say midnight is a reasonable limit, wouldn't you?
Well, since you ask, the guests were leaving rubbish in the hall. I shouldn't have had to clean it up this morning. Had it been a one-off, I'd say nothing, but it has happened before.

That's kind, though not necessary. A sincere apology and a clean hall would be quite enough. Still, I'd gladly accept a pastry, since I skipped breakfast. Thank you for coming, because many neighbors wouldn't bother.
I might just do that, if the music is a bit quieter! Apology accepted, and thank you. Good neighbors are hard to find, so let's keep it that way, shall we?

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing to a friend for missing an important event
scenarios.context: A man apologizes to his best friend for missing her graduation, and they talk about how to repair the friendship.

speakerA.en: Hi Maya, thanks for agreeing to meet. I know you're upset, and you have every right to be. I'd like to apologize in person for missing your graduation. I've been feeling terrible ever since.

I'd be lying if I said I had a good reason. I fell asleep after a night shift, and by the time I woke up, the ceremony was over. If I'd set two alarms, I'd have made it. Not that it excuses it, of course.
I was ashamed, and I didn't know what to say. I'd be lying if I said I wasn't afraid of your reaction. If I had called, I'd have faced it sooner. Looking back, hiding made everything worse.

I can't promise to be perfect, but I can promise to be honest. If I'm ever going to miss something, I'll tell you in advance. I'd be happy to make it up to you. Would you let me take you out to dinner to celebrate?
I'll try, and I mean it. Not that words are enough, but I'd like to see the photos from that day. If I'd been there, we'd have had one together. Do you have any copies?

I've missed you too. Thank you for giving me the chance to explain, since I know you didn't have to. If I could go back, I'd be sitting in the front row, clapping the loudest. Shall we order something to eat?

speakerB.en: Thanks for coming. To be honest, I was really hurt. You were the one person I'd asked to be there, and your seat stayed empty. I'd like to understand what happened. Why didn't you at least call?

I appreciate the honesty. It's easier to hear than a made-up story. Still, what hurt most was the silence afterwards. Had you texted me even a quick message, I'd have felt less abandoned. Why did you stay quiet?

It did, although I understand shame. As far as I'm concerned, the missed ceremony matters less than how you handle it now. On the other hand, I need to know it won't happen again. What can you promise me?

Dinner would be nice, although it won't fix everything on its own. What I really want is for you to show up in the little moments, not only the big ones. Could you try that, even if it's inconvenient?
I do, my parents took a few. And you're right, a photo isn't the same, but it's a sweet gesture. Honestly, I'd rather have you as a friend than hold a grudge. I've missed you these past two weeks.
Let's, and you're paying, as promised! I forgive you, as long as you remember this. Next time, set two alarms, and if you're ever late, just call.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing family background, traditions and local culture
scenarios.context: People talk about their families and cultural habits.

speakerA.en: Do you have a big family?
How many brothers and sisters do you have?
Do you live with your family?
What is your mother's name?
Are there any special festivals or holidays you celebrate in your country?
speakerA.fa: توی کشورتون جشن‌ها یا تعطیلات خاصی دارید که جشن می‌گیرید؟

speakerA.en: What is the typical food in your hometown?
speakerA.fa: غذای معروف شهر شما چیه؟

speakerA.en: In my culture, we always greet older people with respect.
speakerA.fa: در فرهنگ ما، همیشه به بزرگ‌ترها با احترام سلام می‌کنیم.

speakerA.en: Do you have any family traditions during New Year?
speakerA.fa: توی سال نو هیچ سنت خانوادگی دارید؟

speakerA.en: I'm really curious about your customs. Could you tell me more about them?
speakerA.fa: واقعاً درباره رسوم شما کنجکاوم. می‌تونی بیشتر درباره‌شون بگی؟

speakerB.en: Yes, we are six people.
I have one brother and two sisters.
Yes, we live in a big house.
Her name is Maryam.
Yes, we celebrate Nowruz, which is the Persian New Year.
speakerB.fa: بله، ما نوروز رو جشن می‌گیریم که سال نو ایرانی هست.

speakerB.en: We have a dish called 'Chelo Kebab' which is very popular.
speakerB.fa: ما یه غذای معروف به نام 'چلو کباب' داریم که خیلی محبوبه.

speakerB.en: That's beautiful. In our country, we also respect the elderly a lot.
speakerB.fa: خیلی قشنگه. تو کشور ما هم به سالمندان خیلی احترام می‌ذاریم.

speakerB.en: Usually we visit relatives and give presents to children.
speakerB.fa: معمولاً به دیدار اقوام می‌رویم و به بچه‌ها هدیه می‌دهیم.

speakerB.en: Of course! I'd love to. Ask me anything you like.
speakerB.fa: حتماً! خیلی دوست دارم. هر چی دوست داری بپرس.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about parents
scenarios.context: Two classmates talk about their parents.

speakerA.en: Where do your parents live?
What does your father do?
Does your mother work?
Do you like your parents' house?
How often do you see your parents?
What do your parents like to do in their free time?
Are you more similar to your mother or your father?
Do you talk to them on the phone every day?

speakerB.en: They live in Tehran.
He is a teacher.
Yes, she is a nurse.
Yes, I love it.
I visit them every weekend because they live nearby.
My father enjoys gardening, and my mother likes reading.
I'm more like my mother. We both love cooking.
Almost every day. They always ask about my studies.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about brothers and sisters
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about siblings.

speakerA.en: Do you have a sister?
How old is she?
Is your brother older than you?
Do you play together?
Are you close to your brother?
What is your sister studying at university?
Do you ever argue with your siblings?
What did you do together when you were children?

speakerB.en: Yes, I have a little sister.
She is ten years old.
Yes, he is twenty.
Yes, we play every day.
Yes, we are. We talk about everything.
She's studying medicine. She wants to be a doctor.
Sometimes, but we always make up quickly.
We played in the garden and rode our bikes every afternoon.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about grandparents
scenarios.context: A child talks about grandparents.

speakerA.en: Do you see your grandmother?
Where does she live?
Is your grandfather old?
I love my grandparents.
What was your grandmother like when she was young?
Do your grandparents live with your family?
What do you usually do when you visit them?
Did your grandfather teach you anything special?

speakerB.en: Yes, I see her on Fridays.
She lives in a small village.
He is eighty years old.
Me too. They are very kind.
She was a teacher. She told me many interesting stories.
No, they live in a village, but we visit them in the summer.
We help in the garden and have lunch together.
Yes, he taught me how to play chess.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about a family meal
scenarios.context: Two people talk about meals at home.

speakerA.en: Do you eat dinner together?
Who cooks in your family?
What is your favorite food?
Do you help in the kitchen?
Who usually decides what to cook?
Do you have a special dish for family gatherings?
Do you watch TV while you eat?
What was your favorite meal when you were a child?

speakerB.en: Yes, we eat at seven.
My mother cooks.
I like rice and chicken.
Yes, I wash the dishes.
My mother does, but we sometimes help her choose.
Yes, we always make a big pot of stew on Fridays.
No, we prefer to talk during dinner.
My grandmother's rice with chicken. I still love it.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about a national holiday
scenarios.context: Two people talk about a holiday in their country.

speakerA.en: Is today a holiday?
What do you do on holidays?
Do you wear special clothes?
It sounds nice.
What is the biggest holiday in your country?
How long does the celebration last?
Are there any special foods for this holiday?
Would a visitor enjoy it?

speakerB.en: Yes, it is. No school today.
We visit our family.
Yes, we wear new clothes.
Yes, it is a happy day.
It's Nowruz. We celebrate the new year in spring.
About two weeks. Schools and offices are closed for some days.
Yes, we cook herb rice with fish, and we eat sweets.
Definitely. People are friendly and love to invite guests.

scenarios.scenario: Asking about a country
scenarios.context: A person asks a new friend about their country.

speakerA.en: Where are you from?
What language do you speak?
Is your country big?
I want to visit it.
What is the capital of your country?
What is the weather like there in summer?
What food should I try?
What's the best time to visit?

speakerB.en: I'm from Iran.
I speak Persian.
Yes, it is big and beautiful.
You are welcome anytime.
It's Tehran. It's the biggest city, with about nine million people.
It's hot and dry in many areas, but cooler near the mountains.
You should try kebab with rice. It's very popular.
Spring or autumn. The weather is pleasant then.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about family traditions
scenarios.context: Two friends compare how their families celebrate special occasions.

speakerA.en: In my family, we always have a big lunch together on Sundays. What about yours?
Is it a large family? Mine has more than thirty people, counting cousins.
That sounds lovely. Do you have any traditions that are special to your culture?
I love that. Traditions like that bring people closer together.

speakerB.en: We don't do that every week, but we get together for all the big holidays.
About twenty. My grandmother usually cooks, and everyone brings something.
Yes, on New Year's Eve we gather around the table and share a dish that's been in our family for generations.
I agree. I'd like to continue them with my own children one day.

scenarios.scenario: Learning about customs in another country
scenarios.context: A visitor asks a local about customs and manners.

speakerA.en: Before I visit your country, could you tell me a little about local customs?
Is it appropriate to bring a gift if I'm invited to someone's home?
And how about meals? Are there any rules I should know about?
Thanks, that's very helpful. I don't want to offend anyone by accident.

speakerB.en: Of course. People are usually very welcoming, and it's polite to greet everyone when you enter a room.
Yes, flowers or sweets are always appreciated, but avoid giving anything too expensive.
Wait until the host starts eating, and try a little of everything, even if you don't like it.
Don't worry. People understand that visitors don't know everything.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing life in different generations
scenarios.context: A young man and his grandmother talk about how family life has changed.

speakerA.en: Grandma, what was family life like when you were my age?
Did you live with your grandparents as well?
That sounds nice, but I imagine it was also difficult sometimes.
These days, many families only meet a few times a year.

speakerB.en: Very different. We didn't have televisions, so we spent our evenings talking and playing cards.
Yes, three generations lived under one roof, and everyone helped with the work.
It was. There was little privacy, but we learned to respect and support each other.
That's true, and that's why I'm so happy when you visit.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing generational differences in values
scenarios.context: A young woman and her father talk about differing expectations.

speakerA.en: Dad, I'd like to talk to you about my decision to study abroad. I know you have reservations.
Times have changed. Studying abroad is an advantage on a résumé, and I'd return with valuable experience.
I'll always be part of this family, wherever I live. I'd call every week, and visit during the holidays.
I can promise to make the effort. Would you at least think about it before you decide?

speakerB.en: I do, but not because I don't trust you. In my day, families stayed close, and leaving was unheard of.
I understand that. My worry is that you might not come back, and the family would lose you.
You say that now, but distance has a way of loosening ties, however strong they seem.
I will. And I'm proud that you came to talk to me rather than simply go ahead.

scenarios.scenario: Explaining cultural customs to a foreigner
scenarios.context: A local explains a traditional ceremony to a visiting friend.

speakerA.en: I'm fascinated by the ceremony we attended yesterday. What does the ritual of exchanging gifts signify?
That's a lovely idea. In my country, a wedding is seen primarily as a celebration of the couple.
I noticed that the older relatives were treated with great deference. Is that typical?
I find that admirable, although I imagine it can be restrictive for younger people at times.

speakerB.en: It symbolizes the union of two families, not just two individuals. The gifts represent mutual respect.
Here, the whole community takes part, and the elders' blessing is considered essential.
Very much so. Age is associated with wisdom, and it would be unthinkable to contradict an elder in public.
It can, and many of us are renegotiating those norms, but the underlying respect remains strong.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the challenges of raising children between cultures
scenarios.context: Two parents compare their experiences raising bilingual children.

speakerA.en: Our kids understand our language perfectly, but they insist on answering in English.
I worry that they'll lose touch with their heritage if we don't make an effort.
Do they resist? Mine complain that it's unfair to ask them to speak differently from their friends.
I'll try that. I'd also like to take them to visit relatives, so they see the language is alive.

speakerB.en: The same thing happens at our house. The moment they start school, the majority language takes over.
We set aside one evening a week when nobody is allowed to speak anything else, and it has helped.
Initially, but we explained why it matters, and they've gradually come around to the idea.
That's the best motivation. Children learn fastest when they have a real reason to communicate.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing care for an aging parent
scenarios.context: Two siblings discuss how best to care for their elderly mother.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking about Mom. She's insisting on staying in the house, but the stairs are becoming a real hazard.
I'm not suggesting that. Perhaps there's a middle ground, such as a live-in caregiver or moving her into a ground-floor apartment nearby.
Fair. I'm happy to handle the day-to-day arrangements if you can cover a larger share of the expense.
Agreed. She's proud, and I think she'll accept help more readily if it feels like her choice.

speakerB.en: I know, and I worry about her being alone, too. But I don't think she'd forgive us if we pushed her into a care home.
Either would be costly, and I'm not sure we can split it evenly, given that you're closer and I'd be contributing from a distance.
That seems equitable. Let's raise it with her together, though, rather than presenting her with a decision.
Exactly. It's her life, after all. Our job is to make it safer, not smaller.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing heritage language and identity
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about losing the language of their parents' homeland.

speakerA.en: My grandmother called yesterday, and I could barely follow what she was saying. It's embarrassing how much of the language I've lost.
It's strange. I grew up in that language at home, yet at school I worked so hard to sound like everyone else that it simply faded.
Now I feel a quiet sense of grief, as though I'd left behind part of who I am without ever deciding to.
That's encouraging. Perhaps I should join you, if only to be able to talk to my grandmother properly.

speakerB.en: I know the feeling. I understand every word, but when I try to speak, it comes out stilted and childish.
That's common, isn't it? Children want to fit in, and nobody tells them that something will be lost in the process.
Maybe it's not gone, only dormant. I've started taking weekly classes, and it's astonishing how much resurfaces.
I'd welcome the company. Besides, I suspect she'd be delighted to hear you try.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing family obligations against personal ambitions
scenarios.context: A man discusses with a friend whether to turn down a dream job to stay close to his family.

speakerA.en: I've been offered the role of my dreams, but it's in another country, and my father's health has been declining.
That's the complication. My parents insist I should go, but I know they'd never admit how much they need me.
Exactly. I can't tell whether going would be a betrayal or the fulfillment of everything they sacrificed for me.
I hadn't considered that. It's worth asking, even if the answer is no.

speakerB.en: That's an agonizing choice. What does your family say about it?
That's often how it is. People protect their children from guilt by hiding their own needs.
Perhaps it's neither. Is there a way of negotiating a later start date, or some remote arrangement, that would give you time to decide?
It is. Whatever you decide, make sure it's a decision you've made, not one you've drifted into.

scenarios.scenario: Explaining a cultural tradition to an outsider
scenarios.context: A host describes the significance of a ritual that others may find puzzling.

speakerA.en: I noticed you paused when we removed our shoes at the door. It's a custom that appears simple, but it's rooted in rather more than mere tidiness.
The home is regarded as a sanctuary, and shoes carry the outside world's dust and discord across the threshold. Removing them marks a transition.
Every culture has its rituals, though we rarely notice our own until a stranger asks us to explain them.
Perhaps the real value of such customs lies not in their origin but in the sense of belonging they create.

speakerB.en: I'd wondered about that. I assumed it was a matter of cleanliness, but I sensed there was a deeper meaning.
That's rather beautiful. We have nothing comparable, and I suspect we're poorer for it.
Quite so. I've never considered why we shake hands, for instance, and I couldn't justify it with any authority.
A thoughtful observation. I'll gladly leave my shoes at the door from now on, and with a clearer understanding of why.

scenarios.scenario: Navigating generational disagreement over family expectations
scenarios.context: A young adult discusses career choices with a parent who holds different values.

speakerA.en: I know you hoped I would pursue medicine, but I've decided to study design. I wanted you to hear it from me directly.
I'm aware of the sacrifices, and I'm profoundly grateful. That's precisely why I want to do something I can commit to wholeheartedly.
Perhaps not, but a life spent in a profession I dislike would be its own kind of poverty.
It lets me make things that are both useful and beautiful. I can't think of a more satisfying way to spend my working life.

speakerB.en: I'll be honest, I'm disappointed. I made sacrifices so you would have a stable and respectable career.
Stability matters, particularly in uncertain times. Passion is a luxury that doesn't always pay the rent.
That's a mature argument, even if I don't entirely agree. Tell me, what is it about design that draws you?
Then I'll need time to adjust, but I'd rather you were fulfilled than merely secure. Show me your work sometime.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing how family roles differ across cultures
scenarios.context: Two colleagues compare expectations regarding elderly relatives and household responsibility.

speakerA.en: In my family, it would be unthinkable to place an elderly parent in a care home. It would be considered a kind of abandonment.
I suppose each view carries its own logic. Ours emphasizes duty, yours emphasizes expertise.
That's undeniably true. My aunt gave up her career to look after my grandmother, and she never complained, though I suspect she grieved for what she gave up.
A fair point. Perhaps the answer lies in sharing the responsibility more evenly across the family.

speakerB.en: I can understand that, though in my country it's quite normal, and often seen as a responsible choice given the professional care available.
And each has its costs. Caring for a parent at home can be isolating, even punishing, for the one who shoulders the burden.
That's the part rarely discussed. Duty is admirable, but it shouldn't demand that one person absorb the entire cost.
That would be ideal. Though as any family will tell you, an equitable division of labor is easier to propose than to achieve.

scenarios.scenario: Describing a traditional family meal
scenarios.context: A person explains to a colleague how her family celebrates a big meal.

speakerA.en: In my family, we always get together on Sunday for a big lunch.
My grandmother usually cooks, and everyone brings something small, like dessert or drinks.
We talk, laugh, and sometimes play cards. It's the only time we're all in the same place.
You should come with me one day. My grandmother loves meeting new people.

speakerB.en: That sounds lovely. Who usually comes? Is it just your close family?
That's a great tradition. In my family, we only manage something like that once or twice a year.
I think it's important to have those moments. Everyone is so busy these days.
I'd really like that. Thank you for the invitation. I'll bring a cake.

scenarios.scenario: Asking about customs at a family gathering
scenarios.context: A guest asks a friend about the customs at his family's celebration.

speakerA.en: I'm a little nervous about tomorrow. Is there anything I should know before meeting your family?
Should I bring something with me, like flowers or a box of sweets?
And is there anything I should avoid saying? I don't want to offend anyone.
Thank you. That makes me feel much more relaxed.

speakerB.en: Don't worry, they're very friendly. Just remember to take your shoes off when you come in.
A small gift is a nice gesture. Sweets are perfect, because my grandfather has a sweet tooth.
Not really. Just avoid talking about politics at the table, and you'll be fine.
You'll do great. They'll probably ask you a lot of questions about your country.

scenarios.scenario: Comparing family traditions at weddings
scenarios.context: Two coworkers from different countries compare wedding customs.

speakerA.en: I'm going to a wedding in my home country next month, and I've been telling my husband about the customs there.
In my culture, the celebration lasts for three days, and the whole village is invited. There's music, dancing, and enormous amounts of food.
The bride wears several different dresses during the celebration, and the family prepares gifts for all the guests.
Really? It sounds much more relaxed. Do people give gifts to the couple, or do they usually give money?
That's interesting. Where I come from, we also give money in an envelope, but it's not polite to ask how much someone gave.
It's fascinating how many differences there are, yet the main idea is the same everywhere: celebrating love with the people you care about.

speakerB.en: That sounds exciting. How are weddings different there from the ones in your country? I've only been to a few here.
Three days! That's incredible. Here, it usually lasts one evening, and most people go home by midnight.
That's a lovely tradition. Here, the bride typically wears one white dress, and the guests receive a small favor, like a box of chocolates.
Usually money, or something from a list that the couple has prepared. It's a practical way to avoid getting five toasters.
That's a good rule. In my family, people who have been married for a long time often give advice to the couple, which can get a bit awkward.
I couldn't agree more. Traditions may differ, but the feeling is universal, and that's what makes weddings so special.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the role of grandparents
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about how grandparents are involved in family life in their cultures.

speakerA.en: My parents both work full-time, so my grandmother looks after my younger brothers most days. She's practically a second mother.
She lives with us, and she cooks every meal, which is how I learned most of my family recipes. We couldn't manage without her.
Do the grandparents in your family play a big role as well, or is it more common to live separately?
That seems like a good balance. I suppose it depends on how close the family is, and on how much space people have.
My grandmother tells us stories about her childhood almost every evening. I think that's why I feel so connected to my roots.
I think so too. Maybe we could invite your grandparents for a meal with mine one day, and let them share their stories.

speakerB.en: That's lovely. In my family, grandparents are important, too, but they usually live in their own homes, and we visit them on Sundays.
I'm sure she's wonderful. My grandfather taught me to play chess when I was seven, and we still play whenever I see him.
Mostly separately. They like being independent, although they often help us in emergencies, and they babysit when my parents travel.
Yes, and it's also a matter of tradition. Some cultures expect families to look after older relatives at home, while others prefer care homes.
That's beautiful. Stories connect people across generations, and it's a pity that so many families don't take the time to share them anymore.
That would be great. They'd probably get along well, even if they don't speak the same language.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing changing family structures
scenarios.context: Two colleagues compare how family life differs across generations.

speakerA.en: It's interesting how much the idea of family has changed in just two generations. My grandparents lived in the same village all their lives, whereas my siblings and I are spread across three continents.
I think that's partly the reason why people find it harder to maintain family traditions. When everyone lives nearby, customs are passed down naturally, but distance makes it more difficult.
On the other hand, technology has made it possible to stay in contact in ways that my grandparents could never have imagined. We have a weekly video call with the whole family.
That's true, though I sometimes wonder whether it's the same as spending time together in person. It's one thing to see someone on a screen, and another to share a meal.
I agree. Perhaps the answer is to make a point of meeting in person at least once or twice a year, even if it requires planning and some expense.
That's a nice idea. We might even choose a different country each time, which would give the younger members of the family a chance to discover new cultures.

speakerB.en: That's a fascinating change. In my family, it's quite the opposite. My parents moved abroad, but I've returned to live near them, and now we're three generations in the same neighborhood.
That's a valid concern. In my case, the opposite happened. Because we live close, my grandmother has become the keeper of all the traditions, and she makes sure that we continue them.
Absolutely. When my grandmother was ill last year, my cousin in Canada attended every family meeting by video. If it hadn't been for that, he would have felt completely excluded.
It's not identical, but I think that it's better than nothing. Studies suggest that regular contact, even if virtual, strengthens relationships, particularly when combined with occasional visits.
Absolutely. And in some cultures, the family gatherings are so important that people travel across the world for them, regardless of the costs, because they consider it a duty.
I love that. It would be a way of creating new traditions while preserving the old ones, and it might bring everyone closer.

scenarios.scenario: Navigating cultural differences in a mixed marriage
scenarios.context: A person describes how she and her partner handle different traditions.

speakerA.en: My partner and I come from very different backgrounds, so we've had to learn how to compromise on everything from food to how we celebrate the holidays.
At the start, it was quite stressful. His family expected a large celebration, while mine prefers a quiet dinner. We tried to satisfy everyone and ended up satisfying nobody.
Eventually, we realized that we couldn't continue like that. We decided to create our own traditions, drawing on both cultures, and to explain our choices clearly to our relatives.
It wasn't easy, and there were a few awkward conversations, but gradually people began to understand. Now his mother even asks me for my family's recipes.
I'd say that the most important lesson has been to avoid assuming that one's own way is the only right way. Customs that seem strange at first often have a meaningful history.
I think that's the greatest benefit. You see your own culture from the outside, and you appreciate things that you used to take for granted.

speakerB.en: That sounds both enriching and challenging. How did you manage the first few years? I imagine that the holidays were particularly difficult, with each side expecting you to be there.
That's a familiar situation. When two sets of expectations collide, there's a tendency to try to please everyone, but it usually leads to exhaustion and resentment.
That's a wise approach. Rather than choosing between two traditions, you built a third that belongs to both of you. Did your families react positively when you told them?
That's wonderful. It shows that people can adapt, provided they feel respected. Often, resistance comes from a fear that the old ways will be forgotten, rather than from genuine opposition.
I completely agree. Some of the customs that I thought were old-fashioned turned out to be sensible, once I understood the reasons for them. Curiosity is the key to getting along.
That's very true. Do you think your children will grow up feeling that they belong to both cultures, or will they find it confusing?

scenarios.scenario: Discussing care for an elderly parent among siblings
scenarios.context: Two siblings discuss how to arrange care for their mother.

speakerA.en: I think we need to make a decision about Mum. She had a fall last month, and I'm no longer sure that she can safely stay on her own in the house, especially during the winter.
I've looked into a few options. One is a care home, another is a live-in carer, and the third is that she'd move in with one of us, which would involve major changes to our lives.
I know she wants to remain in her own home, and I respect that. But we have to be realistic. If she falls again and nobody is there, the consequences could be very serious.
A live-in carer could be a good compromise, but the cost is considerable. If we divided it equally, it would come to about seven hundred euros a month each, which I could manage, if you could.
That makes sense. We should also ask her opinion, instead of discussing it behind her back. She's entitled to have a say in a decision that affects her so directly.
I'll arrange a family meeting this weekend. It will be a difficult conversation, but I think that it's better to have it now than to wait for an emergency.

speakerB.en: I've been thinking the same thing, but I didn't want to be the one to bring it up. It's hard to see Mum losing her independence, and I feel guilty about even discussing it.
I appreciate your doing the research. A care home might be the cheapest, but she'd hate it. She's lived in that house for forty years, and being surrounded by strangers would make her miserable.
I agree, but we also can't pretend that everything is fine. She's refused help so far, but she can't climb the stairs without holding on to the wall, and that's not safe.
That's possible for me, though I'd need to check my budget. I'd also like to see whether she's entitled to any state benefits for care, because they might cover part of the cost.
Absolutely. If she feels that the decision has been taken without her, she'll resist it. If she's involved in choosing the carer, she'll be much more likely to accept the arrangement.
Thank you. I'll be there. And let's try to stay calm, whatever happens. We both want what's best for her, even if we sometimes disagree about how to achieve it.

scenarios.scenario: Raising bilingual children
scenarios.context: Two parents discuss how to help their children keep two languages.

speakerA.en: I'm starting to worry that our children are losing their ability to speak my language. They answer me in English, even when I speak to them in my own, and it's becoming a pattern.
I was advised by a teacher to use only one language per parent, but it doesn't seem to be working, because they spend most of the day at school, and English naturally dominates.
That's a good idea. If we made it a rule that at home, we only speak the minority language, then they'd get consistent exposure, and the English would take care of itself at school.
I'd also like to organize more contact with my family, so that they can hear it spoken by other people, especially their grandparents, who don't speak a word of English.
I suppose that a bilingual childhood has its challenges, but I'm convinced that the advantages outweigh them. They'll have access to two cultures, and that will give them an important perspective.
Let's start this weekend. I'll find some books and films in my language, and we can make it part of our routine, so that it doesn't feel like a chore.

speakerB.en: I've noticed the same thing. It's common among children in their position. They tend to choose the language that's most useful to them at the time, and at the moment, that's English.
That approach works for some families, but it depends on how much effort is put in. If one parent speaks the minority language only for an hour a day, it's not enough to maintain it.
That sounds sensible. Experts say that children need at least thirty percent of their waking hours in a language to become fluent. It's difficult, but it's achievable if we're consistent.
That's a very good point. Children are much more motivated to speak a language when they have a real reason to use it, such as talking to relatives who don't understand anything else.
I couldn't agree more. Research shows that bilingual children often have better concentration and are more flexible thinkers. It's a gift that they'll be grateful for as adults.
Good idea. We could also start a weekly game evening in the minority language. If we make it fun, they won't see it as a duty, and they might even start to ask for it.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing whether a parent should move in with the family
scenarios.context: Two siblings discuss whether their widowed mother should move into one of their homes or stay in her own house.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking about Mum living alone since Dad passed away. Much as I'd like her to move in with us, I'm not sure it's the right solution. It's not so much the space as the effect on the children that worries me.
Both, to be honest. It's not so much that I mind the extra work as that I'd be stretched far too thin. If it weren't for my job, I'd happily take her in, but I'm out of the house for ten hours a day.

She says she'd prefer to stay, although I think she's lonelier than she admits. If it weren't for her neighbors, she'd hardly see anyone all week. It's not so much that she's unwell as that she's isolated.

That's a practical idea. If it weren't for the distance, I'd go every day. It's not so much a question of time as of organization, so a shared calendar might help. What would you say to a regular Sunday lunch at her place?

They'd love it. If it weren't for the grandchildren, she'd probably feel her life had lost its purpose. It's not so much that she needs looking after as that she needs to feel useful, which makes this arrangement perfect.

Good point. If it weren't for your suggestion, I'd have pushed her into a decision she didn't want. Much as I worry, I'll respect her wishes, and we'll review the situation in six months. Does that sound reasonable?

speakerB.en: I see what you mean, but I'd say we should ask what she wants first. If it weren't for her stairs, she could manage perfectly well at home. Is it the children or your work that makes you hesitate?
That's a valid point. Much as I'd like to offer our spare room, my flat is tiny. It's not so much a lack of willingness as a lack of space. Has she said anything about leaving her house?

Then perhaps the answer is more company, not a new home. Much as I'd like to see her more often, a weekly visit from each of us would make a difference. Could we arrange a rota between the three of us?

I'd say that's ideal, since she loves cooking for us. Much as I'd like to take over the cooking sometimes, it's not so much the meal as the company that she enjoys. Would your children be happy to come along?
Exactly. Much as we'd like to protect her, it's not so much safety as dignity that matters here. If it weren't for the risk of falls, I'd say she's fine, so perhaps we could install a few handrails.
Perfectly reasonable. It's not so much a final decision as a trial, and we can adjust it later. If it weren't for the three of us pulling together, this would be much harder. I'll call her tonight.

scenarios.scenario: Explaining a family tradition to a foreign visitor
scenarios.context: A visitor asks his host why the whole family gathers to bake a special bread each autumn, and the host explains what the tradition means to them.

speakerA.en: That smells wonderful. I'd love to know why your whole family seems to be involved in this cooking. Should I be helping, or would I only be in the way?
I'd be honored. I wish I could say my family had a tradition like this, but we rarely eat together now. What exactly do you celebrate, and why does everyone gather on this particular day?
That sounds moving. Should I ask your grandmother about those stories, or would it upset her? I wish I knew more about the customs here, so that I wouldn't make any mistakes at the table.

That's reassuring. I wish more traditions were passed on so openly. Does every generation take part, or do the younger ones sometimes lose interest, as often happens in my country when children grow up?

I can understand that. I wish I'd grown up with something like this. Should I ever have children, I'd like to start a similar ritual. Once you've experienced something this warm, it's hard to forget it.

I'm sure I will. I wish I could stay longer, but my flight leaves on Sunday. Should I come back next year, would it be possible to join you again? Once you've been welcomed like this, you want to return.

speakerB.en: You're welcome to help. It's a tradition we've kept for four generations, and I wish more families still did it. Once you've kneaded the dough with us, you'll understand why it matters so much. Should you get tired, just say so.

We celebrate the end of the harvest, as our ancestors did. Once you've heard the stories my grandmother tells, you'll see it's not just a meal. I wish you could have met my grandfather, since he started it all.

She'd be delighted, since she loves an audience. Should you make a mistake, nobody will mind, as long as you show interest. Once you've sat at the table, just follow what the oldest person does, and you'll be fine.

It happens here too, I'm afraid. Once you've left home, it's easy to drift away, and I wish my cousins came more often. Should they ever stop coming altogether, we'd lose something precious, which is why we insist.

Then you've already understood the purpose. Should you ever want the recipe, my mother will happily share it. I wish more visitors asked such thoughtful questions, instead of just taking photographs. Once you've tasted the bread, you'll want more.
You'd be most welcome. Should you decide to come, just let us know a month in advance. I wish every guest felt so at home. Once you've been part of the family table, you're always part of it.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a multicultural wedding with two families
scenarios.context: A groom and the bride's mother discuss how to combine two cultural traditions in the wedding.

speakerA.en: Thank you for meeting us, Mrs. Almeida. Sara and I would like your advice about the wedding. To be honest, the last thing we want is to offend either family, since our traditions are so different. Where should we begin?

My mother insists that the ceremony be in church, be it a small one or a large one. On the other hand, Sara would love a garden celebration, with your family's music. I'd say there must be a way to combine both.
That sounds wonderful. As far as food is concerned, my family expects roast lamb, while yours prefers fish. Be it a buffet or a sit-down dinner, we'd need both. Could the caterer manage that?

About a hundred and twenty. The last thing I'd want is to cut anyone out, even distant cousins. Sara thinks fewer would be more intimate, but I feel it would upset my grandparents. What would you recommend?

I like that idea. Then there's the question of language. My relatives speak little Portuguese, and yours speak little English. Be it speeches or toasts, we'd need someone to translate. Could your nephew help, as he's fluent in both?

Perfect, the program will make everyone feel included. Thank you, Mrs. Almeida, you've lifted a weight from my shoulders. I'll talk it over with Sara tonight, and we'll send you the details tomorrow, if that's all right.

speakerB.en: I'm glad you asked. In my family, the ceremony is long, with music and dancing, whereas yours is shorter, I believe. What matters most to you, a traditional ceremony or a modern one? And what does your mother expect?

There is. Why not hold the ceremony in church, and the celebration afterwards in a garden? That way, each family has its part. What matters is that nobody feels excluded, whether it's food, music or customs.

A buffet would be easiest, with a selection from both cuisines. I'd also suggest a vegetarian table, not to mention drinks for guests who don't drink alcohol. Have you thought about how many guests there'd be?

Family is important in both our cultures, so I'd say invite them all, provided the budget allows. If it doesn't, a smaller ceremony followed by a bigger party might work. What matters is that your grandparents feel respected.

He'd be delighted, and he'd be proud to be asked. I'd also propose that the speeches be short, so that translation doesn't slow things down. What do you think about a short printed program in both languages?
Please do. I'm happy to help in any way. To be honest, seeing two families come together is the real joy of a wedding. Whatever you decide, I'm sure it will be a beautiful day.

scenarios.scenario: Deciding how to raise a bilingual child
scenarios.context: Two parents from different countries discuss how to help their two-year-old daughter grow up speaking both of their languages.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking about Lily's language development. She's two now, and to be honest, I'm worried she'll end up speaking only English. Since you speak Polish and I speak English, how should we organize it?

One idea is 'one parent, one language'. I'd always speak English and you'd always speak Polish. It's not until children start school that the majority language takes over, so we need to build the foundation now.

I'd be happy to learn alongside her. Honestly, I've always wanted to. The more I hear Polish at home, the easier it'll be for me too. Besides, your parents will be delighted if Lily can speak with them.

A month is long, but I'd say it's worth it, provided I can work remotely for part of it. The earlier she hears natural conversations, the better her accent will be. Should we also look for Polish books and cartoons?
That's a good point. There's a community center near us with Saturday classes. The sooner we enroll her, the more likely she'll get a place. Do you think two is too young to start?

Agreed. Children often go through phases, and what matters is that we stay consistent. I'm glad we talked, since I felt much less sure before. Shall we write our plan down, so that we can review it in six months?

speakerB.en: I've been wondering too. I'd say the sooner we set a clear system, the better. Research suggests that children need regular exposure to a language, otherwise they won't use it actively. What did you have in mind?

I like that, although it may be harder for me, since we live in an English-speaking country. Were I to speak Polish all day, would you feel left out of conversations? On the other hand, it would be good for your Polish.

That's true, they'd be thrilled. It's not until they video-call that she realizes there's a language she can't use. Were we to visit them every summer, she'd get even more practice. Would you be happy to go for a month?

Definitely. As long as it's fun, she'll absorb it. I'd also suggest finding a weekend Polish school, so that she meets other children. It's not until a child has friends speaking the language that it feels useful to her.

Not for something playful. Songs and games are ideal at that age. I'd rather she enjoy it than feel pressured, since the aim is to love the language. Were she to refuse Polish for a while, we'd have to stay patient.
Yes, let's. As far as I'm concerned, this is one of the best gifts we can give her. Two languages mean two ways of seeing the world, and the sooner she starts, the more naturally it will come.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about sports you play or follow
scenarios.context: Two people discuss their favorite sports or fitness routines.

speakerA.en: Do you like sports?
Do you play football?
Is football popular here?
Do you watch sports on TV?
What's your favorite sport to watch on TV?
speakerA.fa: محبوب‌ترین ورزش برای تماشا از تلویزیون چیه؟

speakerA.en: I go jogging every morning before work. It keeps me fit.
speakerA.fa: هر روز صبح قبل از کار می‌رم دویدن. تناسب اندامم رو حفظ می‌کنه.

speakerA.en: I used to play football, but now I prefer swimming.
speakerA.fa: قبلاً فوتبال بازی می‌کردم، اما الان شنا رو ترجیح می‌دم.

speakerA.en: Have you ever tried yoga? It's great for both body and mind.
speakerA.fa: تا حالا یوگا رو امتحان کردی؟ هم برای بدن و هم برای ذهن عالیه.

speakerA.en: I'm training for a marathon next month. I run about 50 kilometers a week.
speakerA.fa: برای یه ماراتن ماه دیگه تمرین می‌کنم. هفته‌ای حدود ۵۰ کیلومتر می‌دوم.

speakerB.en: Yes, I love playing tennis.
Yes, I play with my friends.
Yes, it is very popular.
Yes, I watch tennis every weekend.
I really enjoy watching basketball, especially the NBA.
speakerB.fa: واقعاً از تماشای بسکتبال لذت می‌برم، مخصوصاً ان‌بی‌ای.

speakerB.en: That's great! I prefer cycling on the weekends.
speakerB.fa: عالیه! من آخر هفته‌ها دوچرخه‌سواری رو ترجیح می‌دم.

speakerB.en: Swimming is fantastic. I should try it more often.
speakerB.fa: شنا فوق‌العاده‌ست. باید بیشتر امتحانش کنم.

speakerB.en: I haven't, but I've heard good things about it. Maybe I'll join a class.
speakerB.fa: نه، اما چیزهای خوبی درباره‌ش شنیدم. شاید برم یه کلاس.

speakerB.en: Wow, that's impressive! How do you find the time with your busy schedule?
speakerB.fa: واو، قابل تحسینه! با برنامه شلوغت چطور وقتش رو پیدا می‌کنی؟

scenarios.scenario: Asking about gym or fitness activities
scenarios.context: In a gym or talking about exercise classes.

speakerA.en: Is there a gym near here?
Is it open today?
Can I join today?
Thank you. See you tomorrow!
How much is the monthly membership?
speakerA.fa: عضویت ماهیانه چنده؟

speakerA.en: Do you offer any group classes like Zumba or Pilates?
speakerA.fa: کلاس‌های گروهی مثل زومبا یا پیلاتس دارید؟

speakerA.en: What time does the gym open in the morning?
speakerA.fa: باشگاه صبح چه ساعتی باز می‌شه؟

speakerA.en: I'm looking for a personal trainer. Do you have any available?
speakerA.fa: دنبال مربی شخصی می‌گردم. کسی در دسترس دارید؟

speakerB.en: Yes, there's one on the next street.
Yes, it opens at six.
Yes, you can. Please sign here.
You're welcome. Have a nice day!
It's $50 per month, with a one-time registration fee.
speakerB.fa: ۵۰ دلار در ماه، با هزینه ثبت‌نام یک‌باره.

speakerB.en: We have yoga, spinning, and HIIT classes every day.
speakerB.fa: ما هر روز کلاس یوگا، اسپینینگ و اچ‌آی‌آی‌تی داریم.

speakerB.en: We open at 6 AM and close at 11 PM.
speakerB.fa: ساعت ۶ صبح باز و ۱۱ شب تعطیل می‌کنیم.

speakerB.en: Yes, we have three certified trainers. I can schedule a free consultation.
speakerB.fa: بله، سه مربی معتبر داریم. می‌تونم یه مشاوره رایگان تنظیم کنم.

scenarios.scenario: Playing football with friends
scenarios.context: Two friends plan a football game.

speakerA.en: Let's play football today.
We can play in the park.
At four o'clock.
Are you ready?
Which position do you usually play?
How many players do we need for a game?
Did you watch the match last night?
Can you play again next Saturday?

speakerB.en: Great idea! Where do we play?
OK. What time?
Good. I'll bring the ball.
Yes, I am. Let's go!
I'm a defender, but sometimes I play in midfield.
Eleven on each team, but we can play five against five.
Yes, it was exciting. Our team won two to one.
I think so. I'll check my schedule and let you know.

scenarios.scenario: Going for a morning run
scenarios.context: Two neighbors go jogging together.

speakerA.en: Do you run every day?
Let's run in the park.
Are you tired?
Sure. Let's drink some water.
How far do you usually run?
Do you have any tips for a beginner?
What time do you start in the morning?
Should I stretch before running?

speakerB.en: No, I run three times a week.
OK. It is a nice place.
A little. Can we stop?
Good idea. I'm very thirsty.
About five kilometers. I'm trying to run ten soon.
Start slowly, and wear comfortable running shoes.
Around six, before it gets too hot.
Yes, always warm up for five minutes first.

scenarios.scenario: Swimming at the pool
scenarios.context: A person asks the staff about a swimming pool.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Is the pool open?
How much is a ticket?
Do I need a cap?
Where are the changing rooms?
Is there a lane for slow swimmers?
Do you offer swimming lessons for adults?
Can I bring my own towel and goggles?
Is there a locker for my things?

speakerB.en: Yes, it is open until nine.
It is five dollars.
Yes, please wear a cap.
They are on the left.
Yes, the lane on the right is for beginners.
Yes, we have classes on Tuesday and Thursday evenings.
Of course. You can also rent them at the desk.
Yes, you need a coin for the locker. You get it back afterwards.

scenarios.scenario: Watching a match on TV
scenarios.context: Two friends watch a sports game together.

speakerA.en: Is the match on TV today?
Which team do you like?
Look! They have a goal!
Who wins today?
Who is the best player on your team?
Why did the referee stop the game?
It's half time. Would you like some snacks?
What was the final score?

speakerB.en: Yes, it starts at eight.
I like the red team.
Wow! That is great!
I think the red team wins.
Number ten. He scored twice last week.
A player was injured, so they need a short break.
Yes, please. I'll have some popcorn.
It was a draw, two all. It was a great game.

scenarios.scenario: Staying healthy
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about exercise and healthy habits.

speakerA.en: Do you exercise every day?
Do you eat healthy food?
I want to be strong.
Can we exercise together?
How many hours do you sleep at night?
Do you try to avoid sugary drinks?
How often do you go to the gym?
What helps you stay motivated?

speakerB.en: Yes, I walk for thirty minutes.
Yes, I eat fruit and vegetables.
Then drink water and sleep well.
Yes, of course. It's fun!
About eight hours. I go to bed early.
Yes, I drink water or tea instead.
Three times a week, usually after work.
Exercising with a friend. It makes it more fun.

scenarios.scenario: Starting a new exercise routine
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about starting to exercise regularly.

speakerA.en: I've decided to get fit this year. I just don't know where to start.
I tried that once, but I got bored after two weeks.
I did enjoy swimming as a kid. Maybe I should look for a pool near my office.
Would you like to join me? I could use the motivation myself.

speakerB.en: Start with something simple, like jogging three times a week.
Then find a sport you enjoy. Swimming or cycling might keep you more motivated.
Good idea. You could also go with a friend, so you encourage each other.
Sure. Let's try it twice a week and see how it goes.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about a recent match
scenarios.context: Two fans discuss the result of a football match.

speakerA.en: Did you watch the match last night? I couldn't believe the ending.
That second goal was incredible. The player was so far from the net.
Do you think we'll win the league this year?
At least we're playing better than we did at the start of the season.

speakerB.en: I did. We were losing until the last ten minutes, and then everything changed.
I know. Our coach made some excellent changes at half time.
It's possible, but we still have some tough games ahead.
True. Let's watch the next one together at my place.

scenarios.scenario: Joining a gym
scenarios.context: A person asks a gym employee about membership options.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'd like to find out more about your membership options, please.
I'm not sure I'll use it regularly. Is there a trial period?
What classes do you offer? I'm interested in yoga and maybe some strength training.
That sounds great. Do I need to bring my own towel?

speakerB.en: Certainly. We have a monthly plan and a yearly plan, which is cheaper in the long run.
Yes, you can try it for a week for free, and we'll show you around.
Yoga takes place every morning and evening, and we have a personal trainer who can help you with a program.
Yes, but we have lockers and showers. I'll sign you up for the trial now.

scenarios.scenario: Recovering from a sports injury
scenarios.context: An athlete discusses recovery with a physiotherapist.

speakerA.en: How is the knee feeling this week? You were struggling with the stairs at our last session.
I understand your impatience, but returning too soon is the most common reason for reinjury.
If you continue to make progress, probably another four to six weeks, though I can't guarantee that.
Better to miss the opening matches than be out for the entire year. Patience now will pay off later.

speakerB.en: Much better, though it still aches after a long day. I'm eager to get back to training.
How long do you think it will be before I can run again without risking further damage?
That's frustrating. The season starts in a month, and I'd hate to be on the sidelines.
You're right. I'll stick to the exercises and resist the urge to push it.

scenarios.scenario: Debating the role of competition in sport
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss whether winning matters most.

speakerA.en: Do you think children's sports should focus on winning, or is taking part more important?
But competition teaches resilience. Learning to lose gracefully is a valuable life skill.
That's true. I've seen some embarrassing behavior at youth matches, mostly from the adults.
That seems sensible. The kids who stick with sport are usually those who feel they belong, not those who win.

speakerB.en: I believe enjoyment should come first. Pressure to win can drain the fun out of it for young players.
I agree, though there's a difference between healthy rivalry and parents shouting from the sidelines.
Perhaps the answer is a balance, where effort is celebrated as much as the result.
Exactly. A trophy gathers dust, but a love of the game lasts a lifetime.

scenarios.scenario: Setting ambitious fitness goals
scenarios.context: A runner explains her training plan to a friend.

speakerA.en: I've signed up for a half marathon in the spring, and I'm hoping to finish in under two hours.
Better than expected. I follow a structured plan, with three short runs and one long run a week.
I'm learning to listen to my body. When my legs feel heavy, I take an extra day off.
I've started eating more carbohydrates the night before, and I notice I have more energy.

speakerB.en: That's quite ambitious, considering you only started running last year. How's the training going?
And do you incorporate rest days? Overtraining is a trap many beginners fall into.
Wise decision. Have you thought about nutrition? It makes a real difference over longer distances.
Excellent. Let me know if you want company on your long runs. I could do with the motivation.

scenarios.scenario: Debating a controversial refereeing decision
scenarios.context: Two fans argue about a disputed call that decided an important match.

speakerA.en: I still can't believe that penalty was awarded. The contact was negligible, and it completely changed the complexion of the match.
Rules aside, there's an unwritten principle that officials shouldn't decide a final on a marginal call. Context matters.
Fair enough, though video review was supposed to eliminate this sort of controversy, and it seems to have amplified it.
Perhaps the real problem is our expectation of perfection. Sport has always been shaped by human error.

speakerB.en: I'd contend it was justified. The defender's arm was clearly extended, and under the current rules, that's a punishable offense.
But that's precisely the danger of making exceptions. Once referees start weighing the occasion, consistency goes out the window.
That's true. It has stripped the game of its flow without delivering the certainty everyone promised.
I suppose so. Still, it's hard to stay philosophical when your team goes out on a technicality.

scenarios.scenario: Coaching an athlete through a setback
scenarios.context: A coach helps a young athlete regain confidence after a painful defeat in a final.

speakerA.en: I know you don't want to talk about it yet, but I think it's worth reviewing the race while it's still fresh.
I'd describe it differently. You made one tactical error under enormous pressure, which is something every elite athlete does at some point.
Nobody feels let down, least of all me. What I saw was an athlete who has improved more this season than anyone I've coached.
Then let's use that replay productively. We'll work on decision-making when fatigued, so that next time the instinct is already in your legs.

speakerB.en: There's not much to review. I froze in the last lap, and I threw away a year of preparation.
It doesn't feel that forgivable when you're the one who let the team down.
I'd like to believe that, but I can't stop replaying the moment I hesitated.
All right. I'd rather turn this into something useful than let it fester.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing up retirement from professional sport
scenarios.context: A veteran athlete discusses with her agent whether to retire at the end of the season.

speakerA.en: I've been putting off this conversation for months, but I think I need to decide whether this is my final season.
Both, really. My body recovers more slowly each year, and the hunger that used to get me out of bed at five has quietly faded.
That's precisely my fear. I'd rather leave while people still remember me at my best than limp out of the sport.
Knowing there's something beyond the finish line makes it easier. It's still strange to imagine an identity without the sport.

speakerB.en: I'm glad you've raised it. What's driving the question, the injuries or something less tangible?
That's an honest assessment, and it's rarer than you might think. Most athletes cling on for a season too long.
There's dignity in that, and there are options. Broadcasting offers have already come in, and the federation has asked about a coaching role.
It will take time, but you'll be leaving with your reputation intact and a considerable amount of choice.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the mental side of competitive sport
scenarios.context: Two athletes reflect on pressure, confidence and recovery from setbacks.

speakerA.en: People assume that sport is predominantly physical, but I'm convinced that most matches are won or lost in the mind.
What helped you most when you were struggling? I went through a spell where I couldn't shake the fear of failing.
That's easy to say, though rather harder to practice. I found myself overthinking every movement, which only made matters worse.
I might try that. It's a strange irony that caring less about the outcome often improves it.

speakerB.en: Entirely. I've seen far more talented players crumble under pressure than those with ordinary ability and steady nerves.
Learning to separate my worth from the result. Once I stopped treating every defeat as a verdict on my character, I played more freely.
Overthinking is the enemy of instinct. I worked with a coach who taught me to focus on the process rather than the scoreboard.
It is, and I suspect it applies well beyond sport. Detachment, properly understood, is simply another form of discipline.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a gradual return to training after an injury
scenarios.context: An athlete consults a physiotherapist about resuming activity safely.

speakerA.en: I'm desperate to get back to running, but I'm wary of undoing the progress we've made. How cautious should I be?
What would you recommend as a sensible progression? I'm prone to overdoing it the moment I feel good.
And if there's discomfort? I can't always tell whether it's normal soreness or a warning sign.
Understood. It's frustrating to proceed so slowly, but I'd rather be patient than injured again.

speakerB.en: Rather more than you'd like, I'm afraid. The tendon has healed, but it hasn't regained its full capacity to absorb load.
Start with alternating walking and jogging in short intervals, three times a week, and increase the duration only if there's no pain the next day.
A dull ache that fades quickly is acceptable. Sharp or lingering pain means you stop and reassess, without exception.
That's the right attitude. Most setbacks I treat come from people who ignored the very advice you're about to follow.

scenarios.scenario: Debating the role of money and ethics in professional sport
scenarios.context: Two fans disagree on whether commercial interests have corrupted the games they love.

speakerA.en: I find it increasingly difficult to enjoy the sport I grew up with. The commercial interests have swallowed the very spirit of the game.
Yes, but at what cost? Ticket prices have become prohibitive, and clubs treat supporters as customers rather than a community.
That's what troubles me most. Sport is supposed to transcend politics, yet it's being used to launder reputations.
I share the skepticism. Still, fans have more leverage than they realize, if they were willing to use it collectively.

speakerB.en: I'd contest that. The money has professionalized the sport and raised standards considerably, and it funds the youth academies that discover talent.
That's a legitimate grievance. I do worry about the sponsorship deals with regimes whose human rights record is, to put it kindly, questionable.
Perhaps the answer is greater regulation, though I'm skeptical whether governing bodies have the will to enforce it.
A boycott would be a bold gamble, but I admit I'd find it hard to resist the lure of the weekend fixture.

scenarios.scenario: Joining a basketball team
scenarios.context: A student asks a classmate about joining the school team.
