speakerA.en: Do you play basketball? We need one more player.
We're not the best, but we have a lot of fun.
Every Tuesday and Thursday after school.
Sports shoes are fine. Come on Tuesday.

speakerB.en: I played a little last year. Is the team good?
When do you practice?
I'd like to try. Do I need special shoes?
Great. I'll see you at the gym.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about an injury
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about a sports injury.

speakerA.en: Why are you walking like that? Are you okay?
Oh no! Did you see a doctor?
That's a long time. Can you do any exercise?
Take care of yourself. Don't play too early.

speakerB.en: I hurt my ankle during the football game.
Yes. She said I must rest for two weeks.
Only some easy stretching at home.
Don't worry. I'll wait until it's completely better.

scenarios.scenario: Planning to run a charity race
scenarios.context: Two friends decide to train for a local charity race.

speakerA.en: Did you hear about the charity race in May? I'm thinking of signing up.
It's only five kilometers, but I haven't run for ages. I need to start training soon.
That would be great. It's much easier to stay motivated when you have a partner.
Perfect. Let's start tomorrow evening, and I'll bring some water for both of us.

speakerB.en: I did. It raises money for the children's hospital, so it's a good cause. Do you want company?
Five kilometers is manageable. We could run three times a week and increase the distance slowly.
Exactly. And if we keep each other accountable, we won't make excuses when it rains.
Sounds like a plan. Just wear comfortable shoes so you don't hurt your feet.

scenarios.scenario: Choosing a sport for the whole family
scenarios.context: Two parents talk about a sport their family can enjoy together.

speakerA.en: We should find an activity the whole family can do together at the weekend.
Cycling might be a good option. The kids can ride safely on the path by the river.
I think so. We'd need helmets for them, and maybe a bike for our youngest.
Good idea. I'll check the prices online tonight and we can decide tomorrow.

speakerB.en: I agree. The children spend too much time indoors. Do you have anything in mind?
That's true, and it isn't expensive. We already have two bikes, don't we?
We could rent one at first, to see if she enjoys it before we buy anything.
Perfect. Maybe we can start this Sunday if the weather is nice.

scenarios.scenario: Signing up for a marathon
scenarios.context: Two runners discuss training for a first marathon.

speakerA.en: I've done it. I've signed up for the city marathon in October, and now there's no way back.
I've been running for about two years, but the longest distance I've done is fifteen kilometers, so I have a lot to learn.
I thought of following a training plan that lasts sixteen weeks, with three runs a week and a long run on Sundays.
That's good advice. I tend to run too fast at the beginning, and then I get tired halfway through, which is exactly the opposite of what I should do.
I'll try that. Would you like to run together on Sundays? It would be great to have someone to keep me motivated.
Fantastic. We can start this weekend with a gentle ten-kilometer run in the park, and see how we feel.

speakerB.en: Congratulations! That's a big decision. I did my first marathon three years ago, and I still remember how nervous I was.
That's a good base to start from. Most beginners can reach the marathon distance if they train consistently and patiently.
That sounds right. Just make sure that you increase the distance gradually, and don't forget to rest. Injuries usually happen when people do too much too soon.
Try to run slowly at the start, even if you feel strong. In a marathon, it's far better to finish the second half faster than the first.
I'd be glad to. I haven't had a running partner for a while, and it would help me get back into a routine as well.
Sounds perfect. Bring plenty of water, and wear shoes that you've already used for a few weeks. New shoes can cause blisters.

scenarios.scenario: Choosing between team and individual sports
scenarios.context: Two friends compare the advantages of team sports and solo exercise.

speakerA.en: I'm trying to decide whether to join a football team or continue going to the gym on my own. What would you do?
I do enjoy the gym, but I often lose motivation, and I find it hard to stay consistent when nobody expects me to be there.
That's what attracts me to football. But I haven't played since school, and I'm afraid I'll be much worse than everyone else.
You may be right. Most amateur teams are happy to have new players, as long as they show up regularly and try their best.
I'll go to the next training session and see how it feels. If I don't like it, I can always go back to the gym.
Thanks. If it goes well, I'll buy you a coffee, since you were the one who encouraged me.

speakerB.en: It depends on what you want. I prefer team sports, because you meet people, and you feel responsible for others.
That's the big advantage of a team. If you know that ten other people are waiting for you, you're far less likely to stay at home.
Don't worry about that. Nobody expects you to be perfect. The most important thing is to have fun and to keep moving.
Exactly. And if you've been going to the gym, your fitness is probably better than you think, so you'll catch up quickly.
That sounds like a good plan. Why don't you ask the coach whether you can try a session before you pay for the whole season?
Deal. And I'll come and watch your first match, so you'll have at least one person cheering for you.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the role of competition in sports
scenarios.context: Two friends debate whether competitive sports help or harm young people.

speakerA.en: I've been wondering whether competitive sports are good for children. My nephew has started playing football in a league, and the pressure seems quite intense for someone so young.
I understand the benefits, such as discipline and teamwork, but I've seen parents shouting from the sidelines, and it makes the children anxious rather than motivated.
That's a fair point. Not every child enjoys competition, though, and those who aren't naturally talented can feel discouraged and eventually give up sport entirely.
I suppose it depends on the attitude of the coaches and the parents. If the emphasis is on participation and improvement, the experience can be positive for everyone.
That makes sense. Perhaps the best approach is to offer both options, so that those who thrive on competition can pursue it, and others can enjoy sport without any pressure.
I'll suggest that to my sister. If my nephew were given a choice, I think he'd be much happier, and he might actually play for longer.

speakerB.en: It's a debate that has been going on for a long time. In my opinion, competition can be very positive, because it teaches children how to cope with both winning and losing.
That's unfortunate, and it's a common problem. A good coach should create an environment where effort is valued more than results, and where mistakes are treated as part of learning.
That's why many clubs now offer recreational leagues alongside competitive ones. Children can try the sport, and if they like it, they can progress to a more demanding level.
Exactly. Research suggests that children who feel supported are more likely to continue exercising in adulthood, whereas those who've been criticized often associate sport with stress.
I think so. Choice is crucial. When children feel that they are participating voluntarily, they tend to develop an internal motivation that lasts a lot longer than external pressure.
Good idea. And if he wants to try something different, like swimming or climbing, that might be an option too, since individual sports have a different dynamic.

scenarios.scenario: Recovering from a sports injury and rebuilding confidence
scenarios.context: An athlete discusses recovery with a coach after a long injury.

speakerA.en: It's been nearly nine months since the injury, and I'm finally allowed to train again. I'd like to talk about how to return gradually, because I'm anxious about reinjuring myself.
Physically, I feel reasonably strong, but mentally it's harder. Every time I land on that leg, I hesitate, as if I were expecting it to give way again.
That's reassuring. I'd hate to lose the progress I've made in rehabilitation by pushing too hard in the first few weeks, but I also don't want to fall behind the others.
I see. So you're suggesting that I should concentrate on technique rather than speed for the time being, and that I should only compete once I've reached specific benchmarks.
I think that's wise. If I hadn't followed the physiotherapist's advice so carefully, I might not have recovered so well, so I'll continue to be patient.
Thank you for being so supportive. Knowing that you're not expecting results immediately takes a lot of pressure off.

speakerB.en: It's good to see you back. First of all, congratulations on completing the rehabilitation. That wasn't easy, and I know how much effort you put into it.

That's very common after a long injury. The body heals faster than the mind, so it's important to build confidence gradually, through controlled exercises, before you return to full-intensity training.
You won't fall behind if you do it properly. Your teammates have been training consistently, but you've kept your fitness at a good level, and your experience is a considerable advantage.
Exactly. We'll set clear targets, and you'll progress only when you're ready. If we hurried, the risk of reinjury would be much higher, and you could be out for another season.
That attitude will serve you well. Athletes who respect the recovery process often return stronger than before, because they've learned to listen to their bodies more carefully.
You're welcome. Remember that you're part of this team, with or without medals. We'd rather have you healthy for ten years than injured after two.

scenarios.scenario: Joining a gym and choosing a membership
scenarios.context: A new member asks about memberships, classes, and cancellation terms.

speakerA.en: Hello. I'm thinking of joining the gym, and I'd like to know a bit more about the different memberships. I haven't exercised regularly for years, so I'd like something flexible.
I'll probably come two or three times a week, in the evenings. What would you recommend, considering that I'm not sure yet how often I'll really use it?
That sounds appealing. Do the monthly passes include group classes, or do they have to be paid for separately? I'd like to try yoga and something more intensive, like spinning.
And what about the contract? I've been caught out before by gyms that make it extremely difficult to cancel, and I don't want to be locked in for a year if it doesn't suit me.
That's much better than I expected. Could I have a free trial week first, to make sure I like the atmosphere and the equipment, before I sign anything?
Wonderful. I'll start tomorrow evening, then. Thank you for being so clear about the conditions, and for not putting any pressure on me.

speakerB.en: Hello, and welcome. We have three options: a pay-as-you-go ticket, a monthly membership, and an annual contract, which is the cheapest per month, but less flexible. What are you hoping to do here?

In that case, I'd recommend the monthly membership. It costs thirty-five euros, and you can use all the equipment, as well as the pool and the sauna, at any time between six in the morning and eleven at night.
Group classes are included in the monthly fee, but you need to book a place in advance, because the popular ones fill up quickly. There are three yoga sessions and two spinning classes every week.
The monthly membership can be canceled at any time with two weeks' notice, and there's no penalty. Only the annual contract has a minimum term, so you wouldn't be tied to anything.
Of course. We offer a seven-day trial, and I can arrange for one of the trainers to give you a tour, and to explain the equipment, since many people find it intimidating at first.
Excellent. Come at six tomorrow, and ask for me at the desk. I'll introduce you to the trainer, and we'll find out which classes would suit you best.

scenarios.scenario: Analyzing a team's defeat
scenarios.context: Two supporters discuss why their team lost an important match.

speakerA.en: I still can't believe that we lost. We were the better side for most of the match, and we conceded two goals in the last ten minutes. It makes no sense at all.
I think the coach made a mistake by bringing on the extra defender. We were winning, but instead of keeping the pressure on, we sat back and invited them to attack.
That's true, though you could say that it was the exhaustion that did us in. We played three matches in a week, and the players just didn't have the energy to defend properly at the end.
I'd say that the real problem is the lack of depth in the squad. If the substitutes were as good as the first team, we wouldn't have such difficulties when people get tired or injured.
I agree that we need a couple of new signings in January. But that depends on the budget, and I doubt that the owner will spend much, given what happened last season.
Still, there's no point in dwelling on it. We've got a few good matches coming up, and if we can win those, we'll be back in contention.

speakerB.en: I know. It was heartbreaking. We dominated, and then it all fell apart. If someone had told me at half-time that we'd lose, I'd have thought they were joking.
I agree, it was a negative decision. In the second half, we stopped passing the ball and just defended. The opposition's confidence grew, and they could feel that we were afraid.

That's a fair point, and the schedule is brutal. But the other team had played just as many matches, and they seemed to find the energy. It's partly a question of mentality and of how the squad is managed.
Quite possibly. The reserves have been poor all season, and that puts pressure on the starting eleven. If one player is out, the whole system suffers, and it becomes predictable.
He might surprise us, but I wouldn't count on it. In the meantime, the coach needs to find a way of using the squad more intelligently, and rest key players when it's possible.
You're right. Let's look at the positives. Our defense was solid for eighty minutes, and the young striker looked promising. If we learn from this, it might even make us stronger.

scenarios.scenario: Deciding whether to compete again after a long injury
scenarios.context: A runner who has spent a long time recovering from an injury talks to her coach about whether to race again or retire from competition.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking about whether I should compete again. Had I known the injury would take eighteen months, I'd probably have retired earlier. If it weren't for the support of my physiotherapist, I'd have given up completely.
Mostly the second, to be honest. If only my times had returned to normal, I wouldn't be doubting myself. Had I known how slowly recovery works, I'd have been more patient with my body from the start.
I have, and I'm about five percent slower. If only I could close that gap quickly, I'd enter the spring marathon. Had I known five percent would feel like so much, I'd have set smaller targets.

That's an interesting suggestion. If only I'd thought of that sooner, I'd have entered a ten-kilometer race months ago. Had I known you'd support the idea, I'd have asked you earlier. Which race would you recommend?
Hills don't frighten me, as long as my knee holds up. I wish I could promise I'd finish well, but I'd be happy just to cross the line. If only I felt as confident as you sound.

Then let's do it. I wish I could say I'm not nervous, but I am. If it weren't for your faith in me, I wouldn't dare try. Had I known how good it would feel to have a goal again, I'd have set one months ago.

speakerB.en: I understand, and I'd say it's a decision you shouldn't rush. If it weren't for your discipline, you wouldn't have recovered this well. Is it the pain that worries you, or the thought of not being as fast as before?

That's natural, but I'd say your times are better than you think. If it weren't for the two months you lost to a minor setback, you'd be much closer to your old pace. Have you compared your latest results with last year's?

Five percent is nothing for someone who has been through what you have. If it weren't for the long break, you'd be right back where you were. I wish you could see your progress as I do. Would a shorter race be a better start?

There's a local ten-kilometer race in April, which is flat and fast. If it weren't for the hills in the first half, I'd call it ideal, but it's still manageable. Had I known you were ready, I'd have mentioned it sooner.

Confidence will come with the first race. If it weren't for your patience over the last year, I'd be more cautious, but you've earned this chance. Had I known how determined you were, I'd have pushed you sooner.

Good, I'll draw up a plan this week. If it weren't for your work in physiotherapy, none of this would be possible. I wish every athlete trained with your attitude. Let's start with easy runs and build gradually.

scenarios.scenario: Advising a newcomer who wants to join a running club
scenarios.context: An experienced member of a local running club answers a nervous beginner's questions on the beginner's first evening.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'm new, and I'm rather nervous. I've only been running for a few months, and I'd appreciate it if you could tell me whether I'm fast enough to keep up with the group.

That's a relief. I'd appreciate it if you could explain how the sessions work, since I don't want to look foolish on my first night. Should I bring anything special, or is ordinary running gear enough?
That's good to know. I'd appreciate it if you could tell me how far we go, as I've never run more than five kilometers, and I'd hate to hold everyone back or get left behind.
That's very kind. I'd appreciate it if you could also give me some advice on avoiding injuries, since I've had a sore knee on and off. Should I see a physiotherapist before I start?
That's sensible advice. I'd appreciate it if you could introduce me to a few people, since I don't know anyone yet. Should I join the social evenings too, or are they only for regular members?
That sounds wonderful. I'd appreciate it if you could show me where we start tonight. Should I just follow you, or is there a particular spot where everyone gathers before the run?

speakerB.en: Welcome, and don't worry. We have several groups, so there's always someone at your pace. Should you find the first group too fast, you can drop back to the second. Once you've done a few sessions, you'll know where you belong.

Ordinary gear is fine, although I'd bring a reflective jacket, since we run in the evenings. Once you've warmed up with the others, the pace is relaxed for the first twenty minutes. Should you need to stop, nobody will mind.

Most evenings are about six kilometers, though beginners can shorten the route. Once you've built up some stamina, you can join the longer runs on weekends. Should anyone get left behind, we always wait at the junctions.

It wouldn't hurt, although it isn't necessary, as long as you build up gradually. Once you've warmed up properly and stretched, the risk drops considerably. Should the knee get worse, rest for a few days and don't push through.

Everyone's welcome. We usually go for coffee afterwards, and once you've been a couple of times, it'll feel like a second family. Should you want to enter a race together, several of us sign up every season.

Follow me. Once you've seen the gathering point by the fountain, you can't miss it next time. Should you be late, just text the group, and someone will wait. Let's get you introduced before we set off.

scenarios.scenario: Setting a realistic marathon goal with a running coach
scenarios.context: A runner asks a coach to help her set a sensible time target for her first marathon.

speakerA.en: Thanks for taking me on, coach. I'd like to run my first marathon in April, and to be honest, I'm aiming for under four hours. I've been running for two years, so I'd say it's realistic. What's your opinion?

My best is fifty-two minutes, and I train four days a week. Only when I started following a plan did I improve, so I'm fairly disciplined. On the other hand, I get injured easily, since I've pushed too hard before. Does that worry you?

Honestly, it's disappointing, but I see your logic. As far as I'm concerned, finishing healthy matters more than hitting a number. Not until I'd injured my knee last year did I realize how costly impatience can be. What would the plan look like?

I think so, although my work schedule is unpredictable. Some weeks I travel, and I can't always run. If I miss a session, would it ruin the plan? I'd hate to push myself to the point where I overdo it to catch up.

That's reassuring. What about nutrition? To be honest, I've never paid much attention, and I've heard that people can hit a wall around thirty kilometers. Is it true that food makes that much difference?

Good to know. I'll start experimenting, and I'll keep a log of what works. Thank you for being so realistic, since I'd rather have honest advice than flattery. Should we set a target for the half marathon in February as a test?

speakerB.en: Happy to help. Before I answer, I'd like to know more. Not until I see your recent race times can I judge whether four hours is sensible. What's your best ten-kilometer time, and how many days a week do you currently train?

It does, a little. Fifty-two minutes suggests a time closer to four hours ten, provided that everything goes well. I'd rather you aim for four-fifteen and beat it than push yourself to the point where you get hurt. How does that sound?

Sixteen weeks, with three runs and one strength session a week. Only when you've built a solid base should we add speed work. Provided that you rest properly, your long run can reach thirty-two kilometers. Would you be able to commit to that?

Never try to catch up. Missing one session hardly matters, provided you stay consistent over the weeks. Not until you miss several in a row do we need to adjust the plan. Just tell me, and we'll rearrange things together.

It makes a huge difference. Only when you practice eating during long runs will your stomach cope on race day. I'd suggest trying gels from week six, provided they don't upset you. Some runners eat so little that they hit a wall early.

Excellent idea. Aim for two hours, provided the training goes smoothly. Not until we see that result can we decide on a final goal for April. I'm confident you'll get there, and I'll send you the first week's schedule tonight.

scenarios.scenario: Reviewing a heavy defeat with the team captain
scenarios.context: A football coach talks with his captain after a heavy defeat, looking honestly at what went wrong.

speakerA.en: Thanks for staying behind, Tom. I wanted to talk about yesterday's defeat. Losing five-one was painful, and I'd like your honest opinion. To be honest, I think we could have played much better. What did you see out there?

That's a fair point, and I should have made that change at half-time. If anything, the mistake was mine. But what concerned me even more was the lack of communication. The defense could have talked more. Did you notice that?

Don't be too hard on yourself. A captain can't control everything. On the other hand, you could have shouted instructions once things started going wrong. Little did I expect you'd be so quiet. Was something bothering you?

I appreciate your honesty. What matters is how we respond. We could have trained harder this week, but we should rest instead, since several players are carrying knocks. How do you think the team's morale is?

I agree. What I'd like is for you to talk to them individually before Thursday's training. Little did they know how much they look up to you. Would you be comfortable doing that? I'd back you up, of course.
Exactly. And we'll review the video together on Friday, so that everyone sees what could have gone better. Thank you, Tom. I'm glad we can be so open, because it makes the team stronger.

speakerB.en: I agree, Coach. We should have kept the ball in the first half. Little did we realize how tired the midfield was, and by the time we reacted, we were already two goals down. It might have been different with an earlier substitution.
I did. Several times we ended up chasing the same man because nobody called who was covering him. I should have organized them better. If anything, I was too focused on my own game, which I regret.

Honestly, I was frustrated with the referee's decision on the second goal. I let it distract me, and I might have lost focus. It's no excuse, but it explains why I stopped leading. As far as I'm concerned, that was my biggest error.

Mixed. Some players are determined to bounce back, but a few seem discouraged. If anything, the younger ones are taking it hardest. They might have expected an easier match. I'd say they need reassurance more than criticism.

Of course, Coach. I should have done it already, to be honest. I'll tell them that one bad match doesn't define us. We could have used the same speech after the cup defeat last year, and it worked then.

Thank you for listening, Coach. I'd say we're closer to a turnaround than the score suggests. If anything, this defeat might be the best thing that could have happened to us. We'll be ready for Saturday.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about devices and apps
scenarios.context: People discuss their phones, social media, or online habits.

speakerA.en: What kind of phone do you have?
Do you like your phone?
Do you have a computer?
Is it new?
Are you on social media? I'd like to connect with you.
speakerA.fa: توی شبکه‌های اجتماعی هستی؟ دوست دارم باهات ارتباط برقرار کنم.

speakerA.en: I spend too much time on my phone these days. I need to cut back.
speakerA.fa: این روزا بیش از حد وقت رو گوشیم می‌ذارم. باید کم کنم.

speakerA.en: Have you tried any of the new AI tools? They're incredibly useful.
speakerA.fa: ابزارهای جدید هوش مصنوعی رو امتحان کردی؟ فوق‌العاده مفید هستن.

speakerA.en: I prefer using messaging apps over calling. It's more convenient.
speakerA.fa: ارسال پیام رو به تماس تلفنی ترجیح می‌دم. راحت‌تره.

speakerA.en: My laptop crashed yesterday and I lost all my files. I'm devastated!
speakerA.fa: دیروز لپ‌تاپم هنگ کرد و همه فایل‌هام رو از دست دادم. حسابی ناراحتم!

speakerB.en: I have an iPhone. It's the newest model.
Yes, it is very fast.
Yes, I have a laptop.
No, it is two years old.
Yeah, I'm on Instagram and WhatsApp. What's your username?
speakerB.fa: آره، توی اینستاگرام و واتس‌اپ هستم. اسم کاربریت چیه؟

speakerB.en: I know the feeling. I try to keep my screen time under two hours a day.
speakerB.fa: حالت رو می‌دونم. سعی می‌کنم زمان استفاده از صفحه رو زیر دو ساعت در روز نگه دارم.

speakerB.en: Not yet. Are they easy to use?
speakerB.fa: نه هنوز. استفاده ازشون راحته؟

speakerB.en: I agree. It's faster and I can reply whenever I want.
speakerB.fa: موافقم. سریع‌تره و هر وقت بخوام می‌تونم جواب بدم.

speakerB.en: Oh no! Did you have a backup? Maybe you can recover them.
speakerB.fa: اوه نه! پشتیبان داشتی؟ شاید بتونی بازیابیش کنی.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for help with technology
scenarios.context: Someone needs assistance with a device or software.

speakerA.en: Can you help me, please?
My phone is not working.
I don't have my charger.
Thank you so much.
My Wi-Fi isn't working. What should I do?
speakerA.fa: وای‌فای‌م کار نمی‌کنه. چیکار کنم؟

speakerA.en: Can you help me set up this app on my phone?
speakerA.fa: میشه کمکم کنی این برنامه رو روی گوشیم نصب کنم؟

speakerA.en: I don't understand how to send a file by email. Could you show me?
speakerA.fa: نمی‌دونم چطور یه فایل با ایمیل بفرستم. میشه بهم نشون بدی؟

speakerA.en: My screen keeps freezing. I think there's a virus.
speakerA.fa: صفحه‌ام مدام یخ می‌زنه. فکر کنم ویروس داره.

speakerA.en: Could you recommend a good editing software for photos?
speakerA.fa: میشه یه نرم‌افزار خوب برای ویرایش عکس پیشنهاد بدی؟

speakerB.en: Sure. What is the problem?
Is the battery low?
You can use mine.
No problem.
Try restarting your router. That usually works.
speakerB.fa: روتر رو ری‌استارت کن. معمولاً جواب میده.

speakerB.en: Sure, let me see your phone. I'll install it for you.
speakerB.fa: حتماً، بذارید گوشیتون رو ببینم. نصبش می‌کنم.

speakerB.en: Yes, just open your email, click on 'attach file,' and select it.
speakerB.fa: بله، فقط ایمیل رو باز کن، روی 'پیوست فایل' کلیک کن و انتخابش کن.

speakerB.en: You might need to run an antivirus scan. I can help you with that.
speakerB.fa: شاید باید یه اسکن آنتی‌ویروس اجرا کنی. می‌تونم توش کمک کنم.

speakerB.en: I recommend Lightroom for professionals, or Snapseed for quick edits.
speakerB.fa: لایت‌روم رو برای حرفه‌ای‌ها توصیه می‌کنم، یا اسنپ‌سید برای ویرایش سریع.

scenarios.scenario: Making a phone call
scenarios.context: Two friends talk on the phone.

speakerA.en: Hello, Anna? It's Tom.
I'm fine. Are you at home?
Can I call you later?
OK. Bye!
Hello, this is Tom. Is this a good time to talk?
I'm calling about the meeting tomorrow.
It starts at ten. Can you hear me clearly? The signal is weak.
No problem. I'll call you back shortly.

speakerB.en: Hi Tom! How are you?
Yes, I am. Why?
Sure. Call me at six.
Bye! Talk to you later.
Yes, I have a few minutes. What's up?
Sure. What time does it start?
Not very well. Could you call me again in a minute?
Thanks. Talk to you soon.

scenarios.scenario: Sending a text message
scenarios.context: Two friends send messages on their phones.

speakerA.en: Did you get my message?
I sent it five minutes ago.
What is your phone number?
Please send me a photo.
I'll text you the address of the restaurant.
I just sent it. Can you see it on the map?
Could you reply to the group message? Everyone is waiting.
My phone is almost out of battery. I'll text you later.

speakerB.en: No, not yet.
Oh, I see it now. Thanks!
OK. I'll send it now.
Great. Please send me your location too.
Yes, I got it. I'll be there in twenty minutes.
Oh, sorry. I didn't see it. I'll answer now.
OK. Send me a message when you arrive.

scenarios.scenario: Connecting to Wi-Fi
scenarios.context: A customer asks for the Wi-Fi at a café.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Do you have Wi-Fi?
What is the password?
The Wi-Fi is slow.
It works now. Thank you!
Is the Wi-Fi free for customers?
I can see the network, but I can't connect.
Could you write the password down for me?
Is there a quiet place where I can work online?

speakerB.en: Yes, we do.
It's on the menu.
Sorry. Please try again.
You're welcome.
Yes, but it's limited to one hour per person.
Try turning your Wi-Fi off and on again.
Sure. It's 'coffee123', all in lowercase.
Yes, the tables by the window are quiet, and there are power sockets.

scenarios.scenario: Using a computer
scenarios.context: A student learns to use a computer.

speakerA.en: Can you turn on the computer?
Where is the mouse?
How do I open the email?
I can do it now!
How do I save this document?
Where did my file go? I can't find it.
The computer is very slow today. What should I do?
Should I back up my files?

speakerB.en: Yes. Press this button.
It's next to the keyboard.
Click on this icon.
Great job!
Click on 'File', then choose 'Save as'.
Check the 'Downloads' folder. You can also use the search box.
Close the programs you aren't using, then restart it.
Yes, always keep a copy on a USB drive or online.

scenarios.scenario: Video call with family
scenarios.context: A person talks to a family member on a video call.

speakerA.en: Can you see me?
Can you hear me?
Is this better?
I miss you.
I can't see you. Is your camera turned on?
The connection is bad. Your voice keeps cutting out.
Could you share your screen so I can see the file?
Shall we have another call next Sunday?

speakerB.en: Yes, I can see you.
No, I can't. Please speak louder.
Yes, it's much better.
I miss you too. Call me again soon.
Oh, sorry. Let me click the camera icon. Is that better?
Let me move closer to the router.
Sure. Can you see it now?
Yes, same time. I'll send you the link.

scenarios.scenario: Helping a relative with a smartphone
scenarios.context: A young woman helps her grandfather use his new phone.

speakerA.en: Grandpa, I'll show you how to send photos to the family group chat.
It's not complicated. First, open the gallery and choose the picture you want.
Tap the share icon, then pick the family group from the list.
You'll see two checkmarks next to your message when it has been delivered.

speakerB.en: Thank you. I still get confused with all these buttons and icons.
Like this one of the garden? What do I press next?
I see it now. And how do I know if everyone has received it?
How clever. I'll practice every day until I get the hang of it.

scenarios.scenario: Dealing with a slow computer
scenarios.context: A coworker asks an IT technician for help.

speakerA.en: My computer has been very slow for the last few days. Do you know what might be wrong?
Not for a week or so. I usually just close the lid at night.
I also have hundreds of files on the desktop. Could that be the reason?
How can I find that out? I'm not very good with computers.

speakerB.en: It could be a lot of things. Have you restarted it recently?
That can cause problems. Programs build up in the memory and slow everything down.
Partly, yes. I'd also check whether the storage is almost full.
I'll come over and take a look. It should take about ten minutes.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about social media habits
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss how much time they spend online.

speakerA.en: I looked at my screen time report yesterday, and I was shocked. I spend four hours a day on my phone.
I feel like I check it without even thinking, like it's a habit.
Maybe I should try that. Do you think social media has a bad effect on us?
On the other hand, it's a good way to stay in touch with friends who live far away.

speakerB.en: That's quite a lot, but I'm probably the same. Most of it is social media for me.
I've started turning off notifications in the evening, and it's helped a bit.
It can, especially if you compare yourself to other people all the time.
True. I suppose the key is finding a balance.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing privacy concerns online
scenarios.context: Two friends debate how much personal information to share online.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking about deleting my social media accounts. It feels as though everything I do is being tracked.
What's the alternative? The companies make enormous profits from our data, and we get nothing in return.
I suppose, but the settings change constantly, and nobody reads the terms and conditions.
Which is why individuals are left to protect themselves, often without knowing how.

speakerB.en: I share your concerns, but I'm not sure quitting altogether is the answer.
You could tighten your privacy settings and limit what you post. It's not perfect, but it reduces your exposure.
That's a fair criticism. Perhaps the real problem is that regulation hasn't kept pace with technology.
Until the rules improve, we should at least be selective about what we share and with whom.

scenarios.scenario: Troubleshooting a video call problem
scenarios.context: Two colleagues try to fix a connection issue before an important meeting.

speakerA.en: I can see you, but your audio keeps cutting out. Is there anything we can do before the client joins?
That's a good idea. Also, close any unnecessary applications, as they might be using up bandwidth.
Much better, although there's a slight echo. Could you try wearing headphones?
While you're doing that, I'll send the client a backup link in case the platform crashes.

speakerB.en: Let me try switching to a wired connection. The Wi-Fi in this room has been unreliable all week.
Done. Can you hear me properly now? I've also moved closer to the microphone.
I'll find a pair. Give me a moment, as they're somewhere in my bag.
Smart thinking. With any luck, we'll be ready with a few minutes to spare.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the pros and cons of artificial intelligence
scenarios.context: Two coworkers share their views on AI in the workplace.

speakerA.en: Our department has just started using an AI tool to draft reports. What do you make of it?
In what sense? As long as someone checks the output, surely it's just a more efficient way of working?
That's a valid point. We'd need clear procedures for reviewing everything it produces.
I understand the fear, but history suggests technology changes the nature of work rather than eliminating it.

speakerB.en: It's impressive, and it saves time, but I worry about how much we're relying on it.
The trouble is that people tend to trust what looks polished, even when it contains errors.
There's also the question of jobs. Some colleagues are anxious that they'll be made redundant.
Perhaps, though the transition could be painful for those who can't adapt quickly enough.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating screen-time boundaries
scenarios.context: A parent and a teenager discuss limits on phone use at home.

speakerA.en: I'd like us to talk about your phone usage. I'm not trying to punish you, but the amount of time you spend on it concerns me.
I don't doubt that, though I've noticed you reaching for it constantly, even during dinner and conversations.
That's a legitimate point, and I don't want to isolate you. What if we agreed on a few phone-free times instead of imposing a strict limit?
Meals, and the hour before bedtime, for all of us, including me. I'm hardly a model of restraint myself.

speakerB.en: I understand, but it isn't as though I'm wasting time. Half of it is homework and keeping in touch with friends.
Everyone does that. If I'm the only one who's offline, I end up missing things and feeling left out.
That's a bit more reasonable. What did you have in mind?
If it applies to you too, I'll agree. But I'm holding you to it, so no checking emails at the table.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting a security breach to the IT department
scenarios.context: An employee reports a suspicious email that may have compromised her account.

speakerA.en: I need to report something urgent. I clicked a link in an email that I now suspect was a phishing attempt, and I entered my password.
About twenty minutes ago. The email appeared to come from our finance director, which is why I didn't hesitate.
Should I be worried that they've already accessed anything sensitive?
I use a variation of it on a couple of other accounts, I'm afraid. I'll change those as soon as we're finished.

speakerB.en: Thank you for coming forward straight away. That makes a considerable difference. When did this happen?
That's how these attacks work; they rely on familiarity. I'll lock your account immediately and force a password reset.
We'll review the login records to see whether there was any unauthorized activity. In the meantime, please avoid using that password anywhere else.
Please do, and consider a password manager. We'll also circulate this email as a warning, without naming you, of course.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the digital divide
scenarios.context: Two colleagues talk about unequal access to technology and its social consequences.

speakerA.en: I read a report suggesting that nearly a fifth of households in the region still lack reliable internet access. That's startling for this day and age.
And it isn't just access. Many older people have the equipment but not the confidence to use it, which leaves them equally stranded.
Do you think the responsibility lies with governments, or should companies that profit from digital services contribute?
That seems fair. Otherwise, we risk building a society where convenience for the majority becomes a barrier for the minority.

speakerB.en: It's more significant than it sounds. When essential services, from banking to healthcare appointments, move online, those without access are effectively excluded.
Right, and the assumption that everyone is digitally fluent leads to poorly designed services that penalize the most vulnerable.
Both, I'd say. Public investment can build the infrastructure, but companies should be obliged to offer genuine non-digital alternatives.
Precisely. Progress that leaves people behind isn't progress at all, merely efficiency for some.

scenarios.scenario: Explaining a technical problem to a non-specialist
scenarios.context: An IT professional translates jargon into plain language for a worried manager.

speakerA.en: I'll try to keep this free of jargon. Essentially, the server that hosts our systems has run out of capacity, and it's affecting performance.
It's serious enough to warrant action, though not catastrophic. If we do nothing, we risk intermittent outages during peak hours.
I'd suggest migrating to a larger instance, which would take about four hours out of hours and cost roughly a fifth more per month.
Minimal, since we'll take a complete backup beforehand and verify it. I'd also schedule the work for a weekend to limit the impact.

speakerB.en: I see. And is that a minor inconvenience, or should I be concerned about it?
What would you recommend, and what are we looking at in terms of cost and disruption?
That's more palatable than I'd feared. Is there any risk of data loss during the migration?
Please proceed, then. And thank you for explaining it plainly; I find that most technical people overestimate how much I wish to know.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the implications of artificial intelligence on work
scenarios.context: Two colleagues contemplate how automation may reshape their profession.

speakerA.en: I can't decide whether the rise of artificial intelligence is cause for optimism or alarm. I suspect it's both, depending on one's vantage point.
That's the crux of it. The technology isn't inherently malign, but the way its benefits are distributed is a matter of political choice.
Yet history also shows that new forms of work have emerged, often ones nobody anticipated at the outset.
A fair point. Perhaps the focus should be on retraining and safety nets, rather than on resisting the technology itself.

speakerB.en: I tend to agree. It will undoubtedly remove tedious tasks, though I worry about how the displaced workers will be supported.
And political choices are rarely made with the interests of the displaced in mind. History suggests the transition will be painful.
True, but that offers little comfort to someone whose skills are rendered obsolete at fifty.
Resistance would be futile in any case. The question is whether we shape the change or merely endure it.

scenarios.scenario: Resolving a misunderstanding caused by an ambiguous message
scenarios.context: Two colleagues sort out a tense exchange that arose from tone lost in writing.

speakerA.en: I wanted to follow up on your email, because I read it as rather curt, and I'd like to be sure I haven't misjudged it.
I suspected as much, but the line about 'as previously discussed' struck me as faintly reproachful.
These things are so easily distorted in writing. A raised eyebrow vanishes, and what remains is simply a block of text.
I'd appreciate that, and I'll try to give people the benefit of the doubt before assuming the worst.

speakerB.en: Curt? Goodness, I'd intended it to be efficient. I was typing between meetings, and I clearly neglected the pleasantries.
Not remotely. I meant it merely as a reference to our earlier conversation. I'm mortified that it came across as criticism.
That's precisely why I should have picked up the phone. I'll bear that in mind whenever the matter is anything more than routine.
A good principle for us both. Shall we agree that when in doubt, we ask rather than assume?

scenarios.scenario: Buying a new phone
scenarios.context: A customer asks a shop assistant about phones.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'm looking for a new phone. Can you help me?
I mostly take photos and use social media.
How much is it?
That's a little expensive. Is there a cheaper one?

speakerB.en: Of course. What do you need it for?
This model has a very good camera and a big screen.
It's four hundred dollars, and it has a two-year guarantee.
Yes, this one is two hundred and fifty, with a smaller camera.

scenarios.scenario: Forgetting a password
scenarios.context: A person asks a friend for help with a forgotten password.

speakerA.en: I can't log in to my email. I forgot my password.
How do I do that?
Now it says that it sent me a code.
Done! This time I'll write it in my notebook.

speakerB.en: Don't worry. You can reset it.
Click on 'Forgot password' and enter your phone number.
Good. Write the code in the box and choose a new password.
Choose something strong, but easy for you to remember.

scenarios.scenario: Troubleshooting a slow internet connection
scenarios.context: A customer calls his provider because the internet is very slow.

speakerA.en: Hello, my internet has been extremely slow for the past two days.
Yes, several times, but it hasn't helped.
Of course. It's really difficult to work from home like this.
How long will it take to fix?

speakerB.en: I'm sorry about that. Have you tried restarting the router?
Let me check your line. Could you hold on for a moment?
I see the problem. There's a fault in your area, and a technician is already working on it.
It should be solved by this evening. We'll send you a message when it works.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about online safety
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss how to protect their accounts.

speakerA.en: Did you hear about the hacking attack on that big online shop?
It makes me nervous. I use the same password for most of my accounts.
But I can't remember them all.
I'll look into it tonight. Do you recommend any particular one?

speakerB.en: Yes, thousands of customers lost their personal information.
That's risky. You should use a different password for each one.
A password manager can do it for you, and it's quite safe.
I use a free one, and I'll send you the name after work.

scenarios.scenario: Setting up a new smartphone
scenarios.context: A customer asks a shop assistant for help transferring data to a new phone.

speakerA.en: Hi. I bought this phone yesterday, but I'm having trouble moving everything from my old one. Could you help me?
I'd like to transfer my contacts, photos, and messages. I tried to do it myself, but the process stopped halfway through.
My old phone is quite slow, and the storage is almost full. I'm afraid I might have lost some of the files.
That's a relief. Is there a way to make sure that this doesn't happen again, so that my photos are stored somewhere safe?
I'd prefer a free option, if there is one. I don't take that many pictures, so I don't need much space.
Thank you so much. I feel much more confident now, and I'll set up the backup as soon as I get home.

speakerB.en: Of course. Let me have a look. Which kind of phone did you have before, and do you remember if you made a backup?
Okay, in that case, it's best to connect both phones with a cable. It's faster than doing it wirelessly, and it's more reliable.
I'll check what's been transferred so far. Don't worry, nothing is deleted from the old phone until you decide to remove it.
I'd recommend a cloud service, which automatically saves your photos every time you connect to the Internet. That way, you won't lose anything if the phone breaks.
Most providers give you about five gigabytes for free, which is usually enough for a few thousand photos. You can pay for more if you need it.
You're welcome. If you have any problems later, just come back, and one of us will be happy to help.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the effects of social media
scenarios.context: Two friends debate how social media influences daily life.

speakerA.en: I've decided to delete my social media accounts. I realized that I was spending almost three hours a day on my phone.
It started as a way to keep in touch with friends, but now it feels like I'm just watching other people's lives instead of living my own.
That's true, and it was useful for finding information and events. But I noticed that I felt anxious when I didn't check my notifications.
I think I'll try it for a month and see how I feel. If I miss it too much, I can always create a new account.
Good idea. I'm going to put my phone in a drawer in the evening and read a book instead. It might help me sleep better, too.
I'll let you know how it goes. Maybe you should try a short break yourself, just to see what happens.

speakerB.en: Really? That's quite a drastic step. Don't you think you'll miss some of the benefits, like staying in contact with people who live far away?
I can understand that. Sometimes I scroll for an hour without realizing it, and afterwards I feel tired rather than entertained.
I think that's something many people experience. Maybe the solution is not to quit completely, but to set limits for how much time you spend.
That's a sensible approach. Some of my friends deleted the applications from their phones and only check them on their computers.
That sounds healthy. I've noticed that when I don't look at my phone before bed, I fall asleep much faster.
Maybe I will. I'd be curious to see how much free time I'd have if I didn't check my messages every few minutes.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing privacy against convenience
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss the trade-off between digital convenience and personal data.

speakerA.en: I've just realized how much information my phone collects about me, from my location to my search history. It's convenient, but it's also slightly unsettling.
Most of us accept the terms without reading them, simply because we want to use the application. I suppose that's what the companies rely on.
I understand the argument that if you have nothing to hide, there's nothing to fear. But privacy isn't only about hiding things. It's about controlling who knows what about you.
I've started to review the permissions on my devices, and I've turned off location tracking for most of the apps. It's a small step, but at least it gives me a sense of control.
Perhaps governments should demand that companies explain in simple language what data they collect and why, instead of burying it in several pages of legal text.
That would certainly be an improvement. In the meantime, I'll try to be more selective about what I share, even if it makes some services slightly less convenient.

speakerB.en: I know what you mean. Last week, my phone suggested a restaurant that I'd only talked about with a friend. I couldn't help wondering whether it had been listening.
That's exactly it. If a service is free, then you're probably paying with your data. Most people understand that in theory, but few change their behavior as a result.
That's an important distinction. Once information has been collected, you can't be sure how it will be used in the future, or who will have access to it, which is the real risk.
That's a sensible approach. You could also use browsers that block trackers, and choose services that don't depend on advertising. It requires some effort, but it's possible.
That would be ideal, and some regulations, like the European data protection law, already require companies to do that. But enforcement is uneven, and many people don't know their rights.
It's a balancing act. Technology offers extraordinary benefits, but we shouldn't have to sacrifice our privacy to enjoy them. We need to demand better standards.

scenarios.scenario: Troubleshooting a remote work setup
scenarios.context: A colleague helps another solve repeated technical problems during video meetings.

speakerA.en: I'm so sorry to bother you, but I keep having problems with my connection during video calls. Yesterday, I was cut off three times in the middle of a client presentation.
I've already restarted the router and updated the software, but it didn't make a difference. The strange thing is that the connection works perfectly well when I'm watching a film.
That's true. My partner also works from home, and she's usually on calls at the same time as I am. Could the problem be that we're using too much bandwidth?
I'd rather avoid buying new equipment if I can help it. Is there any setting that I can adjust that would give priority to my work computer?
That sounds manageable. I'll try connecting my laptop by cable this afternoon, and I'll let you know whether it solves the problem.
Thank you. If I'd contacted you earlier, I might have saved myself a good deal of frustration. I'll have to remember that you're the person to ask.

speakerB.en: No bother at all. Let's work out what's happening. Do you use Wi-Fi or a cable, and does the problem occur at specific times of day, or does it seem random?
That suggests that the issue isn't the speed of your connection, but its stability. Video calls need a steady flow of data, and they're much more sensitive to interruptions than streaming.
That's very likely. If two people are on video calls at the same time, and the signal has to travel through several walls, the quality may deteriorate considerably. Where is the router located?

There's a setting called Quality of Service that allows you to give priority to certain devices. Alternatively, connecting your computer directly to the router with a cable would be the most reliable solution.
Please do. If that fixes it, then we'll know that the Wi-Fi was the weak point, and you can decide whether to move the router or install an extender.
Any time. And if the cable doesn't work, let me know, and I'll ask the technical department to run a few diagnostics. It's what they're there for.

scenarios.scenario: Helping a parent use online banking and video calls
scenarios.context: An adult child patiently explains technology to a parent.

speakerA.en: Mum, I'll show you how to set up the application, and then you'll be able to see your account from your phone. It's much easier than going to the bank every time.
First, you need to download it from the store. Then you have to enter your customer number, and the bank will send you a code by text message to confirm that it's really you.

Don't worry, you don't have to remember all of it. I'll write it down, and we'll save the password in a safe place. But whatever you do, never give it to anybody, even if they say they're from the bank.

Now, let's try a video call, so that you can talk to your grandchildren. Press the green button, and choose the person you'd like to call. It's just like making a normal phone call, but with pictures.
That's it. You've done it. See how simple it is? If anything goes wrong, you can always call me, and I'll talk you through it, so there's no need to feel anxious about it.
I'm proud of you, Mum. You've learned in an hour what many people take weeks to understand. Next time, we'll try ordering your groceries online.

speakerB.en: Oh, dear. I'm not sure about this. I've always preferred going to the branch and talking to a real person. What if I press the wrong button and lose all my money?
A code? How does that work? I'm afraid I'll get confused. Last time, I tried to use my phone to book a taxi, and I ended up ordering a pizza, and I still don't know how.
That's reassuring. I remember reading in the newspaper about people being tricked by fake messages. How can I tell whether a message is genuine? They look so convincing these days.
That sounds wonderful. I miss them so much, and with the distance, we hardly see each other. Is it difficult? I'm worried that I won't be able to hear them, or that it won't work.
Oh, look, I can see Sophie! Hello, darling! Can you hear me? This is marvelous. I never thought that I would be able to do something like this at my age.
Thank you, dear. You're very patient with me. And yes, groceries sound like a good idea. The shop is quite far from here, and my knees aren't what they used to be.

scenarios.scenario: Recovering lost data with a technician
scenarios.context: A user explains data loss to a technician and discusses recovery and prevention.

speakerA.en: Good morning. My laptop stopped working last night, and I'm afraid that I've lost a great deal of important data. There are documents there that I haven't saved anywhere else, so I'm quite worried.
It was working perfectly until yesterday afternoon. Then it began to run very slowly, and finally the screen went black. When I tried to restart it, it just made a strange clicking noise.
I'm self-employed, so most of my work is on that computer, including client files and invoices from the last two years. I should have kept backups, but I always thought that I'd do it later.
How likely is it that you'll be able to recover everything? I'm prepared to pay for it, as the information is far more valuable than the computer itself.
That's good to hear. How long will it take, and can I be told what's happening along the way? I'd like to be able to tell my clients when I'll be able to work again.
Thank you. Once I get everything back, I'll set up an automatic backup. I've learned my lesson, and I won't make the same mistake again.

speakerB.en: Good morning. I'm sorry to hear that. Let me have a look. Don't worry yet, because in many cases we're able to recover the data, even if the computer itself can't be repaired.

The clicking noise is a bad sign. It usually means that the hard drive has a mechanical fault. The most important thing now is that you don't try to switch it on again, because that could make the damage worse.
It's a very common situation. People tend to take backups seriously only after something has gone wrong. I'll take the drive out and connect it to a special device, and we'll see what can be saved.
It depends on how badly the disc has been damaged. In about seventy percent of cases, we can recover most of the files, but it's difficult to give any guarantees until we've examined it.

I'd expect to have a first result by tomorrow evening. I'll call you as soon as I know whether the data is accessible, and I'll give you an estimate of the cost, so that you can decide whether to proceed.
That's a good plan. I'd recommend a cloud service, together with an external drive, so that you have two separate copies. I'll show you how to set it up when you collect your laptop.

scenarios.scenario: Questioning a viral claim about a new app
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss a viral post claiming that a popular new photo app secretly collects its users' data.

speakerA.en: Have you seen that post everyone's sharing? It's widely believed that the new photo app collects your contacts and location even when it's closed. To be honest, I was about to delete it, although I've only had it for a week.

It was on a popular tech page, and thousands of people had shared it by lunchtime. The company is reported to be under investigation, which is why I panicked. The more comments I read, the more worried I became, since nobody doubted it.

Not really, now that you mention it. Everyone just repeats the same screenshot. As far as I'm concerned, that's suspicious in itself, but I can't tell whether the claim is false or the company simply hasn't answered yet. What would you do in my position?

That makes sense. On the other hand, the privacy policy is probably forty pages long, and the more legal language I read, the less I understand. Could you tell me what to look for, as long as it doesn't take all evening?

Mostly the second, I'd say. It's generally expected that companies will ask permission, and I feel I was never given a real choice. If the settings look reasonable, I'll keep the app, but I'll switch off anything it doesn't need.

Yes, please. I'll admit I overreacted, since I shared the post before I'd checked a single detail. It's thought to have reached half my contacts, so I should post a correction too, in case anyone else deletes the app unnecessarily.

speakerB.en: I did see it, but I'd say we should check the facts first. The app is said to have been hacked last year, yet I couldn't find a reliable source for that. Where did you first read the claim, and who posted it?

I understand, but the more a story spreads, the less people bother to check it. It's often assumed that a viral post must be true, although most of them are exaggerated. Did anyone actually link to the investigation itself?

I'd start with the permissions in your settings. The app is believed to ask for your contacts only when you invite friends, but you can verify that yourself. It's also worth reading the policy, in case something has changed recently.

It won't, I promise. Look for the sections on data sharing and third parties. Companies in this sector are known to sell anonymous data, so it isn't necessarily a scandal. Is it the sharing that bothers you, or the fact that you weren't asked first?

That's a sensible compromise. The app is understood to work perfectly well without location access, so you won't lose anything. The more control you take now, the less you'll worry about the next rumor. Shall we go through the settings together?

Good idea, and don't be too hard on yourself. It's estimated that most people share a post without reading beyond the headline. As long as you correct it calmly, nobody will blame you. Let's check the permissions first, and then write the message.

scenarios.scenario: Persuading a manager to tighten password security
scenarios.context: An IT specialist tries to persuade a cautious manager to introduce stricter password rules and two-step verification across the company.

speakerA.en: Thank you for seeing me. I'd like to propose stricter password rules for the whole company. It's essential that we act before the next audit, since our current system would fail it, and I'd rather you heard that from me than from the auditors.

Fair question. Last year's incident cost us about two days of lost work, and a serious breach could cost far more. I'd rather you looked at the actual figures, so it's essential that I send them today. Shall I include the price of the new system too?

I understand, and to be honest, I agree that twelve characters can be tiresome. I suggest that we allow long phrases instead of complicated symbols, since they're easier to remember. It's high time we stopped forcing people to invent passwords they immediately forget.

A password manager helps, although it needs a short introduction. I suggest that we run a trial in one department first. It's important that staff don't feel blamed for old habits, so we could present it as support, not as a punishment.

A lost phone can be replaced using backup codes, which each person keeps in a safe place. It's essential that the codes are stored separately from the device. On the other hand, travelers could use a small security key, which I'd rather you considered, in case phones are unreliable abroad.

Of course. I'll prepare a one-page summary by Friday, written in plain language. I suggest that we present it to the board together, as long as you're comfortable doing so. Thank you for listening, since I know this wasn't an easy request.

speakerB.en: I appreciate you raising it, but I have to be honest: staff already complain about our systems. Why do you think it's so urgent now, and what would the change cost us? I'd rather you gave me figures than general warnings.

Thank you, I'll read them tonight. But twelve characters seems excessive to me. People will simply write them on sticky notes, and then we're less secure than before. I insist that any new rule be practical, as far as I'm concerned. Is there a way to make it easier?

Long phrases do sound easier, I'll grant you that. Would a password manager solve the problem, or would it only create something else for people to learn? I'd rather we avoided anything that needs a week of training.

That sounds more convincing. It's vital that the sales team can still log in abroad, since they rely on their phones. I'd rather we introduced the second step gradually. How would it work if someone loses their phone?

Good. I'd also like the rules written clearly, in case the auditors ask about them. It's essential that the board approves the policy, so I'll need a short summary from you. Can you have it ready by Friday?

Then let's go ahead with the trial. I suggest that we announce it next week, with a short briefing for each department. It's high time we updated the policy, and I'd rather be seen as proactive than defensive. Thank you for persisting.

scenarios.scenario: Questioning a company about how it uses customers' personal data
scenarios.context: A customer calls a company's data protection officer to ask how his personal details were used and whether they were shared.

speakerA.en: Good afternoon. I'm calling about the personal data your company holds about me. To be honest, I received a marketing email from a company I've never dealt with, and I suspect my details were shared. Could you clarify what happened?

It was a travel agency, and I haven't touched my preferences in years. As far as I'm concerned, I never agreed to this, and I'm entitled to know who received my information. On the grounds that this seems a breach, I'd like a full explanation.

Thank you. While you're checking, could you tell me what data you hold? I'd like to see my address, my purchase history and any profile you've built about me. I believe I'm entitled to a copy under the law.

Not at all. Perhaps I ticked a box without reading the small print. Still, on the grounds that the wording was unclear, I'd say the consent isn't valid. Were I to complain to the authority, what would happen?

Yes, please, and I'd like it confirmed in writing. I'd also like my email removed from all marketing, on the grounds that I never requested it. How long will it take for the partner to delete it as well?

That's very helpful, thank you. I appreciate you taking it seriously. To be honest, I expected to be passed from department to department. I'll wait for your email, and I may come back if nothing arrives.

speakerB.en: Good afternoon, and thank you for raising this. Under no circumstances do we sell customer data, but I understand your concern. May I ask which company contacted you, and when you last updated your account preferences?

I understand. In so far as we share data with partners, it's only with those listed in our privacy policy, and only with consent. Were your details to have been shared without consent, that would be a serious matter. Let me check your record.

You are, and I'll arrange it. In so far as the request is clear, we must respond within thirty days. Under no circumstances will we charge you for it. Ah, it appears your email was included in a promotional partnership last spring. Does that ring a bell?

It's your right, and I wouldn't discourage you. In so far as the consent was ambiguous, the authority could ask us to change our process. Under no circumstances should customers feel misled. Would you prefer that I remove your data from the partner list now?

I'll send the confirmation today. As for the partner, in so far as they received your data lawfully, they must delete it within fourteen days of our request. I'll copy you on the message, so that you can check. Would that be satisfactory?

Please do, and don't hesitate. Under no circumstances should you have to chase us. I'll send the confirmation and your data copy by Friday, and I'll review our consent form so that it's clearer for everyone.

scenarios.scenario: Persuading a relative to stop sharing unverified news in a family chat
scenarios.context: A young woman tactfully asks her uncle to check messages before forwarding them to the family group chat.

speakerA.en: Uncle Karim, can I ask you something about the family chat? Yesterday you shared a message saying a common medicine is dangerous. To be honest, I checked, and it doesn't seem to be true. Where did you get it?

I understand the intention, but just because a message looks official doesn't mean it's reliable. The fact that it came without a source should worry us. No matter how convincing it sounds, anyone can write a fake warning.

Good question. First, check who wrote it and whether major news sites mention it. Just because many people share something doesn't mean they've checked it. The fact that it spreads so fast is often a sign of exaggeration, I'd say.

Don't feel bad, it happens to everyone, even to well-informed people. What matters is that we pause before we share. Just because a message makes us feel afraid doesn't mean it's accurate. The fact that fear spreads quickly is exactly why fake news works.

There is. Search the main claim on a reliable site, and if you can't find it, don't share it. It takes under a minute. Far from being complicated, it's a habit, and no matter how busy you are, it protects everyone.
Of course you can, and I'd be glad to help. The fact that you're willing to change your habits says a lot about you. I'll send a short guide to the chat, in case others find it useful too.

speakerB.en: A friend forwarded it, and it seemed convincing. It had a doctor's name on it, and many people were sharing it. Just because it's wrong doesn't mean it isn't worth a warning, does it? Better safe than sorry, I'd say.

Hmm, perhaps. But the fact that so many people shared it makes me think there's some truth in it. Far from being careless, I was trying to protect the family. How can I tell whether a message is real?

I see. Last month I shared a story about a free holiday, and it turned out to be a scam. Far from being harmless, it made a few relatives angry. I suppose I should be more careful, no matter how urgent a message seems.

That makes sense. Is there a simple method I could use? I'm not good with technology, as you know, and I don't want to spend hours checking each message. I'd prefer something quick, as long as it's reliable.
Fair enough. I'll try it. Would it be all right if I asked you whenever I'm unsure? To be honest, I'd rather ask than cause another false alarm. Just because I'm older doesn't mean I can't learn!
Please do. And I'll tell the family that the medicine message was wrong, so nobody worries. Thank you for being patient with me. As far as I'm concerned, you're the family's best fact-checker.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about upcoming holidays and traditions
scenarios.context: People discuss plans for holidays like New Year, Christmas, or Nowruz.

speakerA.en: Do you celebrate Christmas in your country?
What is your favorite holiday?
Do you get a day off?
Do you visit your family?
What are your plans for New Year's Eve?
speakerA.fa: برنامه‌ات برای شب سال نو چیه؟

speakerA.en: In my family, we always have a big dinner on New Year's Day.
speakerA.fa: توی خانواده ما، روز سال نو همیشه شام بزرگ داریم.

speakerA.en: I'm going to visit my hometown for the holidays. I can't wait to see my family.
speakerA.fa: برای تعطیلات می‌رم شهر خودم. بی‌صبرانه منتظرم خانواده‌م رو ببینم.

speakerA.en: We have a tradition of lighting fireworks at midnight.
speakerA.fa: ما یه سنت داریم که نیمه‌شب آتش‌بازی روشن می‌کنیم.

speakerA.en: How do you usually spend Nowruz? I've heard it's a wonderful celebration.
speakerA.fa: معمولاً نوروز رو چطور می‌گذرونید؟ شنیدم جشن فوق‌العاده‌ای است.

speakerB.en: Yes, we celebrate it with trees and gifts.
My favorite is New Year.
Yes, we do. It's great!
Yes, we all eat together.
I'm going to a friend's party. We'll probably stay up until midnight.
speakerB.fa: می‌رم به مهمونی یه دوست. احتمالاً تا نیمه‌شب بیدار می‌مونیم.

speakerB.en: That sounds lovely. We usually have a family gathering and play games.
speakerB.fa: خیلی قشنگ به نظر میاد. ما معمولاً دورهمی خانوادگی داریم و بازی می‌کنیم.

speakerB.en: That's wonderful! I hope you have a great time.
speakerB.fa: خیلی عالیه! امیدوارم اوقات خوبی داشته باشی.

speakerB.en: That sounds beautiful. We do the same thing here.
speakerB.fa: زیبا به نظر میاد. ما هم اینجا همین کار رو می‌کنیم.

speakerB.en: We set up a Haft-Seen table with seven symbolic items and visit relatives.
speakerB.fa: ما یه سفره هفت‌سین با هفت نماد می‌چینیم و به دیدار اقوام می‌رویم.

scenarios.scenario: Wishing someone a happy holiday
scenarios.context: People say happy holiday wishes to each other.

speakerA.en: Happy New Year!
Merry Christmas!
Happy Nowruz!
Have a nice holiday.
I hope you have a wonderful holiday with your family.
Wishing you a happy and healthy new year.
Are you doing anything special this year?
Enjoy your time off, and relax!

speakerB.en: Happy New Year to you!
Thank you! Merry Christmas to you too.
Thank you! Happy Nowruz to you too.
Thanks. You too!
Thank you. We're going to visit my grandparents.
Thank you so much. I wish you the same.
Yes, we're having a big dinner at home.
I will. See you after the holidays.

scenarios.scenario: A birthday party
scenarios.context: Friends celebrate a birthday.

speakerA.en: Happy birthday, Sara!
This is a gift for you.
Here is your cake.
Make a wish.
How old are you today?
Did you open all your presents?
Thank you for inviting us. The party is great.
Would you like to blow out the candles now?

speakerB.en: Thank you!
Oh, how nice! I like it.
Wow! It's beautiful.
OK. I have my wish.
I'm twenty-five. I can't believe it!
Not yet. I'll open them after the cake.
I'm so glad you could come.
Yes, let's do it. Everyone, please sing!

scenarios.scenario: Buying a holiday gift
scenarios.context: Two people shop for a gift.

speakerA.en: What gift do we buy for Mom?
How about a scarf?
How much is it?
OK. Let's buy it.
What does your dad like? He's hard to buy for.
That's a nice idea. Do you know which author he likes?
Could you wrap it as a gift, please?
What's our budget for the gift?

speakerB.en: Let's buy some flowers.
Yes, she likes scarves.
It's twenty dollars.
Good. She will be happy.
He enjoys reading. Maybe we could buy him a good book.
He loves detective stories. Let's ask the shop assistant.
Of course. Would you like a card too?
I think thirty dollars is enough.

scenarios.scenario: Holiday dinner
scenarios.context: A family prepares a holiday dinner.

speakerA.en: What do we cook today?
Do we need more food?
Who comes to dinner?
Dinner is ready!
Could you set the table while I finish cooking?
There will be eight of us. We need more chairs.
Do any of the guests have food allergies?
Would you like some more salad?

speakerB.en: Let's make rice and chicken.
Yes, we need some fruit.
My aunt and uncle come.
It smells so good.
Sure. How many guests are coming?
I'll bring some from the other room.
Yes, my cousin can't eat nuts, so let's check the dessert.
Yes, please. Everything is delicious.

scenarios.scenario: Holiday plans
scenarios.context: Two coworkers talk about their holiday plans.

speakerA.en: Do you have plans for the holiday?
How long is the holiday?
Are you going by car?
Have a great time!
Where are you going for the holiday?
Have you booked your hotel yet?
Are you going to work during the holiday?
Could you send me a photo from there?

speakerB.en: Yes, I visit my parents.
It is five days.
No, I'm going by train.
Thank you. You too!
We're going to the north to see the snow.
Yes, I booked it last week. It wasn't expensive.
No, I'm taking a few days off to relax.
Of course. I'll send you some pictures.

scenarios.scenario: Watching fireworks
scenarios.context: People wait for midnight on New Year's Eve.

speakerA.en: It's almost midnight.
Look at the fireworks!
Are you cold?
Let's take a photo.
Where is the best place to watch the fireworks?
What time do they start?
Let's make a resolution for the new year.
Happy New Year! Let's call our families.

speakerB.en: Yes, only one minute left!
They are so beautiful!
A little. Let's stay together.
Good idea. Smile!
The bridge is good, but it's usually crowded.
At midnight, right after the countdown.
I'm going to exercise more and learn English.
Good idea. They're waiting for our call.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a family holiday dinner
scenarios.context: Two relatives plan the meal for a holiday gathering.

speakerA.en: We should start planning the holiday dinner. How many people are coming this year?
Then we'll need a bigger table. We could borrow one from the neighbors.
I'll try a different recipe this time, with more herbs and a longer cooking time.
Perfect. Let's make a shopping list this weekend so we don't forget anything.

speakerB.en: About fourteen, including the children. My cousin said she might bring a friend.
Good idea. What should we cook? Last year the turkey was a little dry.
I'll take care of the desserts, and maybe a vegetarian dish for my niece.
Agreed. I can't wait. It's my favorite time of the year.

scenarios.scenario: Attending a wedding
scenarios.context: Two guests chat during a wedding reception.

speakerA.en: The ceremony was beautiful, wasn't it? I almost cried when they read their vows.
How do you know the couple? I don't think we've met.
And I work with the groom. He's the kindest person in our office.
Not yet, but I've heard it's wonderful. I'm saving room for the cake.

speakerB.en: I did cry a little. They look so happy together.
I went to university with the bride. We've been friends for almost fifteen years.
The food is excellent as well. Have you tried the lamb?
Me too. After that, I think the dancing will begin.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about a national holiday
scenarios.context: Two coworkers talk about how they spend a public holiday.

speakerA.en: Do you have any plans for the long weekend? The holiday is on Monday.
That sounds fun. Is it a long drive?
I'm staying here this year. I'd like to rest and finish some work on the house.
There are fireworks in the evening, so I might go and watch them with some friends.

speakerB.en: We usually go to my parents' village. There's a parade, and the whole town takes part.
About three hours, but we leave early to avoid the traffic.
That's also a good way to spend it. Aren't there any events in the city?
Enjoy them. I'll send you photos of the parade.

scenarios.scenario: Comparing holiday traditions across cultures
scenarios.context: Two coworkers from different countries compare how they celebrate the new year.

speakerA.en: How do people celebrate the new year where you come from? Here, it's mostly fireworks and parties.
Twelve grapes? That's a charming tradition. Is there a meaning behind it?
I'd probably choke on the first few. Are there other customs I should know about?
That sounds like a wish for travel in the coming year. I like the imagination behind these customs.

speakerB.en: It's more of a family occasion. We gather for a large meal, and at midnight, we eat twelve grapes.
Each one represents a month, and if you finish them all before the last chime, you're said to have good luck.
Some people wear red underwear for luck in love, while others walk around the block with an empty suitcase.
Perhaps you could try some of them this year, even if only for fun.

scenarios.scenario: Feeling lonely during the holidays
scenarios.context: A woman confides in a friend about spending the holidays alone.

speakerA.en: I'm dreading the holiday season this year. It's the first time I'll be spending it by myself.
The flights are exorbitant, and I can't take more than two days off work.
That's very generous, but I wouldn't want to impose on your family at such a personal time.
If you're sure, then I'd be honored. I could bring a dish to contribute.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry. I had no idea. Is there no chance of traveling to see your family?
You're welcome to join us. We have more than enough food, and the more people there are, the livelier it gets.
