scenarios.context: Two people practice a language together.

speakerA.en: Can we practice together?
Let's talk in English.
I'm fine, thank you.
Thank you. Let's meet again.
How about we practice twice a week?
Please correct my mistakes when I speak.
Could you teach me some useful expressions?
Shall we practice in a café or online?

speakerB.en: Yes, that's a good idea.
OK. How are you today?
Very good! Your English is nice.
Yes. See you on Friday.
That sounds good. Tuesday and Thursday work for me.
Of course. I'll tell you after you finish.
Sure. Let's start with some common ones for daily life.
Let's do it online. It's easier for me.

scenarios.scenario: In the classroom
scenarios.context: A teacher helps a student in class.

speakerA.en: Open your book, please.
Page ten.
Please read the first line.
Very good! Now write the word.
Do you have any questions about the lesson?
Let me explain it again with an example.
For homework, please write five sentences.
Please hand them in on Monday morning.

speakerB.en: Which page?
OK. I have it.
Yes, teacher.
Yes. I can do it.
Yes, I don't understand this grammar rule.
Thank you. Now it's clearer.
When do we need to give them to you?
OK. I'll do them over the weekend.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about difficulties in learning English
scenarios.context: Two classmates discuss what is hard about learning English.

speakerA.en: I've been studying English for three years, but I still find the pronunciation difficult.
I try to listen to podcasts every day, but I often can't follow what they say.
That's a good idea. How do you practice your speaking?
That sounds helpful. I get nervous when I have to speak with native speakers.

speakerB.en: Me too. The spelling doesn't match the sound, so I never know how to say a new word.
Maybe you should start with slower material, like audiobooks made for learners.
I talk to a friend online twice a week. We correct each other's mistakes.
Everyone does at first. The more you practice, the more confident you'll feel.

scenarios.scenario: Choosing a language course
scenarios.context: A student asks an advisor about language classes.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'm looking for a Spanish course for intermediate learners.
I work during the day, so the evening class would suit me better.
Will there be an opportunity to practice speaking, or is it mostly grammar?
That's what I need. How much does the course cost, and does it include the books?

speakerB.en: We have two options: an intensive course in the mornings or an evening class twice a week.
It runs for ten weeks, and each lesson lasts ninety minutes.
About half of every lesson is conversation, and the groups are small.
It's three hundred and fifty dollars, and the materials are included.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing tips for learning vocabulary
scenarios.context: Two friends share methods for learning new words.

speakerA.en: How do you remember new words? I forget most of them after a day or two.
I've tried that, but I get tired of it quickly. Isn't there an easier method?
Do you use them every day?
I think I'll try that. I'd also like to learn from movies and series.

speakerB.en: I write them in a notebook with an example sentence, and I review them every weekend.
Flashcard apps work well. They show you a word again just before you forget it.
Yes, for ten minutes before bed. It's short enough that it doesn't feel like work.
That works well too. Turn on the subtitles in the language you're learning.

scenarios.scenario: Overcoming a plateau in language learning
scenarios.context: A learner talks to her tutor about slow progress.

speakerA.en: I feel as though I've stopped improving. I understand a lot, but I can't seem to express myself fluently.
What can I do to break through it? I study every day, yet nothing seems to change.
I'm afraid of making mistakes, which is why I avoid speaking when I can.
I'll try to participate more in conversation groups, even though it makes me nervous.

speakerB.en: That's a common experience. Learners often reach a plateau after the initial rapid progress.
Perhaps you need to shift from passive study to active use. Speaking and writing push you to produce language.
Mistakes are the raw material of progress. Every error you correct is a step toward accuracy.
Start small. A few minutes of conversation a day is worth more than an hour of grammar exercises.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the benefits of immersion
scenarios.context: Two friends compare studying at home with living abroad.

speakerA.en: I'm considering spending three months in France to improve my French. Do you think it's worth it?
But it's expensive, and I'd have to take unpaid leave from work.
I worry about ending up spending time with other English speakers and defeating the purpose.
I hadn't thought of working there. That might solve the financial side as well.

speakerB.en: From my own experience, immersion accelerates learning far more than classes at home.
It's a trade-off, certainly. Yet being forced to use the language for everything, from ordering food to asking directions, makes it stick.
That's a risk. Staying with a host family or taking a local job could help you avoid it.
Look into short-term opportunities. Many cafés and farms welcome foreign volunteers in exchange for accommodation.

scenarios.scenario: Reflecting on the difficulty of idioms and slang
scenarios.context: Two language learners laugh about confusing expressions.

speakerA.en: Yesterday a colleague told me to break a leg, and I was genuinely worried about her intentions.
What makes it harder is that textbooks rarely teach these phrases, though everyone uses them.
Do you keep a record of the ones you discover? I've started a notebook just for idioms.
Smart. Some slang can sound ridiculous or even offensive if used in the wrong setting.

speakerB.en: I had the same reaction when someone said it was raining cats and dogs. I looked out of the window for pets.
That's why listening to native speakers in real situations is so valuable, even when it's bewildering.
I do, and I note down where I heard them, so I remember the context in which they're appropriate.
Exactly. It's a minefield, but it's also the most entertaining part of learning a language.

scenarios.scenario: Giving feedback on a colleague's written English
scenarios.context: A colleague asks for honest feedback on an email she wrote in her second language.

speakerA.en: Would you mind looking at this email before I send it? I want it to sound polished, but I'm never sure whether my phrasing is natural.
Formal in a good way, or in a way that makes me sound stilted?
That's the sort of thing a textbook never teaches. How do I develop that instinct?
I suppose I've been too cautious, relying on formulas that feel safe. Perhaps it's time to take a few risks.

speakerB.en: Happy to. The content is clear, and the structure is excellent. A few phrases sound slightly formal, though.
A little stilted, I'd say. For instance, 'I would like to bring to your attention' is grammatically fine, but 'I wanted to flag' is what most people would write.
Mostly by reading real emails and listening to how colleagues actually speak. Over time, you start noticing the rhythm of it.
Exactly. A slightly imperfect but natural sentence will always serve you better than a flawless one that nobody would say.

scenarios.scenario: Preparing for a high-stakes language exam
scenarios.context: Two classmates discuss strategies for a proficiency exam that will determine a visa application.

speakerA.en: The exam is in three weeks, and my entire visa application hangs on the result. I'm trying not to panic.
That's true. In practice, I do well, but under the clock, my writing falls apart. I run out of time before I can proofread.
That's useful advice. What about the speaking section? I tend to freeze when the examiner stares at me.
I'll try that, though I dread hearing my own voice. Do you want to practice together this weekend?

speakerB.en: I'm in a similar position. What I've found helpful is practicing under timed conditions, since the pressure itself is half the challenge.
Then perhaps you should spend less time perfecting each paragraph. A clear structure with a few errors tends to score higher than a polished fragment.
Record yourself answering random questions and play them back. It's uncomfortable, but you'll quickly spot your habits.
Gladly. Having someone to hold me accountable will probably do more for my score than another textbook.

scenarios.scenario: Debating whether translation apps make learning languages obsolete
scenarios.context: Two friends disagree about whether technology has made language study unnecessary.

speakerA.en: Honestly, I don't see why anyone bothers with years of language study anymore. My phone translates conversations in real time.
That sounds sentimental. For most practical purposes, like ordering food or booking a hotel, an app does the job perfectly well.
Perhaps, though the technology improves every year. In a decade, those gaps may well disappear.
I'll concede that point. I just resent the effort it takes when a shortcut is so readily available.

speakerB.en: It's impressive, I'll grant you, but it can't replicate the experience of actually speaking with someone. Translation is merely a bridge, not a relationship.
For transactions, certainly. But try negotiating, joking, or comforting a friend through an app, and you'll find the nuances simply vanish.
Even so, learning a language reshapes how you think. You notice things about culture and expression that no translation can capture.
Fair enough, but shortcuts rarely teach you anything. The effort is where the real understanding happens.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the plateau that comes with advanced study
scenarios.context: Two learners reflect on the frustration of progress slowing at a high level.

speakerA.en: I've reached a stage where progress feels almost imperceptible. I understand nearly everything, yet I still can't express myself with any elegance.
What worked for you? I'm weary of textbooks, and conversation partners are surprisingly hard to come by.
Deliberate imitation, in other words. It sounds laborious, but I can see its value.
I'll start keeping a notebook of expressions I come across. Perhaps one day they'll surface without effort.

speakerB.en: That's the notorious plateau. The early gains come quickly, but refinement demands a different kind of patience altogether.
Reading widely, and noting down turns of phrase that struck me as idiomatic. I'd then try to use them deliberately in conversation.
It is laborious, but it works. Fluency isn't merely knowing the words; it's knowing which ones native speakers instinctively choose.
They will, if you let them accumulate. It's a slow alchemy, but it eventually transforms your speech.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing immersion against formal study
scenarios.context: A teacher and a student consider the most effective way to reach professional fluency.

speakerA.en: I've been studying grammar diligently for three years, yet I still freeze in real conversations. Where have I gone wrong?
I'm afraid of making mistakes in front of native speakers. The thought alone makes my mind go blank.
Would a period abroad accelerate things, or could I achieve the same results at home with sufficient discipline?
So the decisive factor is deliberate engagement, wherever I happen to be.

speakerB.en: You haven't gone wrong, but you may have favored accuracy over spontaneity. Grammar gives you the structure; fluency requires use.
Mistakes are the raw material of learning. The people who progress fastest are generally those who tolerate looking foolish.
Immersion is undeniably powerful, but it isn't magic. Many expatriates live for years in a bubble of their own language.
Precisely. Surround yourself with the language, force yourself to use it, and accept the discomfort as the price of improvement.

scenarios.scenario: Navigating nuance, register and idiom in a second language
scenarios.context: A translator explains why literal translation often fails.

speakerA.en: I've noticed that a phrase that's perfectly polite in my language can sound brusque when rendered literally into English.
Could you give me an example? I'd like to understand where the pitfalls lie.
That's fascinating, and rather alarming. I've probably misinterpreted countless replies over the years.
It seems that fluency involves a form of cultural literacy that no dictionary can provide.

speakerB.en: That's the central challenge of translation. Words carry cultural baggage that doesn't survive the journey intact.
Take 'I'll think about it.' In some cultures it signals genuine consideration; in others it's a diplomatic refusal.
Almost certainly, as have we all. The solution is to attend to tone, context and what remains unsaid, not merely vocabulary.
Exactly. You aren't merely learning a language; you're learning a way of reading the world.

scenarios.scenario: Practicing speaking with a language partner
scenarios.context: Two people agree to practice their languages together.

speakerA.en: I'd like to improve my English, but I never get a chance to speak it.
I can help you with Spanish in return. Maybe we could meet once a week?
I think an hour is enough. We can spend thirty minutes on each language.
That sounds great. Please correct my mistakes, even if they seem small.

speakerB.en: I know the feeling. I'm learning Spanish, and it's hard to find people who will practice with me.
That would be perfect. I'd love to find a regular language partner. Where should we meet?
Good idea. We could meet at the café near the library on Wednesday evenings.
Of course. And you can correct mine too. It's the best way to make progress.

scenarios.scenario: Preparing for a language exam
scenarios.context: Two students talk about how to prepare for an English exam.

speakerA.en: My English exam is in three weeks, and I'm starting to feel nervous.
Writing is the hardest part for me. I often run out of time and forget the grammar.
That's a good idea. Do you think I should also practice with old exam papers?
Thanks. Do you want to study together at the library on Sunday?

speakerB.en: Don't panic yet. Three weeks is enough time if you practice a little every day.
Try writing one short text each evening, and set a timer so you get used to the pressure.
Definitely. They show you what the questions look like and where you usually lose points.
Sure. I could use the company, and we can check each other's essays.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about the benefits of studying abroad
scenarios.context: Two students discuss whether living in another country helps language learning.

speakerA.en: I'm thinking about spending a semester in Germany. Everyone says that it's the best way to learn a language quickly.
I've been studying German for two years in class, but I can't hold a conversation without feeling nervous or making mistakes.
That's what I'm hoping for. If I were forced to use the language every day, I'd have no choice but to improve.
I'm a bit afraid that I'll end up speaking English with other international students, which wouldn't help much.
Good suggestion. I'll look for a host family, and I'll join a local sports club to meet people outside the university.
Thanks. Your advice makes me feel more confident, and I'll start preparing the application this week.

speakerB.en: It's true, immersion helps a lot. When I lived in France, I learned more in three months than in three years at school.
That's normal. Classes teach you grammar and vocabulary, but you only become fluent when you use the language in real situations.
Exactly. At the beginning, it's tiring, but after a few weeks, you start to understand more, and then it gets easier and more enjoyable.
It can happen, so you have to be disciplined. Try to live with local people, and avoid spending all your time with friends who speak your language.
That's an excellent plan. Also, try to keep a diary in the new language, and write down new words every day.
You're welcome. I'm sure that you'll do well. And when you get back, we can practice together, so that you don't forget anything.

scenarios.scenario: Giving advice on improving listening skills
scenarios.context: A learner asks a more advanced friend how to understand native speakers.

speakerA.en: I have a problem. When people speak English at normal speed, I can't understand them, even though I know most of the words.
In class, I can follow the audio recordings, but in real life, people speak so fast, and they swallow half of the sounds.
I've tried watching films with subtitles, but I end up reading instead of listening. Should I turn them off?
That sounds sensible. Do you have any suggestions for programs or podcasts that are suitable for my level?
I'll start with that. How long should I practice every day in order to notice a difference?
Thanks. I'll start tomorrow, and I'll tell you how it goes in a month.

speakerB.en: That's a very common problem. The good news is that your listening will improve if you practice regularly and in the right way.
That's because natural speech is different from classroom English. People link words together, and they often shorten them, which makes it harder to understand.
First watch with subtitles in English, not in your own language, and then try again without them. Repeating the same scene three times works very well.
I'd suggest short podcasts with transcripts. You can listen first, then read, and then listen again to hear the words you missed.
Twenty to thirty minutes a day is enough, as long as you do it consistently. Don't try to understand every single word. Focus on the general meaning.
Good luck. And remember that it's normal to feel frustrated at first. Everyone goes through that stage when they learn a language.

scenarios.scenario: Debating the best way to become fluent
scenarios.context: Two language learners compare methods and argue about what works best.

speakerA.en: I've been studying Spanish for three years, but I still feel that I'm not fluent. I wonder whether I've been going about it the wrong way, with too much emphasis on grammar.
I've followed a textbook, taken evening classes, and used a few apps. I know the rules, but when I try to speak, I either freeze or make basic mistakes that I know I shouldn't make.
That's an interesting thought. I've always been afraid of making errors, so I tend to avoid speaking until I'm sure that what I want to say is correct.
I suppose that's the problem. If I accepted that errors are part of the process, I'd probably progress more quickly, even though it might feel uncomfortable at first.
That sounds practical. I'll try to find a conversation partner, and set a goal of speaking for at least thirty minutes a week, without worrying about perfection.
Thank you. If I had realized earlier that fluency was a matter of practice rather than knowledge, I'd have started much sooner.

speakerB.en: It's a common experience. Many learners spend years studying grammar and then discover that they can't hold a simple conversation. Knowledge and ability are two different things.
That's the typical pattern. Classes tend to focus on accuracy, whereas real conversation requires speed and spontaneity. You need to practice retrieving words quickly, not just recognizing them.
That fear is one of the biggest obstacles. Children learn languages so well because they're not afraid of sounding foolish. Adults, by contrast, want to avoid embarrassment at all costs.
Exactly. Research suggests that fluency develops fastest when learners are exposed to large amounts of comprehensible input, and when they're forced to produce language in real situations.
Good idea. You could also try shadowing, which means repeating what a native speaker says in real time. It improves pronunciation and rhythm, and it's surprisingly effective.
Don't be too hard on yourself. Three years of study means you've built a solid foundation. Now you just need to activate it by actually using the language.

scenarios.scenario: Preparing for an academic language exam
scenarios.context: A student and a tutor discuss strategies for a high-stakes English exam.

speakerA.en: I'm taking the IELTS exam in two months, and I need a score of at least seven to be accepted by the university. I'm worried that my speaking isn't strong enough.
The examiners seem to expect extended answers with clear reasoning, but I tend to give very short replies, and I don't know how to develop my ideas without repeating myself.
That's useful. So I should state my opinion, give a reason, add an example, and then conclude. It sounds easier to remember than I'd expected.
What about vocabulary? I know many words, but I'm afraid that I use the same ones repeatedly, which could lower my score for lexical range.
That's a helpful suggestion. I'll record myself answering practice questions, and compare my answers with the model responses, to see where I could be more precise.
Thank you. Had I known about these techniques earlier, I might have saved myself a good deal of anxiety.

speakerB.en: That's a realistic goal, and with focused preparation, I think it's achievable. Let's begin by looking at what the examiners are actually assessing, because it isn't just accuracy.
That's a very common weakness. A useful technique is to use a simple structure. For example, state your opinion, explain why, give a personal example, and finish with a brief conclusion.
It works because it gives you a framework for improvising. After a few weeks of practice, you won't need to think about it consciously, and your answers will feel more natural.

That's a valid concern. Try to learn collocations and phrases rather than single words, and practice paraphrasing. If you can express the same idea in two or three ways, you'll sound much more flexible.
Recording yourself is excellent practice. You'll notice hesitations and mistakes that you don't hear while you're speaking. Listen for fillers, too, as they can make you sound uncertain.
That's the way to approach it. Remember that the exam tests your ability to communicate, not to be perfect. Staying calm and keeping talking is more important than avoiding every single error.

scenarios.scenario: Taking a placement interview for a language course
scenarios.context: A prospective student talks with a school adviser to find the right level and class.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'd like to enroll in an English course, but I'm not sure which level would be appropriate. I studied at school years ago, and I've picked up quite a lot through work since then.

I can follow most meetings, and I write emails every day, but I struggle with speaking, especially when people talk quickly. I also make mistakes with tenses, which I wouldn't like to do in front of clients.

I'd say that my main goal is to become more fluent and confident, particularly in professional situations, such as negotiating, presenting, and giving feedback. Is there a course that focuses on that?
That sounds ideal. How many hours per week would I need to attend, and is there any flexibility if I have to travel for work? I wouldn't want to pay for lessons that I can't attend.
And what about the teachers? Are they native speakers, or do they have specific qualifications? I'd like to know that the instruction is of a high standard before I commit.
Thank you. I'll take the placement test this afternoon, and I'll let you know tomorrow whether I'd like to begin next month.

speakerB.en: Good morning, and welcome. Let's begin by finding out where you are at the moment. I'll ask you a few questions, and then you'll take a short written test, which should take about thirty minutes.

That's a very common profile. Many professionals can understand and write quite well, but lack practice in spontaneous speech. A course with plenty of speaking activities would suit you better than a general grammar class.
We offer an advanced business English course on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. It includes role-plays, presentations, and feedback sessions, and it uses real situations from the working world.
It's three hours a week, in two sessions, over twelve weeks. If you miss a class, you can watch the recording online, or make it up in another group. We understand that work sometimes interferes.

All our teachers hold recognized teaching qualifications, and most have worked in business as well. About half are native speakers, but we choose them on their ability to teach, not simply on their accent.
Of course. Here's the test, and you can sit over there. Take as much time as you need, and don't worry if you can't answer everything. The idea is just to find the right level.

scenarios.scenario: Giving feedback to a language exchange partner
scenarios.context: Two language partners discuss mistakes, progress and how to make practice more effective.

speakerA.en: Before we start, I'd like to ask whether you'd mind if I gave you some feedback on your Spanish. I've noticed a few patterns in your mistakes, and I think that pointing them out could help.
The most frequent one is that you use the wrong verb for 'to be'. You say 'estoy' when you should use 'soy', especially when you talk about permanent characteristics, such as jobs and nationalities.
Your vocabulary is impressive, and you're very good at making yourself understood. But sometimes you translate directly from English, which makes the sentences sound unnatural to a native speaker.

Don't be discouraged. These are errors that nearly every English speaker makes, and they disappear with exposure. You've improved enormously since we started, and your pronunciation is already excellent.
I've got an idea. Next time, why don't we choose a topic in advance, and I'll prepare a list of useful phrases that you can try to use during our conversation?
Good. And I'd be glad to hear your own comments on my English. I know that I tend to avoid certain structures, because I'm afraid of making errors.

speakerB.en: I'd be very grateful. To be honest, I'd prefer to be corrected than to continue making the same mistakes without knowing it. I've been feeling that I've hit a plateau, and I don't know why.
Thanks, that's very useful. I always confuse those two. In my language, we only have one verb, so I never know which to choose. Could you give me a simple rule to remember the difference?
I do that all the time. I think in English, and then I translate each word. I know that it doesn't work, but it's an automatic habit, and it's hard to change when I'm trying to speak quickly.
That's encouraging to hear. Sometimes I feel that I'm not making progress, but then I look back at a recording from six months ago, and I realize how much better I've become.
That's a great suggestion. Having specific expressions in mind would give me more confidence, and I'd be less likely to fall back on simple sentences that I know are correct, but boring.
Of course. You tend to say 'make a photo' instead of 'take a photo', and you often leave out articles. But your fluency is excellent, and the mistakes rarely cause any misunderstanding.

scenarios.scenario: Mentoring a new teacher on correcting students' mistakes
scenarios.context: An experienced language teacher gives advice to a newly qualified colleague who is unsure how to correct students' mistakes without discouraging them.

speakerA.en: Thanks for finding time to talk. Having taught for only three months, I still struggle to correct mistakes without discouraging my students. Given that some of them are very shy, I don't want them to stop speaking. What's your approach?

Mostly the grammar ones, like tenses. Given that the exam is in spring, I feel pressure to fix everything immediately. Having listened to a recording of my own lessons, I noticed I interrupt far too often. Is that a bad habit, do you think?

Not yet. Whatever mistakes I hear, I usually correct at once, because I'm afraid they'll become habits. On the other hand, supposing I wrote them on the board instead, would students feel embarrassed, or would they find it useful?

Honestly, not enough. Given that I'm always looking for errors, I forget to praise what's right. Having noticed that, I'll try to mention one strong point per student. Bearing in mind how much they improve, it seems silly not to.
That's encouraging. Supposing a student keeps making the same mistake, though, what should I do? Having corrected it five times, I'm tempted to give up, given that it doesn't seem to help.

I'll try that this week. Having talked to you, I feel far less anxious, given that my confidence was low. Whatever happens, I'll let you know how it goes. Would you mind if I observed one of your lessons?

speakerB.en: That's a common dilemma. Having made the same mistake myself, I used to correct everything, and my students simply fell silent. Bearing in mind how nervous learners can be, I'd say you should choose which mistakes to correct. Which ones bother you most?

It can be, although it's understandable. Provided that students finish their sentences first, correction works much better. Having spoken without interruption, they feel respected, and they remember the correction more easily. Have you tried noting mistakes and discussing them afterward?

As far as I'm concerned, provided that you don't mention names, it works well. Having seen it in my own classes, I can say that students often recognize their own errors and smile. Whatever you do, keep the tone friendly. Do you give any positive feedback as well?

Exactly, and it makes a big difference. Provided that praise is specific, it motivates more than general comments like "good job". Having been told what they did well, students repeat it, since they know it works. Whatever their level, they need to hear that they're making progress.

Be patient. Whatever the mistake, repeated errors usually mean the rule isn't fully understood. Provided that you explain it differently, perhaps with an example from their own lives, it often clicks. Having tried this myself, I'd recommend a short exercise at the start of the next lesson, in case the error returns.

Not at all, provided that you give me some notice, although I'd rather you came when I'm teaching the easier class. Having been observed myself, I know it helps, since it keeps me honest. Come on Thursday morning, and bearing in mind how nervous you've been, I'll let you see the quieter class.

scenarios.scenario: Agreeing a study schedule with a busy language partner
scenarios.context: Two language exchange partners with busy lives negotiate a regular weekly schedule and decide how to use their sessions.

speakerA.en: Before we plan anything, I should explain that my schedule is unpredictable. Rarely do I know my shifts more than a week ahead. Not only do I work irregular hours, but I also have an evening course. Is a fixed weekly time realistic?

Mondays and Wednesdays are usually free, apart from the occasional meeting. Never have I managed to keep a routine for longer than a month, which worries me a little. Not only do I get tired, but I also lose motivation when I don't see progress.

I'd be willing, as long as it's short. Rarely do I have more than half an hour in the evening. Only when I'm relaxed can I speak naturally, so maybe we should avoid Monday, since I'm usually exhausted then.

Splitting equally seems fair. On the other hand, never have I felt comfortable speaking for longer than twenty minutes in a foreign language, though. Only when the topic interests me do I forget my nerves. Could we choose a topic in advance, in case we run out of things to say?

Cooking and football, to be honest. Rarely do I talk about anything else with friends. Not only would I have plenty to say, but I'd also learn useful phrases. What about you, and is there a subject you'd like to avoid?

It does, and I'm happy with that. Never have I had such a clear plan with a language partner. Not only have we agreed on a time, but we've also chosen topics. Shall we start next Wednesday, and then review the arrangement after a month?

speakerB.en: It might be difficult, but I'd say it's worth trying. Seldom do I find a partner who is serious about practicing, so I'd like to make this work. Only when we meet regularly will we really improve. What does a typical week look like for you?

I understand, and honestly I feel the same. Only after I started recording myself did I notice my progress. Not only did it motivate me, but it also showed me which sounds I needed to practice. Would you be willing to try something like that?

As far as I'm concerned, Wednesday would suit us both. Not only is it quieter, but it also leaves the weekend free for homework. Shall we split each session, thirty minutes in your language and thirty in mine, or would you prefer something more flexible?

Good idea. Not only would it reduce the pressure, but it would also help us prepare vocabulary beforehand. Only when you know the words do the conversations really flow. I'd suggest we choose topics we both enjoy. What are you passionate about?

Music and travel for me, and I'd rather avoid politics. Seldom does it lead to a relaxed conversation, and I'm not ready for it yet in your language. Only when we trust each other will we talk about serious topics. Does that sound fair?

Perfect. Rarely do I feel so confident at the beginning, so thank you. Only after a month will we know whether it works, but I'm optimistic. I'll send a reminder on Tuesday evening, in case anything changes. See you on Wednesday.

scenarios.scenario: Persuading a manager to fund language courses for staff
scenarios.context: An employee proposes that the company pay for English courses for the sales team and answers the manager's budget concerns.

speakerA.en: Thank you for making time, Ms. Clarke. I'd like to propose that the company fund English courses for our sales team. To be honest, given that we now work with clients in six countries, I think it's becoming essential. May I explain?

Twelve people, two evenings a week, for six months. The cost would be around eight thousand euros. I'd say that's modest, considering the extent to which poor communication has already cost us deals. Last quarter, two clients complained about misunderstandings.

That's a fair question. We could test everyone at the start and again after six months. Provided that the improvement is measurable, we'd have clear evidence. Also, that's where internal surveys help, since clients could rate our communication.

I think so. One evening and one lunchtime session would be a good balance. Given that people are tired after work, a lunch session might be more productive. As far as I'm concerned, it also shows that we value their development.

That's reasonable, and I'm sure most people would accept it. It also encourages responsibility. Given that some colleagues are already studying on their own, they'd probably welcome the support. Should I ask the team about their interest first?

Understood, I'll send you a comparison with sample programs. Thank you for being so open to it. I believe the extent to which this will help our international clients will surprise everyone, provided that we start soon.

speakerB.en: Please do. I'm open to it, but budgets are tight this year. Given that we've already invested in new software, I'd need a strong case. What exactly are you proposing, and how many employees would be involved?
I remember. That's where the real cost lies, in lost trust. Still, how can we measure the return? Given that language progress is gradual, I'd want to know how we'd see results, and by when.

I like the idea of measurable goals. On the other hand, staff might not take it seriously if it's after work. The extent to which people commit depends on motivation, so I'd want it to be partly during working hours. Would that be possible?

Good point. That's where the company benefits twice, through skills and loyalty. Now, I'd need a commitment. Provided that employees attend at least eighty percent of the classes, we could cover the full cost. Otherwise, they'd share part of it.

Yes, do that, and gather the numbers by Friday. Also, find two or three course providers and compare them. That's where the decision will be made, since price and quality vary widely. I'd rather choose a good one than the cheapest.
I hope you're right. Bring me the figures next week, and I'll present them to the board. Given that you've prepared so carefully, I'm optimistic. Well done, and thank you for the initiative.

scenarios.scenario: Describing an embarrassing misunderstanding in a foreign language
scenarios.context: A friend asks a language learner about an embarrassing mistake she made while staying with a host family in Spain.

speakerA.en: I heard you had an embarrassing moment in Spain last summer. To be honest, I'd love to hear it, since your language stories are always entertaining. What happened, and where were you?
That sounds promising. What exactly did you say? I'd imagine you mixed up a word, since that's the classic mistake. Was it something rude, or just silly?
No! What did they do? I'd have wanted to disappear under the table. As far as I'm concerned, that must have been the most awkward moment of the trip. Did anyone laugh?
That's funny, and kind of them. Did they correct you gently? I've found that people are usually patient with learners, although it depends. How did you react, in the end?
That's a story you'll never forget. Did it change the way you study? I mean, did you start checking words more carefully, or did it put you off speaking?

That's the right attitude. I think mistakes are the fastest way to learn, even if they're embarrassing. To be honest, I envy your courage, and I'd like to try speaking more myself. Maybe I'll take a trip to Spain next year.

speakerB.en: Oh dear, you've heard about it! It was my second day in Madrid, and I wanted to make a good impression on my host family. I could have sworn my Spanish was good enough, but it turned out that I was overconfident.

At dinner, I wanted to say I was embarrassed, so I said 'estoy embarazada'. What I meant was that I felt embarrassed, but it turned out that the word means 'pregnant'. The moment I saw their faces, I realized something was wrong.

The grandmother laughed first, thankfully. I could have sworn the table would go silent, but the whole family burst out laughing. It turned out that it's a very common mistake among English speakers. What a relief!

I laughed too, once I understood. The mother explained the difference between 'embarazada' and 'avergonzada'. What I meant was to say the second one. After that, they teased me for the rest of the week, but affectionately.
Both, at first. I could have sworn I'd never speak again, but it turned out to be the best lesson I've had. Now I check any word that looks similar to English. The moment I'm unsure, I ask.

You should, and don't worry about errors. What I meant to say earlier is that people appreciate the effort. I'll send you a list of false friends, so you can avoid my mistake. Embarazada is number one, obviously!

scenarios.scenario: Reporting or asking for help in an emergency
scenarios.context: Lost items, accidents, or urgent medical situations.

speakerA.en: Help! Please help me!
My friend is hurt. I need a doctor.
Please call the police, too.
Thank you for your help.
Help! I think I'm lost. Can you help me find my hotel?
speakerA.fa: کمک! فکر کنم گم شدم. میشه کمکم کنید هتل‌م رو پیدا کنم؟

speakerA.en: I need to call an ambulance! My friend is having a heart attack.
speakerA.fa: باید آمبولانس بگیرم! دوستم حمله قلبی کرده.

speakerA.en: I've lost my passport. What should I do?
speakerA.fa: پاسپورتم رو گم کردم. چیکار کنم؟

speakerA.en: Is there a police station nearby? I've been robbed.
speakerA.fa: نزدیک اینجا کلانتری هست؟ دزدی شده‌ام.

speakerA.en: I'm stuck in the elevator! Can you call for help?
speakerA.fa: توی آسانسور گیر کردم! میشه کمک بگیرید؟

speakerA.en: My car broke down in the middle of the road. I need a tow truck.
speakerA.fa: ماشینم وسط جاده خراب شده. به یدک‌کش نیاز دارم.

speakerB.en: What's the problem?
Don't worry. I'll call one.
OK. I'm calling now.
You're welcome. Stay calm.
Yes, don't worry. What's the name of your hotel?
speakerB.fa: بله، نگران نباش. اسم هتل‌تون چیه؟

speakerB.en: I'll call 911 right now. Stay with him until they arrive.
speakerB.fa: همین الان به ۹۱۱ زنگ می‌زنم. تا رسیدنشون کنارش بمون.

speakerB.en: You should go to the nearest embassy and report it lost.
speakerB.fa: باید به نزدیک‌ترین سفارت بری و گم شدنش رو گزارش بدی.

speakerB.en: Yes, there's one on the corner. I can walk you there.
speakerB.fa: بله، یکی در گوشه خیابان هست. می‌تونم شما رو ببرم اونجا.

speakerB.en: Stay calm. I'll call the building security right away.
speakerB.fa: آروم باش. همین الان به نگهبان ساختمان زنگ می‌زنم.

speakerB.en: I'll call a towing service for you. Do you have a membership with any company?
speakerB.fa: یه سرویس یدک‌کش برات می‌گیرم. با هیچ شرکتی عضویت نداری؟

scenarios.scenario: Calling an ambulance
scenarios.context: A person calls for an ambulance.

speakerA.en: Hello, I need an ambulance.
My father is not well.
I'm at 10 Main Street.
Please come fast!
My father fell down and he can't breathe well.
He is awake, but he is in a lot of pain.
It's 555 0187. Should I do anything before you arrive?
How long will the ambulance take?

speakerB.en: What is the problem?
Where are you?
Help is coming. Stay there.
They will be there soon.
Is he awake? Can he speak to you?
Don't move him. What is your phone number?
Stay calm and keep him warm. Don't give him food or drink.
About eight minutes. Please stay on the line.

scenarios.scenario: A lost child
scenarios.context: A parent asks for help in a shopping center.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I can't find my son.
He is five.
He wears a red shirt.
Thank you. I'm very worried.
I lost my daughter a few minutes ago near the toy shop.
She's six, with long brown hair and a yellow jacket.
Her name is Mina. Please call me when you find her.
Thank goodness! Is she all right?

speakerB.en: How old is he?
What is he wearing?
Please wait here. We will find him.
Don't worry. Here he is!
Don't panic. Can you describe her for me?
I'll make an announcement. What is her name?
Of course. We'll also check the cameras and the exits.
She's fine. She was waiting at the information desk.

scenarios.scenario: A fire in the building
scenarios.context: People leave a building on fire.

speakerA.en: Fire! Call the fire department!
Is everyone outside?
Don't use the elevator.
Stay away from the building.
I smell smoke. I think there's a fire on the third floor.
Stay low and cover your nose with a cloth.
Please wait for the firefighters. Don't go back inside.
Please meet at the assembly point across the street.

speakerB.en: Everybody, get out!
Yes, we are all here.
OK. Let's use the stairs.
Yes, we are safe now.
I'll press the alarm. Everyone, please leave now!
Good idea. Let's go to the emergency exit.
I understand. My bag is still in my office, but it's not worth it.
OK. I'll count everyone from my team.

scenarios.scenario: A small accident
scenarios.context: A person is hurt on the street.

speakerA.en: Are you OK?
Can you stand up?
Sit here. I'll get help.
Is there a hospital near here?
I think I broke my arm when I fell off my bike.
Yes, please. It hurts a lot.
Could you also tell my wife what happened?
Thank you for staying with me. I was really scared.

speakerB.en: My leg hurts.
No, I can't.
Thank you very much.
Yes, it's five minutes away.
Try not to move it. Shall I call an ambulance?
OK, I'm calling now. I'll stay with you until they arrive.
Of course. What's her phone number?
You're welcome. Help is on the way.

scenarios.scenario: A lost bag
scenarios.context: A traveler reports a lost bag at the police station.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. My bag is gone!
It was on the chair.
My phone and my wallet.
Will you find it?
I left my bag on the train about an hour ago.
The 3:15 train from the city center. I sat near the door.
It's a black backpack with a blue key ring. My passport is inside.
How long will it take to get an answer?

speakerB.en: Where was it?
What is in the bag?
Please fill in this form.
We will try. We'll call you.
Which train was it, and where did you sit?
What does the bag look like?
I understand. Please give me your name and phone number.
We'll contact the train company and call you within a day.

scenarios.scenario: Feeling very sick
scenarios.context: A person feels sick at a pharmacy.

speakerA.en: I feel very sick.
My head hurts.
Yes, I think so.
Should I see a doctor?
I've had a bad stomachache since this morning.
I had some seafood at a restaurant last night.
A little. Could you give me something for the pain?
What if I don't feel better by tomorrow?

speakerB.en: Sit down, please.
Do you have a fever?
Take this medicine and rest.
Yes, please go today.
Did you eat anything unusual yesterday?
It could be food poisoning. Do you feel dizzy?
I can give you something, but please drink plenty of water.
Then see a doctor as soon as possible.

scenarios.scenario: Calling an ambulance for an injured person
scenarios.context: A caller reports an accident to the emergency operator.

speakerA.en: Emergency services. What's your emergency?
Can you tell me exactly where you are?
Is he conscious, and is he breathing normally?
Don't move him. An ambulance is on its way and should arrive in about eight minutes.

speakerB.en: A man has fallen from a ladder, and he can't move his leg. Please send an ambulance.
We're at 25 Oak Street, in the backyard behind the house.
Yes, he's awake and talking, but he's in a lot of pain.
Thank you. I'll stay with him and wait by the gate.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting a fire in a building
scenarios.context: A resident warns the fire department about smoke in an apartment building.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'd like to report a fire. There's smoke coming from the third floor of my building.
It's 18 Park Avenue. Most people have left, but I'm not sure about the older couple on the third floor.
I can hear the alarm, and the smoke is getting thicker.
I will. How long will it take them to get here?

speakerB.en: What is the address, and is everyone out of the building?
Stay outside and don't go back in for any reason. Fire trucks are on the way.
Move away from the building and keep the entrance clear for the firefighters.
About five minutes. Please stay on the line until they arrive.

scenarios.scenario: Dealing with a lost wallet and stolen phone
scenarios.context: A tourist reports a theft at a police station.

speakerA.en: Good afternoon. I'd like to report a theft. Someone took my bag while I was in a café.
My wallet, my phone, and my passport. I don't know what to do now.
Can I get a copy of the report? My insurance company will probably ask for it.
About an hour ago, around two o'clock. The café is on Main Street.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry to hear that. What exactly was in the bag?
First, you should cancel your credit cards. Then we'll write a report you can show to your embassy.
Yes, we'll give you one after you sign the statement. When did it happen?
We'll check whether there are any cameras nearby and contact you if we find anything.

scenarios.scenario: Giving first aid instructions over the phone
scenarios.context: A dispatcher guides a caller through helping someone who has collapsed.

speakerA.en: Please stay calm and tell me exactly what happened. Is the person responsive?
Check whether he's breathing by watching his chest and listening near his mouth. Can you do that?
I need you to place the heel of your hand on the center of his chest and push down firmly, about two compressions per second.
Don't stop until the paramedics take over. They're approximately four minutes away.

speakerB.en: He collapsed in the middle of the street, and he's not answering when I speak to him.
I can't tell. His breathing seems very faint, and his lips are turning blue.
All right, I'm doing it now. How long should I keep going before help arrives?
Understood. Please tell them to hurry, because I don't know how much longer I can keep this up.

scenarios.scenario: Evacuating a building during an alarm
scenarios.context: An employee and a safety officer coordinate an evacuation.

speakerA.en: The fire alarm has just gone off on the fourth floor. Do you know whether it's a drill or the real thing?
Several people are still at their desks. Some are insisting on finishing their work first.
What about the colleague who uses a wheelchair? She's on the sixth floor, and she can't manage the stairs.
I'll stay with her until they arrive. Have you counted everyone at the assembly point?

speakerB.en: We can't take any chances. Everyone must leave immediately through the nearest stairwell.
Make it clear that this isn't optional. Nobody should be using the elevators under any circumstances.
Take her to the designated refuge area near the stairwell and notify the fire crew of her exact location.
We're checking against the attendance list now. Two people remain unaccounted for.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting a natural disaster and seeking shelter
scenarios.context: A resident calls an emergency hotline during severe flooding.

speakerA.en: The water has risen above the doorstep, and my elderly mother and I are trapped upstairs.
We're unharmed, but the power is out, and my mother needs medication she can't do without for long.
It's 14 Riverside Lane, the red-brick house near the bridge. The streets are impassable by car.
Should we try to wade through the water toward higher ground?

speakerB.en: Are either of you injured, and is there anything blocking your exit through a window or roof?
I'll notify the rescue teams of your situation as a priority. What is your address?
Boats are being deployed to your area. In the meantime, gather warm clothing, your documents, and the medication.
Absolutely not. The current is stronger than it looks. Stay where you are and keep your phone charged.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting a gas leak
scenarios.context: A resident calls the gas company's emergency line after smelling gas in her building.

speakerA.en: I'd like to report a gas leak. There's a strong smell in the hallway of my apartment building, and it seems to be getting worse.
I'm in the lobby, and there are a few neighbors here as well. We've left our apartments, but some residents on the upper floors might not have heard.
It's strongest near the basement door. I haven't gone near it, but I think the meter room is down there.
Should I call the fire department as well, or will you notify them?

speakerB.en: Thank you for calling. First, are you inside the building at the moment, and are there any other people with you?
Please don't use any lights, elevators, or phones inside the building, as even a spark could be dangerous. Is the smell strongest in any particular area?
Good. Please move everyone at least fifty yards away and keep the entrance clear. An emergency crew is on its way and should arrive within ten minutes.
We've already alerted them. Please remain at a safe distance, and don't let anyone go back inside until the crew gives the all-clear.

scenarios.scenario: Giving a witness statement after a traffic accident
scenarios.context: A bystander describes a collision to a police officer at the scene.

speakerA.en: Thank you for waiting, sir. I understand you saw the collision. Could you tell me in your own words what you witnessed?
How fast would you estimate the van was traveling, and did you see whether the driver braked beforehand?
Did you notice anything unusual about the driver, such as using a phone or appearing unwell?
That's understood. We'll only record what you're certain of. Would you be willing to sign a written statement and provide your contact details?

speakerB.en: Certainly. I was standing at the corner when a white van ran the red light and struck a cyclist who was crossing the intersection.
I couldn't give you a precise figure, but it was definitely over the limit. I don't recall hearing any braking until the moment of impact.
I couldn't see clearly, but he seemed to be looking down just before it happened. I wouldn't want to state that as fact, though.
Of course. I'd like to help in any way I can. That cyclist was incredibly lucky to survive.

scenarios.scenario: Reviewing an emergency response afterward
scenarios.context: A safety officer and a manager debrief after a fire drill revealed several weaknesses.

speakerA.en: Having reviewed yesterday's evacuation, I'd say the drill exposed some uncomfortable truths about our readiness.
That's accurate, but the figure masks a few problems. The third-floor stairwell was blocked, and two fire wardens weren't at their posts.
Storage boxes had been left there, probably temporarily. In a real fire, that could have delayed people considerably or caused a crush.
I'd also recommend retraining the wardens, since two of them were new and hadn't been briefed on their responsibilities.

speakerB.en: I thought it went reasonably well. Everyone was out within six minutes, which is well within the regulations.
I hadn't realized the stairwell issue. Why was it blocked?
That's unacceptable. I'll have the area cleared today and remind every department of the rules about escape routes.
Agreed. I'd rather discover these flaws in a drill than in an emergency. Please draft a corrective action plan by the end of the week.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting a serious incident to the emergency services
scenarios.context: A caller conveys critical information calmly and precisely under pressure.

speakerA.en: I need an ambulance immediately. There's been a collision at the junction of Harper Street and the ring road, and one driver is unconscious.
He's breathing, but he's unresponsive. The car is smoking slightly, though I can't see any flames. Traffic has stopped.
There's a passenger who appears conscious but is bleeding from the forehead. She's sitting on the pavement.
Understood. I can see the vehicles approaching now. Should I remain here until they arrive?

speakerB.en: Stay on the line with me. Is the person breathing, and is there any danger from traffic or fire?
Please keep a safe distance from the vehicle in case of fire. Is anyone else injured?
Help is on its way and should reach you within six minutes. Don't move either person unless they're in immediate danger.
Yes, please. Stay on the line, and tell the paramedics exactly what you've observed when they reach you.

scenarios.scenario: Coordinating an evacuation during a sudden crisis
scenarios.context: A supervisor directs staff and visitors out of a building during an alarm.

speakerA.en: Attention, everyone. We have an alarm in the east wing, and I need you to proceed calmly to the nearest exit.
Leave everything. Nothing in this building is worth a risk, and I'd rather replace a bag than lose a person.
Marcus is on his way with the evacuation chair. Please do not use the lifts under any circumstances.
Excellent. Report any missing persons directly to me, and don't allow anyone to re-enter until the fire service gives clearance.

speakerB.en: Should we collect our belongings first, or leave immediately? Several visitors are asking.
There's a gentleman in a wheelchair on the second floor who can't use the stairs. Who's assisting him?
Understood. I'll direct the visitors to the assembly point in the car park and take a headcount as they arrive.
Of course. I'll keep the group together and relay any instructions as they come through.

scenarios.scenario: Seeking help after losing documents while abroad
scenarios.context: A traveler reports stolen belongings and seeks assistance from their embassy.

speakerA.en: I'm calling because my bag was stolen this morning, and it contained my passport, my wallet and my phone. I'm rather at a loss.
I've just come from the station and have a report reference. They were courteous but not particularly encouraging.
I have a photocopy of the passport in my hotel safe and a digital scan in my email, if that helps.
That's a tremendous relief. What about the cost? Everything I'd have used to pay is gone.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry to hear that. Have you reported the theft to the local police?
That's typical, I'm afraid. We can issue an emergency travel document, though we'll need proof of identity and a photograph.
It does, considerably. Bring those, along with the police report, and we can process the application within a day.
There's a fee, but we can arrange for a friend or relative to transfer funds. Let's discuss the options when you arrive.

scenarios.scenario: Calling the police
scenarios.context: A woman calls the police after her bike is stolen.

speakerA.en: Police emergency. What's the problem?
When did it happen?
Can you describe the bike?
Okay. A police officer will come to you soon.

speakerB.en: Someone stole my bike from outside my house.
About twenty minutes ago. I was in the shop.
It's red, with a black seat and a small basket.
Thank you. I'll wait here in front of the shop.

scenarios.scenario: Losing a wallet
scenarios.context: A man reports his lost wallet at a station office.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I lost my wallet. Can you help me?
I think on the train from the airport.
It's brown and has my ID card and some money in it.
Thank you. I'm very worried.

speakerB.en: Where do you think you lost it?
What does it look like?
I'll call the train office. Please wait a moment.
Don't worry. People often hand in lost things here.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting a car accident
scenarios.context: A driver calls the emergency number after a crash.

speakerA.en: Emergency services. What's happened?
Is anybody injured?
Please stay on the line. Are you in a safe place?
Good. An ambulance is on its way. Don't move the injured man.

speakerB.en: There's been an accident on the highway near exit twelve. Two cars are involved.
One driver says his arm hurts, but he's conscious and talking.
Yes, I've moved to the side of the road and turned on my hazard lights.
Understood. I'll stay with him until help arrives.

scenarios.scenario: Dealing with a power cut and a gas smell
scenarios.context: A tenant calls the landlord about a smell of gas in the flat.

speakerA.en: Hello, it's an emergency. I can smell gas in my kitchen.
I've done that. Should I leave the apartment?
How long will they take to arrive?
Okay. Thank you for acting so quickly.

speakerB.en: Open the windows immediately and don't turn on any lights or switches.
Yes, go outside now. I'll call the gas company from here.
They promised to come within twenty minutes. Please wait outside.
Of course. Call me when you see the technician.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting a fire to the emergency services
scenarios.context: A caller reports a fire and answers the operator's questions.

speakerA.en: Hello, I need the fire department. There's a fire in the building across the street, and I can see smoke coming from a window.
It's at 14 Maple Street, on the third floor. I think it's an apartment, and there are people on the balcony asking for help.
I don't know exactly how many people are inside. I saw at least two on the balcony, and one of them seems to be a child.
Yes, the main door is open, and some residents are already leaving the building. I'm standing about fifty meters away.
I'll stay on the line. Please hurry. The smoke is getting thicker, and I can hear people shouting.
I see the fire engine arriving now. Thank you so much for your quick response.

speakerB.en: Emergency services. Please stay calm and tell me exactly where you are and what's happening.
Thank you. We're sending fire engines and an ambulance immediately. Can you tell me how many people might be inside the building?
Please don't go near the building yourself, and tell anyone who is outside to stay away from the smoke. Is anyone injured?
That's good. Make sure that the entrance is clear so that the firefighters can get through. Are there any gas cylinders or other hazards that you know of?
Help is on its way, and they should arrive in about three minutes. Stay on the line, and tell me if anything changes.
Well done. You've been very helpful. Keep a safe distance, and wait for the firefighters to tell you what to do.

scenarios.scenario: Helping someone who has fallen
scenarios.context: A passer-by helps an elderly person who has fallen and calls for an ambulance.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, are you all right? I saw you fall. Please don't try to move yet. I'm going to call an ambulance.
I know it's painful, but it's important to stay still until the paramedics have checked you. Do you feel any pain in your head or your neck?
Okay, I'll put my jacket under your head, so that you're more comfortable. Is there anyone I should contact for you?
Hello, I'd like to call an ambulance. An elderly woman has fallen on the pavement in front of the bank on Station Road.
She's conscious and talking, but she thinks that she may have broken her hip. She's about seventy years old.
The ambulance is on its way, so please try to relax. I'll stay with you until they get here.

speakerB.en: Oh, thank you. I tripped on the curb, and I can't get up. My leg hurts terribly, and I feel a bit dizzy.
No, my head is fine. It's my hip that hurts, mostly. I'm afraid I might have broken something.
That's very kind of you. Please call my daughter. Her number is in my handbag, in a small red notebook.
Thank you for staying with me. I don't know what I would have done if you hadn't been here.
I'm sorry to be such a bother. I just went out to buy some bread, and now look at me.
You're very kind. I'm so grateful that there are still people who stop to help others.

scenarios.scenario: Coordinating during a natural disaster
scenarios.context: Two residents discuss how to respond to a flood warning.

speakerA.en: Did you hear the sirens? The authorities have issued an evacuation order for our district, because the river is expected to burst its banks before midnight.
I've already packed documents, medication, and some clothes. The difficulty is my mother, who can't walk far on her own, and I don't have a car.
That's incredibly generous of you. If you could take us to the shelter at the school, it would be a huge relief. We can leave in ten minutes.
Should we take the main road, or is it likely to be blocked by now? I've heard that the bridge on Mill Street has already been closed.
That sounds sensible. I'll tell the neighbors upstairs, in case they haven't heard. Some of them are elderly and may need help getting down the stairs.
Thank you. I don't know what we'd have done without you. Let's hope that the damage isn't as bad as predicted.

speakerB.en: Yes, I heard them about twenty minutes ago. I've been following the news, and the situation is getting worse. We need to leave as soon as possible, and not wait until the last moment.
Don't worry about the car. I have one, and there's room for three. I'll pick you both up in a few minutes, and we can go together. Have you got everything that she'll need?
Of course. It's no trouble. We should also bring blankets and some food. I've heard that the shelters tend to be overcrowded, and supplies may run short.
The main road is probably the safest, but it might be crowded. I'd rather take the one through the hills, even if it's longer, since it's higher up and won't flood.
Good idea. I'll knock on the doors on the ground floor while you finish packing. Make sure the gas is turned off and the electricity is disconnected before you leave.
Let's concentrate on getting everyone to safety. Property can be replaced, but people can't. We'll deal with the rest tomorrow.

scenarios.scenario: Giving first aid instructions to a bystander
scenarios.context: An emergency dispatcher guides a caller through first aid for a person who has collapsed.

speakerA.en: Please help me! A man has collapsed in front of me in the supermarket. He isn't responding, and I don't know what to do. People are standing around, but nobody is helping.
He's lying on his back. I can't see any injuries, and I'm not sure whether he's breathing. His lips seem to be turning a bluish color. Should I move him?
I'm kneeling beside him now. I've put my ear near his mouth, and I can't feel any breath. What should I do next? I've never done this before, and I'm afraid of making things worse.
I've started the compressions. Someone has just brought a defibrillator from the pharmacy. Do I need to stop and use it, or should I continue until the ambulance arrives?
It's talking to me. It says that a shock is advised, and everybody must stand clear. I'm pressing the button now. Please tell me that he'll be all right.
I can hear the siren. The paramedics are coming through the door. Thank you so much for staying with me. I couldn't have done this without your guidance.

speakerB.en: Emergency services. Stay calm, and tell me exactly where you are. I'm sending an ambulance right now. Is the person conscious, and is he breathing normally?
Don't move him unless he's in danger. Tilt his head back gently, and check for breathing for no more than ten seconds. If he's not breathing normally, we need to begin CPR immediately.
You're doing the right thing. Place the heel of your hand in the center of his chest, with the other hand on top, and push hard and fast, about twice a second. I'll count with you.
Continue until the machine tells you to stop. Ask someone to open the defibrillator and follow its instructions. It will tell you exactly what to do, and it's safe to use.
You're doing very well. Make sure that nobody is touching him when the shock is delivered. Afterwards, resume the compressions immediately, and don't stop until the paramedics take over.
You've done everything right, and you may have saved his life. Please tell the paramedics what you did and when. Take a moment to breathe. You've been very brave.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting a car accident to the police and insurance
scenarios.context: A driver gives details of an accident to the police and later calls the insurer.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'd like to report a traffic accident. It happened about twenty minutes ago on Station Road, near the junction with Park Avenue. Nobody seems to be seriously injured, but both cars are damaged.
A silver car pulled out of a side street without stopping, and I couldn't avoid hitting it. I was driving at about forty kilometers an hour, and I braked, but it was too late.
I'm fine, apart from a bruise on my arm, and the other driver says that he's all right as well. His passenger has a pain in her neck, so we've asked for an ambulance to come and check her.
Yes, we've exchanged names, addresses, and insurance details. I've also taken photographs of the damage and of the position of the cars, and there was a witness, who gave me her number.
Hello, I'm calling to report the accident that I told the police about earlier. I've been advised that the police report number is 4471, and I'd like to start the claim.
I've got all the documents ready, including the photographs. Could you tell me how long the process is likely to take, and whether I'll be given a replacement car while mine is being repaired?

speakerB.en: Police emergency line. Is anyone injured, and are the vehicles blocking the road? Please give me your exact location, so that I can send a patrol car and, if necessary, medical assistance.
Thank you. Please stay calm and remain at the scene. Do not move the vehicles unless they're causing a danger. Can you describe how the collision occurred, and who you think was at fault?

I'm sending an ambulance now, and an officer will be with you shortly. In the meantime, please don't admit liability to the other driver. Just exchange the details, and let the police determine what happened.

That's very helpful. Please keep the photographs and the witness's number, since they will be useful for the report. The officer will take statements from everyone when he arrives, and give you a reference number.
Good afternoon. Thank you for the report number. I'll open a claim now. Please send the photographs and the officer's report as soon as you receive it, and we'll start the assessment.

The process usually takes between two and four weeks, depending on whether liability is disputed. If you've chosen the comprehensive cover, you're entitled to a courtesy car, and I'll arrange that today.

scenarios.scenario: Handling a gas leak
scenarios.context: A resident smells gas, calls the utility emergency line, and coordinates with neighbors.

speakerA.en: Hello, I need to report a gas leak. I came home a few minutes ago, and there's a very strong smell of gas in my flat. I haven't switched on any lights, and I've opened all the windows.
The smell seems to be coming from the kitchen. I suspect that I may have left the stove on this morning, but I'm not sure. The ring isn't lit now, but the knob is turned halfway.
I live on the third floor, in a block of twelve flats. I'm in the street outside now, with my neighbors, who have also noticed the smell in the stairwell.
Yes, we've knocked on every door, and as far as I know, everybody's out of the building, except for an elderly woman on the first floor, who is not answering. I'm worried about her.
I'll make sure that nobody goes back inside. I can see the fire engine coming round the corner now. Do you want me to wait here and talk to the firefighters?
Thank you. I'm glad that we acted quickly. I hope that she's all right, and that we'll be allowed back into our homes soon.

speakerB.en: Gas emergency line. Please listen carefully. Don't use any electrical switches, don't smoke, and don't use your phone inside the building. Leave immediately, and call us from a safe distance.
You did the right thing by opening the windows. Do not go back in to turn off the stove, as that could cause a spark. A team is on its way, and the firefighters have been notified, too.
Thank you. Please keep everybody at least fifty meters away from the building, and prevent anyone from entering. How many people live in the block, and has everyone been accounted for?
That's a priority. Tell the firefighters about the woman as soon as they arrive. They have breathing equipment, and they can check her flat safely. Please don't go in yourselves.
Yes, please wait for them, and give them as much information as possible: where you smelled the gas, and when it started. It will help them locate the source quickly.
You've done everything correctly. The engineers will check the building before anyone is allowed back in, which could take a few hours. Is there somewhere that the residents can wait?

scenarios.scenario: Briefing a new employee on fire safety procedures
scenarios.context: A safety officer briefs a newly hired employee on the fire procedures in a busy office and answers questions about what to do in different situations.

speakerA.en: Welcome to the team. Before you start, I'd like to go through our fire procedures, which every new employee needs to know. Should you ever hear the alarm, stop what you're doing immediately. Once you've left your desk, head for the nearest exit.

Never use the lifts, although they may look faster, since they may stop working. Should you be on an upper floor, the stairs at either end of the corridor are marked in green. Once you've reached the ground floor, go to the car park, where we gather by the main gate.

Stay with your visitor and guide them out. Each floor has a warden, who wears a yellow vest. Once you've left, give your name to the warden, so that we know you're safe. Should you see someone in difficulty, tell a warden rather than going back.

That's an honest answer, and a common concern. Should the main exit be blocked, use the emergency door at the back, which opens outwards. Once you've practiced the route twice, you'll do it automatically. I'd say the key is to stay calm and keep low if there's smoke.

Leave everything, even your phone if it isn't in your pocket. Things can be replaced, but people can't. On the other hand, if you're already holding your keys, take them. Once you're outside, stay away from the building, as the fire crew will need space.

We hold a drill every six months, usually without notice, since a real alarm doesn't warn anyone either. Once you've taken part in one, you'll feel more confident. Should you have any more questions, my office is on the second floor, and I'm always happy to help.

speakerB.en: Thank you. I'd appreciate it if you could explain where the exits are, since I haven't had time to look around yet. Should I use the lifts, or only the stairs? And where do we gather outside?
That's clear. I'd appreciate it if you could tell me what happens if I'm with a visitor. Should I stay with them, or look after myself first? And who checks that everybody has left the building?
I see. I'd appreciate it if you could clarify one more thing, though. Should the fire be near the exit, what would I do? To be honest, I'd probably panic, and I'd like to know the alternatives.
That helps. I'd appreciate it if you could show me the route today, in case there's an alarm this week. Should I take my belongings with me, or is it safer to leave everything at my desk?
Understood. I'd appreciate it if you could tell me how often we practice. Should there be a drill, do we receive a warning, or does it happen without notice? I'd rather know what to expect.

Thank you, that's really reassuring. I'd appreciate it if you could send me the written plan by email, so that I can read it again tonight. Should I need anything else, I'll come and see you tomorrow morning.

scenarios.scenario: Preparing an emergency kit with a neighbor before storm season
scenarios.context: Two neighbors discuss how to prepare their households for the storm season and what to keep in an emergency kit.

speakerA.en: Have you heard the forecast for this winter? Much as I'd like to ignore it, they're predicting several severe storms. It's not so much the wind that worries me as the power cuts, which last for days in our street.
It would be the first. Much as I've always meant to, I never found the time. It's not so much a lack of money as a lack of organization. What should be in it, and how much of everything do we need?

That's useful. It's not so much the equipment I'm unsure about as the food. What would you keep, given that we can't cook without electricity? On the other hand, my camping stove might help, as long as we use it outdoors.

My mother takes tablets every day, so yes. What worries me is that the pharmacy might be closed for days. It's not so much the cost as the risk of running out. Could we ask the doctor for a larger supply?

The old couple upstairs, I'd say. It's not so much that they can't cope as that they live alone. What I'd like is to check on them during a storm. Much as they're independent, they'd probably welcome it.

Yes, let's do it next week. It's not so much a formal meeting as a chat over tea, so people feel relaxed. What I'll do is prepare a checklist, as long as you help with the details. Much as I hoped for a mild winter, I feel better prepared.

speakerB.en: I'd say it's wise to prepare. What concerns me most is the water supply, since the pump stops without electricity. Have you ever put together an emergency kit, or would this be the first time?

Water is the priority, about three liters per person per day. What matters is having enough for at least three days. Much as it sounds excessive, it's what the authorities recommend. Flashlights, batteries, and a first-aid kit are essential too.

Good idea, but never use it indoors, in case of fumes. What I'd keep is canned food, nuts, and bread that lasts. Much as I enjoy fresh meals, in an emergency it's about energy, not taste. Do you have any medicines you'd need?

Usually you can, if you explain why. What matters is keeping a list of medications in the kit, with the doses. Much as it feels like a fuss, paramedics find it extremely helpful. Is there anyone else in the building who might need help?

I agree, and we could make a list of vulnerable neighbors. What matters is that everyone knows who to call. Much as we all value privacy, a short phone list could save lives. Shall we organize a meeting in the building?

So do I. What matters now is that we actually follow through. I'll buy the water and batteries this weekend. Much as I'm not looking forward to the storms, to be honest, I'm glad we started this conversation.

scenarios.scenario: Deciding whether to evacuate before an approaching storm
scenarios.context: Two neighbors discuss whether to leave their coastal town after the authorities issue a serious storm warning.

speakerA.en: Have you seen the latest forecast? The storm has been upgraded, and the city is urging people in low-lying streets to leave. To be honest, I can't decide whether to go or stay. What are you planning to do?
What worries me is the river. Should it burst its banks, our street would be flooded within an hour, and we'd have no way out. Had last year's storm been this strong, we would have been trapped.
I'd say they would close it early. Should the water rise, it would be the first thing they shut, and then the only road out would be gone. Had I known that last year, I'd have prepared much better.

My sister lives inland, about forty miles away, and she's offered us her spare room. Were we to wait until tomorrow, the roads would be jammed. Should we leave this afternoon, we'd miss the worst of the traffic.

Documents, medicines, chargers and a few days' clothes, I'd say. We should also move the valuables upstairs. Were the water to get in, at least the important things would be safe. What about your elderly mother next door?
Of course, I'll talk to her now. Were she to see us packing, she'd realize it's serious. Let's leave within the hour, shall we? Better a wasted trip than a tragedy, as far as I'm concerned.

speakerB.en: I've been going back and forth too. Last year's warning turned out to be a false alarm, so part of me thinks we're overreacting. What makes you lean towards leaving this time?

That's a fair point, although the river has never actually flooded our street. Were it to happen, though, the emergency services couldn't reach us quickly. Do you think the bridge would stay open, or would they close it early?

Then staying is a gamble, isn't it? What I keep asking myself is whether the inconvenience of leaving is really worth the risk of staying. Where would we even go, since the hotels are bound to be full?
That settles it, as far as I'm concerned. Had she not offered, I'd have hesitated, but this makes it easy. What should we take, in case the house is damaged and we can't return for a few days?

What worries me is that she'll refuse to leave. Should she say no, we'll have to persuade her gently. Had the city contacted her directly, she might have taken it more seriously. Could you explain it to her?
Agreed. Should anything change, we'll hear about it on the radio. Had we not talked this through, we'd probably still be dithering. I'll start loading the car while you speak to her.

scenarios.scenario: Persuading a manager to fund first-aid training for all staff
scenarios.context: A safety coordinator asks her manager to pay for first-aid training for everyone after a colleague collapsed at work.

speakerA.en: Thank you for making time for me. Since Tuesday's incident, I've been thinking about how well prepared we really are. To be honest, I'd like to propose that the company pay for first-aid training for everyone. What's your first reaction?
