You're welcome. It's never too late to change the way you study. And remember that rest is part of studying. A well-rested brain consolidates information far better than a tired one.
It's completely normal. A certain level of nervousness can even improve your performance. If it becomes overwhelming, speak to a counselor, since there are techniques that can help you manage it.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing a school's new policy on mobile phones
scenarios.context: A parent and a teacher discuss a school's new ban on mobile phones during the school day and how it will affect students.

speakerA.en: Thanks for meeting me. I wanted to ask about the new phone policy. Much as I understand the reasons, I'm worried about my daughter. It's not so much the ban that bothers me as the fact that she can no longer contact me during the day.

She sometimes walks home alone, and I like knowing she's arrived safely. It's not so much a question of convenience as of peace of mind. What I'd like is a way of contacting her, as long as it doesn't disrupt lessons.

I'm glad to hear it, although I'm not sure the improvement is entirely thanks to the ban. On the other hand, I did notice she talks more at dinner. It's not so much that she's changed as that she's less tired. Is there evidence for the benefits?

Interesting. Much as I support the policy, I'm concerned about students who use phones for learning, such as translation apps. It's not so much the phone itself as how it's used. What do you do for those who genuinely need one?

That sounds sensible. What I'd also like to know is how you handle students who break the rule. It's not so much the punishment I'm interested in as the consistency. Much as I'd hate to see my daughter in trouble, fairness matters, in case it happens.

That seems fair. It's not so much a strict policy as a clear one, and I appreciate that. What I'll do is explain it to my daughter tonight, since she's been rather upset. Much as she complains, I think she'll cope.

speakerB.en: I understand your concern, and I'd say it's a common one. What matters is that students can reach you in an emergency, and they can, through the school office. May I ask what specifically worries you, since there may be a misunderstanding?

That's reasonable. Much as the rule is strict, we allow phones to be kept switched off in bags, so students can check them after school. What worries us is the distraction, not the safety. Since the ban, concentration has improved noticeably.

Several studies suggest that grades rise slightly when phones are limited, particularly for weaker students. What matters is that it's the same rule for everyone. Much as some pupils complained at first, most now say they prefer it, to be honest.

Good question. Students with a documented need can apply for an exception. What we ask is that the device is used only for that purpose, and that the teacher supervises. Much as it creates extra work, it seems the fairest approach.

The first time, the phone is kept in the office until the end of the day. What matters is that the response is calm and the same for everyone. Much as we'd like to avoid conflict, repeated cases involve a conversation with the parents.

I'm glad we talked. What matters is that you and the school work together, and I'd say you've shown that today. Much as students grumble, they respond well to parents who support the rules. Please contact me if any problems arise.

scenarios.scenario: Mentoring a first-year student who is struggling to cope
scenarios.context: A university tutor talks to a first-year student who feels overwhelmed by the workload and is thinking about dropping out.

speakerA.en: Thank you for seeing me. Having been here for only two months, I'm already struggling, and I'm thinking about leaving. Given that everyone else seems to manage, I feel there's something wrong with me. Do you think I should quit?

Mostly the reading. Given that I have five courses, I never seem to finish anything. Having stayed up until three last night, I still didn't complete the assignment. I don't know how the others cope, to be honest.

I tried, although I gave up after a few days. Whatever plan I make, something unexpected happens. On the other hand, supposing I did stick to a timetable, would it really make a difference, or would I still feel behind?
Perhaps four, but I don't think I'm using them well. Having read the same page three times, I realized I wasn't concentrating. Given that my phone is always next to me, I get distracted constantly.

I'd say it's worth a try. Having tried everything else, I have little to lose. Whatever happens, I want to give it a fair chance. Supposing it doesn't work, who else could I talk to, since the course is so demanding?
That means a lot. Having spoken to you, I feel much calmer, given that I was close to giving up. Whatever happens next, I'll do my best. Could we meet again in two weeks, as long as you have time?

speakerB.en: I'm glad you came. Having seen many first-year students in your position, I can tell you it's very common. Bearing in mind how big the change is, it's no surprise you're tired. What exactly is making you feel overwhelmed?

Many of them don't, at least at first. As far as I'm concerned, provided that you plan your week, you can reduce the pressure considerably. Having spoken to students who have done well, I notice they usually start tasks early. Have you tried a weekly schedule?

Provided that the timetable is realistic, it makes a big difference. Having overestimated what they can do, most students abandon their plans quickly. Whatever you schedule, leave gaps for the unexpected. How many hours do you actually spend on reading each day?

That's a useful insight. Provided that you put the phone in another room, you'd probably save an hour a day. Bearing in mind that attention is limited, short sessions of forty minutes work better than long ones. Would you be willing to try that for a week?

Provided that you let me know how it goes, we can adjust the plan, in case it proves too ambitious. The university also has a study skills service. Having been through this myself, I can tell you it helps a lot. Whatever you need, you're not on your own.

Of course. Provided that you stick to the plan, we'll review it together. Having taken the first step by coming here, you've already shown courage. Bearing in mind how far you've come, I'm optimistic. Let's book the appointment now.

scenarios.scenario: Deciding whether to move a child to a smaller school
scenarios.context: Two parents discuss whether to change their son's school after he has lost his motivation.

speakerA.en: I've been worried about Daniel for weeks. He used to love school, and now he treats it as if it were a punishment. Honestly, I think it's high time we considered moving him. What's your view?
His teacher told me he rarely speaks up in a class of thirty-two. I wish he felt more comfortable asking for help. He behaves as though he's invisible, and I wish someone had noticed sooner.
There's Riverside, with classes of about eighteen. I'd rather he were somewhere teachers know every child by name. It's high time we stopped assuming he'll simply grow out of it.

That's what I keep asking myself. I wish there were a way to ask him without making him feel responsible. If only he would tell us what he wants, it would be so much simpler. How do you suggest we approach him?
Good idea. It's about time he had a say in this. I'd also like to speak to his current teacher again, in case there's something we've missed. I wish I had done that at the beginning of the term.
That sounds fair, as long as we don't rush him. I'd rather make a slow decision than a bad one. To be honest, I feel better now that we've talked it through. Shall I book the visit for Saturday?

speakerB.en: I've noticed it too, but I'm cautious. Changing schools is a big step, and he's only just made friends. What makes you think the school is the problem, rather than something else going on?

That does worry me. Still, I wish we could be sure a smaller school would solve it, since it would mean a longer commute. It's about time we visited a few places, though, to compare them. Do you have any in mind?
I take your point. On the other hand, Riverside is much more academic, and I wish it weren't so competitive. He talks as if he already feels he's falling behind. Would more pressure really help him?
Gently, I'd say. Perhaps we could visit Riverside together and let him look around, as if it were just an afternoon out. I'd rather he decide for himself than feel we were sending him away.

Yes, let's do both. And let's give ourselves a deadline, because I don't want this dragging on as though nothing were wrong. It's high time we made a decision, but a well-informed one. What about the end of the month?

Please do. I wish we'd had this conversation earlier, but there's no use dwelling on it. Whatever we choose, I want Daniel to look forward to mornings again, as if school were a place where he belonged.

scenarios.scenario: Debating whether coursework or exams should count more
scenarios.context: Two teachers at a secondary school disagree about whether coursework or final exams should carry more weight in students' grades.

speakerA.en: I'd like to get your view on the new grading proposal. Under it, coursework would count for sixty percent and exams for forty. To be honest, I'm not convinced. What's your reaction?

It's not so much the idea that troubles me as the way coursework is done at home. However carefully we supervise, we can't be sure the work is entirely the student's own, especially now that AI tools are so widely available.

It might, although it would take more time than we have. However many staff we assign, grading forty projects each would be exhausting. Whatever we decide, it's the workload that worries me most, since we're already stretched.

Of course, but exams teach something coursework can't: working calmly under pressure. Whatever career they choose, students will face deadlines. However unfair it feels, that's a skill I'd argue they need. Doesn't that count for something?
Frankly, I'd need to see evidence. Whatever the proposal says, I'd want to know how other schools have handled it. It's not so much that I resist change as that I dislike changing without data.

Gladly, as long as we share the findings with the rest of the department before anything is decided. However the vote goes, everyone should feel they had a say. Shall we put it on the agenda for the next meeting?

speakerB.en: I'm in favor, actually. However well a student prepares, a single exam can go wrong on a bad day. Why does the idea trouble you? I'd have thought you'd welcome a fairer system.

That's a valid concern. But it's not so much about catching cheating as about designing better tasks. However much help a student gets, they still have to explain their work in a short interview. Wouldn't that solve it?

Fair enough, but exams have costs too. It's not so much that students learn from them as that they memorize and forget. However hard they study, much of it disappears within a month. Isn't the aim to retain knowledge?
It does, as far as I'm concerned, but I'd say sixty percent on one skill is too much. On the other hand, a fifty-fifty balance might be the best compromise. What would persuade you to accept that?

Reasonable. I could ask the district for results from the schools that piloted it last year. However the numbers look, we'd at least be discussing facts rather than opinions. Would you be willing to review them with me?

Let's do that. Whatever the outcome, I appreciate the discussion. It's not so much about winning the argument as about finding what's best for the students. I'll email the district tomorrow and let you know.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about costs, budgets and spending
scenarios.context: People discuss prices, saving money, or financial plans.

speakerA.en: How much does this cost?
Is that expensive?
I don't have much money.
How much money do you have?
Do you have change for a twenty?
speakerA.fa: برای ۲۰ دلار پول خرد داری؟

speakerA.en: I'm trying to save money. I've cut down on eating out.
speakerA.fa: سعی می‌کنم پول پس‌انداز کنم. غذا خوردن بیرون رو کم کردم.

speakerA.en: Rent is getting more expensive in this city. It's hard to find affordable housing.
speakerA.fa: اجاره‌ها توی این شهر داره گران‌تر می‌شه. پیدا کردن مسکن ارزان سخته.

speakerA.en: I think I need to create a monthly budget to manage my expenses better.
speakerA.fa: فکر کنم باید یه بودجه ماهانه تنظیم کنم تا هزینه‌هام رو بهتر مدیریت کنم.

speakerA.en: Do you usually pay with cash or card?
speakerA.fa: معمولاً با پول نقد پرداخت می‌کنی یا کارت؟

speakerA.en: I've started investing a small portion of my salary every month.
speakerA.fa: هر ماه یه بخش کوچکی از حقوقم رو سرمایه‌گذاری می‌کنم.

speakerB.en: It's $15.99, plus tax.
No, it's cheap.
Let's save some money, then.
I have fifty dollars.
Sorry, I only have cards. You could ask the cashier for change.
speakerB.fa: ببخشید، فقط کارت دارم. می‌تونی از صندوقدار پول خرد بگیری.

speakerB.en: That's a good strategy. I've been cooking more at home too.
speakerB.fa: استراتژی خوبیه. منم بیشتر خونه آشپزی می‌کنم.

speakerB.en: Tell me about it. My rent just went up by 10% this year.
speakerB.fa: بگو نداره! اجاره من امسال ۱۰ درصد بالا رفته.

speakerB.en: That sounds like a smart plan. I should do the same.
speakerB.fa: به نظر برنامه خوبی میاد. منم باید همین کار رو بکنم.

speakerB.en: I mostly use my phone to pay. It's much faster and safer.
speakerB.fa: بیشتر با گوشی پرداخت می‌کنم. خیلی سریع‌تر و امن‌تره.

speakerB.en: That's very forward-thinking. I'm still learning about stocks and bonds.
speakerB.fa: خیلی آینده‌نگرانه‌ست. من هنوز دارم درباره سهام و اوراق قرضه یاد می‌گیرم.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for prices and bargaining
scenarios.context: In a market or store, asking about price and negotiating.

speakerA.en: How much is this shirt?
That's too expensive.
Do you have a cheaper one?
OK. I'll take it.
Is there any discount on this item?
speakerA.fa: برای این کالا تخفیفی هست؟

speakerA.en: Can you give me a better price if I buy two?
speakerA.fa: اگه دو تا بخرم قیمت بهتری می‌دین؟

speakerA.en: That's a bit expensive for me. Is there a cheaper alternative?
speakerA.fa: این یه کم برام گرونه. گزینه ارزان‌تری هست؟

speakerA.en: Could you lower the price to $30? I'll take it right now.
speakerA.fa: میشه قیمت رو به ۳۰ دلار بدید؟ همین الان می‌خرمش.

speakerB.en: OK. How about twenty dollars?
Yes, this one is ten dollars.
Thank you. Here is your bag.
Yes, there's a 20% discount this week.
speakerB.fa: بله، این هفته ۲۰٪ تخفیف داره.

speakerB.en: I can give you 10% off for two items.
speakerB.fa: برای دو تا می‌تونم ۱۰٪ تخفیف بدم.

speakerB.en: We have a similar one in a different color for $10 less.
speakerB.fa: یه نمونه مشابه با رنگ دیگه ۱۰ دلار ارزان‌تر داریم.

speakerB.en: Alright, I'll sell it for $35. That's the best I can do.
speakerB.fa: باشه، به ۳۵ دلار می‌دم. این بهترین قیمتی هست که می‌تونم بدم.

scenarios.scenario: Paying at a store
scenarios.context: A customer pays at the cashier.

speakerA.en: How much is it all?
Can I pay by card?
Here is my card.
Thank you. Goodbye.
Do you accept contactless payment?
It says my card was declined. What should I do?
Do I need to enter my PIN?
Could I get a bag, please?
Can I have a receipt, please?
Can I return this if it doesn't fit?

speakerB.en: It's twelve dollars.
Yes, you can.
Thank you. Here is your receipt.
Goodbye. Have a nice day!
Yes, just hold your card near the machine.
Please try again or use a different card.
Yes, for amounts over fifty dollars.
Of course. It's ten cents extra.
Sure. Would you like it printed or sent by email?
Yes, within thirty days, with the receipt.

scenarios.scenario: Paying with cash
scenarios.context: A customer pays with cash and gets change.

speakerA.en: Here is twenty dollars.
How much is my change?
Is this correct?
Thank you very much.
Sorry, I only have a fifty-dollar bill. Do you have change?
Could you give me the change in smaller bills?
I think you gave me too much change.
Is there an ATM nearby? I need to withdraw some cash.
Do you charge extra for cash payments?
Could I get a receipt for the payment?

speakerB.en: It's fifteen dollars. Here is your change.
It's five dollars.
Yes, it is.
You're welcome.
Yes, no problem. Let me check the register.
Sure. Here are two tens and a five.
Let me count again. You're right. Thank you for telling me.
Yes, there's one at the end of the street.
No, there's no extra charge.
Of course. Here you are.

scenarios.scenario: Saving money
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about saving money.

speakerA.en: I want to buy a new phone.
It's four hundred dollars.
I save ten dollars every week.
Do you save money?
How much do you try to save each month?
Do you have a monthly budget?
Where do you spend the most money?
How can I stop spending so much on small things?
Are you saving for something special?
I think I'll open a savings account.

speakerB.en: How much is it?
That's a lot of money.
That's a good idea.
Yes, a little.
About twenty percent of my salary.
Yes, I write down all my expenses in an app.
On rent and food. Eating out is expensive.
Make a shopping list and avoid buying things you don't need.
Yes, I want to travel to Japan next year.
That's a good idea. Choose one with a good interest rate.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing the cost
scenarios.context: Two friends share the cost of lunch.

speakerA.en: How much is lunch?
Let's share it.
I have only ten dollars.
Thank you. You're kind.
Shall we split the bill equally?
I only had a salad and some water. Could we pay separately?
I'll pay for the taxi, and you can pay for the coffee.
Could you send me your share by bank transfer?
I forgot my wallet. Could you lend me some money?
Let's pay half each for the gift.

speakerB.en: It's thirty dollars.
OK. Fifteen dollars each.
No problem. I can pay the rest.
You're welcome.
Sure. It's easier that way.
Of course. Let me ask the waiter.
That sounds fair.
Yes, I'll do it tonight.
No problem. You can pay me back tomorrow.
Good idea. How much is it?

scenarios.scenario: Buying groceries
scenarios.context: A customer asks about the price of fruit.

speakerA.en: How much are the apples?
And the bananas?
I'll take two kilos of apples.
No, thank you. How much is it?
Are these tomatoes fresh? They look a bit soft.
Do you sell organic vegetables?
Is there a special offer on milk this week?
How much is the cheese per kilo?
Could you weigh these oranges for me, please?
I'll take these. Can I pay by card?

speakerB.en: They are two dollars a kilo.
They are one dollar a kilo.
OK. Anything else?
It's four dollars.
They came this morning. These ones are firmer.
Yes, they're on the left. They cost a little more.
Yes, two bottles for the price of one.
It's twelve dollars a kilo. Would you like to try a piece?
Sure. That's one and a half kilos. It's three dollars.
Yes, please insert it here.

scenarios.scenario: Making a monthly budget
scenarios.context: Two roommates plan how to share their monthly expenses.

speakerA.en: We should write down all our monthly expenses so we know how much each of us has to pay.
Should we split the groceries equally, even though you eat more than I do?
I like that. Would a hundred dollars each be enough for food?
We should also set aside some money for unexpected costs, like repairs.

speakerB.en: Good idea. Rent is the biggest cost, and then we have electricity, internet, and groceries.
That's fair enough. How about a shared account that we both put money into each month?
It might not be, but we can adjust it after the first month.
Agreed. I'll make a spreadsheet so we can both keep track.

scenarios.scenario: Deciding whether to buy or save
scenarios.context: A couple discusses buying an expensive item.

speakerA.en: I'd really like to buy the new laptop, but it costs nearly two thousand dollars.
It's slow and crashes all the time, and I need a better one for work.
I've looked at several, and most of them don't have enough memory.
That's a good point. I can survive a few more weeks with the old one.

speakerB.en: That's a lot of money. What's wrong with the one you have now?
Then it's a reasonable expense, but could you find a cheaper model that does the same?
Maybe we can wait for the sales next month and save a few hundred dollars.
Let's put some money aside now so that we don't have to use our savings.

scenarios.scenario: Splitting costs for a group trip
scenarios.context: Friends discuss how to share the costs of a weekend trip.

speakerA.en: Before we book anything, we should decide how to split the costs.
But two of us aren't going to use the car, so it wouldn't be fair for them to pay.
And who will pay up front? Someone has to book everything online.
That works. Let's keep all the receipts so we can calculate the final amounts.

speakerB.en: The easiest way is to divide everything equally, including the car rental and the cabin.
Good point. Those two could just pay for the cabin and food.
I can use my card, and you can all send me your share by the end of the week.
I'll create a shared note where we write every expense.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing investing and saving
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about how to grow their savings.

speakerA.en: I've got some savings sitting in a current account earning practically nothing. I feel I should be doing more with them.
Mainly for a down payment on an apartment in about five years.
So a savings account with a modest interest rate would be the safer option?
I've heard that fees can eat into returns considerably. How do I avoid that?

speakerB.en: It depends on your goals and how much risk you can tolerate. Are you saving for something specific?
Then I'd be cautious. Stocks can be volatile over a short period, and you wouldn't want to see the value plummet just before you need the money.
For the portion you can't afford to lose, yes. You could invest a smaller amount in a diversified fund.
Look for low-cost index funds, and read the fine print before signing anything.

scenarios.scenario: Handling unexpected financial difficulties
scenarios.context: A man confides in a friend about money problems after a job loss.

speakerA.en: I'm in a bit of a bind. Since losing my job, I've been dipping into my savings, and they won't last long.
I've canceled most subscriptions, but rent and utilities take up the bulk of what I have.
I hadn't considered it. I assumed he'd simply insist on the full amount.
You're right. I'll draft a letter explaining my situation and propose a revised schedule.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry to hear that. Have you looked at where you could cut back in the short term?
Have you spoken to your landlord? Many are willing to arrange a temporary reduction or a payment plan.
It never hurts to ask, particularly if you've been a reliable tenant until now.
And if you need a loan to tide you over, I'd rather you came to me than ran up credit card debt.

scenarios.scenario: Questioning a recurring charge
scenarios.context: A customer calls a company about an unexplained subscription fee.

speakerA.en: I've noticed a monthly charge on my statement that I don't recognize, and I'd like an explanation.
It's twelve dollars, and it seems to have started about four months ago.
I don't recall agreeing to that. I must have missed the fine print when I registered.
I'd like to cancel immediately, and I'd appreciate a refund for the months I didn't use it.

speakerB.en: Certainly. Could you tell me the amount and the date it first appeared?
According to our records, you signed up for a premium service after your free trial expired.
It's possible, as the renewal terms are included in the original conditions.
I can cancel it now and refund the last two months as a gesture of goodwill, but not the full amount.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing financial priorities in a relationship
scenarios.context: A couple discuss how to balance saving for a house with spending on experiences.

speakerA.en: I've been looking at our finances, and I think we need to decide whether we're really saving for the house or just talking about it.
True, but we've also spent a lot on weekends away and dinners out. At this rate, the deposit will take another seven years.
I understand, and I don't want to live like a monk either. Perhaps we could set a monthly spending limit for leisure and treat the rest as untouchable.
Yes, as long as it's a fixed amount and we both stick to it. I'd rather have clear boundaries than recurring arguments.

speakerB.en: That's a bit harsh. We've put money aside every month, even if it hasn't been much.
I don't regret those trips, though. They're the memories that matter to me, and I don't want to postpone life indefinitely.
That's more palatable than cutting everything. Would you agree to a small fund for experiences that we don't touch for the house?
Then let's draw it up this evening. A plan we've both agreed on is a lot easier to follow than one imposed by one of us.

scenarios.scenario: Evaluating a risky investment opportunity
scenarios.context: A man asks a financially savvy friend about an investment he has been offered.

speakerA.en: A colleague has offered me a chance to invest in a startup, promising returns of forty percent within a year. I'm tempted, but something feels off.
He says the founders are experienced and that several other people have already put money in.
And if he can't provide either?
That's helpful. I'd also been worried about how much I could lose if it went badly.

speakerB.en: Your instincts are sound. Returns like that are almost always accompanied by risk, and often by some degree of misrepresentation.
Social proof is a classic persuasion tactic. Before anything else, ask to see audited accounts and a clear explanation of how the company generates revenue.
Then walk away. A legitimate investment can withstand scrutiny, and anyone who discourages questions is telling you something important.
Never invest more than you can afford to lose entirely. If that figure makes you uncomfortable, it's probably too high.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the rising cost of living
scenarios.context: Two colleagues talk about how inflation has reshaped their household budgets.

speakerA.en: I've started keeping a record of my household expenses, and the numbers are alarming. Everything from groceries to utilities has crept up significantly.
How are you coping? I've begun cooking at home more and canceling subscriptions I barely use.
The frustrating part is that careful budgeting only goes so far when the underlying prices are rising so quickly.
That's the part that troubles me. We're inconvenienced, but others are making impossible choices between heating and eating.

speakerB.en: It's the same for me. The grocery bill has jumped nearly a third, and my salary certainly hasn't kept pace.
Much the same, along with switching to a cheaper energy provider. It's remarkable how many small leaks there are in a budget.
True, and it falls hardest on people who had little slack to begin with. A cut in discretionary spending isn't an option when you're already spending only on essentials.
A sobering thought. I suppose gratitude for our own position is warranted, even as we complain about the rising bills.

scenarios.scenario: Confronting a partner about overspending
scenarios.context: A couple discusses their finances candidly without turning it into an accusation.

speakerA.en: I'd like us to look at our spending together. I'm not pointing fingers, but the figures have started to worry me.
Avoidance is understandable, but it doesn't make the numbers disappear. We're spending considerably more than we earn each month.
Mainly subscriptions we've forgotten about, plus dining out. I'd propose we cancel the former and cap the latter.
A sensible compromise. Autonomy within limits tends to breed less resentment than constant scrutiny.

speakerB.en: I suspected this was coming. I'll admit I've been less disciplined recently, and I've been avoiding the statements.
I hadn't realized it was quite so stark. Where do you think the leakage is occurring?
That seems reasonable. I'd also like to agree on a discretionary sum each, so neither of us has to justify every small purchase.
Agreed. Let's draw up a proper budget this weekend and review it monthly, before it becomes a crisis.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating splitting costs among housemates
scenarios.context: Housemates try to divide shared expenses fairly when incomes differ.

speakerA.en: I'd like to raise the question of how we split the bills. I earn considerably less than the two of you, and I've been struggling.
What did you have in mind? I wouldn't want to presume, though an equal division seems to disadvantage me.
I'm comfortable with that, provided it remains confidential among the three of us.
Speaking for myself, I'd be glad to contribute more. A flat division would feel less like fairness and more like convenience.

speakerB.en: I appreciate you raising it. I'd rather address it openly than have resentment build quietly.
We could apportion the costs in proportion to income. It would be more equitable, though it requires everyone to disclose their earnings.
Naturally. Is anyone opposed to adjusting the arrangement, or does someone feel it unfair to the higher earners?
Then it's settled. Let's calculate the ratios tonight and revisit them whenever our circumstances change.

scenarios.scenario: Deliberating over a large, uncertain purchase
scenarios.context: A person weighs the long-term value of an expensive item with a trusted friend.

speakerA.en: I've been contemplating a rather extravagant purchase, and I'd value an honest opinion. It's a high-end camera, and the price is eye-watering.
Mostly travel and portraits. I'd like to take photography more seriously, though I've been telling myself that for years.
A pointed observation, though perhaps a fair one. What if I rented one first, to test my commitment?
I'd rather spend a modest amount on a rental than a fortune on a regret.

speakerB.en: Honesty it is, then. What do you intend to use it for, and how often?
That's the crux. An expensive tool won't make you disciplined, and many such cameras end up gathering dust in a cupboard.
That's a prudent idea. If you're still enthusiastic after a few months, the investment would be easier to justify.
Precisely. And should you decide to buy it, you'll know that it's a considered decision, not an impulse.

scenarios.scenario: Cutting down monthly spending
scenarios.context: A couple talks about how to plan their monthly money.

speakerA.en: We spend too much money every month.
Rent and bills are the biggest costs.
Let's cook at home three times a week.
I'll put that money in a savings account.

speakerB.en: You're right. Let's write down all our expenses.
And food. We eat out too often.
Good idea. We can save about a hundred dollars.
Perfect. Let's check our budget again next month.

scenarios.scenario: Lending money to a friend
scenarios.context: A man asks a friend to lend him some money.

speakerA.en: Could I ask you a favor? I need to borrow fifty dollars.
Yes, my card doesn't work, and I need to pay the rent.
On Friday, when I get my salary.
Thank you so much. I'll return it on time.

speakerB.en: Of course. Is everything okay?
When can you give it back?
That's fine. Here you are.
No problem. Friends help each other.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing an unexpected expense
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about a big car repair bill.

speakerA.en: You look worried. Is everything all right?
That's a lot. Do you have enough savings to cover it?
That's a shame. Have you thought about getting a second opinion?
I'll ask a few more mechanics tomorrow before I decide.

speakerB.en: Not really. My car broke down, and the repair is going to cost nearly six hundred dollars.
Just about, but it means I can't go on holiday this summer.
Good idea. Another garage might charge less.
Let me know if you need to borrow some money in the meantime.

scenarios.scenario: Planning to buy something expensive
scenarios.context: A man tells a friend about saving for a big purchase.

speakerA.en: I've decided to buy a new laptop for my studies, but it's quite expensive.
About a thousand dollars, and I've saved around half of it.
If I put aside a hundred dollars a month, five more months.
The shop offers a payment plan, but the interest is high.

speakerB.en: How much do you need, and how much have you saved so far?
Then you're halfway there. How long will it take to save the rest?
That's reasonable. Is it possible to buy it in instalments?
I'd wait and pay in cash, if you can.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a shared household budget
scenarios.context: Two roommates sit down to plan their shared spending.

speakerA.en: We really need to talk about money. Last month, we spent far more than we planned, and I'm not sure where it all went.
I added up the bills yesterday. Rent, electricity, and the Internet come to about nine hundred euros, and then there's food on top of that.
That's quite a lot, considering that we only eat at home a few days a week. I think we spend too much on takeaway meals.
Good idea. If we limit ourselves to one takeaway a week, we could save around eighty euros a month.
I'd also like to put some money aside for emergencies. Do you think we could each save fifty euros a month?
Perfect. Let's write everything in a shared spreadsheet, and review it at the end of every month.

speakerB.en: I know, and I felt the same way. I'd like to find out what we can cut, without making our lives too boring.
Then we have to count the groceries, which are around three hundred. That leaves very little for anything else, like transport or entertainment.
You're right. We could also try cooking larger portions and freezing them. That would be cheaper and healthier.
That's a realistic target. We can also cancel the streaming service that neither of us uses very often.
That's sensible. If something unexpected happens, such as a broken washing machine, we'll be glad to have some savings.
Good plan. If we stick to it for three months, I'm sure we'll notice the difference.

scenarios.scenario: Deciding whether to buy or rent
scenarios.context: A couple weighs the costs of buying a home against renting.

speakerA.en: I've been looking at apartments online, and the prices are really high. I'm starting to wonder whether buying is realistic for us.
We've saved around twenty thousand euros, but the bank says we'd need at least double that for a down payment.
That's true, and the monthly repayments would probably be higher than our rent, especially with interest rates where they are now.
On the other hand, we'd be paying for something that we'd own in the end, instead of giving our money to a landlord.
I think we should wait a couple of years, save more, and see how the market develops. Renting isn't a failure.
I agree. Let's make a plan, and review it every six months. Then we'll make our decision when we feel ready.

speakerB.en: I've done the same, and I'm shocked. Even small apartments in the suburbs cost more than we expected.
That's a lot of money to find. We'd have to cut our spending dramatically for years, and we wouldn't be able to travel much.
Exactly. If anything went wrong, such as losing a job, we'd be in serious trouble, and we couldn't just leave, as we can with a rented flat.
That's a fair point. But if we found a good deal, the property might gain value, which would be an investment for the future.
I'm not sure we're ready to take that risk yet. I'd prefer to have a larger safety net before signing a mortgage.
Good. In the meantime, we could ask a financial adviser to explain the different options, so that we're better informed.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing saving versus investing
scenarios.context: Two friends compare approaches to managing their money for the long term.

speakerA.en: I've finally managed to save a decent amount, but I'm not sure what to do with it. Leaving it in a savings account feels safe, yet inflation seems to be eating away at its value.
I've heard that investing in funds that track the stock market is one of the best long-term options, but the idea of losing money makes me quite nervous.
That's a reassuring way of looking at it. So the main principle is to invest regularly, over many years, rather than trying to predict the best moment to buy?
And what about an emergency fund? I'd hate to be forced to sell investments at a bad time just because I had an unexpected expense, like a car repair.
That makes sense. I suppose I should start by building that cushion, and then gradually begin investing what remains each month.
Thanks, that's very helpful. I'll read a bit more about index funds before I decide, and I'll try not to be put off by the jargon.

speakerB.en: It's a sensible question, and one that many people struggle with. Savings accounts protect your capital, but with current interest rates, you may well lose purchasing power over time.

Fear of loss is natural, but it's worth remembering that the market tends to rise over long periods, despite short-term fluctuations. The key is to invest only money that you won't need for at least five to ten years.

Exactly. Studies show that most professionals can't consistently beat the market, so spreading regular contributions over time, regardless of conditions, tends to produce better results than speculation.
That's an excellent point. A common recommendation is to keep three to six months of expenses in an easily accessible account before investing anything, precisely to avoid that situation.
I'd say that's the safest strategy. Once you have the emergency fund, you can invest with a clearer mind, because you know that you won't be forced to sell in a downturn.
No problem. And don't be afraid to ask a financial advisor if you feel uncertain, though make sure that they're independent, and not paid on commission.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating who pays for what in a relationship
scenarios.context: A couple discusses how to manage finances fairly after moving in together.

speakerA.en: Now that we're living together, I think we should talk properly about how to split our expenses. I don't want money to become a source of tension between us.
I earn a bit less than you, so an equal division might not be fair. On the other hand, I wouldn't like to feel that I'm depending on you for everything.
That sounds more balanced. If we each contributed according to our income, the percentages would be the same, even if the amounts were different.

We should also decide what happens with larger expenses, like holidays or furniture. I'd prefer that we make those decisions together, instead of one person always paying and the other feeling obliged.
I like that idea. A joint account for shared costs, and separate ones for personal spending, would give us both a sense of independence as well as shared responsibility.
Great. Let's try it for three months and see how it goes. If either of us feels that it isn't working, we can adjust it without any hard feelings.

speakerB.en: I'm glad you brought it up. I was thinking the same thing, and I'd rather deal with it now than wait until it becomes a problem. What do you have in mind?
I understand that, and I wouldn't want you to feel uncomfortable. What if we divided the shared costs in proportion to what each of us earns? That would be fairer than a fifty-fifty split.
Exactly. It also means that if one of us gets a raise or loses a job, we can easily adjust. It's flexible, and it avoids resentment, which can build up silently in relationships.
Agreed. For big purchases, we should discuss them in advance, and agree on a limit above which we both need to be consulted. That way, there won't be any unpleasant surprises.
That's a practical solution. I'd also suggest that we sit down once a month to review how things are going, and that we keep it casual, perhaps over a nice dinner.
Deal. It's reassuring to know that we can talk about this so openly. Honestly, I think it's one of the things that will make us stronger as a couple.

scenarios.scenario: Preparing a tax return with an accountant
scenarios.context: A freelancer discusses expenses and deductions with an accountant.

speakerA.en: Thank you for seeing me. I'm self-employed, and this is the first year that I've had to file a full tax return, so I'm afraid I'm rather confused about what I can and can't deduct.
I've worked from home for most of the year, and I've bought a new computer, some software, and a desk. I've also paid for a course that was related to my work. Are these considered business expenses?
That's a relief. What about my phone and Internet bills? I use them both for work and for personal purposes, so I can't claim the total. How is the proportion calculated?
I see. And what about travel? I took two trips to meet clients, and I stayed overnight on both occasions. I kept all the receipts, including the train tickets and the hotel bills.
Good. One more question: if I haven't paid any advance tax during the year, will I be penalized? I only found out about it a couple of months ago, and I'm worried.
Thank you. I'll gather all the documents this week, and send them to you in a folder, so that you can prepare the return without delay.

speakerB.en: Of course. It can seem complicated at first, but once you understand the principles, it's quite manageable. Let's start with your income. How much did you earn in total, and from how many clients?

Yes, expenses that are directly related to your work are deductible. The computer and the software can be depreciated over a few years, and the course counts as professional training, so that's also deductible.

You can claim a reasonable percentage, based on the proportion of business use. If you work about sixty percent of the time from home, you might claim sixty percent of the bills. Keep a record to justify it.
Excellent. Travel costs for client meetings are fully deductible, as long as you can prove that they were for business. Meals are partly deductible, up to a limit, so keep those receipts, too.
There may be a small penalty, but it depends on the amount. Since it's your first year, the tax office often shows some leniency, particularly if you explain the situation. We can include a note.
That's fine. Please make sure that everything is organized by month, and I'll be able to complete it within a week. And next year, we'll set up a system so that you can pay in installments.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating a salary and benefits
scenarios.context: A candidate negotiates compensation after receiving a job offer.

speakerA.en: Thank you for the offer. I'm very excited about the position, and I'd like to accept, but I'd like to discuss a few points about the compensation package before I finalize my decision.

The salary that you've proposed is slightly below what I was expecting, considering my experience and the responsibilities involved. Based on my research, the market rate for this role is about ten percent higher.

I understand that the budget is limited. In that case, I'd be willing to accept the proposed salary, provided that we review it after six months, with the possibility of an increase if my performance is satisfactory.

I'd also like to ask about the benefits. Is there a possibility of working from home two days a week, and would the company contribute to my professional development, for example by paying for courses?
That sounds fair. And regarding the notice period, I'm currently required to give three months' notice to my present employer. Would it be acceptable to start in the first week of March?
Thank you for being so open. I'm confident that we can reach an agreement, and I look forward to receiving the revised offer in writing.

speakerB.en: We're delighted that you're interested. It was a close decision, and we all felt that you were the strongest candidate. Please tell me what you'd like to discuss, and I'll see what is possible.

I appreciate your frankness. The figure that I mentioned is in line with our salary scale for this grade, but I agree that your experience is substantial. I might have some room for a modest adjustment.

A review after six months is something that we can certainly agree to. I'd have to get approval for a larger increase, but I can offer you five percent more, which would be reviewed again at the end of the year.
We allow two days of remote work after the probationary period, and there's a training budget of fifteen hundred euros per year. If you needed more, we could discuss it on a case-by-case basis.

That shouldn't be a problem. We'd prefer to have you as early as possible, but we respect the notice period. The first week of March works for us, as long as we can arrange for you to attend a few meetings beforehand.
I'll prepare a new contract that includes everything that we've discussed, and send it to you tomorrow. It was a pleasure negotiating with you, and we're looking forward to having you on the team.

scenarios.scenario: Advising a friend to build an emergency fund before investing
scenarios.context: A friend who has just received a bonus asks a more cautious friend whether to invest it all in shares or keep some in savings.

speakerA.en: I've just received a bonus, and I'm thinking of putting all of it into shares. It was a colleague who suggested it, and he's made a lot of money this year. To be honest, I'm tempted, but I'd like a second opinion.

Perhaps two months, although I've never calculated it exactly. It was my brother who always told me to save more, but I never listened. As far as I'm concerned, the market looks safe at the moment. Why do you think I should wait?

I hadn't really thought about that. It's the fear of missing a good opportunity that makes me nervous. On the other hand, I wouldn't want to borrow money in a crisis. How much should I keep aside, in your opinion?

That sounds sensible, although six months is more than I expected. It's the rent that takes most of my income, so it adds up fast. Would it be foolish to invest a small part now, and build the fund gradually?

Honestly, it's the interest rate that puts me off. It's so low that saving seems pointless. But it was you who said safety matters most, and I can see the logic. Which would you choose if you were me?

It does, and I feel more relaxed already. It was a good idea to ask you before I did anything. I'll open the savings account tomorrow, and I'll look at funds next week. Thank you for being so frank with me.

speakerB.en: I'd say slow down a little. It's not the bonus that worries me, but the plan to invest all of it. What I'd ask is whether you have savings for emergencies, since shares can fall quickly. How many months of expenses could you cover?

Because it's usually when everything looks safe that people take the biggest risks. It was in 2008 that several of my relatives lost half their savings, and it was the lack of a cushion that hurt them most. What would you do if you lost your job next month?

I'd suggest at least six months of expenses, in an account you can reach quickly. It's that safety net that lets you sleep at night, as long as you resist the temptation to touch it. Then you can invest the rest, in case you're worried about timing.

Not at all. It's often the people who invest a little each month who do best in the long run. What matters is the habit, not the amount. Is there a particular reason you'd rather start with shares than with a savings account?

I'd split it. It's the first three months of expenses that should go into savings straight away, and the rest could go into a broad fund, since that spreads the risk. It isn't exciting, but it's reliable. Does that feel acceptable?

You're welcome. It's the people who ask first who usually make fewer mistakes, so well done. Let me know what you choose, and I'll help you compare the options. It's a good habit to review everything again in six months.

scenarios.scenario: Regretting an expensive impulse purchase
scenarios.context: A man tells his sister that he bought an expensive camera he can't really afford and asks whether he should return it.

speakerA.en: I did something silly last weekend. I bought a very expensive camera, and now I can't stop worrying about it. If only I'd waited a day, I wouldn't be in this mess. Had I known it would feel like this, I'd have walked away.

Probably not. It cost nine hundred dollars, which is nearly a month's salary. If it weren't for the discount, I'd have ignored it. I wish I could say I needed it, but I don't, since my old one still works, and the shop allows returns within fourteen days.

I took about twenty photos on Sunday. Had I known how complicated it is, I'd have chosen something simpler. If only the salesman hadn't been so persuasive, I'd have left empty-handed. I wish I'd read some reviews first.

Not yet, but I should. If I'd done that on the day, I'd have found a decent camera for half the price. Had I known my own budget better, I'd never have been so reckless. I wish I'd kept better track of my spending.

Yes, please. If only I had your patience, I'd never have got into this. Had I listened to you last year, when you told me to wait before big purchases, I'd have saved a lot of money. I wish I'd taken your advice.
It is, thank goodness. If only every mistake could be fixed so easily, life would be simpler. Had I known you'd be so kind about it, I'd have called you earlier. I wish I could thank you properly.

speakerB.en: Oh dear. How much did it cost, and does the shop accept returns? To be honest, I wish you'd phoned me before buying it. If it weren't for the sale, would you have bought it at all?
Then you've still got time, although not much. Had you bought it online, you might have had less choice, so that's a relief. What made you want it so badly, and have you actually used it yet?

Salespeople are trained to do that, so don't be too hard on yourself. If it weren't for their commissions, they'd probably be more honest. On the other hand, you do enjoy photography, so a cheaper model might suit you. Have you compared prices?

It's never too late to start. If it weren't for the return period, I'd say you were stuck, but you aren't. I wish more people took a day to think before spending. Shall we look at some alternatives together this evening?

We all do things like this. If it weren't for my own mistakes, I wouldn't know what to tell you. I wish I'd had someone to stop me when I bought that expensive coat. Let's return the camera tomorrow, as long as it's still in its box.

Pay for dinner when you get your refund, and we're even. If it weren't for the return policy, I'd be much more worried, so you were lucky. I wish you'd remember this feeling, though. Let's go shopping together on Saturday.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing whether to rent or buy a first home
scenarios.context: A couple discusses whether to keep renting or buy their first apartment now that they have saved a deposit.

speakerA.en: We've finally saved the deposit, so I think it's time to decide: keep renting or buy. To be honest, I'm torn. Buying feels like such a big commitment. How do you see it?

I do, but only when I look at the numbers do I feel nervous. If we had bought five years ago, we would be much better off now, but prices have risen so much that I wonder whether we've missed the moment.

The mortgage rate. Only if it stays below four percent can we afford the apartment comfortably. If rates had been lower last year, we would be paying much less every month now. Do you think they'll fall again?

Yes, please. Meanwhile, what about the extra costs: repairs, insurance, taxes? Only after you own a place do you realize how many bills come with it, my brother says. Renting is simpler, although it's money you never get back.

Somewhere near the station, ideally, so we don't need a second car. Only when I imagined a quiet street did I realize how important a balcony is to me. We'd pay less for a smaller apartment, provided it has one.

Let's start this weekend, provided we agree on a firm maximum price first. Only after we've set it should we look at apartments, otherwise we'll fall in love with something we can't afford. Can we say three hundred thousand?

speakerB.en: I lean towards buying, provided the monthly payments aren't higher than our rent. Why are you torn, though? I thought you wanted a place of our own.

I understand. If we hadn't spent so much on the wedding, we'd have a bigger deposit now, but there's no point regretting it. Only by buying can we build equity. What exactly is the figure you're worried about?

Nobody can say, as far as I'm concerned. Only when the bank offers us a fixed rate for five years will we know exactly what we'll pay. Provided we choose a fixed rate, the risk is smaller. Shall I ask a broker?

True, so we should keep a reserve for repairs, provided we can still afford the mortgage. If I hadn't taken that course last year, I wouldn't have this raise, so I feel confident we can manage. Where would you want to live?

Then we should look at apartments rather than houses. Only then will the budget work. Shall we start viewing places? And what about the deposit, since we'd still need money for the moving costs and the furniture?

Agreed, three hundred thousand at most. To be honest, I feel much clearer now. Only when we talked it through did I see that we're actually ready. I'll contact the broker tomorrow, and we'll take it step by step.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing the cost of an unexpected roof repair
scenarios.context: Two siblings discuss how to share the cost of an unexpected roof repair at their parents' house.

speakerA.en: Thanks for coming over. I wanted to talk about Mom and Dad's roof. The roofer says it needs replacing, and the quote is eleven thousand dollars. To be honest, no sooner had I read it than I started worrying. How should we handle this?

Apparently the damage is so widespread that patching it would only delay the problem. No sooner had he lifted the first tiles than he found rot underneath. Never have I felt so unprepared for an expense like this.

About four thousand, I'd say, and no more, since they need money for everyday expenses. Seldom do they spend on themselves, so I don't want them to dip into the rest. That leaves seven thousand for us to split. What's fair, in your view?

It could, but the roofer wants a deposit as soon as we agree. No sooner will we have signed than he'll order the materials. Could I pay the deposit now, and you pay me back gradually? That way, the work could start before autumn.

None at all. Never would I charge my own brother interest on his parents' roof! What matters is that the work gets done before the rains start. Should we tell Mom and Dad the full amount, or just our share?

You're right. Let's visit on Sunday and explain everything calmly. Never before have I been so glad to have a brother to share this with. I'll ask the roofer for a written breakdown, in case they want to see it.

speakerB.en: That's a lot. Never before have I seen a roofing quote that high, but I suppose the house is old. Why does it need a full replacement, rather than a repair?
I see. Well, Mom and Dad have some savings, haven't they? Rarely do they ask for help, and I'd rather they didn't have to. What do you think they can afford without feeling squeezed?

Splitting it equally seems simplest, although you earn more than I do. Never have I been in a position to give much, as you know. On the other hand, I could contribute monthly, provided it's spread over a year. Would that work?
That's generous of you. Seldom would I accept help like that, but this is different. Let's put it in writing, so there's no confusion later. What interest, if any, do you think is fair?

I'd tell them everything. Never would I keep something like this from them; they'd feel hurt if they found out later. Honesty is the best policy here, as far as I'm concerned. Besides, they might prefer a cheaper roof, so it's worth asking.

Good idea. Seldom do families talk about money so openly, but it makes everything easier. I'll bring a spreadsheet, and no sooner have we shown them the figures than they'll see this is the best option. See you Sunday.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing reading habits and favorite books
scenarios.context: People talk about books they've read or want to read.

speakerA.en: Do you like reading books?
What kind of novels do you like?
Who is your favorite writer?
Is she a good writer?
What kind of books do you enjoy?
speakerA.fa: چه نوع کتاب‌هایی رو دوست داری؟

speakerA.en: I'm currently reading a mystery novel. It's really gripping.
speakerA.fa: این روزا یه رمان معمایی می‌خونم. واقعاً جذابه.

speakerA.en: I mostly read non-fiction. I love learning about history and science.
speakerA.fa: بیشتر کتاب‌های غیرداستانی می‌خونم. عاشق یادگیری تاریخ و علم هستم.

speakerA.en: Have you read any books by Khaled Hosseini? He's a brilliant author.
speakerA.fa: کتاب‌های خالد حسینی رو خوندی؟ نویسنده فوق‌العاده‌ای هست.

speakerA.en: I find reading to be the best way to relax after a long day.
speakerA.fa: به نظر من مطالعه بهترین راه برای استراحت بعد از یه روز طولانیه.

speakerB.en: Yes, I love reading novels.
I like love stories.
My favorite writer is Jane Austen.
Yes, her books are very good.
I'm a big fan of science fiction and fantasy.
speakerB.fa: من طرفدار پر و پا قرص علمی-تخیلی و فانتزی هستم.

speakerB.en: Oh, I love mysteries too! What's it called?
speakerB.fa: اوه، منم عاشق معمایی هستم! اسمش چیه؟

speakerB.en: That's interesting. I like fiction more because it helps me escape reality.
speakerB.fa: جالبه. من داستانی رو بیشتر دوست دارم چون بهم کمک می‌کنه از واقعیت فرار کنم.

speakerB.en: Yes, I've read The Kite Runner. It was heartbreaking and beautiful.
speakerB.fa: بله، بادبادک‌باز رو خوندم. دل‌شکن و زیبا بود.

speakerB.en: I couldn't agree more. Nothing beats a good book and a cup of tea.
speakerB.fa: کاملاً موافقم. هیچی به پای یه کتاب خوب و یه فنجون چای نمی‌رسه.

scenarios.scenario: At a library or bookstore
scenarios.context: Looking for a book and asking for recommendations.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Where is the fiction section?
Thank you. Do you have books in English?
Can you recommend a book?
How much is it?
Do you have this book in stock?
speakerA.fa: این کتاب رو موجود دارید؟

speakerA.en: I'm looking for something by the author J.K. Rowling.
speakerA.fa: دنبال چیزی از نویسنده جی.کی. رولینگ می‌گردم.

speakerA.en: Can you recommend a good book for young adults?
speakerA.fa: یه کتاب خوب برای نوجوانان می‌تونید پیشنهاد بدید؟

speakerA.en: Is this book available as an audiobook?
speakerA.fa: این کتاب به صورت کتاب صوتی هم موجوده؟

speakerA.en: I'd like to borrow this book for two weeks. Is that possible?
speakerA.fa: می‌خوام این کتاب رو دو هفته امانت بگیرم. امکان‌پذیره؟

speakerB.en: It's on the second floor, to your right.
Yes, we do. They are on the left.
Yes. This one is very good.
It's twelve dollars.
Let me check our system. Yes, we have two copies left.
speakerB.fa: بذارید سیستم‌مون رو چک کنم. بله، دو نسخه مونده.

speakerB.en: We have several of her novels. Which one are you looking for?
speakerB.fa: چندین رمان ازش داریم. کدومش رو می‌خواید؟

speakerB.en: I'd recommend 'The Perks of Being a Wallflower' or anything by John Green.
speakerB.fa: 'مزایای گوشه‌گیر بودن' یا هر چی از جان گرین رو توصیه می‌کنم.

speakerB.en: Yes, we have both the paperback and the audiobook version.
speakerB.fa: بله، هم نسخه کاغذی و هم کتاب صوتی رو داریم.

speakerB.en: Sure, just bring it back before the 20th to avoid a late fee.
speakerB.fa: حتماً، فقط قبل از ۲۰ بیاریدش تا جریمه تأخیر نخورید.

scenarios.scenario: Asking what someone is reading
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about the book one of them is reading.

speakerA.en: What are you reading?
Is it a good book?
Who is the writer?
Can I read it after you?
What's the book about?
How many pages have you read so far?
Is the story easy to follow?
Did you buy it, or did you borrow it?
Does it have a happy ending?
I'd love to read it when you finish.

speakerB.en: I'm reading a story book.
Yes, it's very good.
The writer is Jane Austen.
Sure. I will finish it next week.
It's about a young woman who moves to a new city.
About a hundred. I'm reading a chapter every night.
Yes, the language is simple, and the characters are interesting.
My cousin gave it to me for my birthday.
I don't know yet. Please don't tell me!
Sure. I'll lend it to you next week.

scenarios.scenario: Borrowing a book from a friend
scenarios.context: One friend asks to borrow a book.

speakerA.en: Do you have a book about cooking?
Can I borrow one?
When do I give it back?
OK. Thank you very much.
I heard you have a great mystery novel. Could I borrow it?
How long will it take me to read it?
I promise to take care of it.
Could I keep it for two weeks? I'm very busy.
I finished the book. It was fantastic!
Thank you for lending it to me. Here it is.

speakerB.en: Yes, I have two.
Of course. Here you are.
Next Monday, please.
You're welcome. Enjoy it!
Of course. It's one of my favorites.
About a week, if you read every evening.
Thanks. Please don't write in it.
That's fine. Just let me know when you finish.
I'm glad you liked it. Which part did you enjoy the most?
You're welcome. I have another one by the same author.

scenarios.scenario: Joining a library
scenarios.context: A new visitor joins a public library.

speakerA.en: Hello. I want to join the library.
Yes, here it is.
How many books can I borrow?
For how many days?
Is it free to join the library?
What documents do I need to register?
Can I borrow DVDs and magazines too?
Can I access the digital library from home?
What happens if I lose a book?
What are the opening hours on weekends?

speakerB.en: OK. Do you have an ID card?
Please write your name and address here.
You can borrow five books.
For two weeks.
Yes, for residents. Visitors pay a small fee.
A photo ID and a proof of address, like a utility bill.
Yes, you can borrow up to three DVDs at a time.
Yes, you'll get a username and a password today.
You'll need to pay for it, but we can discuss the price.
We're open from ten to four on Saturdays and closed on Sundays.

scenarios.scenario: Buying a book as a gift
scenarios.context: A customer looks for a gift in a bookstore.

speakerA.en: I need a book for my friend.
She likes stories about animals.
How much is it?
Good. I'll take it, please.
My brother loves history. Do you have any good books on it?
Is there a hardcover edition of this book?
Is it suitable for a twelve-year-old?
Could you wrap it as a gift, please?
Can he exchange it if he already has it?
Do you have a gift card for any amount?

speakerB.en: What does your friend like?
This book is very nice.
It's ten dollars.
Do you want a gift bag?
Yes, this one about ancient Rome is very popular.
Yes, but it costs five dollars more.
Yes, it has many pictures and the language is easy.
Of course. Would you like to add a card?
Yes, within thirty days with the gift receipt.
Yes, we do. You can choose from ten to a hundred dollars.

scenarios.scenario: Returning a library book
scenarios.context: A reader returns a book after the due date.

speakerA.en: Hello. I want to return this book.
Sorry, it's late.
Here is the money.
Can I borrow another book today?
I'm sorry. I forgot the due date, and I returned it late.
How much is the fine?
Can I pay it with my card?
Could I check if my reserved book has arrived?
Could you remind me when my next book is due?
Can I renew my membership card today?

speakerB.en: Thank you. Let me check it.
It's two days late. You pay one dollar.
Thank you. Here is your receipt.
Yes, of course.
That's OK. It happens. There's a small fine.
It's twenty cents per day, so it's sixty cents.
Yes, or you can pay at the self-service machine.
Let me look. Yes, it's here. I'll get it for you.
Sure. I'll write the date on your receipt.
Yes, please fill in this form.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about reading habits
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about when and how they read.

speakerA.en: Do you read every day?
How long do you read?
Do you read on your phone?
I read e-books on my phone.
When do you usually find time to read?
Do you prefer fiction or non-fiction?
How many books do you read a year?
Do you ever listen to audiobooks?
Do you finish every book you start?
I'd like to read more. Do you have any advice?

speakerB.en: Yes, I read before bed.
About thirty minutes.
No, I like paper books.
That's nice. It's easy to carry.
On the bus to work and before I go to sleep.
I like both, but I read more non-fiction these days.
About twenty. I set a goal at the beginning of the year.
Yes, when I'm driving or cooking. It saves time.
Not always. If a book is boring, I stop reading it.
Start with short books and read for just ten minutes a day.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for a book recommendation
scenarios.context: A customer asks a bookseller for a good book.

speakerA.en: Can you recommend a good book?
I like adventure stories.
Is it long?
Great. Where can I buy it?
I'd like something relaxing for my holiday. Any ideas?
Is it part of a series?
Who's the author, and what has he written before?
Is this book popular right now?
Have you read it yourself?
OK, I'll take it. Do you have it in paperback?

speakerB.en: Yes. Do you like love stories or adventure?
Read this one. It's very exciting.
No, it's short. It has one hundred pages.
You can buy it here at the front desk.
This novel is light and funny. It's perfect for the beach.
Yes, it's the first of three, so you can continue if you like it.
He's a well-known writer who has published ten novels.
Yes, it was one of our best-sellers last month.
Yes, I finished it in two days. I couldn't stop.
Yes, it's right here for eleven dollars.

scenarios.scenario: Recommending a book to a friend
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about a novel one of them has just read.

speakerA.en: I've just finished a novel that I think you'd love. It's about a family in the 1930s.
It's called The Last Summer. It's long, but once you start, you can't put it down.
Parts of it are, but it's also funny and hopeful. The characters feel very real.
You can borrow it, as long as you promise to give it back.

speakerB.en: What's it called? I need something new to read on my commute.
Is it sad? I'm not in the mood for anything too heavy at the moment.
That sounds perfect. Can I borrow your copy, or should I buy my own?
I promise. I'll let you know what I think when I'm finished.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing e-books and paper books
scenarios.context: Two readers debate which format is better.

speakerA.en: Do you prefer reading on a tablet or holding a real book?
I used to think the same, but an e-reader is much easier when I travel.
And you can change the size of the text, which is useful when you're tired.
Maybe it depends on the kind of book. I read novels on my tablet but textbooks on paper.

speakerB.en: Honestly, I prefer paper books. I like the smell and the feel of the pages.
That's a fair point. I can't carry five books in my bag on a trip.
True, but I find it harder to concentrate on a screen, even if it's an e-reader.
That makes sense. Perhaps I should give e-books another try.

scenarios.scenario: Joining a book club
scenarios.context: A new member talks to the organizer of a book club.

speakerA.en: I saw your poster at the library. Could you tell me how the book club works?
How do you choose the books? Do you take turns?
I mostly read non-fiction. Would that be a problem?
That sounds interesting. What is the next book?

speakerB.en: We meet on the first Monday of every month and discuss a book that we've all read.
Yes, each member suggests a title, and we vote. Last month we read a detective novel.
Not at all. We like variety, and we've read biographies and history books too.
It's a short story collection. I'll email you the title so you can start reading.

scenarios.scenario: Analyzing a novel's themes
scenarios.context: Two book lovers discuss a recently read classic.

speakerA.en: I finished the novel last night, and I'm still wrestling with what the ending was meant to convey.
I thought he was rather unsympathetic, though. It's hard to root for someone so consumed by ambition.
A fair interpretation, although it can come across as heavy-handed in certain chapters.
It is. A few passages were so beautifully written that I had to read them twice.

speakerB.en: I think the author deliberately left it ambiguous, to leave readers reflecting on the choices the protagonist made.
That may be the point. The story seems to warn against pursuing success at the expense of everything else.
I'd agree that the pacing drags in the middle, but the prose is exquisite throughout.
We should recommend it to the book club, even if it divides opinion.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the decline of reading
scenarios.context: Two colleagues consider whether people read less than they used to.

speakerA.en: I read a statistic that fewer than half of adults finish a book in a year. Does that surprise you?
I notice it in myself. I used to read for hours, but now I struggle to concentrate for more than twenty minutes.
Do you think audiobooks count as reading? They've become enormously popular.
Then maybe we're reading more than we realize, just differently.

speakerB.en: Not entirely. Between social media and streaming services, there's so much competing for our attention.
Perhaps the issue isn't lack of interest but the way constant notifications fragment our focus.
I'd say so. The engagement with the story is what matters, not the format.
Possibly, though I still believe there's something irreplaceable about sitting with a physical book.

scenarios.scenario: Recommending literature in translation
scenarios.context: A bookshop customer asks an employee for recommendations.

speakerA.en: I'd like to read something from outside the English-speaking world, but I don't know where to start.
I like character-driven novels with a strong sense of place, preferably not too bleak.
Is the translation good? I've been put off books where the language feels stilted.
That's reassuring. Do you have it in paperback, or only hardcover?

speakerB.en: What kind of stories do you enjoy? That would help me narrow it down.
Then you might enjoy a novel set in a small Italian village, about a family that runs a bakery.
It's widely praised. The translator won an award for capturing the author's voice so naturally.
We have both, and the paperback is considerably cheaper. I'll fetch a copy for you.

scenarios.scenario: Critiquing a flawed biography
scenarios.context: Two readers discuss a biography that they find well researched but poorly balanced.

speakerA.en: I've just finished the biography everyone has been praising, and I'm afraid I came away rather underwhelmed.
The research is impressive, I agree. My problem is the tone. It reads less like a biography and more like a eulogy.
Exactly. A great biography should leave you with a sense of the person's contradictions, not a polished monument.
That's possible, but it's the editor's job to notice. The book could have been far more powerful with a bit more critical distance.

speakerB.en: Really? I thought the research was exhaustive. The author clearly spent years in the archives.
I see what you mean. He glosses over the subject's failings, which makes the portrait feel strangely one-dimensional.
Perhaps the author grew too fond of his subject. It's an occupational hazard after so many years together.
I'll concede that. Still, I'd recommend it to anyone seeking the facts, provided they read it with a skeptical eye.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing an author's influence on a generation
scenarios.context: Two friends reflect on how a celebrated novelist shaped the way their generation thinks.

speakerA.en: I was rereading her first novel last night, and I'm astonished by how much of it has become part of how we talk about everyday life.
What strikes me most is how she captured a mood before anyone else had named it. That sense of restless dissatisfaction felt entirely new.
Do you think the book would have the same impact if it were published today?
That's the paradox of influential literature. It changes the culture so thoroughly that later readers struggle to see what was revolutionary.

speakerB.en: I know what you mean. Phrases from that book have slipped into ordinary conversation, and most people don't even realize where they came from.
And she did it without sermonizing. The characters simply live, and readers recognize themselves in them.
Probably not. So much of its power came from timing. It arrived at a moment when readers were hungry for exactly that voice.
Well said. We've inherited the conversation without remembering who started it.

scenarios.scenario: Debating censorship and banned books
scenarios.context: Two members of a book club discuss whether schools should remove controversial books from their libraries.

speakerA.en: I see the school board has voted to remove several books from the library. Frankly, I find the decision troubling.
Perhaps for the youngest, but removing them altogether treats every teenager as though they can't handle difficult material.
They should have a say about their own children, certainly, but not about everyone else's. That's the difference between guidance and censorship.
There's a line, but it should be drawn through transparent criteria, not through the discomfort of whoever complains loudest.

speakerB.en: I understand the concern, but some of those books deal with explicit themes that parents feel are inappropriate for younger students.
Parents have a legitimate interest in what their children read. Surely they should have a say.
A fair distinction. Yet there must be some line, mustn't there? Not everything belongs in a school library.
I can accept that. A process that's open to scrutiny is far better than one that operates behind closed doors.

scenarios.scenario: Debating whether a literary classic deserves its reputation
scenarios.context: Two readers argue about a celebrated novel they have read.

speakerA.en: I'll risk heresy and say that I found the novel overrated. The prose is magnificent, but I felt very little for the characters.
Perhaps, though detachment can shade into coldness. A book should move me, not merely impress me.
An elegant defense, but it risks excusing any work that's difficult. Some books are difficult simply because they're poorly constructed.
At least we agree on that. Shall we trade recommendations, then? I'll give you something warmer, and you can give me something challenging.

speakerB.en: That's a bold claim. I'd argue that its power lies precisely in its detachment, which compels the reader to draw their own conclusions.
I see your point, yet I'd defend the idea that a great work doesn't always seek to be liked. It's content to be understood.
Touché. I concede that reverence for a classic can discourage honest critique, and that's a disservice to both the book and the reader.
A fair exchange. I'll lend you a novel that I guarantee will make you cry on the train.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing how reading habits are changing in the digital age
scenarios.context: Two friends reflect on how screens have altered the way they read.

speakerA.en: I've noticed that I can no longer sustain the concentration for a long book. My mind wanders after a few pages.
It's a sobering thought. I used to lose entire afternoons to a novel without once reaching for my phone.
I might try that. Do you find that reading on a screen is a different experience from reading on paper?
That's an interesting point. I always thought it was nostalgia, but perhaps there's genuine cognitive substance to it.

speakerB.en: You're hardly alone. I think the constant pull of notifications has eroded our capacity for sustained attention.
I've started leaving the phone in another room while I read. It sounds absurdly simple, but it's made a remarkable difference.
Undeniably. Paper lets me navigate a book spatially, remembering where something appeared on the page, which a screen doesn't replicate.
There may be. At any rate, a physical book has the advantage of never interrupting you with a software update.

scenarios.scenario: Writing a thoughtful critique of a new publication
scenarios.context: A reviewer discusses with an editor how to assess a book fairly.

speakerA.en: I'm struggling with the review. The book is ambitious and flawed, and I don't want to dismiss it unfairly or praise it indulgently.
The author's argument is compelling in its first half, but it unravels as the evidence thins and the rhetoric swells.
Should I mention that the author's earlier work was considerably stronger? It feels slightly unkind.
Understood. I'll aim for a review that's rigorous without being cruel.

speakerB.en: A familiar dilemma. What do you consider its principal weakness?
Then say so plainly, and credit the first half generously. A reviewer who acknowledges strengths earns the right to point out weaknesses.
Comparison is legitimate if it illuminates the present book. Don't use it to settle scores, though.
That's the best any critic can do. Remember that the author will read it, and that a fair review respects the effort behind the work.

scenarios.scenario: Choosing a book as a gift
scenarios.context: A customer asks a bookseller for help choosing a present.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'm looking for a book for my father's birthday. Could you help me?
He enjoys history, especially stories about the Second World War. He doesn't like long novels.
That sounds perfect. Is it available in paperback? He prefers lighter books to carry around.
Wonderful. I'll take it. Could you wrap it as a gift, please?

speakerB.en: Of course. What kind of books does he usually read, and does he have a favorite author?
In that case, I'd suggest this one. It's a collection of true stories, and each chapter is short.
Yes, it is. It's also on offer this week, so you'll save a little money.
Certainly. It will take a few minutes. Would you like a card to go with it?

scenarios.scenario: Talking about a book that changed your mind
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss a book that influenced the way one of them thinks.

speakerA.en: I just finished a book that really changed the way I think about money.
It explains why people spend more than they plan to, and how small habits make a big difference.
Honestly, yes. I've already started saving a little every month, and I track my expenses.
I'll lend it to you if you like. I'd be interested to hear what you think.

speakerB.en: That's interesting. What was it about? I've been trying to manage my budget better.
I recognize that. I always tell myself I'll save more, but then something comes up.
That's impressive. I usually start with good intentions, but I give up after a few weeks.
I'd love that. I'm always looking for something that will help me stay on track.

scenarios.scenario: Describing a book you couldn't put down
scenarios.context: A reader enthusiastically describes a gripping novel to a friend.

speakerA.en: I've just finished the best novel I've read in years. I stayed up until two in the morning to see how it ended.
It's a thriller about a journalist who investigates the disappearance of a famous scientist. Nothing is what it seems at first.
No, I only guessed the ending a few pages before it was revealed. The author really knows how to keep readers guessing.
I'd say it's worth reading even if you don't normally like thrillers, because the characters are so well developed.
