I'd be happy to lend it to you. Just promise to return it, because it's a first edition that my sister gave me.
I'll bring it on Friday. And don't read it before bed, unless you're prepared to lose a night of sleep.

speakerB.en: That sounds like a great recommendation. What was it about, and what made it so hard to put down?
That sounds intriguing. Did you manage to guess who was behind it, or did the ending take you completely by surprise?
I usually avoid thrillers, because they make me anxious, but if it's as good as you say, I might give it a try.
That's true. A story only works for me when I care about the people in it, however exciting the plot is.
That's very kind. I promise to treat it with care. I'll try not to bend the pages or spill coffee on it.
Thanks for the warning. I'll start reading it on a Saturday, so that I won't be tired the next day.

scenarios.scenario: Choosing between reading in a language and in translation
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss reading novels in a foreign language.

speakerA.en: I've decided to read my first novel in English instead of a translation. I wanted to see whether I could manage it.
I chose a book that I already know well in my own language, so that I can follow the story, even if I miss some words.
It's slow at the beginning, and I look up a word every few lines. But I've noticed that I'm understanding more as I go along.
I never thought of that. I'll try to guess the meaning from the context, and only use the dictionary when I'm completely lost.
I believe so. The language feels more natural, and I'm learning expressions that I'd never find in a textbook.
I'll let you know. If I finish it, I might even try a thicker book next time.

speakerB.en: That's brave. How is it going? I've thought about doing the same, but I always worry that it'll be too difficult.
That's a smart choice. Knowing the story in advance helps enormously, because you don't have to worry about every detail.
That's normal. My advice is not to stop every time you meet an unknown word. Otherwise, you'll lose the rhythm and get discouraged.
Exactly. After a while, you'll find that you remember words better when you've seen them in a sentence than when you learn them from a list.
That's the best thing about it. Do you think it's improved your speaking, or just your reading?
I'd love to hear about it. You've almost convinced me to start my own English book this weekend.

scenarios.scenario: Debating physical books versus e-books
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss the advantages and disadvantages of reading formats.

speakerA.en: I recently bought an e-reader, and I have to admit that it's changed my reading habits. I can carry hundreds of books in my bag, which is a real advantage when I travel.
I'll admit that I miss the feeling of turning pages and the smell of an old book. There's something about physical books that a screen can't replicate.
That's an interesting point. Do you think that it affects how well you remember what you read? I've seen studies suggesting that people retain more from printed text.
I haven't noticed a big difference myself, though I probably skim more on a screen. I suppose that's because it's too easy to be distracted by notifications.
Maybe the ideal solution is to use both. Printed books for important or complex works, and the e-reader for lighter reading, or when I'm away from home.
I'd like to try that. In fact, I might swap a few books with you, so that I can get a taste of a real library again.

speakerB.en: I understand why you like it. The portability and the adjustable font size are huge benefits, especially for people with poor eyesight, and the books are often cheaper too.
I feel exactly the same. There's a tactile pleasure in holding a book, and a bookshelf also tells a story about its owner. A list of files on a device just isn't the same.
Some research suggests that comprehension is slightly better with paper, particularly for long, complex texts, though the differences are small, and they vary from person to person.
That's a common complaint. Even if you turn off the notifications, the temptation to check something else is always there, whereas a printed book doesn't compete for your attention.
That seems like a sensible compromise. I use an e-reader on journeys, but at home, I always return to physical books, especially if I want to write notes in the margin.
That would be great. Sharing books is one of the pleasures that digital formats haven't managed to replace, in my view.

scenarios.scenario: Analyzing a controversial novel
scenarios.context: Two members of a book club argue about the message of a challenging novel.

speakerA.en: I found the ending of the novel deeply unsettling, and I still can't decide whether the author wanted us to sympathize with the protagonist or to condemn him.
That's what makes it so provocative. The narrator presents his actions as justified, but the reader gradually realizes that his version of events can't be trusted.
I'd argue that this ambiguity is intentional. By refusing to give a clear moral conclusion, the author forces us to examine our own assumptions about right and wrong.
I see your point, but I'd say that it's also frustrating. Some readers might interpret the book as an endorsement of violence, especially if they don't pay attention to the irony.
That's a risk that any ambitious work faces. Should literature be limited to what can't possibly be misunderstood? I think that would make it very dull indeed.
I suppose you're right. It's a testament to the book that we've been discussing it for an hour, and that we still haven't reached an agreement.

speakerB.en: I felt the same way. For me, the most disturbing aspect was that I found myself understanding his reasoning at certain points, even though I knew it was deeply wrong.
Exactly. It's an unreliable narrator in the classical sense, and the author seems to be inviting us to read between the lines, rather than accepting what we're told at face value.
That's a persuasive interpretation. And it might explain why the novel has divided critics so strongly. Some see it as a masterpiece, while others consider it irresponsible.
It's a legitimate concern, but if every author worried about how a work could be misread, we'd lose many of the most important novels in the canon.
True. Great books often disturb us, and it's through that discomfort that we learn something about ourselves. Comfortable reading rarely leaves a lasting impression.
That's the mark of a significant book. Shall we suggest something more cheerful for next month, or would that be too much of a retreat?

scenarios.scenario: Recommending books for a book club
scenarios.context: Two members choose a book for the next meeting and weigh different options.

speakerA.en: We need to decide on the book for next month. Last time, we all agreed that the novel was too long, so I'd like to propose something shorter, preferably under three hundred pages.

I've been thinking about a collection of essays, which might make a refreshing change from fiction. It would also be easier for the members who don't have much time to read, because they can read it in short sessions.
That's a fair concern. What about a short novel, then? I've heard good things about a book set in a small fishing village, which explores the relationship between a father and his daughter.
I haven't read it, but the reviews describe it as moving without being sentimental. It's also been translated, and I've been told that the translation is excellent, which can make a huge difference.
We could vote at the meeting, but I'd like to know what the others think beforehand. Should I send a message to the group, and ask them to suggest titles?
Good. I'll put together a short list of three books, and send it out tonight. We can decide on Thursday, and then I'll order copies for those who need them.

speakerB.en: I agree. Several of the members told me that they couldn't finish it, and I think they felt a bit guilty about it. A shorter book would encourage everyone to read it, and we'd have a livelier discussion.

Essays are a good idea, but I worry that the conversation might be less lively, because there's usually less of a story to discuss. People tend to have stronger opinions about characters than about arguments.
That sounds promising. I like the idea of a quieter, more intimate story, after the dramatic plot of the last one. And it would be interesting to read something that's been translated.
In that case, I think it's worth trying. The translator can make or break a book, and if the reviews say that it reads naturally, we should be able to appreciate the original style.
Yes, that would be sensible. Some people may have strong feelings about what they'd like to read, and it's good to give everyone a chance to contribute. Ask them to include a sentence explaining why.
Excellent. I'll bring some snacks next time. A good discussion always goes better with something to eat, and I've found a recipe for cookies that match the theme of the book.

scenarios.scenario: Asking a librarian for help with research
scenarios.context: A student asks a librarian for help finding academic sources for a project.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I'm working on a research project about the effects of urbanization on mental health, and I'm having trouble finding reliable sources. Could you help me with the search?

I've tried a few general searches online, but the results are either too basic or hidden behind payment walls. I need peer-reviewed articles, preferably from the last ten years, and I'd like some books, as well.
That sounds very useful. How do I get access to the academic databases from home? I've tried to log in, but it asks for a password, and I'm not sure which one I'm supposed to use.
I see. And if an article isn't available through the library, is there any way of obtaining it? I came across one that seems perfect, but it's published in a journal that you don't subscribe to.
That's a great service. How long does it usually take? My deadline is in two weeks, and I'd need time to read and incorporate it into my paper.
Thank you so much. I'd never have found these without your help, and I feel much more confident about my project now.

speakerB.en: Of course, I'd be happy to help. That's a very interesting topic. Before we begin, could you tell me exactly what you need? How long does the paper have to be, and what kind of sources are required?
In that case, it's best to use the university's databases, rather than a general search engine. I'll show you how to search with specific keywords, and how to filter by date and type of publication.

You need to use your student number and the password for the student portal. Then you can access everything from home. If you have any problems, I'll write down the address of the technical help desk.
We offer an interlibrary loan service. You fill in a request form, and we'll borrow the article from another library, or purchase a copy for you. It's free for students, so there's no need to pay.
Usually, it takes three to five working days, but it can be faster for digital copies. I'd recommend submitting the request today, to be safe. I'll help you fill in the form right now.
It's my pleasure. If you have any other questions, come back to the desk, or send an email. We're here to help, and we'd love to see you use the library more often.

scenarios.scenario: Questioning the hype around a bestselling novel
scenarios.context: Two friends in a book club discuss a novel that has been praised everywhere, although one of them was disappointed.

speakerA.en: I finally finished the novel everyone's talking about, and to be honest, I was disappointed. It's widely regarded as a masterpiece, and it's said to have sold over a million copies. The more people praised it, the less I enjoyed it.

The plot felt predictable, and the characters seemed flat. It's often claimed that the writing is beautiful, but I found it overdecorated. The more I read, the more I wanted the story to move forward, since nothing seemed to happen.

I did, but only because the club meets next week. It's said that the final chapter changes everything, and I'll admit it was moving. On the other hand, it's hard to forgive three hundred pages of waiting for it.

Definitely. It's widely believed that long novels are more serious, but I disagree. The shorter a book is, the more I tend to appreciate each sentence. Do you think the popularity affected your opinion, in case you expected too much?

Only a short story, which was far better. It's thought that the author's early work is stronger, and that this is her least focused book. The less famous a writer is, the more freely they seem to write, in my experience.
Yes, let's. It's expected that most members will love it, so I'd like to explain my view calmly. The more we discuss it, the more I may change my mind, since you've made some good points.

speakerB.en: Really? I'd say it's one of the best books I've read this year. It's thought to be a turning point in modern fiction, and the critics are known to be quite strict. What exactly didn't you like?

I understand, although that's partly the point. The author is believed to have wanted a slow, reflective style, and it's generally accepted that this suits the subject. The more patiently you read, the more rewarding the ending becomes. Did you finish it?

That's fair. It's often argued that a book should earn its ending, and some critics are reported to share your view. As far as I'm concerned, the structure is clever, though. Would you have preferred a shorter version?

Possibly. It's said that high expectations spoil many books. The more I'd heard about it, the more anxious I was to love it, and the more relieved I felt when I did. Have you read anything else by the same author?

That's an interesting theory. It's often assumed that success makes writers cautious, although it isn't always true. I'd say we should raise this at the meeting, as long as we're polite. Should we prepare some questions?

I hope so, but disagreement makes meetings more interesting. It's believed that the best discussions come from opposing views. The more honest we are, the better it will be. I'll bring the questions on Thursday.

scenarios.scenario: Advising a student on reading academic texts efficiently
scenarios.context: A librarian advises a postgraduate student who is overwhelmed by the amount of academic reading on her course.

speakerA.en: Thank you for seeing me. Having started the course only a month ago, I'm already drowning in reading. Given that every module has about fifty pages a week, I can't finish anything properly. Do you have any advice?

From the first line to the last, and slowly. Having read every sentence carefully, I often forget the main point. Given that I want to understand everything, it seems wrong to skip anything, to be honest.
That makes sense. Supposing I read only the introduction and conclusion, though, wouldn't I miss important details? On the other hand, I'd save a lot of time, which is what I need.
No, but I'm willing to try. Given that I forget things quickly, a journal might help. Having had so little time, I haven't organized my notes at all. What should the summary include?

It does, although I worry about quality. Whatever shortcuts I take, I don't want to lose depth. Having been used to long, careful reading, I find skimming uncomfortable. How do I know I'm not missing something?
That's very reassuring. Having spoken to you, I feel I have a plan, given that I was close to panic. Whatever happens, I'll try this method for a month. May I come back to tell you how it goes?

speakerB.en: Of course. Having worked with many students, I can say that almost everyone feels this way at first. Bearing in mind how much you're expected to read, you can't give every page the same attention. How do you read at the moment?

That's the most common mistake. Provided that you read the abstract and conclusion first, you'll know what to look for. Having understood the argument, you can read the middle selectively. Whatever the length, start with the question the author is asking.

Provided that you take notes, you won't miss much. Having identified the key points, go back for details only when you need them. Whatever you read, write one sentence summarizing it. Have you ever kept a reading journal?

The question, the main claim, and one weakness. Provided that you answer these three points, you'll remember the text far better. Bearing in mind how busy you are, ten minutes per article is enough. Does that sound manageable?

Provided that you read the important texts twice, you won't. Having a clear purpose helps, since you know why you're reading. Given that not everything deserves equal effort, I'd say choosing is part of the skill. Ask your tutor which readings matter most, in case you're unsure.

Please do. Provided that you stay consistent, you'll notice a difference within weeks. Having a regular routine matters more than any single trick. Bearing in mind how hard you've worked, I'm sure you'll manage, and we can adjust things as you go.

scenarios.scenario: Choosing between a classic and a new release for the book club
scenarios.context: Two members of a book club argue over whether this month's choice should be a classic or a recent prize-winner.

speakerA.en: We need to pick this month's book, and I'm leaning towards a classic. Since we've read three new novels in a row, I'd say it's time for a change. To be honest, I'd suggest Middlemarch. What do you think?

It's widely believed that classics stay in print because they say something lasting. What I find most rewarding is that they reward slow reading. Although it's long, it's said to be one of the best novels in English.

That's true, and recent books are often more relevant to our lives. On the other hand, what I find disappointing is that prize-winners tend to be forgotten within a few years. Have you read the one you're proposing?
Fair point, a good book club thrives on disagreement. Still, what worries me is that we'd end up arguing about the author rather than the book. Does the novel deal with anything controversial, then?

That's sensible. A short classic tends to suit busy people better. What about Mrs Dalloway? It's about two hundred pages, and it's thought to be among the most influential novels of the twentieth century.

Brilliant idea. What I'd propose is a short comparison at the end of the evening. Then everyone gets something from the choice. Shall I message the group tonight, so people can order copies in case the library is out?

speakerB.en: Hmm, it's very long. I'd say we'd lose half the members by week two. Why a classic, though? What makes you want to go back to the nineteenth century?

I don't doubt that, but what I find difficult is the pace. Modern novels tend to move faster, whereas classics often take fifty pages to get going. Besides, the newest prize-winner is said to be remarkable, and we'd have plenty to discuss.

Yes, twice. What I love about it is the narrator's voice, which is said to be one of the most original in recent fiction. It tends to divide readers, which is exactly what we want for a lively discussion.

It touches on immigration and memory, and it's widely regarded as a challenging read. What I'd suggest is a compromise: a short classic this month and your long one in the summer, when people have more time.
Perfect. What I like is that it's short but dense, so it gives us plenty to talk about. I'd say we might also pair it with a recent novel that echoes it, to keep both sides happy.
Please do. To be honest, I'm more excited now than I was an hour ago. It's widely agreed that a good compromise leaves everyone a little disappointed, but I think we've found one that doesn't.

scenarios.scenario: Rebuilding a reading habit after losing it
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about how one of them lost the habit of reading and wants to get it back.

speakerA.en: I have a confession. I used to read a book a week, but this year I've barely finished two. To be honest, I miss it badly. Do you have any advice for getting back into it?

My phone, mostly. Were it not for the constant notifications, I'd probably still be reading every night. Little did I realize how much time I was losing. Some evenings I'm so tired that I just scroll mindlessly.

That's a great story. Was it something specific that pulled you in, or was it the quiet that helped? I'd say I need something gripping, since my attention span has become so short that long chapters feel exhausting.

Short stories sound ideal. Little did I know that finishing something could feel so rewarding. Were it not for a bit of encouragement, I'd probably keep putting it off. Where do I begin, though? There are so many collections.

I'll try that. Do you think reading before bed is a good idea, or should I find a different time? I'm so exhausted by ten o'clock that I'd probably fall asleep after a page. Although that might not be bad, since I'd sleep better.
Fifteen minutes sounds manageable. Had I known it would be that simple, I'd have started months ago. I'll begin tonight, as long as you promise to ask me about it next week. Would you mind?

speakerB.en: I'm happy to help, although I'm curious about what happened. Was it a lack of time, or did something else change? What do you think made you stop?
I know the feeling. Had it not been for a long train commute last year, I'd have fallen into the same trap. I was so bored one day that I opened a novel, and I was so absorbed that I missed my stop.

Something gripping helps, yes. I'd recommend a thriller or short stories to begin with. Had I started with a heavy classic, I'd never have kept going. The book was so short that I finished it in two sittings, which gave me confidence.

Try a collection by an author you've heard of, so you know what to expect. The anthology I read is so varied that you can dip in and out. And leave your phone in another room, otherwise the temptation will win.

Ha, true! I'd say fifteen minutes before bed is plenty to start with. Were it not for that routine, I wouldn't have finished half the books I did this year. It's so easy to keep going once the habit forms.

Not at all, and I'll expect a full report. To be honest, nothing would make me happier than seeing you enjoy reading again. Just don't pick anything so long that you feel overwhelmed. Shall we swap recommendations on Friday?

scenarios.scenario: Discussing environmental issues and personal habits
scenarios.context: People talk about recycling, pollution, or ways to help the planet.

speakerA.en: Do you recycle at home?
Where do you put them?
Do you recycle glass, too?
That's good. I want to do it, too.
The air quality in this city is getting worse. We need more trees.
speakerA.fa: کیفیت هوا توی این شهر داره بدتر می‌شه. به درخت‌های بیشتری نیاز داریم.

speakerA.en: I always carry a reusable bag to avoid plastic waste.
speakerA.fa: همیشه یه کیسه قابل استفاده مجدد با خودم می‌برم تا زباله پلاستیکی تولید نکنم.

speakerA.en: Climate change is a serious issue. We all need to do our part.
speakerA.fa: تغییرات اقلیمی یه مسئله جدیه. همه‌مون باید سهم خودمون رو انجام بدیم.

speakerA.en: I've switched to using public transport to reduce my carbon footprint.
speakerA.fa: برای کاهش ردپای کربنم، به استفاده از حمل و نقل عمومی روی آوردم.

speakerA.en: Have you heard about the new recycling initiative in our neighborhood?
speakerA.fa: درباره طرح جدید بازیافت تو محله‌مون شنیدی؟

speakerB.en: Yes, we separate plastics and paper.
We put them in different bins.
Yes. There is a glass bin on our street.
It's easy. I can show you.
I agree. I think the government should invest more in green spaces.
speakerB.fa: موافقم. فکر کنم دولت باید بیشتر در فضاهای سبز سرمایه‌گذاری کنه.

speakerB.en: That's great! I'm trying to do the same. Plastic waste is a huge problem.
speakerB.fa: عالیه! منم سعی می‌کنم همین کار رو بکنم. زباله پلاستیکی یه مشکل بزرگه.

speakerB.en: Definitely. I've started composting food waste in my garden.
speakerB.fa: قطعاً. توی باغچه‌م شروع به کمپوست کردن زباله‌های غذایی کردم.

speakerB.en: That's admirable. I'm still struggling to give up using single-use plastics.
speakerB.fa: قابل تحسینه. من هنوز برام سخته که پلاستیک‌های یکبار مصرف رو کنار بذارم.

speakerB.en: Yes, they're organizing a neighborhood clean-up day. I'm going to join.
speakerB.fa: بله، دارن یه روز نظافت محله ترتیب می‌دن. من می‌خوام شرکت کنم.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about natural beauty and outdoor activities
scenarios.context: People discuss parks, hikes, or enjoying nature.

speakerA.en: Do you like spending time in nature?
Do you go every weekend?
Can I come with you?
Great. What time do we go?
Where's the nearest hiking trail from here?
speakerA.fa: نزدیک‌ترین مسیر پیاده‌روی از اینجا کجاست؟

speakerA.en: I love going to the mountains to escape the city noise.
speakerA.fa: عاشق رفتن به کوه هستم تا از سر و صدای شهر فرار کنم.

speakerA.en: The sunset at the beach yesterday was absolutely stunning.
speakerA.fa: غروب دیروز ساحل فوق‌العاده زیبا بود.

speakerA.en: I'm planning a camping trip for next month. Do you have any camping gear?
speakerA.fa: برای ماه دیگه یه سفر کمپینگ برنامه‌ریزی می‌کنم. تجهیزات کمپینگ داری؟

speakerA.en: Birdwatching is a relaxing hobby. You can see so many species in this area.
speakerA.fa: پرنده‌نگری یه سرگرمی آرامش‌بخشه. توی این منطقه می‌تونی خیلی گونه‌های مختلف ببینی.

speakerB.en: Yes, I love going for walks in the park.
Yes, I go on Saturday morning.
Of course. We can take some water and fruit.
Let's meet at eight o'clock.
There's a nice trail about 3 kilometers from here.
speakerB.fa: یه مسیر خوب حدود ۳ کیلومتر از اینجا هست.

speakerB.en: I understand. I feel the same way about the forest near my house.
speakerB.fa: می‌دونم. منم همین احساس رو نسبت به جنگل نزدیک خونه‌م دارم.

speakerB.en: I wish I could have seen it! The beach is my favorite place to unwind.
speakerB.fa: کاش می‌تونستم ببینمش! ساحل جای مورد علاقه من برای آرامشه.

speakerB.en: Camping sounds exciting! I have a tent and sleeping bags you can borrow.
speakerB.fa: کمپینگ هیجان‌انگیز به نظر میاد! من چادر و کیسه خواب دارم که می‌تونی قرض بگیری.

speakerB.en: That's so interesting. I'm more into photography. I like capturing wildlife moments.
speakerB.fa: خیلی جالبه. من بیشتر به عکاسی علاقه دارم. دوست دارم لحظات حیات وحش رو ثبت کنم.

scenarios.scenario: Describing nature around us
scenarios.context: Two friends enjoy a walk in a green park.

speakerA.en: Look at the trees! They are beautiful.
Is the river clean?
Can we see birds here?
I love this place.
What kind of trees are these?
The lake looks so calm and clear.
I like the sound of the birds in the morning.
Is the park open all day?

speakerB.en: Yes, the park is very green.
Yes, it's clean and blue.
Yes, there are many birds in the morning.
Me too. It's quiet and nice.
They are oak trees. They can live for hundreds of years.
Yes, and it's full of fish. Many people come here to fish.
Me too. It's very relaxing after a busy week.
Yes, and it's free. Many families come on weekends.

scenarios.scenario: Recycling at home
scenarios.context: A person asks a roommate how to sort the trash.

speakerA.en: Where does this bottle go?
And this paper?
What about food waste?
Thank you. Now I know.
Do we need to wash the plastic bottles before recycling?
What should I do with old batteries?
When do they collect the recycling?
Can we recycle pizza boxes?

speakerB.en: Put it in the blue bin.
Paper goes in the green bin.
Put it in the small bin in the kitchen.
Good. We help the planet!
Yes, rinse them quickly so they don't smell.
Don't put them in the trash. Take them to the special box at the supermarket.
Every Tuesday morning, so put the bins out on Monday night.
Only if they're clean. Greasy cardboard can't be recycled.

scenarios.scenario: Saving water and electricity
scenarios.context: Two people talk about saving energy at home.

speakerA.en: Please turn off the light.
Don't leave the water on.
A short shower is better.
Let's save energy at home.
Our electricity bill was very high last month.
Let's unplug the devices we don't use.
I fixed the leaking tap in the bathroom.
Could we wash our clothes in cold water?

speakerB.en: Oh, sorry. I forgot.
OK. I'll close the tap.
You're right. It saves water.
Good idea. It also saves money.
We should switch to energy-saving light bulbs.
Good idea. They still use power when they're on standby.
Great. A small leak can waste a lot of water.
Yes, it saves energy, and it works well for most clothes.

scenarios.scenario: Planting a tree
scenarios.context: Two neighbors plant a small tree in a garden.

speakerA.en: I want to plant a tree.
In the garden, near the window.
Yes, I have one here.
Thank you. It needs water every day.
What kind of tree is best for this soil?
How deep should we dig the hole?
Do we need to use fertilizer?
How long will it take to give fruit?

speakerB.en: That's a good idea. Where?
Do you have a small tree?
Let's plant it now. I can help you.
Don't worry. I'll remember.
A fruit tree like an apple tree will grow well here.
About fifty centimeters, and wide enough for the roots.
A little compost is enough. Too much can harm the roots.
About three or four years, if we take good care of it.

scenarios.scenario: Keeping the park clean
scenarios.context: Two people see trash in a park.

speakerA.en: Don't throw your bottle on the ground.
It's over there, next to the bench.
The park looks dirty today.
Do you have a bag?
Someone left a lot of rubbish near the picnic tables.
There should be more trash cans in this area.
Some volunteers clean the park every Sunday.
Please take your garbage with you when you leave.

speakerB.en: Oh, sorry. Where is the trash can?
Thank you. I'll put it there.
Yes. Let's pick up the trash.
Yes, I have one. Let's start.
That's terrible. Let's tell the park staff.
I agree. People throw trash on the ground when they can't find one.
Really? I'd like to join them next time.
Of course. We always leave the place clean.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about air pollution
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about the air in their city.

speakerA.en: The air is bad today.
I don't like the smoke.
Let's take the bus tomorrow.
Bikes are good for the air.
I read that the air quality is poor this week.
What causes most of the pollution in our city?
Do you think more trees would help?
Should we avoid exercising outside today?

speakerB.en: Yes, there are many cars.
Me neither. It's not healthy.
Good idea. Or we can ride bikes.
And good for our health!
Then we should wear a mask when we go outside.
Mainly traffic and factories.
Yes, trees clean the air and make the city cooler.
I think so. It's better to stay inside until the air improves.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a day in the mountains
scenarios.context: Two friends plan a trip to the mountains.

speakerA.en: Do you want to go to the mountains on Saturday?
We need water, food and a hat.
Yes, it's sunny and warm.
Let's leave at seven in the morning.
Should we take warm clothes? It can be cold at the top.
How long is the hike to the top?
Is the path difficult for beginners?
Let's check the weather forecast the night before.

speakerB.en: Yes! What do we need?
I have a backpack. Is the weather good?
Great. What time do we leave?
OK. See you then!
Yes, and a rain jacket in case the weather changes.
About four hours, with a break for lunch.
Not really, but we need good hiking boots.
Good idea. We shouldn't go if there's a storm.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about recycling at home
scenarios.context: Two neighbors discuss how to reduce waste.

speakerA.en: I've been trying to reduce the amount of trash I produce, but it's harder than I expected.
Compost? I live in an apartment. Where would I put it?
That's easier than I thought. What about packaging? Everything seems to come in plastic.
I'd like to do the same. It's a small change, but it adds up.

speakerB.en: I felt the same at first. Now I separate paper, glass, and plastic, and I compost my food waste.
You can buy a small bin for the kitchen, and the city collects it once a week.
I take reusable bags to the shop and buy fresh food from the market when I can.
Exactly. If everyone did a little, it would make a real difference.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing climate change
scenarios.context: Two friends share their concerns about the environment.

speakerA.en: I read an article that said this was the hottest year on record. It's really worrying.
Do you think individuals can make a difference, or does it depend on governments?
I've started cycling to work instead of driving, and I try to fly less.
Maybe we should encourage our friends to do the same.

speakerB.en: I know. We've had floods and droughts all over the world, and they're becoming more common.
Both are important. Governments make the rules, but our daily choices matter as well.
That's a good start. I've also switched to a company that supplies renewable energy.
It's worth trying. Change usually starts with small groups of people.

scenarios.scenario: Organizing a community clean-up
scenarios.context: Two volunteers plan a clean-up day at a local park.

speakerA.en: We need to organize a clean-up day at the park. It's covered in litter after the festival.
At least twenty. Let's post a notice online and put posters up in the neighborhood.
I can ask the local supermarket to donate the bags. They've helped before.
I'll write to them tomorrow. Which date would suit you?

speakerB.en: I agree. How many volunteers do we need to get it done in a morning?
We'll also need gloves, trash bags, and some tools for the larger items.
Great. We should also ask the city council to collect everything afterwards.
How about the first Saturday of next month, if the weather is good?

scenarios.scenario: Debating renewable energy
scenarios.context: Two neighbors disagree about a proposed wind farm.

speakerA.en: I've heard there's a plan to build a wind farm on the hills behind the village. What are your thoughts?
I don't disagree, but the turbines would spoil the landscape that makes this area so special.
There are also concerns about the effect on birds, and the noise might disturb nearby residents.
I'd feel more comfortable if the community had a genuine say in the matter, rather than being presented with a done deal.

speakerB.en: I'm in favor, in principle. We need to move away from fossil fuels, and this would supply power to thousands of homes.
Beauty is subjective, and I'd argue that the consequences of climate change are far uglier.
Studies suggest the impact on wildlife is modest if turbines are positioned carefully.
I'm with you on that. Consultation should be meaningful, not a formality.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing endangered species and conservation
scenarios.context: A volunteer and a visitor talk about protecting wildlife at a nature reserve.

speakerA.en: The population of these birds has fallen by nearly seventy percent in the last twenty years.
Largely, yes, along with pesticides that reduce the insects they feed on, and changing weather patterns.
We've been restoring wetlands and working with local farmers to cut down on chemicals, and we're seeing the first signs of recovery.
Mostly on donations, which is why we try to involve visitors and make them feel invested.

speakerB.en: That's alarming. What's driving the decline? Is it habitat loss?
Is there anything that can realistically be done to reverse the trend?
That's encouraging. Does the reserve rely on public funding?
You've certainly succeeded with me. I'd like to sign up as a member before I leave.

scenarios.scenario: Considering a more sustainable lifestyle
scenarios.context: Two friends reflect on how realistic it is to live sustainably.

speakerA.en: I've been trying to cut my carbon footprint, but the more I learn, the more overwhelming it seems.
I've given up flying for short trips, though my family thinks I'm being extreme.
True. I try not to preach, but I wonder if personal choices count for much when corporations pollute on such a scale.
I suppose that's a hopeful way of looking at it.

speakerB.en: It's easy to feel that way. Perhaps focus on the changes that make the biggest difference, like transport and diet.
People often react defensively when they feel their habits are being criticized.
Both matter. Individual actions send a signal and shift expectations, which eventually influences policy.
It's the only way I can keep going without despairing.

scenarios.scenario: Evaluating corporate greenwashing
scenarios.context: Two colleagues question a company's environmental claims in its latest campaign.

speakerA.en: Have you seen the new advertising campaign? We're apparently a 'carbon-conscious' company now, according to the posters in the lobby.
That's what bothers me. Slogans are easy, whereas genuinely reducing emissions requires investment and, frankly, a change in business model.
Some do, but plenty take it at face value. That's precisely what makes greenwashing so effective, and so corrosive.
Verified targets, published emissions data, and independent audits. If a claim can't be measured and checked, it's marketing, not sustainability.

speakerB.en: I noticed. It would be more convincing if our delivery fleet weren't still running on diesel and our offices left on at night.
Do you think customers see through it, or does the message work regardless?
What would a credible approach look like? Is there a standard we could point to?
I might raise it at the next meeting. Better to be criticized for asking awkward questions than caught making empty promises.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing development against conservation
scenarios.context: Two residents debate a proposed wind farm near a protected landscape.

speakerA.en: I'm genuinely torn about the wind farm. We need clean energy, but the site is one of the last unspoiled stretches of coastline.
Agreed in principle, but I'm worried about the effect on migrating birds. The environmental assessment seemed rather cursory.
Would that be enough? Once the turbines are built, the developer's incentive to protect the habitat will weaken considerably.
I suppose it's less a question of whether to build and more a question of how, and who holds the developer to account.

speakerB.en: I'd argue the climate crisis outweighs aesthetic concerns. Every delay in renewable energy has a real cost, measured in emissions.
That's a legitimate concern, and it should be addressed through conditions such as turbine placement and seasonal shutdowns.
Which is why enforceable commitments and independent monitoring matter. Without them, I'd share your skepticism.
Exactly. Opposition to every project is as unhelpful as approval of every project. The details are what count.

scenarios.scenario: Questioning the value of carbon offsetting
scenarios.context: A traveler and an environmental consultant discuss whether offsetting flights makes a genuine difference.

speakerA.en: I always pay the offset fee when I book a flight, and I'd like to believe it makes a difference. Does it?
That's disheartening. How can I tell the difference?
Even so, wouldn't the simplest solution be to fly less?
That's a sobering way to put it. I've been treating them as a clear conscience for a modest fee.

speakerB.en: It depends enormously on the scheme. Some offsets fund genuine projects, while others pay for forests that were never at risk of being cut down.
Look for independent certification and transparent reporting, and favor projects that remove carbon rather than merely avoid future emissions.
Without question. Offsets are best viewed as a supplement to reducing emissions, not as a license to continue as before.
Many people do. The uncomfortable truth is that there's no substitute for changing behavior, though offsetting is better than doing nothing.

scenarios.scenario: Debating individual versus systemic responsibility for climate change
scenarios.context: Two colleagues discuss whether personal choices can meaningfully address environmental problems.

speakerA.en: I'm increasingly skeptical that recycling and cycling to work will make a material difference when a handful of corporations account for most emissions.
In theory, yes, though the evidence for that trickle-up effect is thin. Structural change seems to come from regulation, not goodwill.
That's fair. I suppose my frustration is with the way responsibility has been shifted onto consumers by those who profit from the status quo.
Which makes me rather suspicious of any message that conveniently places the burden on the individual.

speakerB.en: That's a persuasive point, but I'd be wary of using it as an excuse for inaction. Individual choices shape cultural norms, which in turn influence policy.
Perhaps both are necessary. Regulation provides the framework, but without public support, politicians have little incentive to enact it.
A shrewd observation. The notion of a personal carbon footprint was, after all, popularized by an oil company.
Skepticism is healthy, but I'd urge us not to let it curdle into fatalism. Both pressure from below and legislation from above are needed.

scenarios.scenario: Describing a conservation project to potential donors
scenarios.context: A project lead explains the aims and urgency of a rewilding scheme.

speakerA.en: Our aim is to restore a degraded wetland to a functioning ecosystem, which would provide habitat for dozens of declining species.
Chiefly because we've engaged the local community from the outset. Projects fail when they're imposed from outside rather than embraced from within.
We'll monitor species counts, water quality and the return of key indicator species, and we'll publish the data openly.
We're keenly aware of that. We'd welcome your scrutiny, and any contribution would be spent directly on the restoration work.

speakerB.en: It sounds ambitious. What makes you confident that it can succeed, given how many such initiatives have faltered?
That's persuasive. And how would you measure success, in concrete terms, over the next five years?
I'm glad to hear it. Transparency is what distinguishes a credible venture from an exercise in public relations.
Then I'd like to discuss a multi-year commitment. Sporadic donations strike me as ill-suited to a project of this horizon.

scenarios.scenario: Reflecting on humanity's relationship with the natural world
scenarios.context: Two friends on a hike consider what nature means to them.

speakerA.en: There's a peculiar humility that descends on me in places like this. One feels both utterly insignificant and strangely connected.
And yet we've become so accustomed to dominating it that we've forgotten how to belong to it.
Do you think that's recoverable? I wonder whether people who grow up in cities can ever develop that bond.
Then perhaps we owe it to others to share places like this, rather than guarding them jealously.

speakerB.en: I know exactly what you mean. It's a reminder that the world doesn't revolve around us, which is oddly consoling.
That's the great irony of modernity. We've gained extraordinary power over nature while losing our sense of kinship with it.
I'd like to believe so. Even a few hours in the wilderness can recalibrate one's sense of proportion.
Provided we teach them to tread lightly. Access without respect is merely another form of exploitation.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about reducing plastic use
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss how they can use less plastic in daily life.

speakerA.en: I've been trying to use less plastic lately, but it's surprisingly difficult.
Almost everything in the supermarket is wrapped in it. I carry my own bags, but that's not enough.
Good idea. I'll try the market this weekend. Do you know if they sell loose vegetables?
Thanks. Small changes might not solve the problem, but at least it feels like a start.

speakerB.en: I know what you mean. Even small things, like straws and packaging, add up quickly.
You could buy fresh food at the local market instead. There's much less packaging there.
Yes, most stalls do. And you can bring your own containers for things like nuts and spices.
Exactly. If more people did it, the shops would have to change the way they sell things.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a tree-planting day
scenarios.context: Two volunteers organize an event to plant trees in their neighborhood.

speakerA.en: The city has agreed to give us fifty young trees for the park. We need to organize a planting day.
I'd say the first Saturday of April. The ground will be soft, and the weather should be mild.
I'll contact the local school. I'm sure some of the teachers will bring their students.
Great. I'll make a poster and ask the café if we can hang it in the window.

speakerB.en: That's wonderful news. When do you think is the best time to do it?
Good point. We'll also need shovels and gloves. I can ask the hardware store if they'll lend us some.
That would be perfect. Children love this kind of activity, and it teaches them to care for nature.
Excellent. I'll prepare a list of volunteers and make sure everyone knows where to meet.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the problem of food waste
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about how to waste less food at home.

speakerA.en: I read an article yesterday saying that a third of all food produced in the world is thrown away. It shocked me.
I realized that I'm part of the problem. Every week, I throw away vegetables that have gone bad before I could cook them.
That's the thing. I buy more than I need because the supermarket offers discounts on large packs, and then I can't finish it.
I like that idea. I'll make a weekly menu, and only buy what I need. It would also help me save money.
Good tip. And what about the leftovers? Do you freeze them, or do you simply eat them the following day?
I'll try that. If we all made small changes like this, it would make a real difference to the environment.

speakerB.en: I know. It's terrible, especially considering how many people in the world don't have enough to eat.
Most of us are. The problem is that fresh food doesn't last long, and our lives are so busy that we forget what's in the fridge.
That's a trap. A better strategy is to plan your meals before you go shopping, and to stick to a list.
It certainly would. I've saved almost fifty euros a month since I started, and my fridge is much tidier.
Both. I freeze whatever I can't eat in two days, and I label the boxes with the date, so I know what I have.
Exactly. It's not about being perfect. If everyone reduced their waste by even a little, the total effect would be huge.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about a visit to a national park
scenarios.context: A hiker describes a trip to a national park and what it taught her.

speakerA.en: I've just come back from the national park, and I'm still amazed by how beautiful it was. The silence was incredible.
We hiked for three days, and we camped by a lake. At night, the sky was full of stars, which I'd never seen so clearly before.
The only disadvantage was the rubbish that other visitors had left. It was upsetting to see plastic bottles on such a beautiful trail.
We collected as much as we could and took it with us. The rangers say that the park gets thousands of visitors every summer.
I think it should be compulsory to take your waste home. Places like this need protection if we want future generations to enjoy them.
I'd be glad to. Maybe next year, you could join me, and we could volunteer for a clean-up day.

speakerB.en: That sounds wonderful. I'd love to go there one day. What was the best part of the trip?
That must have been unforgettable. In the city, we hardly see any stars at all because of the lights.
That's a pity. People should know better. If you bring something with you, you should be able to take it away again.
That's good. It's easy to forget how much damage a large number of people can do, even if each of them leaves only a little.
I completely agree. Some parks already charge a fee, which is used to maintain the paths and protect the wildlife.
That would be great. I've been looking for a way to be more active in protecting nature, and this sounds ideal.

scenarios.scenario: Debating individual versus corporate responsibility
scenarios.context: Two friends argue about who should bear responsibility for environmental damage.

speakerA.en: I'm tired of being told that I should recycle more and use my car less, when a handful of large corporations produce most of the world's emissions.
I agree that individual actions matter, but I think the emphasis is unbalanced. It lets companies avoid responsibility, as though the problem were caused by consumer choices alone.
That's true, though consumers do create the demand. If people stopped buying products that harm the environment, companies would have to change what they offer.
But that assumes that people have real alternatives. For many, the greener option is more expensive or simply isn't available where they live.
I think we need both. Regulation to set minimum standards for companies, and incentives that make sustainable choices easier and cheaper for ordinary households.
Well, at least we agree that something has to change. Whatever the solution, it will take cooperation between governments, businesses, and individuals.

speakerB.en: I understand the frustration, and the statistics are striking. Some studies indicate that a hundred companies are responsible for more than seventy percent of industrial emissions.
It's a form of shifting the blame. When advertising campaigns focus on personal carbon footprints, public attention is diverted from the structural changes that really need to happen.
That's a fair point. Market pressure can be powerful, but it's slow, and the damage continues in the meantime. We don't have the luxury of waiting for everyone to change their habits.
Precisely. Not everyone can afford an electric car or organic food. Expecting individuals to carry the entire burden is unrealistic, and arguably unfair to those on lower incomes.
That's the most plausible approach. Governments can set limits, while companies innovate, and individuals contribute through their daily choices. None of them alone is enough.
Absolutely. And the sooner we accept that, the sooner we can stop arguing about who is to blame, and focus on what can actually be done.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing sustainable travel choices
scenarios.context: Two travelers weigh the environmental impact of different ways of getting around.

speakerA.en: I've been trying to reduce the environmental impact of my travel, but it's harder than I expected. Flights are by far the most polluting option, yet they're often the cheapest and quickest.
I recently took a train from Paris to Vienna instead of flying, and although it took nearly twelve hours, I actually enjoyed it. I read, watched the landscape change, and arrived feeling relaxed.
That's a reasonable objection. For longer trips, flying may be unavoidable, but I try to take fewer, longer journeys, so that I'm not constantly taking short flights for weekend breaks.
I've also started choosing accommodation with a sustainable policy, though it's sometimes difficult to know whether a hotel's claims are genuine or just clever marketing.
That's a good tip. I think that being conscious of the issue is already a step in the right direction, even if we can't be perfect in every decision.
Agreed. Maybe next year we could plan a trip by train together, and show that sustainable travel can be an adventure rather than a sacrifice.

speakerB.en: I know the feeling. Airlines are slowly improving, but aviation is still responsible for a significant proportion of global emissions, and the growth in demand is wiping out many of the gains.
That sounds wonderful. The slower pace can actually be a benefit. Traveling overland lets you see the places in between, which you miss when you simply jump from one airport to another.
That's practical advice. A single long trip a year, combined with local excursions by train or bike, has a much smaller footprint than several quick flights, and it's often more rewarding.
The term 'greenwashing' describes exactly that problem. Look for independent certifications, and check whether the hotel publishes concrete data on energy and water use, rather than vague statements.
I think so. If everyone made even modest changes, the combined effect would be significant. It's not about perfection, but about making more thoughtful decisions when we can.
I'd love that. There are some spectacular routes in Europe, and the sleeper trains are making a comeback. It would be a good way to see how enjoyable it can be.

scenarios.scenario: Attending a town meeting on recycling policy
scenarios.context: Two residents discuss a proposal for a new waste collection system.

speakerA.en: I attended the town meeting last night about the new recycling scheme, and I must say that I'm rather skeptical. They want to charge households according to the amount of non-recyclable waste they produce.
In principle, it's a fair idea, since people who produce less waste would pay less. But I worry that some people will simply dump their rubbish in the woods, in order to avoid paying.

That's a risk that other towns have faced. Apparently, illegal dumping increased by thirty percent in the first year of a similar scheme, though it dropped again after a campaign and stricter enforcement.
Perhaps the key is to combine it with better services. If the council provided more collection points for recyclable materials, and made them easy to use, residents would have fewer excuses.
I also think that the council should be clearer about where the money will go. If people see that the revenue is used for environmental projects, they might be more willing to accept it.
I'll write to the councilor, and suggest that they introduce it gradually. Would you like to sign the letter with me, as a joint proposal from residents?

speakerB.en: I was there too. I'm in favor of it overall, but I agree that the details matter. It's not enough to punish people for producing waste, if they don't have a convenient alternative.

That's what the opponents say, and it's a legitimate concern. But the experience in other countries suggests that the overall volume of waste falls significantly, and recycling rates rise considerably.

I read about that. The towns that succeeded were those that spent a lot on education and monitoring. If you introduce a charge without explaining it, you create resentment, and that undermines the whole idea.

Exactly. At the moment, the collection points are far from some neighborhoods, and they're often full. If it's inconvenient to recycle, people will take the easy way out, whatever the financial incentives are.
That's an important point. Transparency builds trust. A public report, showing how the money is spent, would encourage cooperation, and it would also put pressure on the council to deliver.
I'd be glad to sign it. Let's also ask the neighbors, because the more voices we have, the more likely it is that the council will take it seriously.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing energy savings with a home advisor
scenarios.context: A homeowner asks an energy advisor about reducing bills and environmental impact.

speakerA.en: Thank you for coming. My energy bills have increased significantly over the past two years, and I'd like to find out what can be done to reduce them, and also to lower the environmental impact of the house.
It's an old house, built in the nineteen-fifties, with single-glazed windows in some rooms, and I'm not sure how well the roof is insulated. The heating is oil-based, and it's very expensive to run.
That sounds sensible. Which improvement would give the greatest savings for the money? I can't afford to do everything at once, so I'd like to start with the changes that have the most impact.
And what about a heat pump? I've heard that they're efficient, but also expensive to install. Would it be worthwhile in a house like mine, or would I need to improve the insulation first?
Are there any government grants that I could apply for? I read that some programs cover part of the cost for insulation and heat pumps, but the conditions seemed complicated.
Thank you for the clear explanation. I'll wait for your report, and then I'll decide on the order in which to carry out the work.

speakerB.en: Of course. I've done a thorough inspection, and I can already tell you that there's considerable potential for improvement. Let's start with the roof. In houses of this age, up to a third of the heat is lost there.

That's a common situation. Adding insulation in the attic is the cheapest and most effective step. It costs around fifteen hundred euros, and it could reduce your heating costs by up to twenty percent.

After that, I'd recommend replacing the windows, starting with the north side, which is the coldest. And you could seal the gaps around the doors, which costs very little and makes a noticeable difference.
Yes, insulation should come first. A heat pump works best in a well-insulated house. Once the roof and windows have been improved, a heat pump could cut your energy consumption by about half.

There are several grants. The national program covers up to thirty percent of insulation costs, and there's an additional subsidy for heat pumps. I'll prepare a summary of the options, with the forms.
You're welcome. I'll send the full report by the end of the week, with a list of priorities and estimated costs. Don't hesitate to contact me if you have any questions.

scenarios.scenario: Persuading a landlord to install solar panels
scenarios.context: A tenant tries to persuade a landlord to install solar panels on the roof of an apartment building.

speakerA.en: Thank you for meeting me. I'd like to suggest installing solar panels on the roof, since it's mostly unused. It's high time we reduced the building's energy costs, and I'd rather you heard the proposal from a tenant than from a complaint.

A local company estimates around twenty thousand euros, which would be recovered in about eight years. I suggest that we ask for a detailed quote, so that you can compare it. It's important that you see all the numbers before deciding.

You'd gain lower bills for the common areas, and a higher property value. It's vital that the building stays attractive to future tenants, and many people now look for green homes. On the other hand, there are government grants, which I'd rather you checked.

Usually thirty to forty percent, although it depends on the region. I suggest that we contact the energy office this week. It's high time someone in the building took the lead, and I'd be happy to prepare the application, as long as you sign it.

Most would support it, I'd say, especially if lower bills are guaranteed. It's essential that the savings are shared fairly, so I'd rather we agreed on that in writing. The older tenants might be worried about noise during installation.

That sounds fair. I suggest that we set a date for the meeting and invite a representative from the installer. It's high time this project started, and I'd rather it began this spring. Thank you for taking it seriously.

speakerB.en: I appreciate the initiative, but I have to be honest: it sounds expensive. It's essential that any investment pays for itself, so what would it cost? I'd rather you gave me real figures than general enthusiasm.
Eight years is a long time. I insist that any change be profitable for me, as the owner. What do I gain, and who pays for the maintenance, since panels need cleaning and occasional repairs?

Grants would certainly change things. I'd rather we explored that before anything else. It's essential that I understand the conditions, in case there are hidden obligations. Do you know how much they usually cover?

That's generous of you. I'd rather you didn't do all the work yourself, though. It's important that tenants feel involved, so I suggest that we organize a short meeting with everyone. How would the residents react, in your opinion?

Installation takes only a few days, I believe, so that shouldn't be a problem. I insist that the work be done outside working hours. It's vital that nobody loses power, and I'd rather pay extra than upset anyone.

Thank you for the clear proposal. I'd rather decide after the meeting, but I'm much more positive than when you arrived. It's essential that we move carefully, and I suggest that we speak again once the grant results are in.

scenarios.scenario: Reacting to a local plan to cut down a woodland
scenarios.context: Two neighbors discuss a council proposal to cut down a small woodland to build a car park and decide whether to oppose it.

speakerA.en: Have you seen the notice about the woods behind the school? Not only do they want to cut them down, but they also plan to build a car park. Rarely have I felt so angry about a local decision.

Because never before has this town had so little green space. Only when you lose something do you realize its value, and children play there every day. Not only is it a habitat for birds, but it also keeps the air clean.

Not a word. Not only is there no replacement planned, but there's also no environmental study. Rarely do councils skip that, so it looks rushed. As far as I'm concerned, that alone justifies a protest.

The parents' association would help, since they use the woods most. Only when the school supports us will the council take it seriously. Not only could they sign a petition, but they could also speak at the meeting.

Deal. Not only will I collect signatures, but I'll also ask the local newspaper to cover the story. Rarely does a council ignore the press, I'd say. Only after they've seen public pressure will they reconsider, in my experience.

That's brilliant. Not only would it save the trees, but it would also be cheaper. Only a quick look at the map will show whether it's realistic, so let's check it tonight. Never have I been so glad to have a neighbor like you.

speakerB.en: I saw it this morning. To be honest, I'm not sure what to think. Seldom do I walk there, and the school really does need parking. Why do you feel so strongly about it?

I understand, but the council says the parking situation is dangerous at the moment. Hardly ever do I see anyone using the woods, though. Only if the plan included new trees elsewhere would I support it. Does it say anything about that?

That's a good point. On the other hand, a protest only works if many people join. Never have I seen this street so united, so maybe you're right. Who else could we ask, in case the council ignores us?

Good idea. Rarely do I get involved in local politics, but I'd regret staying silent. Only when people write letters do councils seem to listen. Shall I draft a petition, as long as you collect the signatures?

I agree. Never have I thought a few trees could matter so much, but they do. I'd suggest we also offer an alternative, since complaining alone isn't enough. Could the car park be built on the unused tennis courts instead?
Same here. Rarely do I feel so motivated, so let's make the most of it. Not only will we sign the petition, but we'll also present the alternative at the meeting. See you at seven, and bring the map.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about food preferences and cooking skills
scenarios.context: People discuss what they like to eat and their cooking experience.

speakerA.en: Do you like cooking?
What do you cook?
Is pasta easy to cook?
Can you cook for me?
What's your favorite dish to cook?
speakerA.fa: بهترین غذایی که دوست داری بپزی چیه؟

speakerA.en: I can cook simple things like pasta and omelettes.
speakerA.fa: می‌تونم چیزهای ساده مثل پاستا و املت درست کنم.

speakerA.en: I'm trying to learn how to cook Persian food. It's a bit complicated but delicious.
speakerA.fa: سعی می‌کنم غذای ایرانی پختن رو یاد بگیرم. یه کم پیچیده‌ست ولی خوشمزه‌ست.

speakerA.en: I love experimenting with spices. They totally change the flavor of a dish.
speakerA.fa: عاشق آزمایش با ادویه‌ها هستم. طعم غذا رو کاملاً تغییر می‌دن.

speakerA.en: I've been following a plant-based diet for a few months now. It's been great for my health.
speakerA.fa: چند ماهه که رژیم گیاهی گرفتم. برای سلامتی‌م عالی بوده.

speakerB.en: Yes, I find it very relaxing.
I cook pasta and soup.
Yes, it's very easy. It takes ten minutes.
Of course! Come on Saturday.
I love making homemade pizza. It's so much better than takeout.
speakerB.fa: عاشق پیتزای خانگی هستم. خیلی بهتر از پیتزای بیرونیه.

speakerB.en: That's a good start. I also recommend learning to make soup. It's easy and healthy.
speakerB.fa: شروع خوبیه. منم توصیه می‌کنم سوپ درست کردن رو یاد بگیری. راحت و سالمه.

speakerB.en: Oh, I love Persian food! I'd love to try some of your dishes someday.
speakerB.fa: اوه، عاشق غذای ایرانی هستم! دوست دارم یه روزی غذاهای شما رو امتحان کنم.

speakerB.en: I agree. A pinch of cinnamon or cumin can make a huge difference.
speakerB.fa: موافقم. یه کم دارچین یا زیره می‌تونه تفاوت خیلی زیادی ایجاد کنه.

speakerB.en: That's inspiring. I'm thinking of reducing meat in my diet too.
speakerB.fa: الهام‌بخشه. منم به کاهش گوشت در رژیم غذاییم فکر می‌کنم.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing a recipe or asking for cooking advice
scenarios.context: Someone asks how to cook a specific dish or requests a recipe.

speakerA.en: Could you teach me how to make that cake?
speakerA.fa: میشه بهم یاد بدی اون کیک رو چطور درست کنم؟

speakerA.en: What's your secret to making this curry so flavorful?
speakerA.fa: راز اینکه این کاری رو اینقدر خوش‌طعم می‌کنی چیه؟

speakerA.en: Could you write down the recipe for me?
speakerA.fa: میشه دستور پخت رو برام بنویسی؟

speakerA.en: How long do you need to bake the bread for?
speakerA.fa: این نان رو چقدر باید توی فر بذاری؟

speakerA.en: I always overcook the rice. Do you have any tips for perfect rice?
speakerA.fa: همیشه برنج رو بیش از حد می‌پزم. نکته‌ای برای برنج عالی داری؟

speakerB.en: Sure! The main ingredients are flour, eggs, and sugar. Let me show you.
speakerB.fa: حتماً! مواد اصلی آرد، تخم‌مرغ و شکر هستن. بذارید نشونتون بدم.

speakerB.en: I add a bit of coconut milk and fresh herbs at the end.
speakerB.fa: تهش یه کم شیر نارگیل و سبزی تازه اضافه می‌کنم.

speakerB.en: Of course, I'll send it to you later.
speakerB.fa: حتماً، بعداً برات می‌فرستم.

speakerB.en: About 30 minutes at 180 degrees Celsius.
speakerB.fa: حدود ۳۰ دقیقه در دمای ۱۸۰ درجه سانتی‌گراد.

speakerB.en: Try rinsing the rice several times and soaking it before cooking. That helps.
speakerB.fa: سعی کن برنج رو چند بار آبکشی کنی و قبل از پخت خیسش کنی. این کمک می‌کنه.

scenarios.scenario: Deciding what to cook for dinner
scenarios.context: Two people decide what to make for dinner.

speakerA.en: What do we cook for dinner?
Do we have tomatoes?
We need cheese. I'll go to the shop.
How long does it take?
What would you like to eat tonight? I'm tired of pizza.
Do we have all the ingredients for it?
I'll go to the supermarket. What else do we need?
Shall we make a salad as well?
Should we cook enough for tomorrow's lunch too?
Do you want rice or bread with it?
I don't like spicy food. Please don't add much pepper.
Dinner will be ready in about forty minutes.

speakerB.en: Let's make pasta.
Yes, we have three tomatoes.
Thanks. I'll start with the pasta.
About thirty minutes.
How about chicken soup? It's healthy and easy to make.
We have chicken and carrots, but we need some potatoes.
Some onions, garlic, and fresh parsley, please.
Yes, I'll prepare a simple one with cucumber and tomatoes.
Good idea. Soup tastes even better the next day.
Bread is fine. There's some fresh bread in the kitchen.
OK. I'll add just a little salt and black pepper.
Perfect. I'll set the table in the meantime.

scenarios.scenario: Making breakfast
scenarios.context: A person asks a family member to make breakfast.

speakerA.en: Can you make breakfast?
Yes, please. Two eggs.
Boiled, please. And a cup of tea.
Thank you. Do you need help?
What time is breakfast usually ready?
Could you make me an omelet with cheese?
No, just cheese and tomatoes, please.
Is there any orange juice in the fridge?
Could you toast some bread for me?
I'll have jam, please. Do you need any help?
I think the tea is ready.
This is a delicious breakfast. Thank you for making it.

speakerB.en: Sure. Do you want eggs?
Do you want them fried or boiled?
OK. It takes five minutes.
No, just sit down. Breakfast is ready soon.
Around eight, before everyone leaves for work.
Of course. Do you want mushrooms in it?
OK. It will take about ten minutes.
Yes, but only a little. I'll make some fresh juice.
Sure. Would you like butter or jam?
Yes, could you put the plates and cups on the table?
Great. Please pour it for everyone.
You're welcome. I enjoy cooking in the morning.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for a simple recipe
scenarios.context: A friend explains how to make a salad.

speakerA.en: How do you make a salad?
Then what?
What do I put on top?
That's simple. Thank you!
Could you tell me how to make pasta salad?
What should I do after that?
Which vegetables do you usually add?
Do I need a special dressing?
Can I add some chicken or tuna?
How long should I keep it in the fridge?
Can I make it a day before the party?
This sounds easy. I'll try it this weekend.

speakerB.en: It's easy. First, wash the vegetables.
Cut the tomatoes and the cucumbers.
Add a little oil, lemon and salt.
Enjoy your salad!
Sure. First, boil the pasta for ten minutes.
Drain it and rinse it with cold water.
I add tomatoes, corn, and some green peppers.
Just mix olive oil, lemon juice, and a little salt.
Yes, tuna works very well, and it adds protein.
About thirty minutes, so that it gets cold.
Yes, but add the dressing just before you serve it.
Good luck! Tell me how it turns out.

scenarios.scenario: Finding things in the kitchen
scenarios.context: A guest asks where things are in the kitchen.

speakerA.en: Where is the salt?
Where is the big pan?
Do we have any rice?
Where are the spoons?
Where do you keep the cooking oil?
Do you have a knife for cutting vegetables?
Where can I find a cutting board?
Do you have any clean towels?
Could you pass me that big bowl, please?
Where do you put the leftover food?
I can't find the can opener anywhere.
Where should I put the dirty dishes?

speakerB.en: It's on the shelf, next to the sugar.
It's in the cupboard under the sink.
Yes, there is a bag in the cupboard.
They are in the drawer.
It's in the cupboard above the stove.
Yes, it's in the second drawer, next to the forks.
It's hanging on the wall, next to the fridge.
Yes, there are some in the bottom drawer.
Sure. Here you are. Be careful, it's heavy.
Put it in a plastic box and place it in the fridge.
It's in the drawer under the microwave.
Just leave them in the sink. I'll wash them later.

scenarios.scenario: Cooking rice
scenarios.context: One person shows another how to cook rice.

speakerA.en: How much rice do we need?
Do I wash the rice first?
How long do I cook it?
Is it ready now?
Should I soak the rice before cooking it?
How much water do I need for two cups of rice?
Do I cover the pot while it's cooking?
Should I stir it during cooking?
How can I tell when it's ready?
Can I add some butter at the end?
What can I serve with the rice?
Thanks for teaching me. It looks perfect!

speakerB.en: Two cups for four people.
Yes, wash it with water.
About twenty minutes.
Yes. Let's eat!
Yes, soak it for thirty minutes to make it softer.
About three cups of water, and a teaspoon of salt.
Yes, and turn the heat to low after it boils.
No, don't stir it, or it will become sticky.
The water will disappear, and the rice will be soft.
Of course. It makes the rice taste richer.
Grilled chicken and a fresh salad go well with it.
You're welcome. You'll make it even better next time.

scenarios.scenario: Tasting the food
scenarios.context: A host asks a guest to taste the soup.

speakerA.en: Please try this soup.
Is it too salty?
Do you want more?
Thank you for dinner.
I made this stew for the first time. What do you think?
Does it need more salt or spices?
I put some herbs in it. Can you taste them?
Would you like some bread to go with it?
Is it too hot for you?
Do you want to try the dessert as well?
It's a homemade chocolate cake. I baked it this morning.
I'm glad you liked everything. Would you like the recipe?

speakerB.en: Mmm, it's very tasty.
No, it's just right.
Yes, please. A little more.
You're welcome. I'm happy you like it.
It's very good. The meat is really soft.
Maybe a little salt, but the flavor is great.
Yes, I can taste the mint. It's a nice touch.
Yes, please. I'd love to dip it in the sauce.
A little. I'll wait for a minute.
Definitely. What is it?
It smells wonderful. May I have a small slice?
Yes, please. I'd love to cook it at home.

scenarios.scenario: Helping in the kitchen
scenarios.context: Two people cook together.

speakerA.en: Can I help you cook?
Sure. How many?
Is the oven hot?
OK. What's next?
What should I do first?
How thin should I slice the carrots?
Do you want me to heat the oil in the pan?
Can I add the onions now?
Could you taste the sauce and tell me if it needs anything?
The timer is ringing. Is the chicken ready?
Where should I put the hot pan?
Shall I clean the kitchen while you serve?

speakerB.en: Yes, please. Can you cut the onions?
Two onions, please.
Yes, be careful! It's very hot.
Now please put the plates on the table.
Please wash the vegetables and peel the potatoes.
About half a centimeter, so they cook quickly.
Yes, on medium heat, please. Don't let it burn.
Yes, fry them until they're golden brown.
It needs a little more salt and some pepper.
Let me check. Yes, it's cooked. Please turn off the oven.
Put it on the board here. Use a cloth to hold the handle.
That would be great. Thanks for your help!

scenarios.scenario: Asking for a recipe
scenarios.context: A guest asks the host how to make a dish she enjoyed.

speakerA.en: This soup is wonderful. Would you mind telling me how you made it?
Then what do you add? Is it a tomato base?
How long do you let it cook, and do you blend it afterwards?
What gives it that rich flavor? I can taste something smoky.

speakerB.en: Thank you. It's easy. You start by frying onions and garlic in olive oil.
Yes, canned tomatoes, a little stock, and some roasted red peppers.
About thirty minutes on a low heat, and then I blend it until it's smooth.
A teaspoon of smoked paprika. It makes all the difference.

scenarios.scenario: Cooking dinner together
scenarios.context: Two roommates prepare dinner and share tasks.

speakerA.en: I'd like to make pasta tonight. Could you help me chop the vegetables?
Yes, please. Cut them into small pieces so that they cook quickly.
Let's wait for the water. In the meantime, could you grate some cheese?
Not yet. Thanks for reminding me. It makes a big difference to the taste.

speakerB.en: Sure. How many do you need, and should I peel the carrots first?
Done. Shall I start on the sauce, or is the water not boiling yet?
Of course. By the way, did you add enough salt to the pasta water?
Dinner should be ready in fifteen minutes. I'll set the table.

scenarios.scenario: Fixing a cooking mistake
scenarios.context: A person has trouble with a recipe and asks for advice.

speakerA.en: I've made a mistake with the sauce. I added too much salt, and now it's almost inedible.
Does that really work? I've never heard of it.
I have some cream in the fridge. How much should I use?
That's better already. Thanks for saving the dinner!

speakerB.en: Don't throw it away. Try adding a peeled potato and cooking it for a few minutes.
It absorbs some of the salt. You could also add a little cream or lemon juice.
Start with a few spoonfuls and taste it. You can always add more.
Anytime. Next time, add the salt gradually and taste as you go.

scenarios.scenario: Adapting a recipe for dietary restrictions
scenarios.context: A host asks a guest about preparing a meal for a vegan friend.

speakerA.en: I'm hosting dinner on Saturday, and one of the guests is vegan. I'm a bit out of my depth.
I was planning a creamy mushroom pasta. Could I replace the cream with something else?
What about dessert? I'd rather not serve fruit salad as an afterthought.
That sounds intriguing. I'd better test it beforehand, so there are no disasters on the night.

speakerB.en: It's easier than you'd think. Many traditional dishes can be adapted by swapping out butter, cream, and eggs.
Cashew cream works well, or you could use coconut milk, provided you don't mind a slight sweetness.
A dark chocolate mousse made with avocado is surprisingly rich, and nobody would guess it's dairy-free.
Wise idea. And check the labels carefully, as some wines and sauces contain hidden animal products.

scenarios.scenario: Learning a traditional cooking technique
scenarios.context: A learner asks an experienced cook to demonstrate bread-making.

speakerA.en: I've tried making sourdough several times, and it always turns out as dense as a brick.
It's a little sluggish, I suppose. I've been feeding it every few days rather than daily.
And how long should I let the dough rise? The instructions I followed were rather vague.
I've been cutting it short because I was afraid of overproofing it.

speakerB.en: The most common culprit is the starter. Is it active and bubbly before you use it?
That's probably the problem. It needs regular feeding and warmth to be strong enough to lift the dough.
It depends on the temperature, but you're looking for it to roughly double in size, which can take anywhere from four to eight hours.
Patience is the secret. Try again with a healthier starter, and you'll notice the difference immediately.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing food culture and eating habits
scenarios.context: Two friends reflect on how attitudes to food differ across cultures.

speakerA.en: What struck me during my stay abroad was how seriously people take mealtimes. Nobody eats at their desk.
I found that sitting down to eat with others made me appreciate what I was eating far more.
Do you think fast food has eroded the tradition of cooking from scratch?
That's encouraging. I'd like to host regular dinners myself, if only to encourage more conversation.

speakerB.en: Here, lunch is often a sandwich eaten while answering emails. We treat food as fuel rather than as an occasion.
It probably aids digestion as well, and it strengthens relationships.
To a degree, but I've noticed a revival among younger people who are curious about where their food comes from.
Start small, with one shared meal a week, and see whether it becomes a habit.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing seasonal cooking
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about why cooking with seasonal ingredients matters to them.

speakerA.en: I've been trying to cook only with seasonal produce this year, and it's changed my whole relationship with food.
It's limiting in the best way. Constraints force creativity, and I've discovered root vegetables I'd never have considered before.
Exactly. When something is in season, it tastes of itself, and you barely have to do anything to it.
Often less, since seasonal produce is abundant and therefore cheaper. The real investment is in learning to preserve and pickle.

speakerB.en: How so? I'd have thought it would be limiting, particularly in winter.
I can see the appeal. A tomato in January is rarely worth eating anyway.
Does it cost more or less? I've always assumed that eating well means spending more.
That might be the push I need. I could start with a batch of preserved lemons before the season ends.

scenarios.scenario: Running a busy restaurant kitchen
