That's what worries me. Volumes of letters have been falling for years, and many post offices have closed. It seems that the service is slowly being phased out.
True, but the postal service also plays a social role, especially in rural areas, where it may be the only link to the outside world for elderly residents.
That's an interesting point. Perhaps postal workers could take on additional tasks, such as delivering medication or checking on isolated people, to justify the cost of maintaining the network.
I like that idea. It would give the service a new purpose, and it might be more sustainable than simply trying to compete with email and messaging.
In the meantime, I'll try to write more letters myself. There's something special about receiving something that someone has taken the time to write by hand.

speakerB.en: Probably, though not in the form that we're used to. Letters will decline, but parcels have increased dramatically because of online shopping, so the postal services are changing rather than disappearing.
It's a delicate transition. Some countries have already stopped daily delivery, and others have introduced digital mailboxes. The challenge is to adapt without leaving vulnerable people behind.
That's what is often overlooked. For older people, a postal worker may be the only person they see in a day. Closing a post office can have a significant social impact on the community.
Some countries have experimented with exactly that. In Japan, for example, postal workers visit elderly customers regularly, and in some regions, they also provide basic banking services.
It's the kind of creativity that might help the sector survive. If the postal system is regarded as a public service, rather than purely a business, the priorities change.
I agree. A letter has a personal quality that no message on a screen can match. I still keep the ones that my grandfather wrote to me, and I treasure them.

scenarios.scenario: Sending a valuable item with insurance and customs documents
scenarios.context: A customer ships a valuable item abroad and learns about insurance, tracking and customs.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'd like to send this watch to my brother in Canada. It's a family heirloom, worth about two thousand euros, so I want to make sure that it arrives safely. What would you recommend?
I'd prefer the most secure option, even if it's more expensive. Is it possible to insure it for the full value, and to require a signature on delivery, so that nobody else can accept it?

That's very reassuring. And what about customs? Will my brother have to pay any duties when it arrives? It's a gift, and not something that has been bought, but I'm not sure whether that makes a difference.
I see. Could you help me fill in the customs declaration? I've never sent anything of this value abroad, and I'm afraid of making a mistake that could cause delays or problems.
Thank you. How long will it take, and will I be able to follow the parcel on the Internet? I'd like to be able to tell my brother exactly when to expect it.
Perfect. I'll pay now, and I'll make sure that my brother knows to look out for the notification. Thank you for explaining everything so carefully.

speakerB.en: Good morning. For an item of that value, I'd strongly recommend our registered express service, with full insurance. It's tracked at every stage, and the recipient has to sign for it, so it can't be left unattended.

Yes, insurance for up to two thousand euros costs thirty-five euros in addition to the postage. A signature will be required on delivery, and the recipient will have to show identification, so it will be handed over only to your brother.

Gifts are treated differently, but they aren't completely exempt. In Canada, gifts under a certain value, usually around sixty dollars, are free of duty. A watch of that value would probably be subject to taxes, and your brother might have to pay.
Certainly. You need to state the contents, the value, and the reason for sending it. Write 'gift', and attach a letter or a receipt, if you have one. Accurate information avoids problems at customs.
The express service takes four to six working days. You'll receive a tracking number, which you can enter on our website, and your brother will also get an email when the parcel is on its way.
You're welcome. Please keep the receipt and the tracking number safe, in case there's any problem. And remember that the insurance claim must be submitted within thirty days of the shipping date.

scenarios.scenario: Redirecting mail after moving
scenarios.context: A resident arranges for mail to be forwarded and updates official records.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'm moving to a new address at the end of the month, and I'd like to arrange for my mail to be forwarded, so that I don't miss any important letters. How does that work?

I'd like it to start on the first of next month, and continue for as long as possible. I'm worried about bank letters and official documents, which might go to the wrong place if I forget to notify anyone.
That's a relief. What do I need to bring, and is there a charge? I've heard that it can be rather expensive, and I'd like to know the total before I decide.
A year is probably enough. Could I also have my mail forwarded to my sister's address for a few weeks, since I won't have my own place ready until the middle of the month?
That's very convenient. Besides the post office, who else should I tell about my change of address? I'm afraid I might forget somebody, and then I'd have to chase them.
Thank you. I'll fill in the form now, and I'll make a list of everyone I need to inform before the move.

speakerB.en: Good morning, and congratulations on the new home. We offer a mail forwarding service for periods of three, six, or twelve months. You can start it from a specific date, so that it's smooth.

It's an excellent idea, as many people overlook that. All mail addressed to your old address will be redirected to the new one automatically. You'll also be given a reference number in case you need to make a change.
You need to bring a proof of identity and a document that shows your old and your new address, such as a rental contract. The fee is twenty-five euros for three months, or sixty for a year.
Yes, you can set up a temporary redirection to a second address, then update it when you move into the final one. It's free to change, as long as you inform us at least three days beforehand.

I'd recommend that you inform your bank, your insurance company, your employer, the tax office, your doctor, and any subscriptions. Many of them let you do it online. We also provide a checklist on our website.

You're welcome. If you fill in this form, I'll register it today. Please remember that the service is meant to help during the transition, and that it's still important to update your details with everyone.

scenarios.scenario: Claiming compensation for a damaged parcel
scenarios.context: A customer asks a post office clerk how to claim compensation for a parcel that arrived damaged.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'm afraid this parcel arrived with the box crushed and the vase inside smashed, although I'd paid extra for fragile handling. I'd appreciate it if you could tell me how to claim compensation, since I'd rather not simply lose the money.

Yes, I kept everything, including the box and the tracking slip. To be honest, I took photographs as soon as I opened it, in case the sender asked for proof. Do you think that will be enough for the claim?

Frankly, it was an oversight. Had I known the cover would be that cheap, I'd have paid for it without hesitation. As far as I'm concerned, the counter staff should have mentioned it. Does that weaken my claim in any way?

About ninety dollars, although it was a gift, so its sentimental value is far greater. I'd appreciate it if you could tell me how long the process takes, because I'd like to replace it before my sister's birthday on the twentieth.

A refund, please, since I'd rather choose the replacement myself. Had I known about the claims procedure earlier, I'd have filed it online, but I'm glad I came in. I'd appreciate it if you could confirm that the form has been received.
Only that I'd like to be informed by email as well as by text. To be honest, I'm relieved, since I was expecting a long argument. Thank you for being so helpful, and I'll wait to hear from you.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry to hear that. Should the item have been insured, you'd be entitled to a full refund, so I'll need to check your receipt first. Once you've shown it to me, we can start the claim. Did you keep the original packaging?

That's very sensible, and I'd say it will help considerably. Once you've filled in this form, we'll send it with your photos to the claims department. Could you explain why you chose the standard service rather than the insured one?

Not necessarily, since you paid for fragile handling, and that's recorded on the label. Should the investigators find the packing adequate, you'd have a strong case. On the other hand, the payout may be only partial. What was the vase worth?

Normally it takes about three weeks, but if you mark the claim as urgent, it can be faster. Should you need a decision sooner, you could call the helpline with your reference number. Would you prefer a refund or a replacement voucher?

Of course. Once you've signed here, I'll stamp your copy and scan everything into the system. You'll get a confirmation text within the hour. Is there anything else you'd like me to note down before I submit it?

You're welcome, and I'd say you've done everything correctly. Should anything go wrong, quote your reference number and ask for me by name. On the other hand, I'm confident you'll hear back soon. Have a pleasant day.

scenarios.scenario: Choosing a courier for a small online shop
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss which delivery service a small online business should use for its parcels.

speakerA.en: I've been comparing delivery services for my online shop, and honestly I'm lost. Much as I'd like to use the cheapest one, I've heard its parcels often arrive late. What would you say matters most when choosing a courier?

Mostly within the country, although about a fifth of my orders go abroad. If it weren't for those, I'd simply choose the national post office, as long as it offered tracking. Why do you think tracking is so important?

Roughly five dollars on average, although I'd stretch to seven for heavier items. Much as I'd like to offer free shipping, my margins are too thin, so I'm thinking of charging a flat fee. Would that put customers off, in your opinion?

Not yet. Had I known how complicated this was, I'd have started with a simpler product. It's not so much the logistics as the unpredictability that worries me. What happens if a courier damages an order?

Two of them do, and one of them includes free packaging materials. Much as I'd love to try the newest company, I'm wary of trusting my stock to a business without a long track record. Is that overcautious, as far as you can tell?

It does, and it gives me a clear plan. If it weren't for your advice, I'd probably have signed up with the cheapest company this afternoon. Let me buy you a coffee, since you've saved me a lot of trouble.

speakerB.en: I'd say it's not so much the price as the reliability. Customers forgive a slightly higher delivery charge, but they rarely forgive a missing parcel. Since you sell fragile ceramics, how often do you expect to ship abroad?

Because it's not so much about knowing where the parcel is as about reassuring the buyer. If it weren't for tracking, you'd spend hours answering anxious emails. Had I known that earlier, I'd have saved myself months of complaints. What budget do you have per parcel?

To be honest, a flat fee is easier for them to understand, as long as you state it clearly before checkout. On the other hand, free shipping above a certain amount might encourage larger orders. Have you tried calculating what that threshold would be?

Then it depends on the contract. If it weren't for the insurance clause I negotiated, I'd have lost hundreds last year. I'd advise you to read the compensation terms carefully, in case you ever need to claim. Does any provider offer collection from your door?

Not at all. It's not so much caution as common sense, since a new service can't prove its reliability yet. I'd suggest a trial month with the established courier, and comparing the results before committing to a long contract. Does that sound manageable?

Gladly, although I'd say the real work is still ahead of you. Once the trial month ends, bring me the figures, and we'll compare them over lunch. On the other hand, I'm confident your shop will do well.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about neighbors and their habits
scenarios.context: People discuss their neighbors and experiences in the neighborhood.

speakerA.en: Do you know your neighbors well?
My neighbor Anna is very kind.
Yes, we talk every day.
Say hello to them. It's easy!
I have a really helpful neighbor. She often waters my plants when I'm away.
speakerA.fa: یه همسایه خیلی کمک‌کننده دارم. وقتی نیستم، گاهی به گل‌هام آب میده.

speakerA.en: The new neighbors are a bit noisy. They play loud music every night.
speakerA.fa: همسایه‌های جدید یه کم سروصدا می‌کنن. هر شب موسیقی بلند می‌ذارن.

speakerA.en: I'm lucky because my neighbors are very friendly and we look out for each other.
speakerA.fa: خوش‌شانسم چون همسایه‌هام خیلی خوش‌برخورد هستن و مواظب هم هستیم.

speakerA.en: We've organized a neighborhood watch to improve security in our area.
speakerA.fa: ما یه گشت محله‌ای برای بهبود امنیت منطقه سازماندهی کردیم.

speakerA.en: I want to build a better relationship with my neighbors. Any suggestions?
speakerA.fa: می‌خوام رابطه بهتری با همسایه‌هام برقرار کنم. پیشنهادی داری؟

speakerB.en: Not really. We just say hello.
That's nice. Do you talk often?
I want to meet my neighbors too.
OK. I'll say hello tomorrow.
That's nice. I wish my neighbors were that kind.
speakerB.fa: خوبه. کاش همسایه‌هام اونقدر مهربون بودن.

speakerB.en: That sounds annoying. Have you talked to them about it?
speakerB.fa: آزاردهنده به نظر میاد. باهاشون در این باره صحبت کردی؟

speakerB.en: That's really nice. It feels safer when you know you can count on them.
speakerB.fa: واقعاً خوبه. وقتی می‌دونی می‌تونی رویشون حساب کنی، احساس امنیت بیشتری داری.

speakerB.en: That's a great initiative. I wish my neighborhood would do something like that.
speakerB.fa: ابتکار فوق‌العاده‌ایست. کاش محله منم یه همچین کاری می‌کرد.

speakerB.en: Why not start a small community event? A potluck or a garage sale could work.
speakerB.fa: چرا یه رویداد کوچیک محله‌ای شروع نمی‌کنی؟ یه مهمونی یا حراج حیاط خلوت می‌تونه خوب باشه.

scenarios.scenario: Meeting a new neighbor
scenarios.context: A person says hello to a new neighbor.

speakerA.en: Hello. I'm your new neighbor.
Nice to meet you, Peter. I'm Maria.
I live in apartment six.
Is this a good building?
If you need anything, please let me know.
Would you like to come over for tea this weekend?

speakerB.en: Welcome! My name is Peter.
Nice to meet you too. Which apartment do you live in?
Oh, I live in apartment five. We are neighbors!
Yes, it's quiet. Call me if you need help.
Thank you. That's very kind of you.
I'd love to. What time is good for you?

scenarios.scenario: Borrowing something
scenarios.context: A person asks a neighbor to lend something.

speakerA.en: Hello. Sorry to bother you.
Can I borrow some sugar?
Just one cup, please.
Thank you. I'll bring it back tomorrow.
Could I borrow your ladder for an hour? I need to change a light bulb.
Thanks for lending it. I'll return it this afternoon.

speakerB.en: Hi. What do you need?
Sure. How much do you need?
OK. Here you are.
Don't worry. It's OK.
Of course. It's in the garage. I'll get it for you.
No hurry. Just bring it back when you're finished.

scenarios.scenario: A noise problem
scenarios.context: A neighbor politely asks someone to turn the music down.

speakerA.en: Hello. Sorry, but your music is very loud.
Yes. My baby is sleeping.
Can you turn it down, please?
Thank you very much.
I understand you have guests tonight, but could you keep it quiet after eleven?
I appreciate it. I have to get up early tomorrow.

speakerB.en: Oh, I'm sorry. Is it too loud?
Oh, I didn't know. I'm sorry.
Yes, of course. I'll turn it down now.
No problem. Sorry again.
Sure. We'll be quiet by then.
I'll make sure everyone knows. Thanks for telling me politely.

scenarios.scenario: Looking after a neighbor's home
scenarios.context: A person asks a neighbor for help before going on vacation.

speakerA.en: I'm going on vacation next week.
To Spain. Can you help me, please?
Please water my plants and take my mail.
Here is the key. Thank you!
Could you check the apartment every two days?
I'll call you if there's any problem. Here's my phone number.

speakerB.en: Nice! Where are you going?
Sure. What can I do?
OK. No problem.
You're welcome. Have a nice trip!
No problem. I'll also turn on the lights in the evening.
OK. Have a safe trip, and don't worry about anything.

scenarios.scenario: Asking about the neighborhood
scenarios.context: A new resident asks a neighbor about shops and services nearby.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Is there a supermarket near here?
Is there a park?
Where is the bus stop?
Is this a safe area?
Is there a good pharmacy nearby?
Which supermarket do you recommend for fresh vegetables?

speakerB.en: Yes, there is one on Oak Street.
Yes, there is a nice park near the school.
It's at the end of this street.
Yes, it's very safe and quiet.
Yes, there's one next to the bank. It's open until ten.
The one on Oak Street. They also have a market on Saturdays.

scenarios.scenario: A neighborhood event
scenarios.context: Neighbors plan a small party in the park.

speakerA.en: Hello. We have a party for the neighbors on Saturday.
It's in the park. Can you come?
At four o'clock. Please bring some food.
Great! See you there.
Could you help us put up the tables on Saturday morning?
Around two. We need to set everything up before the guests arrive.

speakerB.en: Oh, nice! Where is it?
Yes, I can. What time?
OK. I'll bring a cake.
See you on Saturday. Thank you for asking me.
Of course. What time should I come?
OK. I'll bring some chairs from my house too.

scenarios.scenario: Complaining politely about noise
scenarios.context: A resident speaks to a neighbor about loud music.

speakerA.en: Hi, I'm sorry to bother you, but I wanted to talk about the noise in the evenings.
A little, especially after eleven. I have to get up at six for work.
Thank you, I really appreciate that. I don't want any problems between us.
I will. By the way, I love your garden. The flowers are beautiful.

speakerB.en: Oh, I'm sorry. Has the music been too loud?
I didn't realize it was so loud. I'll turn it down after ten from now on.
Neither do I. If it ever bothers you again, just knock on my door.
Thanks. Come over some time, and I'll give you a few plants.

scenarios.scenario: Organizing a neighborhood meeting
scenarios.context: Two residents plan a meeting about a local problem.

speakerA.en: Many people in our street are unhappy about the traffic. We should do something.
Maybe we could organize a meeting and invite the local council.
Where should we hold the meeting? My living room is too small.
I'll make a flyer and put it in everyone's mailbox this week.

speakerB.en: I agree. Cars drive too fast, and there are a lot of children around.
Good idea. We could ask them to put in speed bumps or a crossing.
The community center has a hall we can use on weekday evenings.
Great. I'll talk to some of the neighbors who live near the corner.

scenarios.scenario: Welcoming a new neighbor
scenarios.context: A resident greets a person who has just moved in.

speakerA.en: Hello! I live next door, and I wanted to welcome you to the neighborhood.
If you need anything, just let me know. Do you know where the nearest supermarket is?
It's about five minutes on foot. There's also a good bakery on the corner.
Very quiet. Everyone looks after each other, and we have a street party every summer.

speakerB.en: That's very kind of you. We've only just arrived, so everything is still in boxes.
Not yet. We're still finding our way around.
That's useful to know. Is it a quiet area in general?
That sounds lovely. We'd love to come when the time comes.

scenarios.scenario: Resolving a dispute over a boundary
scenarios.context: Two neighbors discuss a disagreement about a fence.

speakerA.en: I wanted to speak to you about the fence. It appears to be a foot or so inside my property line.
I had the land surveyed last month, and the measurements suggest otherwise. I'd rather settle this amicably.
Of course. I'll bring a copy over this evening. I don't want it to become a source of tension between us.
That's more generous than I expected, and I'm grateful. We've always got along well, and I'd hate to jeopardize that.

speakerB.en: Really? I always assumed it followed the original boundary. It was there when we bought the house.
I appreciate that. Could I see the survey, so we can both be sure we're working from the same facts?
Neither do I. If it turns out you're right, I'd be willing to share the cost of moving it.
Then let's agree to review the survey together and decide on a solution over a cup of coffee.

scenarios.scenario: Organizing neighbors to address a local issue
scenarios.context: Two residents plan a petition about a dangerous intersection.

speakerA.en: Another near miss at the crossroads this morning. A car ran the stop sign and almost hit a child.
I've been thinking of starting a petition to ask the council for traffic lights or a pedestrian crossing.
We could go door to door and set up a table outside the supermarket on weekends.
I'll contact the local newspaper as well. Public pressure often prompts quicker action.

speakerB.en: It's only a matter of time before someone is seriously hurt. We have to do something.
That could work, but we'd need a substantial number of signatures to be taken seriously.
Good idea. We should also compile statistics on accidents, because evidence carries more weight than anecdotes.
Excellent. Let's draft the wording tonight, and aim to submit it within a month.

scenarios.scenario: Reflecting on community spirit
scenarios.context: Two longtime residents discuss how their neighborhood has changed.

speakerA.en: It's remarkable how much this street has changed. When we first moved here, everyone knew everyone else.
Part of it is the rise in rented housing. Tenants don't tend to put down roots in the same way.
I sometimes wonder whether we could revive the old street parties, to bring everyone together.
I'll put a note through every door and offer to host the first gathering in my garden.

speakerB.en: True. Now people come and go so quickly that I hardly recognize half the faces.
There's also the fact that people spend so much time indoors, absorbed in their screens.
It might take effort at first, but I'm sure there are plenty of newcomers who'd welcome the opportunity to meet their neighbors.
That's the spirit. It only takes one person to get the ball rolling.

scenarios.scenario: Addressing persistent parking conflicts
scenarios.context: A resident speaks to a neighbor whose guests regularly block her driveway.

speakerA.en: I hope you don't mind me knocking. I wanted to raise something that's been bothering me, and I'd rather do it face to face.
It's about the parking. Several times recently, your guests' cars have blocked my driveway, and I've been late for work as a result.
I appreciate that. I don't mind the occasional inconvenience, but it's become quite frequent over the past few months.
That would be wonderful. And if it ever happens again, please knock rather than leaving me to guess whose car it is.

speakerB.en: Not at all. Please come in. Is something wrong?
I'm so sorry. I had no idea it was causing a problem. My guests tend to park wherever they find space.
That's entirely reasonable. I'll make sure everyone knows to park on the side road, and I'll put a note on the door if we're expecting visitors.
Of course. I'm glad you came to me directly. It's much better than letting resentment build.

scenarios.scenario: Proposing a community garden
scenarios.context: A resident presents an idea to the residents' association for turning a vacant lot into a shared garden.

speakerA.en: Thank you for letting me address the association. I'd like to propose converting the vacant lot on Maple Street into a community garden.
There's a program that lets residents lease unused land for a nominal fee, provided there's an organized group to manage it. I've already read the guidelines.
That's a legitimate worry, which is why I'd propose a rota and a small committee. Several neighbors have already volunteered.
I'd estimate around two thousand dollars to begin with, which we could raise through donations and a grant from the local council.

speakerB.en: It's an appealing idea, but the lot belongs to the city. What makes you think they'd allow it?
And who would maintain it? Gardens tend to start with great enthusiasm and end up neglected.
What about the costs? Soil, tools, and water access won't come free.
I'm inclined to support it. Could you put together a written proposal for the next meeting so we can vote on it?

scenarios.scenario: Supporting an elderly neighbor discreetly
scenarios.context: Two neighbors discuss how to help an older resident who is struggling without wounding her pride.

speakerA.en: Have you noticed that Mrs. Alvarez hasn't been out much lately? Her curtains were drawn all day yesterday, and she looked quite unsteady last week.
The difficulty is that she's fiercely independent. If we offer help too directly, she'll probably take offense.
That's thoughtful. I could offer to carry her shopping up the stairs, framing it as something I'm doing anyway.
Agreed. Should we let her daughter know, or is that overstepping?

speakerB.en: I noticed too. I'd hate to interfere, but I'm worried she may be struggling to manage on her own.
Perhaps we could do it indirectly. I often cook too much, so I could bring her a portion and say I'd made extra.
And we should keep an eye on her without making a show of it. If she hasn't appeared for a couple of days, one of us should knock.
I think a quiet word is justified, provided we explain that our intention is simply to look out for her.

scenarios.scenario: Addressing a noise problem with a neighbor
scenarios.context: A resident raises a sensitive issue without souring the relationship.

speakerA.en: I hope you won't mind my knocking. I've been reluctant to raise this, but the music has been quite loud late in the evening.
I assumed as much, which is why I thought a conversation would be preferable to a complaint. The walls are thinner than we'd like.
I'm not asking you to stop, naturally. Perhaps we could agree on a cut-off time, say ten o'clock on weeknights?
Thank you. I appreciate your understanding, and for what it's worth, you play remarkably well.

speakerB.en: Oh dear, I'm mortified. I had no idea it was reaching you. I'd never intentionally disturb anyone.
That's good of you. I tend to lose track of time when I'm playing, and I'm afraid I'm not very mindful of the hour.
That's entirely reasonable. I'll use headphones after that, and please don't hesitate to tell me if I slip.
You're very kind. If you'd like to hear it properly sometime, you're welcome to come over at a civilized hour.

scenarios.scenario: Organizing neighbors to oppose a local development
scenarios.context: A resident rallies others against a proposal that threatens the character of their street.

speakerA.en: Have you seen the planning notice? They intend to demolish the old orchard and build forty flats on it.
I'm arranging a meeting at the community hall next Thursday. If we present a united front, the council will be obliged to take notice.
Excellent point. I know a retired engineer on the next street who may be willing to help, at least informally.
Agreed. We must present ourselves as constructive, not merely obstructive, and propose a more sensitive alternative.

speakerB.en: I have, and I'm appalled. The site is one of the few green spaces left, and the infrastructure here can scarcely cope as it is.
Count me in. Have we considered commissioning a traffic assessment? Objections grounded in evidence carry far more weight.
And I could draft a letter for everyone to sign. A well-argued, courteous submission tends to be more persuasive than an angry one.
Precisely. Opposition is most effective when it offers a vision, not just a refusal.

scenarios.scenario: Mediating a boundary dispute between two households
scenarios.context: A community volunteer helps neighbors who disagree over a hedge and a fence line.

speakerA.en: Thank you both for agreeing to this conversation. My role is simply to help you find common ground, not to rule on who's right.
With respect, the survey is unambiguous. The line runs a good meter inside the hedge, which is why I felt entitled to build the fence.
That's a fair criticism, and I apologize. I didn't grasp that the hedge carried such sentimental value.
Then perhaps we can honor that. What if I set the fence back and leave the hedge exactly where it is?

speakerB.en: I appreciate that. I've lived here for thirty years, and the hedge has always marked the boundary, regardless of what the survey now claims.
Entitled, perhaps, but you might have consulted me first. A courtesy would have spared us all this unpleasantness.
It was planted by my late husband. I'm less concerned about the strip of land than about what it represents.
That would mean a great deal to me. In return, I'd be happy to trim it so that it doesn't encroach on your garden.

scenarios.scenario: Collecting the mail for a neighbor
scenarios.context: A neighbor asks for help while she is away.

speakerA.en: Hi, Peter. Could you do me a favor next week?
I'm going to visit my sister for five days.
Yes, please. And could you water my plants?
I'll leave it with you tomorrow morning.

speakerB.en: Sure. What do you need?
Would you like me to collect your mail?
No problem. Where do you keep the key?
Perfect. Have a good trip!

scenarios.scenario: Inviting neighbors to a barbecue
scenarios.context: A man invites a neighbor to a small summer party.

speakerA.en: Good afternoon, Mrs. Davis. We're having a barbecue on Sunday.
It starts at one o'clock in the garden.
Maybe a salad or some fruit, if you like.
Wonderful. The children are going to play games too.

speakerB.en: That sounds lovely. What time is it?
Can I bring something to eat?
I'll make a big fruit salad.
They'll love it. Thank you for inviting us.

scenarios.scenario: Looking for a lost cat
scenarios.context: A girl asks her neighbor about her missing cat.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, have you seen a small gray cat?
This morning. She went out of the window.
Her name is Luna. She has a white spot on her nose.
Thank you so much. Here's my phone number.
I hope so. She's very important to me.

speakerB.en: No, I haven't. When did you lose her?
What's her name? I'll call her if I see her.
I'll look in the garden behind the building.
Don't worry. We'll find her soon.
I understand. I'll call you if I find her.

scenarios.scenario: Helping with heavy shopping bags
scenarios.context: A neighbor sees an older woman with heavy bags.

speakerA.en: Hello, Mrs. Brown. Let me help you with those bags.
Which floor do you live on?
No problem. I can carry them up the stairs.
Thanks, but I have to go to work now.

speakerB.en: Oh, thank you. They're very heavy today.
The fourth floor, and the elevator is broken.
You're very kind. Would you like a cup of tea?
Then please come another day. I'll make a cake.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about the building rules
scenarios.context: Two neighbors talk about rules in their apartment building.

speakerA.en: Did you read the new notice in the lobby?
I didn't know that. I usually take it out later.
Is it also quiet time after ten at night?
That's fair. I'll tell my children.

speakerB.en: Yes. The rubbish must be outside by eight in the morning.
The bins are collected early now.
Yes, and no loud music on weekdays.
Thanks. We all want a quiet building.

scenarios.scenario: Asking to use a neighbor's parking space
scenarios.context: A man asks his neighbor about parking for guests.

speakerA.en: Hello, Mr. Evans. Could I ask you something?
My parents are visiting on Saturday. Can they park in your space?
Thank you. They'll stay for the whole day.
I will. I'll bring you some cake as a thank-you.

speakerB.en: Of course. What is it?
I'm not going out on Saturday, so it's fine.
No problem. Tell them to park carefully.
That's very nice of you.

scenarios.scenario: Cleaning the street together
scenarios.context: Two neighbors take part in a street cleaning day.

speakerA.en: Are you coming to the street cleaning day on Sunday?
At ten. We're going to clean the park and plant some flowers.
Just some gloves. They'll give us bags and tools.
That's great. After that, we'll have lunch together.

speakerB.en: Yes. What time does it start?
Do we need to bring anything?
I'll bring my children, too.
What a nice way to meet the neighbors.

scenarios.scenario: Borrowing a tool from a neighbor
scenarios.context: A man asks his neighbor if he can borrow a tool for a small repair.

speakerA.en: Good evening. I'm sorry to disturb you, but could I ask you for a favor?
I'm trying to hang a shelf, but my drill has stopped working. Could I borrow yours for an hour?
That's very generous. I'll be careful with it and bring it back before dinner.
Thank you so much. If you ever need anything from me, please just ask.

speakerB.en: Not at all. What can I do for you? You look like you're in the middle of something.
Of course. It's in the garage. Do you need any screws or drill bits as well?
Take your time. I won't need it until the weekend, so there's no rush at all.
I will, thanks. Actually, my car won't start in the cold, so maybe I'll need a push someday!

scenarios.scenario: Joining a community garden
scenarios.context: A resident asks about joining the community garden in her area.

speakerA.en: Hello, I heard there's a community garden nearby. How can I take part?
I've never grown vegetables before, but I'd love to learn. Is there a fee?
That's very reasonable. When do you usually meet, and what should I bring?
Perfect. I'll be there on Saturday morning. I'm really looking forward to it.

speakerB.en: Yes, there is, and we're always happy to welcome new members. Have you done any gardening before?
That's no problem. Several of us are experienced and can show you the basics. It costs ten euros a year.
We meet every Saturday at nine. Just bring a pair of gloves, and we'll lend you the tools.
Wonderful. You'll meet some lovely people, and you can take home some fresh vegetables.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing a shared garden problem
scenarios.context: Two neighbors talk about a disagreement over a shared courtyard.

speakerA.en: Good evening. I hope I'm not disturbing you, but I'd like to talk about something that's been bothering me for a while.
It's about the courtyard. Recently, there have been bicycles and boxes left in front of my door, and it's difficult to get in and out.
I understand that there isn't much storage space, but it's also a safety issue. If there were a fire, people couldn't leave the building quickly.
That would be great. Perhaps we could ask the rest of the residents to contribute to a small shed where everyone can store things.
I'll write a note and put it in everyone's mailbox. Would you be willing to come to a meeting next week to discuss it?
Thank you. I think it's much better to solve this together than to complain to the landlord.

speakerB.en: Good evening. Not at all. Please come in. Is something wrong? You look a little worried.
Oh, I'm sorry. I hadn't realized that. The bike belongs to my son, and we've been looking for a place to keep it since we moved in.
You're absolutely right. I'll move it inside tonight. We can keep it in the basement, if we can find some space down there.
That's a good idea. I'm sure that other people have the same problem, and a shared solution would be better for everybody.
Of course. Tuesday evening would suit me. We could also ask the landlord whether he'd be willing to pay for part of the costs.
I agree. Thank you for coming to me first, instead of making a complaint. That's the way neighbors should treat each other.

scenarios.scenario: Helping an elderly neighbor
scenarios.context: A young resident offers help to an elderly neighbor and learns about her situation.

speakerA.en: Good morning, Mrs. Green. I saw that you were carrying heavy shopping bags. Would you like me to help you with them?
It's no trouble at all. I'm on my way to the university, but I have plenty of time. Let me take them upstairs for you.
I've been wondering whether you need help with anything else. If you give me your phone number, I could go shopping for you once a week.
I wouldn't mind in the least. I'm only a few doors away, and I enjoy talking to you. You always have such interesting stories.
Then it's settled. I'll come by every Saturday morning, and you can give me a list of what you need.
It's my pleasure. Everyone needs a little help sometimes, and I'm happy to be of use.

speakerB.en: Oh, thank you, dear. That's very thoughtful of you. My knees aren't what they used to be, and the stairs are becoming difficult.
You're very kind. I've lived in this building for forty years, and I can't remember the last time that someone offered to help me.
That would be wonderful, but I don't want to be a burden. You have your studies, and I know how busy young people are.
Well, if you're sure, I'd be very grateful. And I can pay you back with some of my homemade cakes. I still bake every Sunday.
That sounds perfect. I'll write the list on Friday evening, and leave it by the door so that you can pick it up.
God bless you. It's lovely to know that there are still such good people in the world.

scenarios.scenario: Mediating a conflict between neighbors
scenarios.context: A community mediator speaks with a resident about a long-running dispute.

speakerA.en: Thank you for agreeing to meet with me. I understand that the situation with your neighbor has been going on for some time, and I'd like to help both of you find a solution.
I'd like you to feel free to describe how you see things. I won't take sides, and whatever you tell me will remain confidential unless you decide otherwise.
That sounds very frustrating. When did the problem begin, and have you tried to talk to him directly, or has communication mainly been through letters and complaints?
It's often the case that disputes escalate because people stop speaking. I wonder whether it would be possible to arrange a meeting where both of you could express your concerns, with me present.
I understand your reluctance. Perhaps we could begin by exchanging short written messages through me, outlining what each person would need in order to resolve the matter.
That's a constructive attitude. I'll contact your neighbor this afternoon, and I'll get back to you by the end of the week.

speakerB.en: Thank you for coming. Honestly, I'm at the end of my patience. For two years, his dog has barked all night, and every time I mention it, he accuses me of exaggerating.
It began when he moved in. At first, I tolerated it, but then I started losing sleep. I wrote him a polite note, and he responded with an aggressive letter, and things have deteriorated since then.
We haven't spoken in months. When we meet in the corridor, he looks the other way, and I do the same. It's a ridiculous situation, but I don't know how to break the silence.
I'm willing to try, provided that he is prepared to listen. I don't want a fight, just peace and quiet. But I'm worried that he will interpret the invitation as an accusation.
That could work. If he could see that I'm not trying to humiliate him, he might be more flexible. Maybe there are things that I've done which have bothered him, too.
Thank you. It's a relief to feel that someone is willing to listen. I hope we can find a way of living side by side without the constant tension.

scenarios.scenario: Organizing a neighborhood initiative
scenarios.context: Two residents plan a community project to improve a shared space.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking about the empty lot at the end of our street. It's been neglected for years, and I wonder whether we could turn it into a community garden or a small playground.
I've already spoken to a few neighbors, and the response has been positive. Several people have offered to help with the labor, and one of them is a landscape designer who'd contribute her time.
The main obstacle is permission. The lot belongs to the council, so we'd need an agreement, and possibly some insurance, as they'll be concerned about liability if someone is injured.
That's an excellent suggestion. If we had a representative group with a clear plan and a budget, it would be much easier to persuade the authorities that we're serious.
We could apply for a small grant, too. I've read that the local government has funds for projects that improve public spaces, provided the application shows a genuine benefit for the community.
I'll draft an outline this week, and we can hold a first meeting at the community hall. Let's hope that enough people come to make it worthwhile.

speakerB.en: That's a wonderful idea. I've always found it a shame that such a large space is wasted. If we organized it properly, it could become the heart of the neighborhood.
That's encouraging. Having someone with professional experience would make a big difference, particularly when it comes to drainage and choosing plants that would survive in that soil.
That's what I feared. Perhaps we should form a residents' association, which would give us a legal identity and allow us to negotiate more effectively with the council.
I'd be glad to help with that. We'll need a simple constitution, a treasurer, and a few active members. Once that's in place, we can approach the council with a concrete proposal.
That's worth investigating. Some grants require that the community contributes a percentage of the cost, so we might organize a small fundraising event, such as a bake sale or a street party.
I'll prepare some flyers and put them in everyone's mailbox. With a bit of effort, I'm sure we can create something that the whole neighborhood will be proud of.

scenarios.scenario: Welcoming a new family and explaining local customs
scenarios.context: A long-term resident explains local routines and expectations to newcomers.

speakerA.en: Welcome to the street! I wanted to introduce myself, and to explain a few things, since I remember how confusing it was when I first moved here. If you have any questions, please don't hesitate to ask.

First of all, the refuse collection is on Monday morning for general waste, and on alternate Thursdays for recycling. The bins must be put out the evening before, but not earlier, as the council will fine you.

There's also a custom that we have a street party once a year, usually in June. Everyone brings food, and we close off the road for the afternoon. It's a good opportunity to meet people, and the children love it.

One thing that you might not know is that quiet hours are observed from ten at night until seven in the morning. It's not a legal rule, but everyone respects it, and it keeps the neighborhood peaceful.
If you need a reliable plumber or electrician, I can recommend people. And if you ever go away, we usually keep an eye on each other's houses, and collect the post, so that it doesn't pile up.
I'm delighted to have you here. Please come to dinner when you've settled in, and I'll introduce you to some of the other neighbors.

speakerB.en: Thank you so much for coming over. It's very kind of you, and we really appreciate it. We're finding it a bit overwhelming at the moment, with the boxes and all the paperwork, so any advice is welcome.
That's very helpful. We were told that the system here is quite strict, and we'd have been bound to make a mistake. Do we have to separate the glass from the plastic, or is it all collected together?

That sounds wonderful. In our previous neighborhood, people hardly spoke to one another, so a community event would be a nice change. Is there anything we should do to prepare, or can we just show up?
That's good to know. We have two young children, so we'll make sure that they understand. Is there anything else that we should be careful about, such as parking, or rules about the garden?

That's incredibly generous. We might well take you up on the recommendations. And we'd be happy to do the same for you, if you're ever away. It's reassuring to know that people look out for each other.
We'd love to. Thank you again for the warm welcome. It's making us feel that we've made the right decision in moving here.

scenarios.scenario: Handling noise from a renovation project
scenarios.context: A resident discusses building noise with a neighbor who is renovating.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I hope that I'm not disturbing you, but I wanted to speak to you about the building work. I understand that you're renovating the whole flat, and I'd like to know how long it will take.

I don't want to complain, and I know that renovations are unavoidable. But the drilling begins at seven thirty, and it continues until late afternoon. I work from home, and it's very difficult to concentrate.
I appreciate that. Would it be possible to restrict the noisiest work to certain hours, for instance between ten and four, so that I can plan my day around it? It would be a great help.
That would be wonderful. I could also arrange to be out of the flat on the days when the work is loudest, if you let me know in advance. It would save us both a lot of stress.
Thank you. I really appreciate your cooperation. In return, I'd be happy to collect any deliveries for you during the day, since I'm at home anyway.
That's very kind. I'm glad that we could talk about it so openly. It makes the whole situation much more bearable, and I'm sure that it will go smoothly.

speakerB.en: Good morning. Please come in. I'm sorry that you're having trouble, and I should have spoken to you earlier. We wanted to finish before the summer, but it's turned out to be a bigger job than we expected.

I completely understand. It's a nuisance for everyone, and I'm trying to make it as short as possible. The builders say that the heavy work, such as removing walls, will be finished in about three weeks.

That's a reasonable request. I'll talk to the foreman and ask him to avoid the loudest work before ten and after four. There might be a few exceptions, but I'll make sure that they're kept to a minimum.
I'll message you the day before any particularly noisy work, such as demolition or drilling in the concrete. That way, you can plan accordingly, and perhaps work somewhere else if it's too difficult.
That's very generous of you, and it would be a big help. The delivery companies tend to come when we're not here, and it's a nuisance to collect parcels from the depot.
I agree. Thank you for being so understanding. When the work is finished, I'll invite you over for a drink, as a way of making up for the inconvenience.

scenarios.scenario: Resolving a parking dispute on a shared street
scenarios.context: Two neighbors discuss a parking problem on their narrow street and look for a fair solution.

speakerA.en: Morning, Dave. I wanted to catch you before work, since the parking situation has become rather difficult. I wish I didn't have to raise it, but your van has blocked my driveway twice this week. Could we talk?

Tuesday evening and again this morning, although I understand there's little space on this street. I'd appreciate it if you could park on the other side, since that's where the other residents leave their cars. Is there a reason you can't?

It would, as long as I could still reverse out safely. Much as I'd like to avoid complaining to the city, I can't keep missing appointments, since I'm often called out at short notice. Do you work early shifts yourself?

I'd say we should ask the city about residents' permits, since those would reserve a few spaces. Meanwhile, I'd appreciate it if you could leave a note on my door whenever you're planning to park there. Would that be acceptable?

There's an officer for our district. Once you've written down the times when the street is fullest, I'll put them in a letter with mine. If it weren't for evidence like that, they'd probably ignore us. Can you manage that this week?

That would be wonderful, and I'd appreciate it if you could send me a copy before posting it. To be honest, I'm relieved we sorted this out calmly. I wish every disagreement could be settled like this.

speakerB.en: Of course, and I'm sorry if I've caused trouble. I honestly had no idea it was a problem. If only you'd knocked on my door, I'd have moved it immediately. When exactly did it happen?

Well, I wish there were a simpler answer. It's not so much that I'm careless as that my van is wide, and the other side is narrow. Had I known you needed access, I'd have found another space. Would a few inches make any difference?

Yes, I leave at six, which is exactly why I park near the corner. If it weren't for my tools, I'd keep the van at the depot. To be honest, I'd rather find a compromise than argue. What would you suggest?

That sounds fair, as long as the permits don't cost too much. On the other hand, I wish the city would simply paint lines on the road. Had I known they listened to residents, I'd have contacted them years ago. Who should we speak to?

Certainly. It's not so much an effort as a good idea, since the evidence will help everyone. I'll ask the other neighbors to sign it as well, in case the city wants more support. Should I draft the letter?
So do I, and I'm glad you spoke to me directly. As far as I'm concerned, good neighbors should talk first and complain later. I'll move the van tonight, and I'll send you the draft by Friday.

scenarios.scenario: Responding to a planned development at a residents' meeting
scenarios.context: Two residents discuss a proposed apartment block at a neighborhood meeting and decide how to respond.

speakerA.en: Did you read the proposal for the new apartment block by the park? Much as I'd like the area to develop, I'm worried about the traffic. I'd say it's not so much the building as the loss of green space that bothers me.

It's the only place where children can play safely, and the plans reduce it by almost half. Had I known how much land they intended to use, I'd have attended the first meeting. As far as I'm concerned, there must be a better site. Do you agree?

Not yet, and I wish they were more open about it. If only the city had consulted residents earlier, we wouldn't be arguing now. I'd appreciate it if you could join the committee, since we need someone who understands the housing side.

About two hundred, although many are undecided. Much as I'd like to say everyone is against it, that wouldn't be honest. If it weren't for the traffic concerns, support would be much stronger. What would persuade the undecided residents, in your opinion?

I have, and I'd appreciate it if you could help me draft the invitation. Had I known how many people were willing to speak, I'd have booked the larger hall. Do you think the architect would agree to answer questions directly?

Tomorrow works, and I'm grateful for your support. If it weren't for people like you, nobody would speak up. To be honest, I started this expecting an argument, and I'm pleased we found common ground.

speakerB.en: I did, and to be honest, I'm torn. If it weren't for the housing shortage, I'd oppose it outright. Since my daughter can't afford to rent here, though, I wonder whether we're being selfish. What exactly worries you about the park?

Partly, although the developers claim the other sites are contaminated. Should they be telling the truth, the park may be the only practical option. On the other hand, I'd like to see the surveys. Do you know whether they've been published?

I'd be glad to, as long as the committee remains open to compromise. It's not so much opposition I want as a fairer plan. Once you've gathered everyone's concerns, we could present balanced proposals. How many residents have signed so far?

Concrete guarantees, I'd say. If the developers promised to build a smaller block and keep the playground, many would accept it. Should they refuse, the opposition would grow. Have you thought about asking them for a public meeting?

Probably, since a refusal would look bad in the local press. It's not so much a favor as an obligation, given the public money involved. Once you've confirmed the date, I'll contact the newspaper and the school. Shall we meet tomorrow?
So am I. Much as we disagree on some details, we both want a neighborhood that works for everyone. As far as I'm concerned, that's worth a few evenings of effort. I'll see you at six.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about aspirations and life goals
scenarios.context: Two people share their dreams for the future.

speakerA.en: What do you want to do in the future?
speakerA.fa: توی آینده می‌خوای چیکار کنی؟

speakerA.en: Why do you want to be a doctor?
Is it a hard job?
I think you will be a good doctor.
I hope to travel around the world one day.
speakerA.fa: امیدوارم یه روزی دور دنیا سفر کنم.

speakerA.en: My dream is to start my own business and be my own boss.
speakerA.fa: رویای من اینه که کسب‌وکار خودم رو راه بندازم و رئیس خودم باشم.

speakerA.en: I'm planning to move to a bigger city next year for better career opportunities.
speakerA.fa: برنامه دارم سال دیگه برای فرصت‌های شغلی بهتر به یه شهر بزرگ‌تر نقل مکان کنم.

speakerA.en: I've always wanted to learn how to fly a plane. It sounds so freeing.
speakerA.fa: همیشه دوست داشتم هواپیما خلبانی کنم. خیلی حس آزادی داره.

speakerA.en: In ten years, I see myself living abroad with a family and a stable career.
speakerA.fa: ده سال دیگه خودم رو خارج از کشور، با خانواده و یه شغل پایدار می‌بینم.

speakerB.en: I want to become a doctor.
speakerB.fa: می‌خوام دکتر بشم.

speakerB.en: I like to help people.
Yes, but I will study hard.
Thank you. I hope so.
That's a great goal! I'd love to see the mountains in Nepal.
speakerB.fa: هدف فوق‌العاده‌ایست! من دوست دارم کوه‌های نپال رو ببینم.

speakerB.en: That's brave. I'm not sure I could handle the risk.
speakerB.fa: شجاعانه‌ست. مطمئن نیستم بتونم ریسکش رو تحمل کنم.

speakerB.en: That sounds like a smart move. What field are you interested in?
speakerB.fa: به نظر حرکت عاقلانه‌ای میاد. به چه زمینه‌ای علاقه داری؟

speakerB.en: I've always admired that. Maybe you should go for it!
speakerB.fa: همیشه به این کار حسادت می‌کردم. شاید باید بری دنبالش!

speakerB.en: That's a beautiful vision. I hope you achieve it. I'm more focused on the present myself.
speakerB.fa: چشم‌انداز قشنگیه. امیدوارم بهش برسی. من خودم بیشتر روی حال حاضر متمرکزم.

scenarios.scenario: Plans for next year
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about what they will do next year.

speakerA.en: What are your plans for next year?
Where will you study?
Are you going to travel too?
That sounds great!
What are you going to do after you finish your English course?
Do you think your English will be good enough?

speakerB.en: I'm going to study English.
I'll study at a language school.
Yes. I'm going to visit my uncle in Canada.
Thank you. I'm very excited.
I'm going to look for a job in an international company.
I hope so. I'm practicing every day to improve it.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about a dream job
scenarios.context: A student tells a friend about the job they want.

speakerA.en: What job do you want in the future?
Why do you like that job?
Do you need to go to university?
I'm sure you will be a good engineer.
What do you need to do to become a doctor?
Do you think it will be a hard job?

speakerB.en: I want to be an engineer.
I like to build things.
Yes, I do. I will study for four years.
Thank you. That's kind of you.
I need to study medicine for six years and then work in a hospital.
Yes, but I want to help people, so it's worth it.

scenarios.scenario: A travel dream
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about a place they want to visit.

speakerA.en: Which country do you want to visit?
Why Japan?
When do you want to go?
Can I go with you?
How are you going to travel around the country?
How long are you going to stay?

speakerB.en: I want to visit Japan.
I love Japanese food and the old temples.
Maybe next summer. I'm saving money now.
Of course! It will be more fun with a friend.
I'll take trains. They're cheap and comfortable.
Two weeks. I hope to visit as many places as possible.

scenarios.scenario: Dreaming about a future home
scenarios.context: Two friends describe the home they want one day.

speakerA.en: Where do you want to live one day?
Do you want a big house?
Do you want a pet?
That sounds like a beautiful home.
Would you prefer a house in the city or in the countryside?
What will you do if you can't afford it?

speakerB.en: I want to live near the sea.
Yes, with a small garden.
Yes, I want a dog.
It's my dream. I hope it comes true.
In the countryside. I want fresh air and a peaceful life.
I'll start with a small apartment and save for a bigger place.

scenarios.scenario: Saving money for a goal
scenarios.context: A person tells a friend about a plan to buy something.

speakerA.en: I want to buy a car next year.
Not yet. I save money every month.
I save two hundred dollars a month.
I hope so. I will work hard.
Have you opened a savings account for the car?
Would you buy a new car or a used one?

speakerB.en: That's a good plan. Do you have enough money?
How much do you save?
That's good. You will have it soon.
Good luck with your plan!
Yes, I did last month. It has a good interest rate.
A used one. It's cheaper, and I can save more money.

scenarios.scenario: Learning a new skill
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about something new they want to learn.

speakerA.en: What do you want to learn this year?
When will you start?
Is it difficult?
You can do it!
How are you going to learn it? Will you take lessons?
How long will it take to get your license?

speakerB.en: I want to learn to drive.
I'll start next month.
A little, but I will practice every day.
Thanks! You are a good friend.
Yes, I've found a good school. The lessons start next week.
About three months, if I pass the tests the first time.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about career goals
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss where they see themselves in five years.

speakerA.en: Where do you see yourself in five years? Do you still want to work in marketing?
That's a good goal. What do you need to do to get there?
I'm thinking about changing careers completely and becoming a teacher.
I've always enjoyed explaining things to people, and I want to do something more meaningful.

speakerB.en: I think so, but I'd like to be in a managing position by then.
I'll have to take some courses and gain more experience leading projects.
Really? That's a big change. What made you think about it?
I think you'd be great at it. Just make sure you plan the move carefully.

scenarios.scenario: Dreaming about living abroad
scenarios.context: A couple imagines living in another country one day.

speakerA.en: Do you ever think about living abroad? I dream about it more and more.
We could try Spain or Portugal. Many people work remotely from there.
We could take lessons now, so we'd be ready when the time comes.
It's a big dream, but I think we could make it happen if we plan properly.

speakerB.en: All the time. I'd love to live somewhere warm, near the sea.
That would be ideal, but we'd have to learn the language and find a place to live.
And we should save enough money to survive the first year, just in case.
Let's make a list of things we need to do and set a date.

scenarios.scenario: Setting personal goals for the new year
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about their resolutions.

speakerA.en: Have you made any resolutions for the new year?
I'd like to finally run a marathon. I've been talking about it for years.
Not seriously, but I've signed up for a race in October, so I have no excuse now.
Why not? We could train together on weekends and encourage each other.

speakerB.en: I want to read more and spend less time on my phone. What about you?
That's ambitious. Have you started training yet?
That's a clever way to stay motivated. I might join you for a shorter distance.
It's a deal. Let's make a plan next week.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing up a career change in mid-life
scenarios.context: A man discusses leaving a stable job with his wife.

speakerA.en: I've been seriously considering leaving the firm to start my own business. I need to know what you think.
I'm aware of that, which is why I'd put aside enough to cover our expenses for a year.
I've done the calculations, and I believe we'd break even in eighteen months, though I'll admit that's optimistic.
That's a reasonable compromise. It would reduce the risk without extinguishing the dream.

speakerB.en: It's a daunting prospect. We have a mortgage and the children's education to consider.
A year might not be long enough if the business is slow to take off. Have you drawn up a realistic plan?
I don't want to dampen your enthusiasm, but I'd feel better if you worked part-time for a while before taking the plunge.
Then I'm with you. I'd rather support you in trying than watch you regret never having done so.

scenarios.scenario: Imagining life after retirement
scenarios.context: Two colleagues nearing retirement discuss their plans.

speakerA.en: With only two years to go, I've started to wonder what I'll do with all that free time.
That sounds ambitious. I suspect I'll spend the first few months simply catching up on sleep.
A little. My job has given me a sense of purpose, and I'm not sure what will replace it.
That's a thought. I could mentor young people starting out in the field.

speakerB.en: I've been making a list of things I never had time for, including learning to sail and writing a memoir.
I've heard that many retirees feel lost without the structure of work. Does that worry you?
Perhaps volunteering would help. There are plenty of organizations that benefit from experienced professionals.
I'm sure they'd be fortunate to have you. And I'll expect regular reports on your progress.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing whether to pursue a passion or a practical path
scenarios.context: A student seeks advice from a mentor about choosing a career.

speakerA.en: I'm torn between studying music, which I love, and engineering, which my parents consider a safer choice.
Honestly, music. But I'm afraid of the uncertainty and of disappointing my family.
Not really. I've avoided the conversation because I know it will turn into an argument.
Perhaps I could combine the two, studying sound engineering, for instance.

speakerB.en: It's a difficult decision, and there's no universally right answer. What do you think would make you happiest in ten years?
Their concern comes from love, though it's your life. Have you discussed your fears openly with them?
I'd suggest trying anyway. They might respond better than you expect, particularly if you present a concrete plan.
That could be an excellent middle path, and it might reassure everyone while keeping you close to what you love.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the risks of starting a business
scenarios.context: A friend considers leaving a stable job to launch her own company and asks for a candid opinion.

speakerA.en: I've decided to hand in my notice and start my own consultancy. I wanted to hear your honest opinion before I do anything irrevocable.
About eight months of savings, and a few contacts who have promised work. Not exactly a safety net, I admit.
That would take some of the pressure off, but I'm afraid I'd end up half-committed to both.
You're right. I've been romanticizing the leap, when I should be thinking about how to land.

speakerB.en: I admire your courage, and I think you have the skills for it. But how much runway do you have if the first year is slow?
Eight months is thin. Most ventures take longer than expected to become profitable, so you might consider keeping part-time work in the beginning.
It's a risk, but so is running out of money. Sustainability is more valuable than the symbolic gesture of a clean break.
Exactly. And I'll be your first referral, regardless of how you structure it.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a sabbatical
scenarios.context: A professional talks to her manager about taking a year off to pursue a long-held dream.

speakerA.en: I'd like to discuss something I've been considering for a long time. I'd like to request an unpaid sabbatical for twelve months.
Not at all. I've wanted to write a book for years, and I've realized that if I don't do it now, the opportunity will keep slipping away.
I understand, and I'm willing to help with the handover. I could even train a successor and remain on call for emergencies.
I'd be grateful for any arrangement that leaves the door open. I'd rather return to a similar role than lose the connection altogether.

speakerB.en: That's a significant request. May I ask what's behind it, and whether it signals any dissatisfaction with your role here?
I respect that. From the company's perspective, though, a year is a long absence, and we'd need to arrange cover for your responsibilities.
That's generous. I can't promise your position would be waiting, but I'd certainly like to find a way of keeping you.
Let me take it to the directors. I think there's a reasonable chance they'll agree, given your record.

scenarios.scenario: Reassessing priorities after a setback
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss how a failed venture has changed what each of them wants from the future.

speakerA.en: It's been six months since the company folded, and I'm still trying to work out what I actually want. The old plan no longer feels like mine.
What's strange is that I feel less devastated than relieved. I'd been chasing a version of success that I'd inherited rather than chosen.
Something smaller and more deliberate. I'd like to teach, perhaps, and spend more time with people rather than spreadsheets.
Not yet. I want to be certain it's a conviction, not merely a reaction to disappointment.

speakerB.en: That's understandable. A failure of that scale forces you to examine assumptions you'd never questioned.
That's a valuable realization, even if it came at a high price. What are you drawn to now?
That sounds like a considerable shift. Have you told anyone? Some people may struggle to understand.
A wise precaution. Give it a few months, and if it still feels right, trust it.

scenarios.scenario: Contemplating a radical career change
scenarios.context: Two friends explore the practical and emotional implications of leaving a stable profession.

speakerA.en: I've been seriously contemplating leaving law to open a bakery. I realize how absurd that sounds, but the thought won't release me.
Sheer practicality, mostly. I'd forfeit a secure income, and I'd be starting from nothing in a field where I have no credentials.
I've considered working part-time at a bakery to learn the trade. It would reduce my income, but it would also reduce the risk.
That's what frightens me. I'm afraid the reality may disappoint me, and then I'll have no dream left to retreat to.

speakerB.en: It doesn't sound absurd; it sounds like something you've wanted for years. What's holding you back?
Those are serious considerations, but are they insurmountable? Could you test the idea gradually before committing entirely?
A pragmatic compromise. It would show you whether the reality matches the romance, which is the crucial thing to discover.
A dream you never test isn't a dream, it's a refuge. I'd rather find out and be disappointed than wonder indefinitely.

scenarios.scenario: Setting ambitious goals while remaining realistic
scenarios.context: A mentor helps a young entrepreneur calibrate vision against constraints.

speakerA.en: I want to build a company that transforms how people manage their health. I know it's ambitious, but I refuse to think small.
I have a vision. What I lack, I suppose, is a clear sense of the stages between here and there.
I could build a basic version and test it with a small group of users. That would tell me whether anyone genuinely needs it.
That's sobering, but I take your point. Most failures probably result from scaling something that was never proven.

speakerB.en: Ambition is admirable, but it's worth distinguishing between a vision and a plan. The first inspires; the second executes.
Then let's begin with the first step. What could you accomplish in six months that would validate the core idea?
Excellent. Resist the temptation to build the grand edifice before you've established that the foundation is sound.
Precisely. The ambitious founders who endure are those who remain humble about the first small step.

scenarios.scenario: Reflecting on how aspirations change over a lifetime
scenarios.context: Two older friends consider how their dreams have shifted since youth.

speakerA.en: When I was young, I wanted to change the world. Now I'd settle for changing a few lives in a modest way.
Though I sometimes wonder whether I've merely made peace with disappointment and dressed it up as maturity.
Honestly, a bit of both. There are moments when I mourn the person who believed everything was possible.
A generous way to see it. I find that my aspirations are now less about achievement and more about presence.

speakerB.en: I suspect that's a form of wisdom, not a retreat. The grand ambitions of youth often yield to a clearer sense of what's within reach.
A shrewd question. The difference, I think, is whether you feel diminished or simply refocused.
I mourn him too, but I wouldn't swap what I've learned for what I've lost. Dreams, like people, ought to be allowed to mature.
That's perhaps the final dream worth having, to be fully where you are while there's still time.

scenarios.scenario: Planning to learn to drive
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about driving lessons.

speakerA.en: I'm going to learn to drive this year.
Yes, there's a good one near my house.
About thirty dollars an hour. I'll take two lessons a week.
I hope so. I want to buy a small car next year.

speakerB.en: That's a great plan. Have you found a school?
How much are the lessons?
Then you can pass the test in a few months.
I'm sure you'll do it. Good luck!

scenarios.scenario: Talking about studying abroad
scenarios.context: Two students discuss their dream of studying in another country.

speakerA.en: Where would you like to study after school?
Do you speak German?
I want to study art in Italy.
But it's expensive. I need to find a scholarship.

speakerB.en: I'd like to study engineering in Germany.
A little. I'm taking a course on Saturdays.
That sounds wonderful. Italy has famous art schools.
Let's search for some together this weekend.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a small business
scenarios.context: A woman tells a friend about her plan to open a bakery.

speakerA.en: I have news. I'm going to open a small bakery.
I've saved some money, and my cousin will help me.
Near the school, because many people walk there.
Bread, cakes and cookies. All fresh every morning.
Thank you. I'm a little afraid, but I'm also very happy.

speakerB.en: Really? That's a big step!
Where are you going to open it?
Good choice. What will you sell?
I'll be your first customer.
That's normal. You'll be great.

scenarios.scenario: Getting fit this year
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about their health goals for the year.

speakerA.en: What is your goal for this year?
That's difficult in winter. It's so cold.
I'd like to join a swimming class.
Maybe we can go together on Fridays.

speakerB.en: I want to be healthier. I'm going to run every morning.
I know, but I'll start slowly with ten minutes.
Good idea. Swimming is good for your whole body.
Yes, that would make it more fun.

scenarios.scenario: Plans after graduation
scenarios.context: Two students talk about what they will do after they finish university.

speakerA.en: What are you going to do after you graduate?
Do you want to stay in this city?
I'm thinking about traveling for a few months first.
Maybe Turkey and then Spain. I've never been there.
What about you? Will you start work immediately?

speakerB.en: I want to find a job in a big company.
No, I'd like to move to the capital.
Where would you like to go?
That sounds like a great adventure.
Yes, but I'll visit you during my first holiday.

scenarios.scenario: Planning to learn English better
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about improving their English.

speakerA.en: I want to speak English much better next year.
I'm going to study for half an hour every day.
Let's have a talk in English once a week.
In a year, I hope I'll understand everything.

speakerB.en: Me too. How are you going to do it?
I'd like to watch movies with subtitles.
Good idea. We can start this Sunday.
I'm sure we will. We just need to keep going.

scenarios.scenario: Dreaming about a small house in the country
scenarios.context: A couple dream of moving out of the city.

speakerA.en: One day, I'd like to live in a small house in the country.
We could have a garden with vegetables and flowers.
But we need to save some money first.
How many years do you think it will take?

speakerB.en: Me too. It would be quiet and peaceful.
And maybe a dog and some chickens.
Yes. Let's save a little every month.
Maybe five or six. But it's worth it.

scenarios.scenario: Planning to start a small business
scenarios.context: A person tells a friend about her plan to open a small shop.

speakerA.en: I've decided to leave my job next year and open a small bakery.
I've been saving for three years, and I've already found a small place near the station.
I'm nervous, of course. But I'd regret it if I never tried. Do you think it's a good idea?
Thank you. It means a lot that you believe in me. I'll let you know how it goes.

speakerB.en: Really? That's a big step. Have you thought about how you'll pay for everything?
That sounds like you've planned carefully. What will you do if business is slow at first?
I do. You've always been a wonderful baker, and people will love it. Just be patient at the beginning.
Please do. And I'll be your first customer on the opening day.

scenarios.scenario: Planning to apply to a university overseas
scenarios.context: Two students discuss their plans to study in another country.

speakerA.en: I'm thinking of applying to study in Canada after I finish my degree here.
My English isn't perfect yet, but I'm taking extra classes to improve it.
I know, it's expensive. I'm planning to apply for a scholarship, and I'll work part-time if necessary.
Thanks. If I get in, I'll send you photos and tell you everything about it.

speakerB.en: That's a great goal. Have you looked into how much it would cost?
That's good. You'll need a strong score on the language test to be accepted, won't you?
It sounds like you've thought it through. Hard work will pay off in the end.
I'd love that. Maybe I'll come and visit you when you're settled.

scenarios.scenario: Planning a career change
scenarios.context: A person talks to a friend about leaving an office job to become a teacher.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking seriously about changing my career. I've worked in an office for eight years, but I don't feel fulfilled anymore.
I'd like to become a teacher. I've always enjoyed explaining things to people, and I think I'd find it much more meaningful.
I'd need to study for another two years to get the qualification, which means I'd have to reduce my working hours, and my income would fall.
I know it's a risk, but I'd rather try now than regret it in ten years. I've already started saving, and I've talked to my partner.
That's reassuring. Do you think I'm too old to start again? I'll be thirty-eight when I finish the course.
Thanks. You've given me confidence. I'll apply for the program next month, and let you know how it goes.

speakerB.en: That's a big decision. What's making you consider it now? Has something happened at work, or is it just a feeling?
I can see you as a teacher. You're patient, and you always have a way of making complicated things sound simple.
That's the difficult part. Have you thought about how you'd pay your bills during that time? It might be hard, but it's not impossible.
It's good that you've discussed it with your partner. Support from the people around you can make a huge difference.
Not at all. Many people change their careers in their thirties and forties, and your life experience will be an advantage in the classroom.
I'm really proud of you. And if you need help with anything, like practicing a lesson, I'll gladly be your first student.

scenarios.scenario: Imagining life in ten years
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about where they hope to be in a decade.

speakerA.en: Where do you see yourself in ten years? I was thinking about it last night, and I couldn't decide what I really want.
I hope to have my own business by then. I'd like to run a small travel agency that organizes trips for people who love nature.
I haven't decided yet. But I'd like to live somewhere warm, close to the sea, where I can work from home and take long walks.
That sounds nice. Do you think that you'd stay in your job, or would you like to change direction at some point?
I think that's a healthy attitude. I'd rather have a flexible plan than a fixed one, because life rarely goes the way we expect.
Let's meet in ten years and see how close we got. We can write our predictions down now, and open them then.

speakerB.en: That's a big question. I've always wanted to live abroad, but I'm not sure whether that's still my dream, or only something I used to want.
That sounds like a wonderful idea, and it suits you perfectly. You're organized, you love meeting people, and you've been to so many places.
I would prefer to have more time for the things I enjoy, like writing and traveling, even if it means earning a little less.
I'd probably stay in the same field, but I'd like to manage a team and help younger colleagues to develop their skills.
That's true. Ten years ago, I'd never have imagined being where I am now, and I'm sure the next ten will bring even more surprises.
That's a great idea. If we're still friends then, I'm sure we'll have plenty to talk about. I'll buy the first coffee.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing stability against adventure
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss whether to follow a secure path or take a risk.

speakerA.en: I've been offered a permanent position at a good company, but I've also been invited to join a start-up that could either succeed spectacularly or collapse within a year. I can't decide which to choose.
The secure job pays more, and it offers good benefits and a clear career path. But I know I'd probably spend the next thirty years wondering what might have happened if I'd taken the other chance.
That's what my head says, but my heart says something different. I'm only twenty-eight, and if I don't take a risk now, when I have few responsibilities, I might never do so.
I've thought about that. If the start-up failed, I'd have to find another job, but I'd have gained experience that most people never get, and I'd still be employable.
